families.title: Cyclotomic degrees, Galois fibres and trace transport
families.central_question: What exact structure follows from conductor 1680, and which additional certificates are needed to connect it to another representation?
families.synopsis: The number 384 becomes mathematically productive when assigned a specific role: it is the degree of Q(ζ₁₆₈₀), not the order of a primitive root, the largest Galois-element order, a Lie algebra dimension or a category rank. Distinguishing those meanings allows a much stronger construction. The subgroup corresponding to Q(ζ₃₀) produces uniform fibres of size 48; trace transport is then a theorem of the field tower and can be checked through finite residue classes. This organizes a recurring numerical framework into an auditable arithmetic object. The same discipline applies to trace orthogonality: a coefficient p, rather than p+1, follows from which residue sums are actually being taken. Any proposed passage to an integral E₈ lattice must exhibit a basis matrix, its Gram form and an intertwining equation. Equal degree or a handful of coincident traces cannot supply those maps.
definitions: For N≥1, ζ_N=exp(2πi/N); Gal(Q(ζ_N)/Q) identifies with U_N=(Z/NZ)× by σ_a(ζ_N)=ζ_N^a.
The Ramanujan sum c_N(n)=Σ_(a∈U_N)ζ_N^(an) is an integer and equals Σ_(d|gcd(N,n))d μ(N/d).
For L⊆K and x∈L, Tr_(K/Q)(x)=[K:L]Tr_(L/Q)(x). Relative trace is a linear map, not a choice of an integral basis.

theorem.statement: Let K=Q(ζ₁₆₈₀), L=Q(ζ₃₀), and η=ζ₁₆₈₀^56. Then [K:Q]=384, [L:Q]=8, [K:L]=48; reduction U₁₆₈₀→U₃₀ is onto with every fibre of size 48. Hence Tr_(K/Q)(η^n)=48c₃₀(n). The Galois group of K is C₄²×C₂³×C₃ and has exponent 12.
theorem.proof: Since 1680=16·3·5·7, the totient product is 8·2·4·6=384; φ(30)=1·2·4=8. The order of ζ₁₆₈₀^56 is 1680/gcd(1680,56)=30, giving L⊆K and the tower degree. A class coprime to 30 can be extended to a unit modulo 1680 by prescribing a compatible odd residue modulo 16 and a nonzero residue modulo 7; CRT proves surjectivity. A surjective finite-group homomorphism has fibres equal to kernel cosets, all of size 384/8. Summing η^(an) across these fibres proves the trace formula. For the group structure CRT gives U₁₆×U₃×U₅×U₇≅(C₄×C₂)×C₂×C₄×C₆, and C₆≅C₂×C₃. The least common multiple of these cyclic orders is 12, so the group cannot be cyclic of order 384. These conclusions use classical cyclotomic irreducibility as a structural input; the residue enumeration independently verifies the finite arithmetic.

worked_example.setup: Count the fibres and compute four exact traces without floating-point roots of unity.
worked_example.calculation: Enumerating 0≤a<1680 with gcd(a,1680)=1 gives 384 residues. Reducing modulo 30 produces precisely 1,7,11,13,17,19,23,29, each 48 times. Inclusion–exclusion gives c₃₀(1)=−1, c₃₀(2)=1, c₃₀(15)=−8 and c₃₀(30)=8. The associated K-traces are −48,48,−384,384. Complex conjugation is the nontrivial involution a↦−a, so its fixed maximal real subfield has degree 192. This is distinct from the extension degree 48 and the number of target phases eight.
worked_example.meaning: The arithmetic framework now supports a real interactive finite model: every displayed multiplicity is an exact residue count and every displayed trace has an integer formula.

progression.narrative: The explicit user conductor framework supports the degree and Galois computation; the fourth-power counterexample and corrected trace coefficient delimit what that arithmetic can imply.
The later treatments correct the totient to 384 and derive the concrete conductor-30 field tower. The uniform phase fibres are the strongest exact transport statement supported by these entries.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A matrix C on one lattice and D on another are intertwined only after an explicit B satisfies CB=BD; then C^nB=BD^n follows by induction.
connections.scope: Trace coincidences give necessary diagnostics, not an integral lattice isomorphism.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The primitive phase pushforward is an exact finite distribution with uniform multiplicity 48.
connections.scope: It does not determine a fusion category, quantum dimension or Hamiltonian.

connections.mathematical_bridge: CRT enumeration, group-element orders and integer Ramanujan sums give independent finite checks.
connections.scope: The field-degree interpretation still cites cyclotomic irreducibility.

interactive_contract.inputs: Select a supported divisor m of 1680; the default target is m=30.
interactive_contract.outputs: All reduced unit classes, their fibre sizes, source and target counts, and a uniformity verdict. The trace identities are explained in the family and replayed by verify.py; the current lab has no trace-exponent control.
interactive_contract.validation: Enumerate every gcd-one residue modulo 1680; compare target counts with 384/φ(m). At m=30 assert eight fibres of size 48.
interactive_contract.status: Implemented residue-fibre worked model; trace controls are a specified extension

The sources do not supply arithmetic continuity back to 2023, so this family’s chronology begins with the supported 2025 conductor treatment.

For a general divisor M of N, can the interface expose the CRT proof of surjectivity alongside the uniform reduction fibres, while retaining exceptional small-conductor conventions?

families.title: Quadratic units, complete Pell orbits and congruence populations
families.central_question: When does a recurrence describe every integer solution, and how do finite congruence filters change an infinite population?
families.synopsis: A norm-preserving recurrence generates solutions immediately; proving that it generates all of them is the substantive step. The D=2 Pell equation has an elementary descent to the identity, while the negative equation x²−2y²=−7 requires two distinct canonical seeds. A compact reduction interval makes the seed count finite and proves uniqueness. This exposes an important difference between a finite list, an infinite parametrized family, and a complete classification. Once completeness is established, modular arithmetic is useful again: the unit recurrence is invertible modulo every q, so its state orbit is genuinely periodic. Counting accepted index classes gives an exact density within the orbit and a logarithmic coefficient in a height-bounded population. The same quadratic-unit mechanism explains Fibonacci matrix eigenvalues, but geometric length normalizations must still be declared separately.
definitions: In Z[√2], conjugation sends x+y√2 to x−y√2 and the norm is x²−2y². The norm-one unit ε=3+2√2 has inverse 3−2√2.
Multiplication by ε sends (x,y) to (3x+4y,2x+3y), an integral matrix of determinant one.

A canonical seed is a norm solution reduced to a specified half-open interval under multiplication by ε. A modular filter is a predicate on the full residue state, not solely on a visually selected coordinate.

theorem.statement: Every solution x,y≥0 of x²−2y²=1 is ε^j for a unique j≥0. Every solution of x²−2y²=−7 with y>0 belongs uniquely to (1+2√2)ε^j or (5+4√2)ε^j, j∈Z. For the positive Pell orbit, a modulo-q predicate accepting w positions in its period P yields a population (w/P)log N/log ε+O(1) under y≤N.
theorem.proof: For norm one and y>0, y≥2 and √2<x/y≤3/2. The inverse step gives x′=3x−4y>0 and 0≤y′=3y−2x<y; iteration reaches (1,0), proving coverage. For norm −7, α=x+y√2 is positive whenever y>0. Multiply by a unique power of ε to put β in [√7,ε√7). Since β̄=−7/β, its coordinates satisfy x_β=(β−7/β)/2≥0 and y_β=(β+7/β)/(2√2), which lies below 3√(7/2)<6. Thus y_β∈{2,3,4,5}; the required squares 2y_β²−7 are 1,11,25,43. Exactly two seeds remain. The interval is half-open, so seed and exponent are unique. For the positive orbit, conjugation gives y_j=(ε^j−ε^(−j))/(2√2), hence j≤log N/log ε+O(1). The determinant-one recurrence permutes a finite modular state set, so its orbit has no transient tail. A periodic acceptance pattern with w of P positions contributes w/P of the indices, up to a bounded endpoint error.

worked_example.setup: Generate the two negative-norm seeds, then apply an even-index filter to the positive-norm orbit.
worked_example.calculation: The first seed (1,2) maps to (11,8), and 11²−2·8²=−7. The second (5,4) maps to (31,22), also of norm −7. The inverse sends (11,8) back to (1,2). The positive norm-one sequence begins (3,2),(17,12),(99,70),(577,408). Modulo 3 its full states (x,y) are (1,0),(0,2),(2,0),(0,1), followed by (1,0); the period is four. The condition y≡0 mod 3 accepts precisely the even indices, so the filtered count has coefficient 1/(2log ε).
worked_example.meaning: Completeness rests on descent and seed reduction; finite modular enumeration then safely determines the accepted fraction of that already complete family.

progression.narrative: The recovered catalog name is developed into an elementary complete D=2 Pell example, with a proof explicitly authored for the annual treatment rather than claimed as recovered historical wording.

The later treatments connect quadratic units to matrix decay, periodic filters and logarithmic populations, then make the multiple-seed issue explicit through the negative-norm equation. No intervening 2025 Pell source is invented.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The recurrence is an invertible integer map preserving a quadratic invariant; its finite reductions are permutation dynamics.
connections.scope: Modular periodicity does not by itself prove completeness over the integers.

connections.mathematical_bridge: An exact conjugate formula turns exponential orbit growth into logarithmic population growth.
connections.scope: The O(1) counting remainder is tied to this orbit model, not to arbitrary Diophantine families.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A compact seed bound plus exact square testing proves that every unit orbit is represented.
connections.scope: A finite search without a derived reduction bound is not a global theorem.

interactive_contract.inputs: Choose negative-norm seed (1,2) or (5,4), then an integer unit power from −20 to 20.
interactive_contract.outputs: Exact transported coordinates, signed step and norm −7. Positive-Pell sequences and modular acceptance periods are proved in the family and replayed by verify.py; they are not current lab controls.
interactive_contract.validation: Compute with arbitrary-precision integers and assert x²−2y²=−7 after each displayed transport. The accompanying half-open seed interval proves completeness.
interactive_contract.status: Implemented two-seed negative-Pell worked model; positive-orbit and congruence-filter controls are specified extensions

Floating-point logarithms may display growth but are not used to certify integer membership. No unsupplied global shift-uniqueness theorem follows from the population calculation.
open_questions: For each additional quadratic core, can all seeds be bounded and enumerated with a proof of descent coverage before attaching any congruence filter?
Can an exact interval method decide a height cutoff without rounding error when ε^j lies close to the chosen bound?

families.title: Number fields, norm forms and arithmetic obstructions
families.central_question: Which field, ideal and lattice data are sufficient to turn a norm identity into a complete arithmetic statement?
families.synopsis: A defining polynomial is the beginning of a number-field calculation. Irreducibility, the polynomial-order index, ramification, unit structure and the actual sublattice representing the original equation each impose additional requirements. The squarefree discriminants −23 and −283 give unusually clean maximal-order certificates, while nonabelian Galois closure supplies a decisive obstruction to cyclotomic containment. The class-field examples add a second kind of obstruction: an extension with the right degree can still ramify at finite or real places. Finally, the 2026 norm forms show why unit transport alone need not classify a two-variable equation. Multiplication preserves a cubic norm surface, but often leaves the binary plane that encoded the original problem. Retaining the embedding lattice makes this loss visible and turns a plausible reduction into a mathematically correct one.
definitions: For an algebraic integer α, the discriminant of Z[α] equals the field discriminant times [O_K:Z[α]]². A squarefree polynomial discriminant therefore forces index one.
The field norm N_(K/Q)(x) is the determinant of multiplication by x on K. In a specified integral order, norm ±1 implies a unit of that order.

A binary cubic equation can embed in a norm equation only together with a rank-two lattice condition; the full norm surface has an extra coordinate. An exceptional unit is an algebraic integer z for which both z and 1−z are units.

theorem.statement: For f(T)=T³−T+1, irreducibility and discriminant −23 imply S₃ Galois closure and exclude every root from every cyclotomic field. Separately, in the order Z[z] with z³=−4, N(a+bz+cz²)=a³−4b³+16c³+12abc; norm-one transport need not preserve c=0.
theorem.proof: The only possible rational roots of the monic cubic are ±1, neither of which is a root. Its discriminant is −4(−1)³−27=−23, not a rational square. An irreducible cubic has transitive Galois group A₃ or S₃; the discriminant-square criterion excludes A₃. Every subfield of a finite abelian Galois extension is itself Galois because every subgroup is normal. A nonnormal cubic with S₃ closure therefore cannot be contained in a cyclotomic field. For the norm formula, multiplication by a+bz+cz² in basis (1,z,z²) has matrix [[a,−4c,−4b],[b,a,−4c],[c,b,a]]. Its determinant is the displayed form, giving an exact integral certificate without approximate roots. The unit ε=1−z−z² has norm one. Multiplying the binary element −1−3z by ε gives −13−2z+4z². Both have norm 107, but the latter has nonzero third coordinate. Consequently unit-orbit completeness in the ambient order, even if independently proved, would still require an exact return-to-plane test to solve u³+4v³=107.

worked_example.setup: Contrast a correct unramified class-field candidate with a wrong one, then retain a Thue lattice.
worked_example.calculation: For K=Q(√10), the quadratic discriminant is 40 and the class number is two. The biquadratic L=Q(√2,√5) has discriminant 8·5·40=1600=40², so its relative discriminant has norm one; L is totally real, giving no real-place ramification. The alternative K(i) has discriminant 40·(−4)·(−40)=6400 and relative norm four, so it is ramified. For H(u,v)=−3u³+9uv²−2v³ and β³−27β−18=0, determinant expansion gives N(−3u−βv)=9H(u,v). The relevant lattice is −3Z+Zβ, not every norm element of the field.
worked_example.meaning: Degree, discriminant, class-field identification and binary-lattice membership answer different questions and require distinct certificates.

progression.narrative: Quadratic splitting in Q(i) supplies a small exact local-to-global model and illustrates how local factors depend on prime ideals rather than solely rational primes.
Ray classes, nonprincipal ideals, ramification tests and finite-field descent make several independent meanings of arithmetic obstruction concrete.

The later sources expose nonabelian field obstructions, exceptional-unit symmetries and binary norm-plane restrictions. The Mordell equation adds a genuinely complete proof using a norm-Euclidean quadratic ring.

connections.scope: Matching discriminants alone does not identify coordinates or embeddings.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The S₃ closure distinguishes a cubic field from subfields of abelian cyclotomic extensions.
connections.scope: A common numerical degree gives no representation equivalence.

connections.mathematical_bridge: An exact multiplication matrix certifies a norm identity; unit bases and lattice-return constraints are additional obligations for exhaustive solving.
connections.scope: No unreplayed global unit search is promoted to a theorem.

interactive_contract.validation: Expand determinants over integers; verify substitutions both ways; distinguish polynomial from field discriminants and unit transport from exhaustive orbit coverage.

families.title: Modular forms, Hecke relations and arithmetic local factors
families.central_question: Which identities genuinely characterize modular arithmetic, rather than an arbitrary prime-indexed statistic?
families.synopsis: A modular-form assertion includes the group, weight, character, normalization and transformation law. Once those are fixed, dimensions, Hecke recurrences and Euler factors become exact algebraic constraints. The number 24 enters the logarithmic derivative of Dedekind eta through a specific product normalization; it is not interchangeable with a root count or an abstract dimension. Similarly, a genuine Frobenius trace is tied to a point count and determinant p. Its symmetric square has three eigenvalue products, not a guessed two-factor denominator. This family places q-expansion calculations beside local arithmetic while retaining the distinction between an Eisenstein series, a cusp eigenform and an elliptic-curve L-function. Modular symbols supply a boundary algebra that can later support periods, but their elementary relations alone do not execute a modular-symbol algorithm or establish modularity.
definitions: For the full modular group over C, the graded ring of holomorphic modular forms is C[E₄,E₆], with weights 4 and 6. Δ=(E₄³−E₆²)/1728 has weight 12.
For weight k, a normalized Hecke eigenform satisfies a_(p²)=a_p²−p^(k−1), with suitable unramified and normalization hypotheses.
For an elliptic local factor, α+β=a_p and αβ=p. The symmetric square eigenvalues are α²,p,β².

theorem.statement: The weight-38 full-level modular-form space has basis E₄⁸E₆, E₄⁵E₆³, E₄²E₆⁵ and dimension three; its cusp subspace is ΔM₂₆ of dimension two. For elliptic eigenvalues α,β, the symmetric-square denominator is 1−(a_p²−p)t+p(a_p²−p)t²−p³t³.
theorem.proof: A monomial E₄^aE₆^b has weight 4a+6b. Solving 4a+6b=38 in nonnegative integers gives b=1,3,5 and a=8,5,2. Polynomial independence in C[E₄,E₆] proves that these monomials form a basis. Multiplication by the nonzero Δ identifies cusp forms of weight 38 with weight-26 forms, whose equation 4a+6b=26 has solutions (a,b)=(5,1),(2,3). The structural description of the modular-form ring and its cusp ideal are classical inputs, while the dimension calculation is elementary. For the symmetric square, α²+β²=(α+β)²−2αβ=a_p²−2p. Adding the middle eigenvalue p gives sum a_p²−p. The sum of pairwise products is p(α²+β²)+p²=p(a_p²−p), and the triple product is p³. Expanding the three linear factors gives the stated polynomial. The determinant p is essential: substituting an unrelated prime-power ratio destroys this derivation.

worked_example.setup: Check an Eisenstein Hecke relation and an elliptic symmetric-square factor.
worked_example.calculation: The normalized nonconstant coefficients of E₄ are σ₃(n). At p=2, σ₃(2)=9 and σ₃(4)=73=9²−2³. The constant coefficient of E₄ is also compatible with T₂E₄=9E₄ under the stated weight-four convention. For p=2 and a_p=−2, the symmetric-square denominator becomes 1−2t+4t²−8t³. For eta, its defining product gives q d(log η)/dq=1/24−Σ_(n≥1)σ₁(n)q^n=E₂/24. The translation phase of an eta quotient must still be tested; a q-series with appealing coefficients is not automatically invariant under τ↦τ+1.
worked_example.meaning: Small exact coefficient tests make the hypotheses auditable, while the theorem of transformation or modularity remains a separate structural obligation.

progression.narrative: The exact Hecke formula, full-level weight-38 dimension and eta normalization make distinct modular invariants calculable.

Transformation phases, modular-symbol boundaries and local eigenvalue products impose additional consistency tests. The later Hecke critique explains why an arbitrary prime-index statistic cannot be substituted for those invariants.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A point-count trace fixes a_p and determinant p, supplying the exact local quadratic factor that feeds the symmetric square.
connections.scope: A local factor alone does not prove modularity, analytic rank or BSD.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The modular-symbol relation {a,b}+{b,c}={a,c} is realized by [b]−[a], a degree-zero cusp boundary.
connections.scope: The elementary relation is a precursor to relative homology and periods, not the whole theory.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Eta logarithmic derivatives and Eisenstein Dirichlet series connect products to coefficient convolutions in their convergence domains.
connections.scope: Analytic continuation and modular transformation require their own theorems.

interactive_contract.outputs: Dimension and monomial checks, Hecke coefficient residuals, eta phases and local symmetric-square factors.
interactive_contract.validation: Check transformation conventions and coefficient normalization before applying recurrences; distinguish finite coefficient consistency from a universal modularity proof.

Can each proposed arithmetic statistic pass the exact p² Hecke recurrence and a finite certified comparison bound after all normalization choices are stated?

families.title: Euler products, prime sums and the analytic burden of identification
families.central_question: How do multiplicative identities become analytic formulas without losing signs, prime powers, convergence or main terms?
families.synopsis: The divisor algebra gives formal identities; absolute convergence permits their interpretation as analytic functions. This transition is where several recovered proposals needed repair. Pointwise μΛ is a negative prime indicator weighted by logarithm, while convolution μ*log equals the positive prime-power function Λ. A prime-ideal sum changes again when norms and splitting types enter. An Euler product in Re(s)>1 is nonvanishing there, but this fact does not settle zeros after analytic continuation. Likewise π(x) and x/log x are not interchangeable at square-root error scale: the omitted x/log²x term is much larger. The family organizes these issues around exact operation and domain. Spectral determinants, sampled zeta layouts and prime oscillatory tones can be valid mathematical objects while their proposed identification with arithmetic zeros remains an additional, explicitly missing theorem.
definitions: The von Mangoldt function Λ(n) is log p when n=p^k, k≥1, and zero otherwise. The Möbius function μ vanishes on integers with a squared prime factor.
A Dirichlet series is absolutely convergent where Σ|a_n|n^(−σ) is finite; only in a justified domain may one freely multiply, rearrange or differentiate the relevant series.
The arithmetic prime sums θ(x)=Σ_(p≤x)log p and ψ(x)=Σ_(p^k≤x)log p differ by prime-power contributions. A spectral zeta requires its own operator, eigenvalue domain and summability.

theorem.statement: The exact convolution identity μ*log=Λ gives −ζ′(s)/ζ(s)=ΣΛ(n)n^(−s) for Re(s)>1. Also Σφ(n)n^(−s)=ζ(s−1)/ζ(s) for Re(s)>2, and for real σ>2 its tail after N is at most N^(2−σ)/(σ−2).
theorem.proof: For n=∏p_i^a_i, log n=Σ_(d|n)Λ(d), since the prime powers dividing n contribute Σ_i a_i log p_i. Convolution with μ, using μ*1=ε, gives μ*log=Λ. Absolute convergence in σ>1 justifies differentiating the Euler product and summing its geometric prime-power expansions. By contrast μ(n)Λ(n) is −log p at n=p and zero elsewhere, because μ(p^k)=0 for k≥2; its sum is −θ(x), not ψ(x). For the totient identity, n=Σ_(d|n)φ(d) means id=1*φ. Multiplication of absolutely convergent Dirichlet series in σ>2 gives ζ(s−1)=ζ(s)Σφ(n)n^(−s); the Euler product ensures ζ(s)≠0 there. Since 0≤φ(n)≤n, the remaining tail is bounded by Σ_(n>N)n^(1−σ)≤∫_N^∞x^(1−σ)dx. This explicitly states both the stronger half-plane required by φ(n) and an error certificate for truncation.

worked_example.setup: Compare the two operations at n=12 and bound a real totient series.
worked_example.calculation: The divisors of 12 with nonzero μ are 1,2,3,6. Thus (μ*log)(12)=log 12−log 6−log 4+log 2=0, agreeing with Λ(12)=0. At n=8 the convolution is log 8−log 4=log 2, while μ(8)Λ(8)=0. At n=3 the latter product is −log 3. For σ=4 and N=100, the totient tail is at most 100^(−2)/2=1/20000. This is a deterministic truncation error, not an empirical convergence observation or a zero-location theorem.
worked_example.meaning: A single symbol change between multiplication and convolution changes the arithmetic object; a single half-plane change can invalidate an analytic manipulation.

progression.narrative: The strongest supported early thread is operation and analytic-domain repair: signs, convolution, prime powers, Euler tails and the correct prime-counting main term.
Valuation-shell integrals and divisor convolution give exact analytic models. Prime oscillatory sums retain valid finite calculus without gaining a zero correspondence merely from their construction.

The later sources distinguish sampled layouts from invariants and give a totient-series tail on its correct domain. The cyclotomic Mellin kernel supplies an exact special identity, not a universal spectral realization.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Mellin transforms, logarithmic derivatives and Euler products connect coefficient algebra to analytic functions once a common absolute-convergence domain is proved.
connections.scope: Continuation outside that domain needs a separate theorem.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A claimed spectral realization must state an operator, domain, determinant regularization and an equality to the normalized L-function.
connections.scope: Finite spectral data or finitely many zero checks cannot supply that global equality.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A bijective zeta sampling layout preserves the sampled multiset but may change adjacency statistics.
connections.scope: A visualization statistic must specify its dependence on ordering and truncation.

interactive_contract.inputs: Cutoff N, real σ in the declared half-plane, explicit arithmetic coefficient function and operation type.
interactive_contract.outputs: Finite sums, rigorous tail bounds, prime-power contributions and a table distinguishing pointwise from convolution operations.
interactive_contract.validation: Check exact divisor identities first; attach analytic domain and explicit tail before reporting a limit.
interactive_contract.status: Mathematical recipe; no general solver implemented

families.limits: The worked integer checks certify arithmetic identities, while the convergence proof supplies infinite validity. No Riemann hypothesis, BSD conclusion or arithmetic-spectral identification is inferred. Floating-point samples on a line do not certify unsampled zeros or a global distribution.
open_questions: Can every proposed spectral equality state its exact normalization, analytic domain and continuation theorem, rather than only matching selected terms?
For a chosen arithmetic transform, what explicit tail bound is strong enough to support the claimed precision uniformly across its parameter region?

families.title: Algebraic maps, singularities and the choice of smooth model
families.central_question: Which geometric information is preserved by a parametrization, a birational coordinate change or a normalization?
families.synopsis: An equation is not yet a complete specification of the geometric object being studied. An affine curve may be singular, its normalization smooth, and its projective closure may acquire additional points at infinity. A parametrization can be injective and still lose differential information. Conversely, an explicit rational change of coordinate can identify function fields even when the displayed equations look unrelated. This family builds a hierarchy of certificates: substitution proves that a map lands on the curve; an inverse on a dense open proves birationality; an integral-closure argument proves normalization; Jacobian or local-ring calculations detect singularities; ramification on the smooth compact model determines genus. Cross-ratio symmetry supplies a finite quotient of ordered configurations, but singular special values and ramification must be handled before treating a parameter as a moduli coordinate.
definitions: A normalization replaces an integral curve by the curve whose coordinate ring is integrally closed in its function field. A birational map is an isomorphism of function fields, not necessarily an everywhere-defined isomorphism.
For a plane curve F=0 in characteristic zero, a point with F=F_x=F_y=0 is singular. Local intersection multiplicity measures the length of the corresponding local quotient when finite.
For squarefree P of degree m and d≥2, the superelliptic curve means the smooth projective normalization of y^d=P(x), with δ=gcd(d,m) points over infinity.

theorem.statement: The cusp y²=x³ is normalized by t↦(t²,t³), and its intersection multiplicity with y=0 at the origin is three. For squarefree P of degree m, the smooth projective model of y^d=P(x) has genus g=((d−1)(m−1)−gcd(d,m)+1)/2.
theorem.proof: The ring A=C[t²,t³] has fraction field C(t), since t=t³/t², and t is integral over A because it satisfies T²−t²=0. C[t] is integrally closed and finite over A, so it is the normalization. The cusp is singular at the origin because the two partial derivatives of y²−x³ vanish there; the parametrization derivative is also zero there, explaining why injectivity does not imply an immersion. Quotienting the local equation by y gives C[x]_(x)/(x³), whose length is three. In the blowup chart y=ux, the total equation is x²(u²−x)=0 and the strict transform u²−x=0 is smooth. For the superelliptic genus, each of the m simple finite zeros has ramification index d, contributing d−1. At infinity there are δ points, each of index d/δ, contributing d−δ in total. Riemann–Hurwitz gives 2g−2=−2d+m(d−1)+(d−δ). Rearrangement yields the stated formula. Both the squarefree assumption and the use of the smooth compact normalization are essential.

worked_example.setup: Compare a cusp, two compact superelliptic models and an exact corner-coordinate substitution.
worked_example.calculation: For y²=x³−x, d=2,m=3,δ=1 gives genus one. For y³=x⁴−1, d=3,m=4,δ=1 gives genus three; its compact surface therefore has Euler characteristic −4. The rational function R(z)=(1−z)³/z² on P¹ has divisor 3[1]−2[0]−[∞]. Setting u=(z−1)/z transforms R(z)=1 into u³−u+1=0, with inverse z=1/(1−u). The equation excludes z=0,1 and u=0,1, so the denominators introduce no missing or extraneous solutions. A matching discriminant would not have proved this coordinate identification; the forward and inverse substitutions do.
worked_example.meaning: Each model supports a different valid question: singular local structure, smooth genus, ordered branch data or arithmetic field identity. The chosen object must remain explicit throughout.

progression.narrative: Rational parametrization and the ordered cross-ratio provide early concrete maps with domains and exceptional points already visible.
Rational-coordinate and cusp treatments separate set-theoretic parametrization, ambient dimension and differential regularity.

Jacobian algebras quantify isolated hypersurface singularities, while the Legendre j-map makes finite cross-ratio collisions explicit. These are related geometric tools rather than a claimed single historical construction.
The later cusp blowup, birational corner coordinate and superelliptic ramification calculations supply increasingly complete map-and-model certificates.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A simple branch point has local coordinate x−a=t^d, and analytic continuation multiplies y by exp(2πi/d); Gauss–Bonnet converts the compact genus to total curvature.
connections.scope: Local covering monodromy is distinct from an arbitrary connection holonomy.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The Möbius corner substitution identifies the cubic fields, while the divisor of R records zeros and poles exactly.
connections.scope: Neither an approximate root match nor a common discriminant supplies the rational map.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Substitution, inverse-domain checks, Jacobian rank and local quotient length form complementary certificates.
connections.scope: A finite sample of mapped points proves none of the universal map properties.

interactive_contract.inputs: An explicit polynomial curve, a rational map with denominators, and a declared affine, normalized or compact model.
interactive_contract.outputs: Exact substitution identities, excluded loci, singular points, local intersection length and genus under verified squarefree hypotheses.
interactive_contract.validation: Verify forward and inverse maps on their stated domains; count ramification at infinity as well as at finite roots.
interactive_contract.status: Mathematical recipe; no general solver implemented

families.limits: The genus formula does not apply unchanged to repeated roots, positive characteristic dividing d or an unreduced affine equation. A normalization is not automatically an embedding, and a blowup chart does not by itself prove global resolution. General singularity classification requires more than a handful of invariants.
open_questions: For a proposed parameter family, where do repeated roots or denominator poles change the normalization and branch profile?
Can every claimed moduli identification exhibit its exact finite symmetry group and distinguish generic fibres from special ramified fibres?

families.title: Elliptic arithmetic: local counts, global points and height lattices
families.central_question: How far can exact local and group-law certificates take us toward rational rank, and where do descent and global conjectures enter?
families.synopsis: Elliptic arithmetic joins several structures whose numerical outputs must not be conflated. A point count over a finite field gives a Frobenius trace. A rational group-law calculation gives an exact point and its multiples. Good reduction can rule out rational torsion, producing a rank lower bound from one nonzero point. A height pairing then certifies independence and measures the covolume of a chosen subgroup, while a Selmer computation can give an upper bound with an additional Tate–Shafarevich contribution. Each is valuable on its own. The most coherent cross-year example is E:y²+y=x³−x, of discriminant 37: exact finite counts in 2024 recur as group and rank certificates in 2026. That continuity supports a reusable arithmetic laboratory recipe, while the stronger assertions of exact rank, BSD or complete integral points need separate proofs.
definitions: For a good prime p, a_p=p+1−#E(F_p) and the local polynomial is 1−a_p t+pt². Good reduction means the discriminant is nonzero modulo p.
For E:y²+y=x³−x, negation is (x,y)↦(x,−y−1). Rational points form an abelian group with identity O.
The canonical height pairing is positive definite on E(Q) modulo torsion. A Gram determinant for a subgroup of index I is I² times the full-lattice regulator.

theorem.statement: For E:y²+y=x³−x, the rational torsion subgroup is trivial and P=(0,0) has infinite order, so rank E(Q)≥1. The exact point counts #E(F₅)=8 and #E(F₇)=9 suffice, provided the prime-to-p restriction on torsion reduction is respected.
theorem.proof: The discriminant is 37, so both primes are good. Suppose there is a rational torsion point of prime order ℓ. If ℓ≠5, injection of ℓ-torsion under reduction at 5 forces ℓ|8 and thus ℓ=2. Reduction at 7 then forces 2|9, impossible. If ℓ=5, reduction at 7 instead forces 5|9, also impossible. Every nontrivial finite abelian torsion group contains an element of prime order, so all rational torsion is excluded. The point (0,0) is nonzero and lies on E, hence has infinite order. This proves a rank lower bound without computing an L-function. For heights, bilinearity gives G′=MᵀGM under a generator-coordinate matrix M and therefore det G′=(det M)²det G. A positive Gram determinant proves independence of the displayed points but says nothing about saturation unless the index is certified. The exact Selmer sequence adds the separate quotient Sha[n] to E(Q)/nE(Q); a Selmer cardinality is therefore not automatically a count of visible rational generators.

worked_example.setup: Count the two finite reductions and verify exact rational multiples.
worked_example.calculation: Enumerating y²+y=x³−x over F₅ gives seven affine points plus O, while over F₇ it gives eight affine points plus O. At P=(0,0), the tangent slope is (3x²−1)/(2y+1)=−1, yielding 2P=(1,0). The line through P and 2P has slope zero, yielding 3P=(−1,−1). Exact addition gives 7P=(−5/9,8/27), where both sides of the equation are 280/729. Independently, for a short Weierstrass curve y²=x³+ax+b, clearing the denominator in the doubling formula gives a quartic condition on the x-coordinate of a half-point; every candidate must still satisfy the original curve and group equation.
worked_example.meaning: The finite reductions establish the global non-torsion result through a stated theorem; the visible multiples verify the arithmetic implementation but are not themselves the proof of infinite order.

progression.narrative: Finite-field zeta factors, the discriminant-37 counts, a non-torsion proof and height-lattice interpretation establish four distinct arithmetic certificates.
Weierstrass invariants, true local traces, independence and Selmer bounds sharpen the distinction between a displayed subgroup and the full arithmetic object.

The later sources make hidden torsors, CM local traces, higher-genus Frobenius reconstruction and multiplication fibres explicit. The same discriminant-37 curve supplies a supported return to the earlier rank lower bound.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Finite counts determine a_p and the determinant p, supplying local factors and the input to Hecke and symmetric-square identities.
connections.scope: A list of factors does not alone prove analytic continuation or BSD.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The exact Selmer sequence separates E(Q)/nE(Q) from Sha[n].
connections.scope: A cohomological upper bound is not automatically a constructive list of rational points.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A positive height Gram matrix certifies independence and supports metric optimization on the free quotient.
connections.scope: Torsion is collapsed, and index or saturation must be certified before claiming the full regulator.

interactive_contract.inputs: Exact Weierstrass coefficients, a good prime, rational points and optional certified height-pairing data.
interactive_contract.outputs: Point counts, Frobenius traces, exact group-law residuals, torsion exclusions and basis-dependent Gram determinants.
interactive_contract.validation: Count every finite-field point including infinity; check good reduction; respect prime-to-p injection; substitute every rational output exactly.
interactive_contract.status: Mathematical recipe; no general solver implemented

families.limits: No general elliptic solver or certified height engine is implemented here. The rank-one lower bound is not an upper bound, and an analytic determinant analogy is not BSD. Halving quartics yield candidates requiring sign and exceptional-case checks. Genus-two counts require their own Frobenius degree and cannot use an elliptic quadratic factor.
open_questions: Can a documented descent give an independent upper bound matching the exhibited non-torsion subgroup, with saturation certified?
For multiplication fibres, can the field of definition, rational torsion kernel and all exceptional doubling cases be incorporated into a complete exact candidate procedure?

families.title: Divisors, compactification and projective positivity
families.central_question: What separate certificates establish a smooth quotient, a well-behaved boundary, positivity and an actual projective embedding?
families.synopsis: The early arithmetic-geometry material becomes coherent when organized around distinct geometric properties. Neatness removes finite stabilizer phenomena in an open arithmetic quotient. A compactification adds boundary strata. Regular cones make local toric charts smooth. A positive canonical or log-canonical divisor controls a birational growth property. A sufficiently positive line bundle supplies sections that define an embedding. None of these steps is interchangeable with the others. Modular curves make this hierarchy unusually explicit: X(3) is a smooth genus-zero compact curve, while its four-punctured interior is hyperbolic and of log-general type. Divisor intersection on P¹×P¹ then gives a second exact arena for positivity and invariant classes. The family’s strongest result is a curve embedding criterion whose proof states exactly why enough sections separate both points and tangent directions.
definitions: For a smooth compact curve X of genus g, deg K_X=2g−2; with c reduced boundary points D, deg(K_X+D)=2g−2+c.
A line bundle L is very ample when its complete linear system gives a closed projective embedding. On a smooth curve, separation of every length-two subscheme is the relevant section criterion.
A two-dimensional toric cone with primitive generators u,v is regular when |det(u,v)|=1. Smoothness is local lattice regularity; projectivity additionally requires a compatible support function.

theorem.statement: For a smooth projective curve of genus g and a line bundle L of degree d≥2g+1, h⁰(L)=d+1−g and the complete linear system embeds X into P^(d−g). On the principal modular curve X(3), deg K=−2 while deg(K+D)=2; at level seven these degrees are four and 28.
theorem.proof: For any length-two subscheme Z, Serre duality gives H¹(L(−Z)) dual to H⁰(K_X⊗L⁻¹(Z)). Its degree is 2g−2−d+2≤−1, so it has no nonzero section. The restriction sequence therefore makes H⁰(L)→H⁰(L|_Z) surjective. Distinct points and doubled points give point separation and tangent separation; the length-one version also gives base-point freeness. The standard embedding criterion then proves very ampleness. Vanishing of H¹(L), followed by Riemann–Roch, yields h⁰(L)=d+1−g. For a torsion-free effective modular group of index μ and c cusps, Gauss–Bonnet gives 2g−2+c=μ/6. Principal level N has c=μ/N. At N=3, μ=12,c=4,g=0; at N=7, μ=168,c=24,g=3. The degree formulas then distinguish ordinary from logarithmic general type. These arguments use the declared smooth projective curve and classical modular-curve inputs; they do not algebraize an arbitrary analytic space.

worked_example.setup: Compare a toric boundary chart, a divisor lattice and two projective embeddings.
worked_example.calculation: The cone generated by (1,0),(1,2) has determinant two and a singular toric chart. Adding (1,1) gives determinant-one adjacent cones, producing a smooth local toric modification. On P¹×P¹, classes (a,b) have intersection pairing (a,b)·(c,d)=ad+bc and self-intersection 2ab; for a,b≥0, h⁰(O(a,b))=(a+1)(b+1). Swapping the factors fixes the line a=b in the real divisor space. For g=1,d=3, the embedding theorem gives three sections and a plane cubic. For g=3,d=7, it gives five sections and an embedding into P⁴.
worked_example.meaning: Boundary regularity, divisor intersections and sections now have computable meanings rather than being treated as interchangeable claims of geometric richness.

progression.narrative: The foundational cluster already separates arithmetic quotient smoothness, compactification charts, canonical positivity, embedding sections and adjunction dimensions. The atlas links these explicit treatments without upgrading their higher-dimensional scope.
Picard and Néron–Severi calculations, invariant divisor classes and a finite-index modular quotient give complementary algebraic descriptions of the same questions of class, quotient and positivity.

The cusp area example makes finite volume distinct from compactness, while the product abelian-surface locus fixes a specific moduli discriminant. Neither is claimed as a general compactification theorem.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Hyperbolic area and cusp widths determine genus in the modular-curve case; q=exp(2πiτ/N) fills each puncture.
connections.scope: Finite area does not imply compactness, and neatness does not choose a higher-dimensional smooth fan.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Averaging a finite group action projects the real Picard class space to its invariants; factor swap leaves (1,1).
connections.scope: Fixed-space linear algebra does not classify the whole Picard group or its torsion.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Determinants of adjacent primitive rays certify regularity of a two-dimensional subdivision.
connections.scope: Global projectivity and arithmetic admissibility remain additional conditions.

interactive_contract.inputs: Genus g, degree d, boundary count c; or lattice rays and a specified divisor-class basis.
interactive_contract.outputs: Canonical and log-canonical degrees, section counts, projective target dimension, intersection values and cone determinants.
interactive_contract.validation: Check smoothness assumptions, integral lattice primitiveness, cohomology-vanishing hypotheses and exact effective quotient indices.
interactive_contract.status: Mathematical recipe; no general solver implemented

families.limits: The degree criterion is sufficient, not necessary. A projective curve is an input to its proof, so the theorem cannot establish algebraization from scratch. A local toric subdivision is not a proof of a global arithmetic compactification. Higher-dimensional general type needs explicit boundary and ramification contributions.
open_questions: For a specified higher-dimensional arithmetic quotient, what canonical-divisor formula and admissible fan give simultaneous smoothness, projectivity and a proved positivity bound?
Can an intended analytic compactification exhibit a concrete ample bundle and enough sections to verify its claimed algebraization and embedding?

families.title: Cohomological realizations, Hodge filtrations and comparison types
families.central_question: Which information survives a realization, and what additional structure is required before two cohomology theories can be compared?
families.synopsis: Cohomology provides several forms of organized information: dimensions, graded pieces, mixed structures, integral torsion, Frobenius action and functorial maps. A numerical realization may preserve addition and multiplication while forgetting almost everything else. This is why an Euler characteristic can be zero for a nontrivial elliptic curve, and why multiplying it by Shannon entropy cannot automatically become a positive complexity index. The same caution governs comparison theorems: a characteristic-p variety has no complex analytic space until appropriate characteristic-zero data have been supplied, and a motivic chain index is not a singular cohomology degree. A finite monodromy model makes the loss of information especially concrete. Rational ranks can remain unchanged while integer coinvariants gain torsion; the nilpotent operator determines a weight filtration but not an entire limiting mixed Hodge structure.
definitions: The Grothendieck ring of complex varieties imposes [X]=[Z]+[X minus Z] for closed Z and multiplication by Cartesian product. A motivic realization is a declared ring homomorphism out of that ring.
Compact-support Euler characteristic is χ_c(X)=Σ_i(−1)^i dim H_c^i(X); it is additive but need not be positive or separating.
A monodromy weight filtration centered at one obeys N(W_k)⊆W_(k−2) and N^j:Gr_(1+j)^W→Gr_(1−j)^W isomorphically. A Hodge filtration and polarization are extra data.

theorem.statement: For V=Qe₁⊕Qe₂ and N(e₂)=e₁,N(e₁)=0, the centered weight filtration is W_k=0 for k<0, W₀=W₁=Qe₁ and W_k=V for k≥2. For integral monodromy M_n=I+nN, n>0, the coinvariants are Z⊕Z/nZ, although all these rational models have the same ranks.
theorem.proof: The image and kernel of N are both Qe₁. The proposed filtration lowers by two under N, and its only nonzero graded pieces are Gr₀ and Gr₂, both one-dimensional. N maps the class of e₂ to the class of e₁, an isomorphism, while all higher required isomorphisms concern zero spaces. Thus the defining conditions are satisfied. On the integer lattice, (M_n−I)Z²=nZe₁, so the quotient is generated freely by e₂ and by e₁ modulo n. Tensoring with Q removes the latter torsion. For realization loss, the scissor relation A¹={0}⊔G_m gives [G_m]=L−1. Compact-support cohomology of G_m has one copy of the coefficient field in degrees one and two, so its Euler characteristic is zero despite nonzero cohomology. A projective genus-g curve has Betti numbers (1,2g,1) and Euler characteristic 2−2g. Therefore χ_c(X)H(p) can vanish or be negative for a positive entropy H(p). Additivity alone gives no positivity or faithful geometric encoding.

worked_example.setup: Test comparison types on P¹ and exhibit a failure of an unrestricted motivic–Betti isomorphism.
worked_example.calculation: P¹ over F₅ has six points and its standard smooth lift has cohomological ranks (1,0,1). Frobenius acts by 1 in degree zero and 5 on the hyperplane class in degree two, giving trace count 1+5=6; over F₂₅ it gives 1+25=26. This is a useful consistency test, not a proof of the general comparison theorem. At Spec C, the weight-one motivic group H^{1,1}=C× is nonzero, whereas singular H¹ of a point vanishes. Even after tensoring with C the source is nonzero, since log|·| maps C× onto R and R⊗_Z C maps nontrivially to C. The universal isomorphism claim therefore fails at a point.
worked_example.meaning: Small examples discriminate a valid comparison with explicit coefficients and hypotheses from a false formula that merely passes a rank coincidence.

progression.narrative: The early Hodge treatment supplies concrete Betti and Hodge-number constraints for curves and P¹×P¹, making geometric compatibility a prerequisite for proposed tables.
Motivic scalars, finite-field trace counts and prismatic structure introduce distinct realization targets. Their codomains and additional data must be kept visible.
Monodromy, localization, a point counterexample and typed étale–crystalline statements sharpen the information-loss and comparison questions. No unsupported 2026 continuation is added.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Localization and compact-support cohomology explain a subtraction in a Grothendieck group without implying a direct-sum decomposition of actual objects.
connections.scope: Equality of virtual classes is weaker than an isomorphism of complexes or mixed Hodge structures.

connections.mathematical_bridge: The integer coinvariant torsion and filtered Frobenius residual retain information erased by rational ranks or insufficient digits.
connections.scope: Rational comparison cannot by itself recover integral torsion.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A scalar geometric realization can be multiplied by entropy only after a codomain is fixed and desired positivity and sensitivity are tested.
connections.scope: The resulting authored functional is not an intrinsic nonnegative complexity measure.

interactive_contract.inputs: Exact nilpotent matrix and integer lattice; or a variety, cohomology theory, coefficient ring, base and proposed comparison degree.
interactive_contract.outputs: Weight graded dimensions, integer coinvariants, Euler realizations and explicit type checks for comparison formulas.
interactive_contract.validation: Verify N-action on each graded piece; preserve torsion before tensoring; test proposed universal comparisons on a point and projective line.
interactive_contract.status: Mathematical recipe; no general solver implemented

families.limits: The finite matrix model is not a general degeneration or mixed-Hodge solver. A limiting Hodge filtration, polarization, geometric origin and admissibility remain extra requirements. Étale–crystalline comparison uses stated lifting or period-ring hypotheses; numerical agreement of a cellular test object is insufficient.
open_questions: Can a proposed comparison specify an actual functor and a correctly graded natural map before asking whether it is an isomorphism?
Which integral or filtered invariants must a proposed geometric complexity measure retain to distinguish objects with identical Euler characteristic?

families.title: Typed operations, quotients and finite algebraic structure
families.central_question: Which operations, equations and equivalences actually determine an algebra, and which information survives quotienting?
families.synopsis:
The algebraic backbone of the collection is the move from a named collection of symbols to a multiplication law whose identities can be proved. A field, a monoid, a ring and a partial resource algebra have different admissible operations. Their quotients therefore require different compatibility conditions. The useful revised question is not whether a construction looks algebraic, but whether its carrier, operations, units, domains of definition and notion of equality have all been specified. This viewpoint makes the number-system comparisons, transported operations, finite maximal ideals, capped trace monoids and squarefree branch decomposition parts of one coherent programme.

Transport of structure is the first constructive tool. Given a bijection, pulling all operations back creates an isomorphic object, so associativity and distributivity are inherited by proof. This gives a complete model of a coordinate deformation while explaining why it supplies no new intrinsic field invariant. Quotients then remove information in a controlled way: a ring congruence is determined by a two-sided ideal; a monoid quotient requires a multiplication-compatible equivalence; a partial algebra needs its composability relation retained. Approximate numerical closeness cannot silently serve as any of these equalities.

Finite models make the distinction executable. Enumerating ideals of a finite ring can produce maximal ideals and field quotients. Capping an additive counter produces an absorbing top layer, but does not turn its semigroup kernel into a linear nullspace. The latter distinction matters throughout the atlas: a minimal two-sided ideal, a kernel of a homomorphism and a vector-space kernel answer different questions. Algebra becomes useful for interactive reconstruction precisely when the requested invariant is named before its computation.
definitions: For a unital ring R, a quotient R/I is defined by a two-sided ideal I; multiplication of classes is [a][b]=[ab].
For a finite monoid S, K(S) denotes its unique minimal nonempty two-sided ideal. It is not a matrix nullspace.
For k≥1, L_k={0,…,k} has operation a⊕b=min(a+b,k); k is absorbing.
For a bijection φ:X→Y, transported multiplication is x⋆y=φ⁻¹(φ(x)φ(y)), with all other required operations transported likewise.

theorem.statement: For a finite monoid S and positive integers k_1,…,k_r, K(S×∏L_{k_i})=K(S)×{(k_1,…,k_r)}. Thus adding saturated counters preserves the cardinality of the minimal ideal, although it enlarges the monoid.
theorem.proof: Let P=S×∏L_{k_i}. The displayed product J is a nonempty two-sided ideal: multiplication preserves K(S), while every capped coordinate remains at its maximum. Let I be any nonempty two-sided ideal of P and choose (s,a)∈I. Multiplication by (1,k_1,…,k_r) puts (s,k_1,…,k_r) in I. The set of x∈S for which (x,k_1,…,k_r)∈I is a nonempty ideal of S. It contains K(S), hence I contains J. Therefore J is the unique minimal ideal. For completeness, existence and uniqueness of K(S) in a finite monoid follow by choosing a minimal nonempty ideal and observing that the product of any two nonempty ideals is nonempty and lies in their intersection. Minimality then forces the two chosen minimal ideals to agree. This proof concerns multiplication ideals only; no vector-space structure is used.

worked_example.setup: Take S=C₂={1,g}, g²=1, and one counter L₂. Also compare the finite commutative ring Z/12Z.
worked_example.calculation: The six monoid elements are (1,0),(g,0),(1,1),(g,1),(1,2),(g,2). Their product is (g^a,i)(g^b,j)=(g^{a+b mod2},min(i+j,2)). Exactly (1,0) and (1,2) are idempotent. The minimal ideal is {(1,2),(g,2)}, a copy of C₂. Exhaustive multiplication proves associativity on all 216 triples and finds no smaller nonempty ideal. In Z/12Z the maximal ideals are (2)={0,2,4,6,8,10} and (3)={0,3,6,9}; their quotients have two and three elements. These outputs distinguish minimal monoid ideals from maximal ring ideals rather than relying on the shared word ideal.
worked_example.meaning: A small exact multiplication table can certify an invariant of the declared model. It cannot identify an unnamed historical transition object with that model without a multiplication-preserving map.

progression.narrative: Number systems and transported operations supply the operation-first theme; the historical topics do not themselves establish a new field.
The capped monoid and partial-share models sharpen which products are total and which equalities are legitimate.
Saturation, finite maximal ideals and quotient branch splitting give finite certificates of retained or discarded structure.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A transition congruence must preserve all future outputs before a machine quotient represents behaviour.
connections.scope: A multiplication table alone does not establish observational equivalence.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Coprime factors and Bézout identities construct orthogonal idempotents and branch inverses.
connections.scope: Repeated factors require local or primary methods.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A homomorphism killing relations factors uniquely through their generated ideal.
connections.scope: The category and type of ideal must be declared.

interactive_contract.inputs: Finite multiplication table, distinguished identity, chosen capped-counter sizes or finite ring table.
interactive_contract.outputs: Associativity certificate, units, idempotents, relevant ideals and explicit quotient map.
interactive_contract.validation: Exhaustive finite products; ideal closure; no conflation of ring, semigroup and linear kernels.
interactive_contract.status: Worked mathematical recipe; no dedicated general algebra user interface is implemented.

families.limits: No unspecified M29 table is reconstructed. Transport is an isomorphism construction. Enumeration scales exponentially, and finite maximal-ideal search proves no algorithmic result for arbitrary infinite rings.
open_questions: Given a recovered finite transition table, which multiplication congruence is also complete for its actual observations?
For a squarefree polynomial quotient, which sign or arithmetic admissibility conditions survive the algebraic product decomposition?

families.title: Exact matrix structure, metrics and spectral certificates
families.central_question: Which finite identities certify rank, spectrum and decomposition, and which metric is each certificate using?
families.synopsis:
Linear algebra is a common language across the source years, but a useful synthesis must preserve the question encoded by each matrix. Rank counts independent directions, singular values quantify amplification after metrics are fixed, Jordan structure measures nilpotent mixing, and a projector certifies a subspace only through its defining identities. A large Frobenius norm, a symmetry label and an eigenvalue list cannot replace one another. The revised framework starts with a domain, codomain and scalar field, then attaches the appropriate certificate.

The exact approach is particularly effective when a numerical claim can be reduced to polynomial identities. A verified factorization A=UV supplies a rank upper bound; a nonzero minor supplies a lower bound. Reduction modulo a prime can certify that a rational minor is nonzero, while a rank drop modulo that prime can arise from arithmetic cancellation. A spectral polynomial p(T)=0 gives projectors only when its roots are distinct; actual nonzero support witnesses are still needed to certify that every advertised eigenvalue occurs. These are constructive, inspectable statements rather than a generic reliance on diagonalization software.

Metrics are part of this structure. A diagonalizable matrix with real spectrum can be self-adjoint in a suitable positive metric without being symmetric in the original coordinates. Conversely a nontrivial Jordan block cannot be made self-adjoint by a positive metric, because an isometric change to ordinary Euclidean coordinates would make it diagonalizable. The same rule governs anisotropy and whitening: coordinate changes preserve metric singular values only when both source and target metrics transform. This family supplies algebraic certificates which the inverse, control and statistical chapters can then use with their own observation and error models.
definitions: A rank certificate pairs an exact rank-r factorization with a nonzero r×r minor.
A positive metric η defines ⟨x,y⟩_η=x*ηy; η-self-adjointness is A*η=ηA.
For commuting idempotents P_i, define E_ε=∏_i P_i^{ε_i}(I−P_i)^{1−ε_i}, ε∈{0,1}^m.
For a squarefree polynomial p(t)=∏_{λ∈S}(t−λ), Lagrange polynomials e_λ(t)=∏_{μ≠λ}(t−μ)/(λ−μ) define spectral projectors when p(T)=0.

theorem.statement: If P_1,…,P_m are commuting idempotents on a finite-dimensional vector space, the E_ε are pairwise annihilating idempotents summing to I, and im(E_ε) is the simultaneous eigenspace P_i v=ε_i v. Hence the nonzero blocks give an exact direct-sum decomposition.
theorem.proof: All factors in E_ε commute, and each factor is idempotent, so E_ε²=E_ε. If ε≠δ, some index i has one product containing P_i and the other containing I−P_i. Their product is zero, proving E_εE_δ=0. Expanding ∏_i(P_i+(I−P_i)) gives Σ_εE_ε=I. Multiplication by P_i gives P_iE_ε=ε_iE_ε. Conversely, if v satisfies all simultaneous eigenvalue equations, every factor of E_ε acts as identity on v, so E_εv=v. Thus its image is exactly that eigenspace. Any v equals ΣE_εv; applying each projector to a supposed zero sum proves directness. The proof requires commutativity: arbitrary idempotents can have incompatible images and the product construction can fail even to be idempotent.

worked_example.setup: Use P=diag(1,1,0,0), Q=diag(1,0,1,0), and T=2P−Q.
worked_example.calculation: The Boolean blocks E_11,E_10,E_01,E_00 are the four coordinate projections. T has respective eigenvalues 1,2,−1,0, so p(T)=T(T−I)(T−2I)(T+I)=0. Every block is nonzero, witnessed by its coordinate basis vector. A separate rank example is A=[[1,2,3],[2,4,6],[0,1,1]]: its factorization into its first two independent columns times coefficient rows gives rank at most two, while the minor on rows 1,3 and columns 1,2 equals one. It remains nonzero modulo every prime. In contrast, [[2]] has rational rank one and rank zero modulo two; modular rank loss is not a rational vanishing certificate.
worked_example.meaning: The examples provide independent upper and lower witnesses. The eigenvalue list is supported by actual vectors, and no conditioning statement is inferred from exact rank alone.

progression.narrative: Norm, block-energy and rank distinctions establish the finite matrix vocabulary.
Jordan nullities separate generalized eigenspaces from a bare list of eigenvalues.
Positive metrics, modular minors, Perron projections and nilpotent mixing identify the hypotheses behind spectral claims.
Boolean blocks, annihilating polynomials and integer intertwiner kernels provide exact reconstruction certificates.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A matrix kernel becomes an invisible state direction only after a specific observation map is declared.
connections.scope: Exact rank gives no noise margin without singular values.

connections.mathematical_bridge: W*ΣW=I is a metric normalization, distinct from an invariance equation P*ΣP=Σ.
connections.scope: A singular covariance can be whitened only on its range.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A characteristic polynomial or equitable quotient can certify a conditional spectrum.
connections.scope: A spectrum alone does not construct the graph.

interactive_contract.inputs: Exact matrix, field, input/output metrics and proposed projectors or factors.
interactive_contract.outputs: Rank bounds, exact residuals, Boolean blocks, spectral support and metric-aware singular directions.
interactive_contract.validation: Check products over rationals; use only certified prime reductions; report exact identity separately from numerical conditioning.
interactive_contract.status: Related worked-model labs expose rank and singular-value effects; the general matrix recipe is documented.

families.limits: Finite exact identities do not settle infinite operator domains or asymptotic boundedness. Rational rank, integral torsion and floating-point effective rank remain different invariants.
open_questions: Which nonzero projector witnesses suffice to make a proposed finite spectral rigidity theorem independently replayable?
For a family of varying metrics, can the smallest retained singular value be bounded uniformly on the declared parameter domain?

families.title: Symmetry as an action, representation and orbit calculation
families.central_question: What does a specified symmetry force, and which numerical features remain free after imposing it?
families.synopsis:
A symmetry label becomes mathematical information only after a group acts on a stated space. The collection repeatedly returns to Weyl groups, permutation characters, signed permutations, crystals and branching. These topics connect through invariant subspaces and orbit decompositions, not through shared large integers. The useful question is what the actual action fixes, which representations occur, and what independent parameters survive in the commuting algebra.

The elementary averaging projector is the organising construction. It turns a finite group action into an exact invariant subspace over a field where the group order is invertible. Character traces then measure multiplicities, and orbit splitting gives concrete restrictions and induced representations. Low-rank Weyl calculations provide a more structured version: a signed orbit sum becomes a polynomial identity after fixing the root coordinates and normalization. The A₂ denominator can be expanded completely; a nonconstant Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial requires its actual Bruhat interval and Hecke convention. Neither object is a universal score of computational complexity.

The signed-permutation examples are especially useful because they expose the limit of a symmetry inference. Over F₃, sign changes interchange the two nonzero entries, so the B₄ orbits are exactly the five Hamming-weight classes. Over the reals, invariance of a symmetric matrix under all independent sign changes kills off-diagonal entries, and permutation invariance makes its diagonal entries equal. This forces a scalar matrix on that irreducible coordinate representation, but two copies of a representation still admit independent scalar blocks and hence arbitrary positive frequency ratios. Symmetry narrows a model class; it need not pick a numerical constant, an empirical rank or a physical scale.
definitions: A representation is a homomorphism ρ:G→GL(V); its invariants are V^G={v:ρ(g)v=v for all g}.
The character χ_V(g)=trρ(g) records the trace of the actual action, not just dimV=χ_V(1).
The signed permutation group B_n=C₂^n⋊S_n changes coordinate signs and permutes coordinates.
A Weyl denominator is an alternating group-algebra sum; its signs and root lattice are part of the input.

theorem.statement: If G is finite and |G| is invertible in k, R=|G|⁻¹Σ_gρ(g) is an idempotent with image V^G. For the B_n action on F₃^n, the orbits are indexed by Hamming weight j and have sizes 2^j binom(n,j).
theorem.proof: For h∈G, ρ(h)R=|G|⁻¹Σ_gρ(hg)=R because left multiplication permutes G. Hence every vector in imR is invariant. If v is invariant then Rv=v, so imR=V^G and R²=R. The division hypothesis is essential; in characteristic dividing |G| this formula is unavailable and invariant functors need not be exact. For the orbit claim, every group element preserves the number of nonzero coordinates. Conversely, two vectors of equal weight can first have their supports matched by a coordinate permutation, then have their entries matched by sign changes, since F₃\{0}={1,−1}. Thus weight is a complete orbit invariant. Choose the support in binom(n,j) ways and independently choose each nonzero sign in 2^j ways. This proves both completeness and the sizes without enumerating all group elements.

worked_example.setup: Enumerate B₄ orbits on F₃⁴, and compare a symmetry constraint on a real 5×5 quadratic form.
worked_example.calculation: The orbit sizes are 1,8,24,32,16 and sum to 81. Their stabilizer sizes are 384,48,16,12,24, giving orbit×stabilizer=384 in each case. For a symmetric real κ invariant under every coordinate sign flip, choose the flip of coordinate i; its conjugation reverses every off-diagonal entry in row or column i, forcing those entries to zero. Conjugation by coordinate permutations then forces all diagonal entries equal. Thus κ=cI. On V⊕V, however, K=diag(a²I,b²I) commutes with ρ(g)⊕ρ(g) for every a,b>0. Its two oscillation frequencies have freely chosen ratio b/a, so no particular ratio follows from equivariance alone.
worked_example.meaning: An orbit computation can be complete at a stated finite level while a proposed exceptional-group action remains unconstructed. Large familiar orders are consistency constraints, not replacements for matrices or relations.

progression.narrative: Weyl denominators, Hecke polynomials and compact-group cutoffs turn symmetry into finite calculations.
Character tables, branching diagrams and invariant averaging add actual representation-theoretic maps.
Signed-permutation orbits, Mackey splitting and rank-one crystals separate group actions from speculative numerical identifications.
Intertwiner kernels and completeness of invariant maps frame exactly what an action can reconstruct.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Hamming-weight orbit counts and stabilizers are finite counting certificates.
connections.scope: The count does not identify unrelated datasets.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Character orthogonality yields exact observable projection loss in compact-group examples.
connections.scope: Noncentral functions need matrix coefficients, not characters alone.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A splitting-field group acts on roots and preserves field operations.
connections.scope: An automorphism is not an evolution in physical time.

interactive_contract.inputs: Generators with explicit matrices or permutations, scalar field, proposed invariant and representation space.
interactive_contract.outputs: Orbits, stabilizers, invariant projector, character traces and intertwiner kernels.
interactive_contract.validation: Verify generator relations and the actual action; compare independent orbit counts or kernel certificates.
interactive_contract.status: The finite-counting lab illustrates enumeration; the representation-specific calculations are worked recipes.

families.limits: This family does not construct Monster moonshine, every KL polynomial, an E₈ crystal or a faithful W(E₈) action on F₃⁴. Equality of coefficients or dimensions requires a separately defined representation before it gains that meaning.
open_questions: Which invariant map is injective on the declared orbit space, rather than merely locally independent?
For a proposed exceptional symmetry, can its generator matrices and exact intertwiner ranks be supplied over a stated field?

families.title: Lie brackets, octonion associators and exceptional weight structure
families.central_question: Which identities survive a nonassociative or graded product, and what additional data turn exceptional dimensions into a Lie algebra?
families.synopsis:
This family joins two recurring themes: bracket consistency and exceptional symmetry. The starting point is a declared multiplication convention. Associative multiplication produces a commutator satisfying Jacobi; graded associative multiplication produces the super-Jacobi identity with parity signs. Octonionic multiplication is alternative rather than associative, so its commutator carries a nonzero Jacobiator. These are different algebraic structures, each with identities that can be derived and tested exactly.

The octonion model is especially productive because it turns regrouping into a measurable defect. Under a fixed Cayley–Dickson convention, the triple e₁,e₂,e₄ has associator 2e₇. Norm multiplicativity then yields a sharp universal bound for every triple, with a complete equality criterion. This gives a rigorous invariant of the multiplication, while preventing an illicit reassociation of three unrelated factors. The same discipline applies to superalgebras: in gl(1|1), the bracket of the two odd off-diagonal matrix units is an anticommutator and equals the identity, not an ordinary commutator.

Exceptional Lie algebras enter at the representation level. The decomposition so₁₆⊕S⁺ has dimension 120+128=248, and its D₈ roots together with the half-spin weights form the 240-element E₈ root set. That is a substantial and checkable weight calculation. It is still distinct from constructing the bracket: the so₁₆ action on S⁺ and an equivariant map Λ²S⁺→so₁₆ must be specified with a normalization satisfying spinor Jacobi. The magic-square dimension arithmetic likewise organises candidate structures without replacing their multiplication. This synthesis keeps the genuine exceptional mathematics while making its missing construction obligations visible.
definitions: Use quaternion units ij=k, jk=i, ki=j and octonion product (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−conj(d)b, da+b conj(c)).
The associator is [a,b,c]=(ab)c−a(bc); the octonion norm is multiplicative.
For homogeneous parity |X|∈{0,1}, [X,Y]_s=XY−(−1)^{|X||Y|}YX.
The E₈ root set is {±e_i±e_j:i<j} together with {(±1/2,…,±1/2):an even number of minus signs}.

theorem.statement: For real octonions, ||(ab)c−a(bc)||≤2||a||||b||||c||. For nonzero norm product, equality holds exactly when (ab)c=−a(bc), and the constant two is sharp. Independently, the displayed E₈ root set has 240 vectors of squared length two.
theorem.proof: Write u=(ab)c and v=a(bc). Multiplicativity gives ||u||=||v||=n=||a||||b||||c||. Hence ||u−v||≤||u||+||v||=2n. If n>0, equality in the triangle inequality requires u and −v to have the same direction; equal norms make this exactly u=−v. The declared multiplication gives e₁e₂=e₃, e₃e₄=e₇, e₂e₄=e₆ and e₁e₆=−e₇, proving sharpness. For the root count, choosing two positions among eight and two independent signs gives 4·binom(8,2)=112 integer roots. Of the 2⁸ half-integral sign vectors exactly half have even parity: flipping one chosen sign pairs the two parity classes. Thus there are 128 such roots and 240 total. Each integer root has norm squared 1+1=2; each half-integral vector has 8/4=2. No Jacobi identity for an exceptional Lie bracket is implied by this count.

worked_example.setup: Compare a maximally nonassociative triple, an associative quaternion triple, and a small superalgebra.
worked_example.calculation: For (e₁,e₂,e₄), the two groupings are e₇ and −e₇, so the defect is two. For (e₁,e₂,e₃), both groupings equal −1, so the defect is zero. In gl(1|1), Q₊=E₁₂ and Q₋=E₂₁ are odd. Their superbracket is E₁₁+E₂₂=I, while Q₊²=Q₋²=0. Taking N=E₁₁ gives [N,Q₊]_s=Q₊ and [N,Q₋]_s=−Q₋. Expanding associative triple products with parity signs proves super-Jacobi. A finite exact verifier can check the octonion basis associators and all E₈ root lengths without asserting that either computation constructs a physical model.
worked_example.meaning: Convention-sensitive multiplication and root enumeration are complete finite tasks. A dimension match remains a consistency check until the actual bracket maps are present.

progression.narrative: The octonion multiplication convention and sharp defect bound make nonassociativity quantitative.
Superbrackets, Virasoro central terms and magic-square dimensions introduce graded and exceptional structure with explicit hypotheses.
The Jacobiator and infinitesimal SO(3) commutator distinguish bracket identities from informal rotation analogies.
The 120+128 decomposition provides exact E₈ weight accounting while leaving bracket construction separate.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Matrix rotation generators satisfy [J_x,J_y]=J_z and encode second-order commutation defects.
connections.scope: A bracket does not by itself specify a connection or PDE.

connections.mathematical_bridge: Associators and Jacobi identities are algebraic consistency conditions for proposed deformed products.
connections.scope: Ordinary associative matrices cannot faithfully realise a nonassociative product while preserving all multiplications.

connections.mathematical_bridge: A square-zero differential needs a graded bracket and its compatibility law.
connections.scope: An odd symbol alone does not give a differential graded algebra.

interactive_contract.inputs: Declared octonion table or graded multiplication, norm and parity assignments; explicit root lattice.
interactive_contract.outputs: Associators, defect bounds, bracket residuals, root counts and weight norms.
interactive_contract.validation: Exact basis multiplication; polarization when extending finite identity checks; root parity and norm checks.
interactive_contract.status: Worked finite multiplication and root-enumeration recipes; no exceptional Lie-algebra constructor is implemented.

families.limits: The octonion defect theorem does not classify every zero-associator orbit. Root counts do not prove anomaly cancellation, physical field content or a full E₈ bracket. Real forms and normalization must accompany any further comparison.
open_questions: Can an explicit normalized map Λ²S⁺→so₁₆ be supplied and its spinor Jacobi identity verified in a chosen basis?
Which automorphism orbits of unit octonion triples attain each fixed associator norm?
