families.title: Discretization, truncation and controlled approximation
families.central_question: Which finite approximation preserves the model’s invariants, and what bound connects it to the intended continuous object?
families.synopsis: Approximation becomes usable when its error sources are separated and bounded. The archive includes positive diffusion stencils, CFL conditions, distributed halo exchange, lattice anisotropy, FFT differentiation, Newton error and inverse cutoffs. They share a need to distinguish consistency from stability and implementation correctness. A correct communication pattern cannot repair an unstable time step; a stable matrix cannot recover frequencies never observed. The periodic heat stencil below has sharp positivity conditions, exact mass conservation and an explicit Fourier symbol. It is therefore a fully inspectable worked model. Its continuum error additionally needs smoothness and a consistency estimate. The inverse-cutoff lab L04 uses a different, explicitly declared observation model: bias decreases with cutoff while noise amplification increases. The common capability is selecting a finite scale under a proved error budget, not one universal algorithm.
definitions: For N≥3 with indices modulo N, define (T_r u)_j=ru_(j−1)+(1−2r)u_j+ru_(j+1), r=κΔt/(Δx)².

Positivity means T_r maps every coordinatewise nonnegative vector to a nonnegative vector. Fixed-grid identities use the sum-of-squares norm; continuum error rates use the normalized norm (N^(−1)Σ|u_j|²)^(1/2).
Consistency compares the discrete equation with a sufficiently smooth exact solution; it is distinct from finite-dimensional conservation and positivity.

theorem.statement: T_r preserves Σu_j for every r. It preserves nonnegativity exactly for 0≤r≤1/2. In that range it contracts the discrete ℓ² norm, with Fourier amplification 1−4r sin²(πk/N). For a smooth heat solution, the forward-Euler centered-space residual is O(Δt+Δx²) on a fixed bounded time interval with bounded derivatives.
theorem.proof: Cyclic summation makes each old value appear with coefficient r+(1−2r)+r=1, proving mass conservation. If all three coefficients are nonnegative, every new coordinate is a convex combination. Conversely a coordinate basis vector detects a negative off-diagonal coefficient when r<0 or a negative central coefficient when r>1/2, proving the sharp positivity condition. Convexity of z↦|z|² then gives |(T_ru)_j|²≤r|u_(j−1)|²+(1−2r)|u_j|²+r|u_(j+1)|². Sum over j to get contraction. Substituting the discrete character e^(2πikj/N) gives the amplification symbol r e^(−2πik/N)+(1−2r)+r e^(2πik/N)=1−4r sin²(πk/N), an independent spectral check. Finally Taylor expansion yields [u(t+Δt)−u(t)]/Δt=u_t+O(Δt), and [u(x+Δx)−2u(x)+u(x−Δx)]/Δx²=u_xx+O(Δx²). The heat equation cancels the leading terms. In the stable range, summing the resulting one-step defects gives a global fixed-time error of the same order under the stated smoothness in the normalized grid norm, with a uniform bound on the sampled consistency defect. A reaction term or boundary update changes these steps and must be analyzed separately.

worked_example.calculation: The next vector is (1/2,1/4,0,0,1/4). Its mass remains one, and its squared norm falls from one to 1/4+1/16+1/16=3/8. At r=3/4 the same central value becomes −1/2, disproving positivity immediately. For a separate cutoff recipe with bound B(N)+δS(N), a valid choice must drive both terms to zero; specifying only N→∞ is insufficient.
worked_example.meaning: The finite stencil certificate is exact and independent of a continuum limit. The cutoff lab exposes the parallel bias–amplification tradeoff with its own supplied singular values and source-class assumptions.

families.title: Regular-singular equations, normalized bases and monodromy
families.central_question: How should a parameter-dependent local basis be chosen so logarithms, resonances and continuation data remain meaningful?
families.synopsis: Frobenius and Picard–Fuchs questions recur in scalar connections, elliptic periods, gauge changes and Hill equations. A differential equation is not determined by an evocative period name: its coefficients, singularities, normalization and initial or cycle data must be supplied. Once the operator is known, coefficient recurrence and a Wronskian provide concrete local information. When exponents collide, a raw basis can appear singular even if the solution space varies regularly. The divided-difference model below makes the logarithm appear explicitly and proves which pole is removable. It also exhibits nontrivial unipotent monodromy with eigenvalues equal to one, explaining why those eigenvalues do not imply trivial continuation. General Fuchsian systems require additional resonance compatibility conditions; the model is a constructive baseline rather than a replacement for the missing operator.
definitions: For t>0 let θ=t d/dt and L_ε=θ(θ+ε). Its indicial exponents are 0 and −ε.
For ε≠0 define g_ε(t)=(t^(−ε)−1)/ε. A branch of log t must be fixed for complex continuation.
A fundamental pair of scalar solutions has nonzero Wronskian. Monodromy records how a chosen basis changes after analytic continuation around a singular point.

theorem.statement: g_ε extends analytically in ε to g₀=−log t. The pair (1,g_ε) remains independent with Wronskian −t^(−ε−1). Writing g_ε=Σ_{r≥0}ε^r g_r yields g_r=(−1)^(r+1)(log t)^(r+1)/(r+1)!, θ²g₀=0 and θ²g_r=−θg_(r−1) for r≥1.
theorem.proof: Choose a simply connected punctured domain and one analytic logarithm. Then t^(−ε)=exp(−ε log t) is entire in ε for each fixed t. Its exponential Taylor expansion shows that the numerator vanishes to first order at ε=0, so division removes the apparent pole and gives the stated coefficients. Both 1 and t^(−ε) solve L_εf=0, hence so does their divided difference. Direct differentiation gives g_ε′=−t^(−ε−1), never zero on the chosen domain; the Wronskian therefore has a finite nonzero limit −1/t. This proves independence even when the original pair (1,t^(−ε)) coalesces. Substituting the ε-series into (θ²+εθ)g=0 and equating coefficients gives the triangular hierarchy. It can also be checked directly using θ(log t)^k=k(log t)^(k−1). After a positive loop around zero, log t gains 2πi, so the limiting second solution −log t gains −2πi times the first. In the basis (1,−log t), continuation is represented by a nonidentity unipotent matrix, although both of its eigenvalues are one. The construction distinguishes a removable basis pole from genuine singular boundary data. For an actual Picard–Fuchs operator, its Frobenius recurrence and resonance equations must still be derived from that operator, rather than imported from this Euler example.

worked_example.setup: Take t=e² and ε=1/10, and compare the exact divided difference with its first three ε terms.
worked_example.calculation: g_(1/10)(e²)=10(e^(−1/5)−1)≈−1.812692469. The first three terms give −2+1/5−1/75=−136/75≈−1.813333333. families.title: Asymptotic expansions, singular scales and exponentially small data
families.central_question: What does a finite asymptotic expansion determine, and how can its remainder and missing exponential contribution be made explicit?
families.synopsis: The asymptotic strand includes renormalization flows, spectral gaps, elliptic logarithms, cubic folds, Mathieu perturbation, and a factorial Borel model. Its common requirement is to state the small parameter, the approach sector and the uniformity of a remainder. A formal series can be useful while diverging everywhere; convergence and asymptotic accuracy are distinct. Conversely, a few perturbative coefficients cannot determine a global continuation, a Stokes constant or a nonlinear front law. The one-pole Borel example makes the distinction fully constructive. Its coefficients, exact integral, finite error bound and exponentially small solution ambiguity are all explicit. The cubic fold supplies a complementary algebraic scale: coalescing critical points produce a three-halves action difference and a two-thirds transition parameter. Each model has its own hypotheses and should not be promoted to a universal description by analogy.
definitions: The formal series F(z)=Σ_{n≥0}n!z^(n+1) has zero radius of convergence. Its Borel transform is B(t)=Σt^n=1/(1−t) near t=0.
For a>0 define the nonsingular negative-ray sum F(−a)=−∫₀∞e^(−u/a)/(1+u)du.
An asymptotic expansion controls the error after each fixed finite truncation as a parameter tends to a limit; it need not converge when infinitely many terms are added.

theorem.statement: For every a>0 and N≥1, |F(−a)−Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}n!(−a)^(n+1)|≤N!a^(N+1). The corresponding Laplace sums solve z²F′−F=−z. Any two solutions differ by Ce^(−1/z); with above-minus-below bypasses of the positive Borel pole, the lateral difference is 2πi e^(−1/z).
theorem.proof: The exact finite geometric identity gives 1/(1+u)=Σ_{n=0}^{N−1}(−u)^n+(−u)^N/(1+u). Integrate against −e^(−u/a). The nth term evaluates to (−1)^(n+1)n!a^(n+1) by the Mellin moment. The absolute remainder is bounded by ∫₀∞e^(−u/a)u^Ndu=N!a^(N+1), since 1/(1+u)≤1. This proves a genuine finite-order error estimate on the negative ray even though the coefficient ratio makes the infinite power series divergent for every nonzero argument. Differentiation under the convergent integral, or integration by parts in its Laplace form, gives the inhomogeneous equation. Subtracting two solutions gives H′=H/z², hence H=Ce^(−1/z), which is smaller than every power as z↓0 on the positive ray. To compare the two lateral integrals, their difference closes clockwise around t=1. The residue of e^(−t/z)/(1−t) is −e^(−1/z), giving +2πi e^(−1/z) in that convention. The exponential ambiguity is therefore visible without guessing it from several factorial coefficients. A complete sectorial asymptotic proof must keep the bypass and decay contour fixed in a compatible sector; the explicit negative-ray bound is the directly verified remainder used here.

worked_example.setup: Use a=1/10 and N=5. Separately consider Φ(x;t)=x³/3−tx for t>0.
worked_example.calculation: The Borel-model truncation is −1/10+1/100−2/1000+6/10000−24/100000=−11455/125000=−0.09164, with error at most 120/10⁶=0.00012. The fold saddles are x_±=±√t and Φ(x_−;t)−Φ(x_+;t)=4t^(3/2)/3. Scaling x=h^(1/3)y in Φ/h yields y³/3−(t/h^(2/3))y, so the nontrivial transition occurs at t of order h^(2/3).
worked_example.meaning: These examples attach a bound or exact scaling identity to an asymptotic statement. They do not identify the Stokes data or thimbles of an unspecified amplitude.

families.title: Stability in the right metric, including transient and hybrid behavior
families.central_question: Which norm or storage function certifies decay when eigenvalues, Euclidean growth and switching tell different stories?
families.synopsis: The stability strand is unusually consistent across the years: feedback can be asymptotically stable and still amplify an initial perturbation, a spectral gap depends on the modes actually observed, and changing metrics can reveal coercivity absent in the Euclidean symmetric part. A positive quadratic Lyapunov function supplies a constructive certificate. Its matrix also quantifies the cost of a coordinate change, forcing, switching and resets. These are capabilities with distinct inputs: an eigenvalue calculation, a transient-gain calculation and a hybrid dwell-time bound are related but answer different questions. The two-dimensional triangular model below is deliberately small enough to solve exactly. It proves decay in one metric while displaying temporary growth in another, giving a positive explanation for the archive’s repeated cautions about nonnormality.
definitions: For P=Pᵀ>0, define V(x)=xᵀPx and ||x||_P=√V(x). A Hurwitz matrix has all eigenvalues with negative real part.
A quadratic Lyapunov certificate is AᵀP+PA≤−2αP for α>0. It implies ||e^(tA)x||_P≤e^(−αt)||x||_P.
For hybrid switching, a metric jump ratio ρ≥1 bounds V_after≤ρV_before; an average dwell-time bound controls how often this cost can be incurred.

theorem.statement: For A=[[-1,3],[0,−1]] and P=[[1/2,3/4],[3/4,11/4]], P>0 and AᵀP+PA=−I. Since P≤3I, ||e^(tA)x||_P≤e^(−t/6)||x||_P. Nevertheless the Euclidean squared norm has positive derivative at x=(1,1).
theorem.proof: The leading principal entry of P is 1/2 and det P=11/8−9/16=13/16>0, so the two-by-two Sylvester criterion proves positive definiteness. Direct multiplication gives AᵀP+PA=−I. Along x′=Ax, V′=xᵀ(AᵀP+PA)x=−||x||₂². The matrix 3I−P has positive first entry 5/2 and determinant (5/2)(1/4)−9/16=1/16>0, so P≤3I. Therefore ||x||₂²≥V/3 and V′≤−V/3. Integration and square roots give the rate 1/6 in the P norm. In contrast, at x=(1,1), Ax=(2,−1), so d||x||₂²/dt=2xᵀAx=2>0. The eigenvalues of A are both −1; their location does not prohibit this initial Euclidean amplification. Because A=−I+3N with N²=0, its exact exponential is e^(−t)(I+3tN), explicitly displaying the polynomial transient. If continuous segments obey V′≤−2αV and jumps cost at most ρ, then V(t)≤ρ^N(t)e^(−2αt)V(0). Under N(t)≤N₀+t/τ, this becomes ρ^N₀ exp[−2(α−logρ/(2τ))t]V(0). Thus switching consumes a precise logarithmic decay budget rather than preserving stability merely because each mode is stable.

worked_example.setup: Use x₀=(0,1) for the continuous model, and compare two rank-one orthogonal projections whose lines meet at angle θ.
worked_example.calculation: The exact trajectory is x(t)=e^(−t)(3t,1). At t=1 its Euclidean norm is √10/e>1 although it eventually tends to zero. For projections P₀ onto (1,0) and Q onto (cosθ,sinθ), P₀QP₀=cos²θ P₀. Thus a cycle restricted to im P₀ contracts by cos²θ, while ||[P₀,Q]||=|sinθ cosθ|. These are different quantities, even though both depend on the same angle.
worked_example.meaning: The Lyapunov example has a globally valid certificate for its linear flow. The L05 projection component provides another exact model of convergence and noncommutation, without identifying either number as a universal holonomy invariant.

families.title: Local bifurcation, exact cycles and the boundary of chaos claims
families.central_question: Which changes of stability can be derived from a return map, and what additional work separates a local bifurcation from global chaos?
families.synopsis: The dynamics archive repeatedly returns to logistic period doubling, oscillator locking, pitchfork regulation, scalar flip equations and return-map jets. These are best organized around a local map or flow, its invariant branches and its multipliers. A nonlinearity is not itself chaos, a symbolic analogy is not a conjugacy, and a local germ is not a global attractor. The logistic family offers an unusually complete positive example: the first fixed-point instability, the born two-cycle and its entire linear-stability interval follow from exact algebra. Later 2026 questions enrich this with explicit transcendental flip candidates, square-root branching and cubic coefficients of the second iterate. Those mechanisms can be compared once the local coordinates and nondegeneracy conditions are stated.
definitions: Let f_r(x)=rx(1−x), r>0. A point has exact period two when f_r²(x)=x and f_r(x)≠x.
The multiplier of a k-cycle is the product of derivatives along it. Absolute multiplier less than one proves local attraction; equality is a boundary case requiring higher-order analysis.
A local flip occurs when a fixed-point multiplier crosses −1 transversely with an appropriate nonzero nonlinear coefficient.

theorem.statement: The nonzero logistic fixed point is stable for 1<r<3. For r>3 its genuine two-cycle has points x_±=[r+1±√((r−3)(r+1))]/(2r) and multiplier m₂=−r²+2r+4. It is linearly attracting exactly for 3<r<1+√6.
theorem.proof: Solving f_r(x)=x gives zero and x*=1−1/r. At x*, f_r′(x*)=r(1−2+2/r)=2−r, whose absolute value is less than one exactly when 1<r<3. To locate period-two points, expand f_r²(x)−x and divide by the known fixed-point factors. The remaining equation is r²x²−r(r+1)x+(r+1)=0. Its discriminant is r²(r−3)(r+1), giving the displayed distinct real roots for r>3. Their sum is (r+1)/r and product is (r+1)/r². Consequently f_r′(x_+)f_r′(x_-)=r²[1−2(x_++x_-)+4x_+x_-]=−r²+2r+4. For r>3 this polynomial decreases strictly, starts at +1 at r=3 and reaches −1 at r=1+√6. Hence |m₂|<1 precisely on the stated interval. At the first endpoint the two-cycle merges with the fixed branch; at the second, its multiplier reaches the next flip boundary. This calculation establishes neither every later doubling nor Feigenbaum universality. A complementary jet calculation explains why higher terms matter: if R(s)=−s+as²+bs³+O(s⁴), direct composition gives R²(s)=s−2(a²+b)s³+O(s⁴); the quadratic term cancels and the sign or vanishing of a²+b is relevant. A multiplier of −1 alone omits that information.

worked_example.setup: Take r=16/5. Also compare the regulator m↦tanh(am) near a=1.
worked_example.calculation: The logistic two-cycle is (21±√21)/32, and its multiplier is 4/25. It is therefore locally attracting. For the regulator, tanh(am)=am−a³m³/3+O(m⁵); a nonzero fixed point satisfies m²=3(a−1)/a³+O((a−1)²) as a↓1. This square-root branch is a pitchfork mechanism, distinct from the logistic two-cycle despite a shared critical-scaling vocabulary.
worked_example.meaning: Exact branch formulas make hypotheses testable. They provide a foundation for a numerical bifurcation diagram, while the diagram itself cannot certify an infinite cascade or a global chaotic invariant set.

families.title: Mechanics, dimensional modeling and invariant flow coordinates
families.central_question: Which quantities and scaling laws survive a change of coordinates, units or time parameter?
families.synopsis: The modeling strand includes mechanics, population and asset recurrences, conductance gates, mass balances and renormalization flows. Its common discipline is to identify state variables, units, conserved quantities and the meaning of the time parameter before interpreting a formula. Dimensional consistency narrows possible equations but does not determine numerical coefficients, boundary conditions or a physical mechanism. Hamiltonian mechanics supplies a precise constructive invariant: energy conservation. A simple turning point then exhibits two different exponents for physical time and abbreviated action. Their difference is caused by the measure being integrated, not a contradiction. The RG examples use the same chain-rule discipline to distinguish an invariant linearization exponent from coordinate-dependent higher coefficients. These are typed bridges between calculations, rather than a claim that every model in the family describes the same physics.
definitions: For a unit-mass one-dimensional Hamiltonian H(q,p)=p²/2+V(q), Hamilton’s equations are q′=p and p′=−V′(q).
At energy E, a simple turning point q* has E−V(q)≈F(q*−q) with F>0 on the allowed side.
A scalar autonomous flow g′=β(g) transforms under h=φ(g), φ′≠0, to β_h(h)=φ′(g)β(g). The meaning of the time variable remains part of this definition.

theorem.statement: For the stated Hamiltonian, H is conserved. If V(q)=E−F(q*−q) exactly on q≤q*, then with δ=q*−q the remaining travel time is T(δ)=√(2/F)δ^(1/2), while the action length is S(δ)=(2/3)√(2F)δ^(3/2). At any scalar-flow fixed point, dβ_h/dh=β′(g*) under a smooth invertible state-coordinate change.
theorem.proof: Energy conservation is a direct chain-rule calculation: H′=V′(q)q′+pp′=V′p−pV′=0. On the increasing branch p=√[2(E−V(q))]=√(2Fδ). Physical travel time integrates dq/p, so T(δ)=∫₀^δ(2Fs)^(−1/2)ds=√(2/F)√δ. The abbreviated action integrates p dq, giving S(δ)=∫₀^δ√(2Fs)ds=(2/3)√(2F)δ^(3/2). The two powers therefore concern different observables. For a smooth potential with a nonzero turning derivative, Taylor’s theorem produces these leading terms with controlled local remainders; a degenerate turning point has different exponents. For the scalar coordinate calculation, differentiate β_h=φ′β with respect to h using d/dh=(φ′)^(−1)d/dg. The result is β′+(φ″/φ′)β. At a fixed point β(g*)=0, the second term vanishes and the linearized exponent is unchanged. This conclusion uses a state-coordinate change with φ′ nonzero and the same time. A rescaling of time multiplies the rate and must not be silently included. Exact flow integration makes the same point: for g′=bg², 1/g(t)=1/g₀−bt on every interval avoiding its pole. The finite-time wall is a property of that stated flow, not a physically meaningful singularity without an identified scale convention.

worked_example.setup: Let F=2 in the turning-point model, and separately let g′=g² with g₀=1/4.
worked_example.calculation: The travel time from distance δ to the turn is √δ, whereas the action is (4/3)δ^(3/2). The exact flow is g(t)=1/(4−t) for t<4. Replacing g by h=2g changes the beta function to h′=h²/2, but the same solution and wall time remain. At a nonzero fixed point of a flow with β(g)=−εg+bg², the derivative is ε, and the state-coordinate argument preserves that number.
worked_example.meaning: Each formula carries its own dimensions and clock. A mass balance similarly needs an actual volume, molar conversion and yield; an area alone cannot recover an amount.

families.title: Memory, recurrence and the information needed for a closed evolution
families.central_question: When does a reduced state determine its own future, and what exact memory or symbolic data repair a failure of closure?
families.synopsis: A final dynamics strand connects hidden-variable elimination, damped recurrences, rotations, substitutions, cellular automata and path-dependent accumulators. The shared question is what information must be retained for a well-defined next state. Eliminating a hidden coordinate usually creates a memory kernel and an initial-state source. Forgetting either can turn an exact reduction into a different equation. Symbolic models pose the discrete analogue: an observed label may not encode the phase or history needed for the future. At the same time, deterministic aperiodicity can be highly structured. A rotation coding has exact balance, and a dense quasiperiodic orbit can have zero entropy. The family therefore organizes recurrence by a declared state, observation and equivalence relation rather than grouping every irregular-looking sequence under chaos.
definitions: Consider x′=−ax+by and y′=cx−dy with constants a,b,c,d and given (x₀,y₀). A closed scalar evolution in x alone must determine x′ from retained data.
The memory convolution (K*x)(t)=∫₀ᵗK(t−s)x(s)ds retains past x values. The source be^(−dt)y₀ carries the hidden initial condition.
A mechanical word is w_n=⌊(n+1)α+ρ⌋−⌊nα+ρ⌋ for 0<α<1. It codes a rotation with an explicitly retained phase.

theorem.statement: Eliminating y gives exactly x′(t)=−ax(t)+be^(−dt)y₀+bc∫₀ᵗe^(−d(t−s))x(s)ds. For a=d=b=c=1 and (x₀,y₀)=(1,0), x(t)=(1+e^(−2t))/2. Moreover every length-m block of the mechanical word has either ⌊mα⌋ or ⌈mα⌉ ones.
theorem.proof: Multiply the y-equation by e^(dt). Its derivative is c e^(dt)x(t); integrate from zero to t and divide by e^(dt) to obtain y(t)=e^(−dt)y₀+c∫₀ᵗe^(−d(t−s))x(s)ds. Substitution into the x-equation proves the exact Volterra equation and shows why the initial source cannot be omitted. In the stated symmetric example, s=x+y satisfies s′=0 and r=x−y satisfies r′=−2r. With s₀=r₀=1, x=(s+r)/2=(1+e^(−2t))/2 and y=(1−e^(−2t))/2. Dropping the memory would give e^(−t), which has the wrong long-time limit. This is an exact closure failure, not an approximation estimate. For the mechanical word, sum from n=j to j+m−1: the floors telescope to ⌊(j+m)α+ρ⌋−⌊jα+ρ⌋. Writing jα+ρ as integer plus θ∈[0,1) gives ⌊mα+θ⌋, which is either floor or ceiling of mα. Any two length-m blocks therefore differ in their number of ones by at most one. Dividing the prefix count by m yields limiting frequency α. If α is irrational, a periodic binary word would have rational frequency, so the word is aperiodic. These two examples demonstrate distinct constructive repairs: keep a memory term for the continuous reduction, or keep the rotation phase for the symbolic coding. Neither irregular recurrence nor aperiodicity alone proves positive entropy or unpredictability.

worked_example.setup: Compare the exact continuous reduction at t=log2 with a mechanical word of slope α=(√5−1)/2 and ρ=0.
worked_example.calculation: At t=log2, x=(1+1/4)/2=5/8, while the memory-free approximation is 1/2. The mechanical word begins 0,1,0,1,1,0,1,0; its first eight symbols contain ⌊8α⌋=4 ones. Every block of eight contains four or five ones. The compact floor formula supplies all finite blocks without asserting an independent random-symbol model.
worked_example.meaning: The archive’s symbolic Perron models, substitutions and relative periodic cellular automata can be compared through their declared coding maps and retained state. They are not automatically interchangeable realizations of the same process.

families.title: Probability laws, moments and joint dependence
families.central_question: Which parts of a conclusion follow from marginal probabilities, and which require a full joint law?
families.synopsis: A probability model is an assignment of mass to compatible outcomes before it is a formula for an average. The earliest finite probability questions, the distinction between population and amplitude weights, reliability calculations, Bayesian prediction and the final three-item surplus model all converge on this point. Linearity of expectation survives dependence, whereas the probability of a conjunction generally does not. The most productive revision is to preserve the entire compatibility structure until the requested functional has been calculated. A mean, a variance, a tail probability and an optimal action use different parts of that structure. This family therefore treats uncertainty as a mathematical input with explicitly stated moments, rather than as a single decorative error bar.
definitions: A finite law is p(ω)≥0 with Σωp(ω)=1; E f=Σωp(ω)f(ω). A covariance requires finite second moments.
For Bernoulli indicators B_i, marginal success probabilities p_i=E B_i specify only n linear constraints on their joint table.
Population-weighted energy is Σp_i|a_i|²=‖diag(√p)a‖²; replacing √p by p changes the quantity.
A posterior predictive probability integrates a conditional law against the posterior; its repeated outcomes can be dependent after the latent parameter is integrated out.

theorem.statement: For events A_1,…,A_n with probabilities p_i, max(0,Σp_i−n+1)≤P(∩A_i)≤min_i p_i. For any integrable B_i, EΣB_i=ΣE B_i without independence. If p is random, conditionally independent future Bernoulli outcomes have unconditional covariance Var(p), so their joint success probability is E p² rather than (E p)².
theorem.proof: The upper intersection bound follows from containment. For the lower bound apply the union bound to the complementary events: P(∩A_i)=1−P(∪A_i^c)≥1−Σ(1−p_i), then combine with nonnegativity. Linearity is a finite rearrangement of sums, or the linearity of the Lebesgue integral. For two future indicators, conditional independence gives E[B_1B_2|p]=p², and the tower property yields E B_1B_2=E p². Each mean is E p; subtraction gives Var(p). Thus independence conditional on one variable cannot be silently transported through marginalization. The proof also identifies the missing datum: a coupling or a latent-parameter distribution.

worked_example.setup: Three indicators each have success probability 4/5, and an illustrative surplus is Π=10(B_1+B_2+B_3)−95/4.
worked_example.calculation: The mean is 30·4/5−95/4=1/4 for every compatible coupling. Profit requires three successes, whose probability lies between 2/5 and 4/5. The lower endpoint is attained by assigning mass 2/5 to 111 and 1/5 each to 110,101,011. The upper endpoint is attained by mass 4/5 at 111 and 1/5 at 000. Independence instead yields 64/125. In a Beta(4,2) posterior, the mean success probability is 2/3 but the probability of two future successes is 4·5/(6·7)=10/21, exceeding 4/9 by 2/63.
worked_example.meaning: A positive expectation and a frequent positive outcome are separate objectives. These exact fixtures give a practical diagnostic: ask whether the claimed conclusion remains constant over all joint laws with the supplied marginals. If it does not, the dependence model belongs in the question itself. This is also the common starting point for distributionally robust decisions.

families.title: Random filtrations, weighted sampling and exact inclusion laws
families.central_question: How can random selection be transported into an exact expectation of a combinatorial or topological observable?
families.synopsis: Random filtrations connect probability with topology by making the event that a face is present explicit. The source trajectory runs from elementary denominators and collision probabilities to fractal measures, random birth times and weighted fixed-size samples. A random complex cannot be understood solely by calling it random: its vertex law, face rule, dependence and filtration parameter must be declared. Once those inputs are fixed, indicator expansion often turns a seemingly global expected invariant into a short exact sum. This family organizes three scales of the same idea: finite subset enumeration, order statistics of random birth times, and weak approximation of measures by coupled partial constructions.
definitions: For positive weights w_1,…,w_N and fixed size m, assign a subset S probability proportional to ∏_{i∈S}w_i. The normalizer e_m(w) is the degree-m elementary symmetric polynomial.
For a prescribed face F with b vertices, the inclusion indicator is 1_{F⊆S}. A simplicial complex is induced by the selected vertices only after the face rule is specified.
The Euler characteristic of a finite complex is χ=Σ_F(−1)^{dim F}; expectation commutes with this finite sum.
A filtration K_t is increasing in t. Independent uniform vertex birth times create correlated face births via the maximum over each face.

theorem.statement: Under weighted fixed-size sampling, P(F⊆S)=w_F e_{m−b}(w_{F^c})/e_m(w), taking e_r=0 outside valid degrees. Consequently Eχ(K[S])=Σ_F(−1)^{dim F}P(F⊆S). In the equal-weight case this becomes binom(N−b,m−b)/binom(N,m).
theorem.proof: Every selected subset containing F is uniquely F∪T with T⊆F^c and |T|=m−b. Its unnormalized mass is w_F∏_{i∈T}w_i. Summing over T gives the numerator; summing over all size-m subsets gives the denominator. The Euler formula follows by inserting one inclusion indicator per face and using linearity, with no independence assumption between faces. The normalizers satisfy E_{j,r}=E_{j−1,r}+w_jE_{j−1,r−1}, because each size-r subset either excludes j or includes it. This dynamic program is an exact coefficient computation, not a Monte Carlo estimate. Equal weights reduce both symmetric polynomials to binomial coefficients and recover the hypergeometric law.

worked_example.setup: Select two vertices from four with weights (1,2,3,4). Separately, let the four vertices of a cycle appear at independent uniform times, with edges appearing when both endpoints are present and the filling two-cell arriving at time one.
worked_example.calculation: Here e_2=2+3+4+6+8+12=35. Vertex one is selected with probability (2+3+4)/35=9/35; the pair {1,2} is selected with probability 2/35. If K is the four-cycle, Eχ=Σ_iP(i∈S)−Σ_edgesP(edge⊆S)=2−(2+6+12+4)/35=46/35. In the birth-time model, the loop appears at B=max(U_1,…,U_4), hence P(B≤t)=t^4. Its barcode is [B,1), and E(1−B)=∫_0^1t^4dt=1/5.
worked_example.meaning: The expected Euler characteristic needs only face inclusion probabilities, whereas expected Betti numbers usually require joint rank information. The barcode example is exactly solvable because the topology has one possible loop. The distinction prevents a facewise expectation formula from being mistaken for a general persistent-homology estimator.

families.title: Stochastic dynamics, Itô correction and finite-horizon prediction
families.central_question: Which drift, noise and observation model determines the uncertainty at a future time?
families.synopsis: The stochastic strand becomes coherent when a process is specified before its spectrum, stationary law or prediction error is computed. Finite reversible chains, a two-spin Gibbs model, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics, bridge functionals and exact linear propagation supply complementary levels of resolution. The key unification is the generator: transition rates in a finite state space and second derivatives in a diffusion both encode how expectations evolve. They do not make deterministic gradient descent, white noise and colored fluctuations interchangeable. The prediction problem adds a second layer: an observation changes the present conditional law, then a common transition propagates that law and introduces fresh process noise. Reversibility supplies a complementary finite certificate: detailed balance makes a Markov generator symmetric after weighting by its stationary law, so its relaxation modes can be checked spectrally. That self-adjoint reduction is specific to the declared chain and is not available for arbitrary driven dynamics.
definitions: An Itô diffusion satisfies dX=b(X,t)dt+σ(X,t)dW; its generator is Lf=b·∇f+(1/2)tr(σσᵀD²f).
For dX=AXdt+LdW with deterministic coefficients, F=e^{AΔ} and Q=∫_0^Δe^{As}LLᵀe^{Aᵀs}ds describe the exact transition.
An OU process has drift −κX, κ>0; a stationary variance solves the scalar Lyapunov equation −2κv+σ²=0.
A Brownian bridge B_t=W_t−(t/T)W_T conditions the endpoint, changing covariances and all integrals sensitive to constants.

theorem.statement: For dX=−κXdt+σdW and deterministic X_t=x, E[X_T²|X_t=x]=e^{−2κτ}x²+σ²(1−e^{−2κτ})/(2κ), τ=T−t. More generally a linear Gaussian prior covariance P propagates to FPFᵀ+Q. A common propagation preserves Loewner order between two posterior covariances.
theorem.proof: The integrating factor gives X_T=e^{−κτ}x+σ∫_t^Te^{−κ(T−s)}dW_s. The stochastic integral has mean zero and, by Itô isometry, variance σ²∫_0^τe^{−2κs}ds. Squaring and taking expectations gives the displayed expression. The generator gives the same conclusion: L(x²)=−2κx²+σ², where the constant σ² is the Itô correction. For the matrix process use the variation-of-constants formula, independence of future Wiener increments and the matrix isometry. If P_1≤P_2, then F(P_2−P_1)Fᵀ≥0. Adding the same Q preserves the order. Different terminal times require different F and Q and therefore are outside that comparison.

worked_example.setup: Let X=(position,driver), A=[[0,1],[0,0]], prior P=I, horizon Δ=10, and a scalar sensor with noise variance r=1/100. Compare measuring position with measuring driver, both at the present time.
worked_example.calculation: F=[[1,10],[0,1]]. A measurement of position gives posterior diag(1/101,1), so terminal position variance is 100+1/101. A driver measurement gives diag(1,1/101), hence variance 1+100/101=201/101. The indirect sensor is better for this future target. If L=(0,1)ᵀ, process covariance is [[Δ³/3,Δ²/2],[Δ²/2,Δ]]; at Δ=2 it has determinant 4/3 and must be added for either sensor. For OU Euler–Maruyama, stationary variance is σ²/(2κ−κ²h), existing only for 0<κh<2.
worked_example.meaning: A good present measurement and a good future-target measurement are different design questions. The exact transition separates structural ignorance, current sensor noise, future noise and numerical discretization bias. Each has a different remedy and a different mathematical certificate.

families.title: Scaling limits, stable laws and the geometry of approximation
families.central_question: When does repeated averaging simplify a law, and which quantitative information survives the limit?
families.synopsis: Averaging, renormalization, heavy tails, multiplicative products and infinite-dimensional Gaussian models share a demand for explicit scaling. A Gaussian fixed point is a theorem about normalized sums with finite variance, not a universal fate of every noise source. Cauchy stability provides an exact countermodel, and multiplicative products become additive only after taking logarithms. The fractal measure construction adds a different kind of approximation: convergence follows from a direct coupling bound rather than from a central limit theorem. This family distinguishes exact finite identities, limiting distributions and numerical approximations, preserving the assumptions that make each useful.
definitions: For independent copies X_1,X_2 of a centered variable, the averaging renormalization is R(X)=(X_1+X_2)/√2.
The characteristic function is φ(t)=E e^{itX}; independent summation multiplies characteristic functions.
An α-stable fixed law for R_α=(X_1+X_2)/2^{1/α} has characteristic function exp(−c|t|^α) in the symmetric model.
A Gaussian series X=Σ√q_nZ_ne_n is H-valued in mean square when Σq_n<∞; cylindrical coordinate consistency alone does not guarantee H-valued samples.

theorem.statement: If a centered nondegenerate finite-variance law is fixed under R_α, then α=2; under R_2 its characteristic function is Gaussian. More generally R^k(X) converges in distribution to the centered Gaussian of variance v when EX=0 and EX²=v<∞.
theorem.proof: A fixed law has v=2·2^{−2/α}v, so nonzero finite v forces α=2. In that case the characteristic-function equation implies φ(t)=[φ(t/√n)]^n for dyadic n. Finite variance and centering give φ(s)=1−vs²/2+o(s²). Inserting s=t/√n and letting n grow yields exp(−vt²/2), proving the fixed-law assertion. The same expansion applied to the normalized sum of n independent copies proves convergence of characteristic functions, and hence convergence in distribution, for dyadic n and for the usual all-n central limit theorem. If higher cumulants exist, the rth cumulant scales as n^{1−r/2}; this records the disappearance of finite higher-order cumulants without asserting a uniform density approximation or a rate from only two moments.

worked_example.setup: Let U_j be independent uniform variables on (0,1), κ_k=∏_{j=1}^kU_j and Y_j=−log U_j. Also compare a standard Cauchy sample mean.
worked_example.calculation: Each Y_j has exponential density e^{−y} for y>0, mean and variance one. Therefore k^{−1}logκ_k→−1 almost surely and (logκ_k+k)/√k converges to N(0,1). The transform Eκ_k^{−βγ}=(1−βγ)^{−k} is finite precisely for βγ<1. For a Cauchy variable, φ(t)=e^{−|t|}; averaging n copies yields [φ(t/n)]^n=e^{−|t|}, so the mean never concentrates and P(|X̄_n|≤1)=1/2 for every n. For a Cantor coupling whose omitted tail is at most 3^{−n}, every L-Lipschitz test has expectation error at most L3^{−n}.
worked_example.meaning: Different mechanisms supply different error statements: a weak Gaussian limit, exact Cauchy stability, a transform convergence threshold, or a deterministic transport bound. Choosing among them begins by stating which observable must be approximated and in which metric. A visual similarity between histograms does not substitute for that choice.

families.title: Covariance geometry, nonlinear uncertainty and hidden-target risk
families.central_question: Which uncertainty is reducible by precision, and which requires a different observation?
families.synopsis: The covariance strand connects finite quadratic forms, data fusion, singular maps and statistical observability. Its central revision is to separate an exact law from a linearized uncertainty approximation, and to separate noise in an observed coordinate from a target component that the observation never determines. Positive semidefiniteness is a structural constraint on covariances, not merely a numerical preference. The observation sigma-algebra determines what can be estimated; the loss determines what error means. Together these ideas give a precise route from a hidden coordinate to an irreducible risk, while preventing a zero Jacobian from being read as zero nonlinear uncertainty.
definitions: For X∈L², Σ=E[(X−EX)(X−EX)ᵀ] is positive semidefinite; singularity records an almost-sure linear relation.
The exact output law under f is the pushforward f_#μ. The delta approximation ε²JΣJᵀ applies to f(x_0+εZ) only as an asymptotic statement with appropriate moments and remainders.
For target T∈L² and observation Z, the squared-loss Bayes estimator is E[T|Z] and its risk is E Var(T|Z).
The Markov condition T→Z→Y means Y supplies no target information beyond Z; this includes adding independent measurement noise to Z.

theorem.statement: Under T→Z→Y, E Var(T|Y)=E Var(T|Z)+E Var(E[T|Z]|Y). Thus the best noisy-observation risk is at least the noise-free hidden-target floor. Separately, for X∼N(0,σ²), Var(X²)=2σ⁴ even though the derivative of x² at zero vanishes.
theorem.proof: Write m=E[T|Z], e=T−m. Conditional independence gives E[e|Z,Y]=0, hence E[T|Y]=E[m|Y]. Expand T−E[T|Y]=e+m−E[m|Y]. Conditioning on Z,Y kills the cross term, so the mean squared error is E e²+E(m−E[m|Y])². Conditional-mean optimality itself follows by decomposing T−a(Y) into T−E[T|Y] and E[T|Y]−a(Y). The nonlinear example uses E X²=σ² and E X⁴=3σ⁴. Its full density follows by the two inverse branches ±√y and their Jacobians. The nonzero variance is of order σ⁴; the failed linear term would have been order σ², so the issue is an altered leading order rather than a contradiction.

worked_example.setup: Take independent X_1 and Z_3∼N(0,σ²), target T=X_1+Z_3², and observe X_1 exactly. Compare independent repeated sensors with identical copies of one sensor.
worked_example.calculation: The best estimate is X_1+σ² and risk is 2σ⁴. Repeating a noiseless observation of X_1 leaves the observation sigma-algebra unchanged. A sensor informative about Z_3 can improve the risk because it enlarges that sigma-algebra. For n independent observations of a scalar mean with noise variance s², averaging has variance s²/n. For n identical copies of one noise realization, Σ=s²11ᵀ and every unbiased weighted average has variance s². If local covariances C_j and means μ_j are mixed with p_j≥0, total covariance is Σp_jC_j+Σp_j(μ_j−μ)(μ_j−μ)ᵀ, preserving positivity.
worked_example.meaning: This family connects experimental design directly to target information. More repetitions can remove measurement noise; a new kind of observation can remove hidden-target ambiguity. A coordinate covariance, a worst-case fibre width and a Bayes risk are distinct quantities with distinct units and quantifiers. The atlas makes those distinctions operational in its worked examples.

families.title: Entropy contraction, channel information and Fisher geometry
families.central_question: Which information quantity is monotone under a declared transformation, and what geometry does it induce?
families.synopsis: Entropy appears across finite chains, communication channels, softmax models, quantum states and gradient diffusion. The synthesis needs a reference measure and a transformation before it needs a slogan about disorder. Shannon entropy can decrease under a nonuniform Markov equilibrium while relative entropy to that equilibrium decreases as well. Mutual information describes a joint distribution and contracts along a Markov channel; it does not assign a causal arrow. At small scale, relative entropy generates Fisher geometry, whose null directions express parameter redundancy. These facts connect probabilistic coarse-graining, differential geometry and optimization through explicit maps rather than through a shared word.
definitions: For positive finite q, D(p||q)=Σp_i log(p_i/q_i), with 0 log0=0; Shannon entropy is H(p)=−Σp_i logp_i.
A stochastic channel T maps input distributions to output distributions. Mutual information is D(p_XY||p_Xp_Y).
For logits u, A(u)=logΣe^{u_i}, p_i=e^{u_i−A(u)}, and F=diag(p)−ppᵀ. A common additive logit is unidentifiable.
For a faithful density matrix σ, its modular Hamiltonian is −logσ. Matrix entropy and classical entropy agree on diagonal states, but their full differential geometry requires operator calculus.

theorem.statement: Every finite stochastic channel satisfies D(Tp||Tq)≤D(p||q). For softmax probabilities, F≥0, F1=0, and D(p(u)||p(u+h))=(1/2)hᵀFh+O(‖h‖³). At uniform p on m outcomes, F=(I−11ᵀ/m)/m and H=logm.
theorem.proof: For each output j, apply the log-sum inequality to a_i=T_{ji}p_i and b_i=T_{ji}q_i. Summing the inequalities over j and using Σ_jT_{ji}=1 gives contraction. Equality requires the likelihood ratio p_i/q_i to be constant across every collection of inputs mixed into a positive output. For the geometric statement, differentiating A gives ∇A=p and ∇²A=F. The quadratic form vᵀFv=Σp_iv_i²−(Σp_iv_i)² is a variance, hence nonnegative and zero on constants. The KL expression is exactly A(u+h)−A(u)−p(u)·h; Taylor expansion supplies the local quadratic term. This proves the geometry on the quotient by common logits rather than pretending the full Fisher matrix is invertible.

worked_example.setup: Take a Markov matrix whose every row is π=(9/10,1/10), and initial p=(1/2,1/2). Then compare a fair bit passed through two binary symmetric channels with flip probability 1/10.
worked_example.calculation: One Markov step sends p to π, reducing H from log2 to −.9log.9−.1log.1, while D(p||π)=log(5/3) falls to zero. In the channel cascade the effective flip probability is 2(.1)(.9)=.18. Information therefore falls from 1−h_2(.1)≈.531004 bits to 1−h_2(.18)≈.319923 bits. At m=97 uniform classes, entropy is log97≈4.574711 nats and the 96 nonzero Fisher eigenvalues are 1/97. Neither uniform entropy nor a small parameter step reports classification accuracy.
worked_example.meaning: The correct monotone depends on the experiment: relative entropy for a fixed reference law, mutual information for a channel, or KL locally for a parameterized model. This provides a useful common language while preserving their distinct arguments, units and equality conditions. An information quantity can be mathematically exact even when its proposed application lacks data.

families.title: Identifiability, calibration and honest statistical validation
families.central_question: What mathematical contract turns a fitted pattern into a justified inference about unseen outcomes?
families.synopsis: The inference strand develops from an identifiable logistic design and calibrated residual energy to finite strategy search, PAC–Bayes bounds, rank statistics and exact randomization. Its organizing distinction is between fitting a chosen sample, identifying a model parameter, calibrating a test under a null, and predicting a new draw. Each asks a different question. A low residual proves a relation within a specified sample geometry; it does not automatically validate a causal mechanism or a future performance claim. This family supplies positive mathematical tools for stronger questions: declare the sampling law, expose the selection step, reserve independent data, and report an uncertainty statement whose quantifiers survive that selection.
definitions: A parameter is identifiable if distinct admissible values produce distinct observation laws at the stated design.
For a fixed predictor f and bounded loss in [0,1], true risk R(f) is the expected loss under a declared sampling distribution, while empirical risk is the sample mean.
A valid p-value obeys P_0(p≤α)≤α for every α∈[0,1] under the stated null. Pairing alone does not supply the null.
AUROC is P(s_+>s_−)+(1/2)P(s_+=s_−) for independent uniform empirical positive and negative choices; its tie rule belongs to the definition.

theorem.statement: For K fixed candidates evaluated on n iid validation observations with loss in [0,1], with probability at least 1−δ all risk errors are at most ε=√(log(2K/δ)/(2n)). The empirically best candidate then has true risk at most 2ε above the best candidate. A paired fair-sign randomization test has a finite superuniform p-value under its exchangeable sign null.
theorem.proof: Hoeffding's bound gives P(|Rhat_k−R_k|>ε)≤2e^{−2nε²} for one fixed candidate. A union bound over K choices yields δ at the stated ε. On the simultaneous event, R(fhat)≤Rhat(fhat)+ε≤Rhat(f*)+ε≤R(f*)+2ε. The candidates must be fixed independently of this validation sample, or their entire adaptive selection must be included in a stronger valid argument. For the randomization result, condition on the observed magnitudes and enumerate every equally likely sign assignment. Ranking the test statistic within that finite null population makes the upper-tail rank p superuniform; ties only make it conservative. This proof is finite and requires no normal approximation.

worked_example.setup: Eight paired differences have illustrative magnitudes all one, and the observed signs are all positive. A separate two-class score example has positive scores (2,1) and negative scores (1,0).
worked_example.calculation: There are 2^8=256 sign vectors. Only one gives signed sum eight, so the one-sided exact p-value is 1/256. The absolute statistic has two extremes, giving 1/128. For AUROC, the four positive-negative comparisons yield wins 1,1,0,1 with the tied comparison replaced by 1/2, so the total is 7/2 and AUROC=7/8. Every strictly increasing score transformation preserves these comparisons. Multiplying all paired magnitudes by a positive constant leaves randomization p unchanged, demonstrating that statistical evidence and practical effect size are different outputs.
worked_example.meaning: The sources on regressions, periodic contrasts, spectral fits and normalized residuals become useful when attached to this contract. A period-matched difference can identify an exact trend in a declared model; a nested regression always improves training fit; neither alone supplies a future-risk bound. The best revised question names both the estimand and the independent evidence that could challenge it.

families.title: Finite information, observation equivalence and diagnostic statistics
families.central_question: How much can an observation distinguish, and what information does a summary discard?
families.synopsis: Several source questions use entropy, spectral flatness, phase concentration, compression or correlation as a proxy for a richer structure. Their strongest mathematical development begins by specifying the observation map and its fibres. A summary can be exactly computed and still fail to separate the objects relevant to the question. Conversely, an injective finite encoding supports exact recovery regardless of whether its values resemble a preferred statistical distribution. This family organizes capacity and diagnostics as distinct operations: counting distinguishable messages, preserving information under a reversible map, and measuring one chosen feature of a data object.
definitions: An observation h:X→Y induces equivalence x∼x′ when h(x)=h(x′). Exact reconstruction from h exists precisely when the required target is constant on each fibre.
A lossless finite encoder E has a decoder D with D(E(x))=x, hence must be injective.
A b-ary prefix X_1,…,X_k has entropy H_k; its increment is conditional entropy, lying between zero and log b.
For positive powers P_i, spectral flatness is (∏P_i)^{1/n}/((ΣP_i)/n). For phases θ_j, circular resultant is |Σe^{iθ_j}|/n.

theorem.statement: A lossless fixed-length binary code for N objects needs b≥ceil(log_2N). No injective binary encoder can strictly shorten every binary string of lengths at most b. Prefix entropy obeys H_{k+1}−H_k=H(X_{k+1}|X_1,…,X_k), independently of a metric contraction placed on the symbolic space.
theorem.proof: Injectivity follows by applying D to a collision E(x)=E(x′). A b-bit codomain contains only 2^b addresses, so N≤2^b. For universal shortening, the number of strings of lengths at most b is 2^{b+1}−1, whereas all shorter outputs through length b−1 number only 2^b−1; the pigeonhole principle rules out injectivity. The entropy chain rule follows by factoring p(x_1,…,x_{k+1}) into p(x_1,…,x_k)p(x_{k+1}|x_1,…,x_k) and expanding the logarithm in the expectation. Conditional entropy is nonnegative and at most log b. No property of an externally imposed ultrametric enters this algebra, so a metric contraction alone cannot prove an entropy decrease.

worked_example.setup: Suppose five feasible objects are indexed by three bits, and examine two phase populations: all phases zero, or half zero and half π. Compare flat and nonflat power arrays.
worked_example.calculation: Three bits suffice because ceil(log_25)=3. Drawing a uniform three-bit address and rejecting 5,6,7 yields each valid object with probability 1/5. Taking the address modulo five instead gives probabilities (2,2,2,1,1)/8. The all-zero phase population has resultant one; the two-opposite-cluster population has resultant zero despite being sharply concentrated in two directions. Powers (1,1,1,1) have flatness one, while (1,1,1,9) have flatness √3/3<1. Neither flatness nor resultant defines a false-acceptance exponent without an observation and null model.
worked_example.meaning: The useful output is a hierarchy of observables, each with a declared invariance and a known failure mode. AUROC preserves ranking but discards calibration. Spectral power discards phase. A finite entropy calculation records empirical symbol balance but cannot establish decimal normality. A reversible code preserves object identity but does not imply shorter descriptions for every object. These distinctions turn diagnostics into well-typed tools.

families.title: Convex duality, singular quadratic programs and global certificates
families.central_question: What finite certificate proves global optimality, including null directions and boundary cases?
families.synopsis: The optimization strand is strongest when an answer arrives with a lower bound and a feasible point attaining it. The source sequence links constrained covariance minimization, Fenchel conjugates, polyhedral actions and semidefinite primal-dual gaps. These are several forms of one principle: weak duality gives an inequality valid over the entire feasible set, and a matching construction turns it into a global theorem. The singular cases deserve equal status with the invertible ones. A pseudoinverse is meaningful only after the nullspace has been checked against the constraint; stationarity alone cannot provide the missing boundedness or convexity.
definitions: For convex f, its conjugate is f*(p)=sup_x(p·x−f(x)); the domain of x is part of f and changes the conjugate.
A symmetric covariance matrix Σ≥0 defines the objective wᵀΣw. The affine budget is cᵀw=1 with c≠0.
The Moore–Penrose inverse Σ⁺ inverts positive eigenspaces and vanishes on the nullspace.
An SDP primal feasible X≥0 and dual slack S=C−Σ_i y_iA_i≥0 satisfy constraints Tr(A_iX)=b_i.

theorem.statement: If some z∈kerΣ has cᵀz≠0, the constrained quadratic minimum is zero. Otherwise c∈rangeΣ and, with q=cᵀΣ⁺c>0, all minimizers are Σ⁺c/q+z for z∈kerΣ, with minimum 1/q. For every SDP feasible pair, the objective gap is Tr(SX)≥0; a zero gap certifies global optimality without requiring a separate strong-duality theorem.
theorem.proof: In the first quadratic case scale z by 1/(cᵀz); feasibility and zero energy follow, while nonnegativity proves minimality. Otherwise decompose w into positive spectral and null components. The constraint sees only the positive part. Cauchy–Schwarz applied to Σ^{1/2}w and Σ^{+1/2}c gives 1=(cᵀw)²≤(wᵀΣw)(cᵀΣ⁺c), so the objective is at least 1/q. Equality gives the displayed positive component, with arbitrary invisible null addition. For the SDP, subtract the objectives, insert the primal equalities, and obtain Tr(SX). This is nonnegative because Tr(SX)=Tr(X^{1/2}SX^{1/2}) and the enclosed matrix is PSD. A feasible zero-gap pair therefore sandwiches the optimum exactly.

worked_example.setup: Minimize w_1²+4w_2² subject to w_1+w_2=1. Compare Σ=diag(0,4), then Σ=11ᵀ. A separate SDP minimizes Tr(diag(1,2)X) subject to Tr X=1 and X≥0.
worked_example.calculation: For the positive definite quadratic, q=1+1/4=5/4 and w*=(4/5,1/5), giving value 4/5. For diag(0,4), the null vector e_1 satisfies the budget and achieves zero. For 11ᵀ, every feasible point has value one; the nullspace is budget-invisible. In the SDP, X*=diag(1,0), y=1 and S=diag(0,1) are feasible and give Tr(SX*)=0. Finally, the conjugate of kx² on all real x is p²/(4k), but restricting x≥0 changes it to max(p,0)²/(4k).
worked_example.meaning: The same computational discipline applies across these examples: inspect feasibility, preserve the actual domain, identify nullspaces, and produce a global inequality. A solver residual can guide a candidate, while an exact rational primal-dual pair can turn it into a reviewable certificate. Boundary constraints may alter the optimum and cannot be repaired by postprocessing an unconstrained answer.

families.title: Proximal maps, projected descent and stable optimization dynamics
families.central_question: Which update respects the feasible geometry and comes with a descent or contraction theorem?
families.synopsis: The source development repeatedly distinguishes an intended variational objective from an informal update rule. Soft thresholding, radial shrinkage, ridge regularization, projected gradient, Mahalanobis steps, resolvents and Wasserstein proximal maps all become coherent when the update is defined as a minimizer. This family uses that minimization property to derive an inequality, then studies what remains invisible in a projected or singular geometry. Continuous dissipation and discrete stability are related but separate claims. A small gradient, a clipped direction or an Armijo line search is not a substitute for the exact hypotheses needed by the chosen method. Exact proximal examples also show what the objective preserves: radial shrinkage keeps direction, soft thresholding can change support, and a subspace projector can permanently preserve invisible components.
definitions: For a proper convex g, prox_{ηg}(z)=argmin_x[g(x)+‖x−z‖²/(2η)] where the minimizer exists; the quadratic supplies strict convexity.
Projection Π_C is the proximal map of the indicator of a nonempty closed convex set C.
An M-weighted step uses ‖d‖_M²=dᵀMd with M>0; the metric is part of the algorithm.
For differentiable f with L-Lipschitz gradient, the descent lemma is f(y)≤f(x)+∇f(x)·(y−x)+(L/2)‖y−x‖².

theorem.statement: For x∈C closed convex and x+=Π_C(x−η∇f(x)), f(x+)≤f(x)−(1/η−L/2)‖x+−x‖². Thus 0<η<2/L gives strict descent unless the step vanishes. For a quadratic local model with Hessian H, the resolvent step δ=−η(I+ηH)^{-1}g is the unique minimizer when I+ηH>0.
theorem.proof: The projection variational inequality gives (x−η∇f(x)−x+)·(x−x+)≤0. Rearranging yields ∇f(x)·(x+−x)≤−‖x+−x‖²/η. Substitute this into the descent lemma to obtain the bound. Convexity is used for the projection inequality; smoothness controls the objective. The resolvent follows by differentiating q(δ)=g·δ+(1/2)δᵀHδ+‖δ‖²/(2η). Its Hessian H+I/η is positive definite under the stated condition, so the stationary point is the global unique minimizer. In an H eigenbasis each component is −ηg_i/(1+ηλ_i), making curvature damping and a possible negative-curvature obstruction explicit.

worked_example.setup: For z=(3,4), compare the minimizers of (1/2)‖x−z‖²+λ‖x‖_1, with λ‖x‖_2, and with (λ/2)‖x‖² at λ=1. Also inspect a four-cycle quadratic energy.
worked_example.calculation: The three updates are respectively (2,3), (12/5,16/5), and (3/2,2). Componentwise sparsity, radial shrinkage and uniform rescaling are different objectives. families.title: Objective design, discrete selection and certified finite search
families.central_question: Which feasible set and objective make a proposed improvement mathematically meaningful?
families.synopsis: Many optimization questions initially hide their most consequential choice: what is being optimized over which alternatives. Clustering weights can duplicate one scatter identity; capacity quotas are different from score weights; Pareto points can resist every linear selector; a QUBO is meaningful only after the binary variables and constraints are fixed. The later equivalence-class and separator constructions improve search by preserving the cost of every legal continuation. This family unifies these questions around a typed feasible set and a certified objective, while distinguishing an abstract optimum from a measured implementation cost.
definitions: A feasible optimization problem is (X,J), with optimum inf_{x∈X}J(x); changing X or J changes the problem.
A vector objective is Pareto nondominated when no feasible competitor improves all coordinates and at least one strictly.
A QUBO minimizes a quadratic polynomial on {0,1}^n; a graph-cut objective is one exact finite instance.
A frontier state in dynamic programming is sufficient only when its signature retains all information connecting processed choices to future feasibility and cost.

theorem.statement: For fixed data, total scatter T equals within-cluster scatter W plus between-cluster scatter B. Therefore maximizing aB−bW with a,b≥0 and a+b>0 is equivalent to minimizing W over the same partitions. Separately, if a frontier signature determines every future interaction, retaining only the cheapest prefix per signature preserves the global optimum.
theorem.proof: For the scatter identity, insert x_i−μ=(x_i−μ_{c(i)})+(μ_{c(i)}−μ). Cross terms vanish within each cluster because Σ_{i∈c}(x_i−μ_c)=0. Hence T=W+B and aB−bW=aT−(a+b)W, differing from −W only by a positive scale and constant. For frontier compression, take two partial solutions with the same sufficient signature. Every legal completion contributes the same added cost and has the same feasibility for both; replacing the dearer prefix with the cheaper one can only improve the total. Induct over processed layers. The proof requires equality of continuation behavior, not merely equality of the currently best continuation or the present objective value.

worked_example.setup: Use the triangle maximum-cut problem and a two-state repeated-layer transfer. Also consider minimization of two costs at feasible points A=(0,2), B=(1,3/2), C=(2,0).
worked_example.calculation: The triangle has eight binary labelings: the two constant ones cut zero edges and all six nonconstant ones cut two, proving optimum two by enumeration. In min-plus algebra, M=[[∞,2],[3,∞]] has M⊗M=5I_minplus. Thus with initial costs (0,∞), the minimum terminal sequence is 0,2,5,7,10,… and d_{L+2}=d_L+5. In the Pareto fixture all three points are nondominated. For positive weights α,β, choosing B over A requires α≤β/2, while choosing B over C requires α≥3β/2, impossible. The middle Pareto point cannot be reached by a positive linear selector.
worked_example.meaning: The scatter identity shows how a proposed extra criterion can collapse algebraically; the Pareto example shows how a single scalarization can omit legitimate tradeoffs; the transfer identity shows how finite search can be compressed without losing its optimum. Together they support a stronger design practice: simplify the objective symbolically, preserve deployment constraints, and certify both the search reduction and the final feasible candidate.

families.title: Shared uncertainty, robust margins and decision-sufficient measurement
families.central_question: What must be measured to certify the decision, rather than reconstruct every uncertain score?
families.synopsis: The final decision strand ties the archive together especially well. Earlier finite thresholds, singular covariance optimization, normalized residual margins and later target-observation questions lead to a precise endpoint: compare the competing actions under the same compatible state. Independent score intervals can erase cancellation and make an easy decision look unresolved. A decision difference may depend on only a small part of a high-dimensional uncertainty set. The best experiment can therefore be one that resolves the sign of that difference, even if it leaves most of the system unknown. This is a mathematical design principle with deterministic quantifiers, distinct from a posterior preference or an empirical forecast.
definitions: Let X be a nonempty uncertainty set and J_A,J_B:X→R be scores, with larger preferred; δ(x)=J_A(x)−J_B(x).
A strict robust certificate is a proved m>0 with δ(x)≥m for every x∈X; the infimum need not be attained.
A bounded-error measurement h(x)≈z restricts compatibility to X_z={x∈X:|h(x)−z|≤ε}.
A decision-sufficient finite test makes each nonempty outcome fibre certify one action. Its objective may be worst-case cost rather than expected estimation error.

theorem.statement: Joint comparison satisfies inf_X(J_A−J_B)≥inf_XJ_A−sup_XJ_B, often strictly. Restricting to a measurement fibre cannot decrease the lower margin for A. In the shared model J_A=c+d, J_B=c, c∈[0,100], d∈[7/4,9/4], the exact robust A-margin is 7/4 although subtraction of separate score intervals yields lower bound −393/4.
theorem.proof: For every x, J_A(x)≥inf J_A and J_B(x)≤sup J_B, so subtraction and then infimization prove the inequality. Separate extrema may occur at incompatible x, explaining strictness. If X_z⊆X, every lower bound valid on X remains valid on X_z. In the shared example δ=d because the common c cancels before minimization. The independent ranges are J_A∈[7/4,409/4] and J_B∈[0,100], whose separate lower difference is 7/4−100=−393/4. The distinction is about preserving the same state in both scores. In a finite test tree, a recurrence V(S)=min_t[c_t+max_oV(S∩t^{-1}(o))], with V=0 on decision-certified states, computes the cheapest guaranteed procedure when the admissible tests and stopping certificates are fixed and a terminating strategy exists.

worked_example.setup: The L08 worked model uses a common nuisance score and an interval for the decision difference. A second fixture measures d with absolute error at most 1/10.
worked_example.calculation: For c∈[0,100] and d∈[7/4,9/4], every compatible state prefers A with margin at least 1.75, regardless of nuisance width. Changing c's range changes the separate-score bound but leaves the joint margin unchanged. A measurement z=1/4 implies d≥z−1/10=3/20>0, certifying A. A result z=1/20 yields d∈[−1/20,3/20], which certifies neither direction. With affine δ=aᵀx+b on a box, its exact lower bound is b+Σ_j min(a_jl_j,a_ju_j); shared-variable simplification should precede this bound.
worked_example.meaning: This creates a bridge from information to action: the required observation need distinguish states only when they demand different actions. Reconstructing nuisance coordinates can be unnecessary. Conversely a confident score estimate without a defensible compatibility set cannot become a robust theorem. L08 exposes the common-variable cancellation directly; arbitrary semialgebraic positivity and automatic measurement-tree synthesis remain specified extensions. L08 centers the nuisance interval as [−C,C]; C=50 gives the same width and independent lower bound as [0,100], with both scores translated by −50. It does not implement the bounded-error measurement or test-tree extensions.

families.title: Exact populations: products, recurrences and reversible addresses
families.central_question: How can a finite combinatorial population be counted, optimized and indexed without confusing objects with their statistics?
families.synopsis: The recurring constructive idea is to make an object contribute exactly once to a finite sum. A partition contributes a monomial through its part multiplicities; a tableau contributes through the position of its largest entry; a project selection contributes through one factor for every labeled project. These constructions give independent descriptions of the same population rather than a fit to its reported size. They also explain why equal weights do not merge labeled selections and why a terminal in a reduced decision diagram can represent many assignments. Once completion counts are available, enumeration becomes an address system: the same integers support counting, conditional queries, exact uniform sampling, and an optimum proved by a threshold population of size one. The mathematical advance is the unification of these operations under a single disjoint decomposition. It does not require trusting an optimizer or assuming that a compact diagram has already retained every multiplicity.
definitions: A completion count C(q) is the number of feasible objects extending a prefix q; it counts original objects, unless a quotient population has explicitly been chosen.
For labeled binary choices with nonnegative vector weights w_i and capacity b, C(i,b) counts feasible assignments of coordinates i,…,n−1.
The generating polynomial ∏_i(1+z^{w_i}t^{p_i}) records vector weight and integer profit with multiplicity; a coefficient counts choices, not distinct numerical sums.
A species a_1≥a_2≥…≥0 corresponds bijectively to differences d_j=a_j−a_{j+1}; its least representative is ∏_j P_j^{d_j}, where P_j is the jth primorial.

theorem.statement: For nonnegative weights, C(i,b)=C(i+1,b)+C(i+1,b−w_i), with C(i,b)=0 if a capacity coordinate is negative and C(n,b)=1 otherwise. These counts yield inverse bijections rank:Ω→{0,…,|Ω|−1} and unrank. A feasible object of profit v is the unique maximizer if the count of feasible objects with profit at least v equals one.
theorem.proof: Split each population according to its next bit. The two pieces are disjoint and correspond exactly to the smaller residual capacities, proving the recurrence by induction. If the entire suffix fits, every remaining bit is free and contributes 2^{n−i}; an omitted block of g coordinates therefore contributes a factor 2^g. In lexicographic order the zero branch occupies an initial address interval of length C(q0); the one branch occupies the next interval. Unranking compares an address with C(q0), subtracting that count in the one branch; ranking performs the inverse additions. Induction down the tree proves a bijection, including empty branches. A uniform address consequently induces a uniform object. Finally a singleton threshold population includes the supplied feasible witness, excludes every higher-profit object and excludes every competing equal-profit object. This proves optimum and uniqueness together.

worked_example.setup: Use three distinct projects with weights (2,3,4), capacity 5 and profits (3,4,5). Also compare a small partition problem.
worked_example.calculation: The feasible words in zero-before-one order are 000,001,010,100,110. Their profits are 0,5,4,3,7, so addresses 0,…,4 enumerate the complete population and 110 is uniquely optimal. The prefix 1 has two completions. Three unbiased random bits can sample an address by rejecting 5,6,7; direct reduction modulo 5 instead gives probabilities (2,2,2,1,1)/8. Independently, for species with least representative at most 12, the inequality 2^{d_1}6^{d_2}≤12 gives representatives 1,2,4,6,8,12. A partition dynamic program gives p(5)=7, while corner removal gives five standard tableaux of shape (3,2). These different integers count different declared objects.
worked_example.meaning: An exact count is useful infrastructure: it supports reversible inspection, unbiased sampling and optimality witnesses while preserving which population was actually counted.

families.title: Graph observations: spectra, cut censuses and stronger energy probes
families.central_question: Which graph features survive an observation, and what extra measurement separates a known collision?
families.synopsis: The graph thread develops from a warning about incomplete spectral observations into an exact hierarchy of finite invariants. A graph can be encoded by its adjacency matrix, its Laplacian, a heat operator, a heat trace, diagonal heat signatures, binary cut statistics or integer-height energy coefficients. These are different observation maps. Equality at one level need not imply equality at a richer level, and a numerical agreement at several parameters does not prove equality of a polynomial invariant. The productive method is to construct a full exact collision, identify the discarded correlations, then design a stronger finite observation. Incidence identities provide a parallel constructive route: singular values of a point-line incidence matrix determine the spectrum of its bipartite Levi graph. The centered Green matrix adds a variational capacity, translating a graph operator into an exact energy required to force one coordinate while maintaining zero mean.
definitions: For a simple graph G, L=D−A and E_G(h)=hᵀLh=Σ_{uv∈E}(h_u−h_v)^2.
The binary census records all pairs (Σh_i,E_G(h)) for h∈{0,1}^V; on binary heights E_G is a cut boundary size.
The formal integer-height series F_G(x,q)=Σ_{h∈Z_≥0^V}x^{Σh_i}q^{E_G(h)} has finitely many terms at every fixed x-degree.
For λ>0 and Π=I−11ᵀ/n, the centered Green matrix K=Π(λI+L)^{-1}Π is the inverse of λI+L on 1⊥.

theorem.statement: The explicit seven-vertex graphs G and H below have identical complete binary size-energy censuses but different integer-height series: [x³](F_G−F_H)=q³(1−q)(1−q³)²(1−q⁴)². Separately, for any graph with n≥2, min{vᵀ(λI+L)v:1ᵀv=0,v_i=a}=a²/K_ii.
theorem.proof: For the collision, enumerate every one of the 128 binary subsets and store its size and cut size as an integer histogram. For total height R enumerate all weak compositions of R into seven coordinates, recording energy. Exact subtraction at R=0,1,2 is zero; at R=3 its coefficient polynomial factors as stated. This finite computation is a proof certificate for these explicit graphs. For the variational theorem, QK=Π on 1⊥. Thus v_i=(Ke_i)ᵀQv and Cauchy–Schwarz in the positive Q-inner product gives a²≤K_ii vᵀQv. Equality holds at v=aKe_i/K_ii; its mean is zero and its ith component is a. The inverse is positive on 1⊥, so K_ii>0. This proves both the sharp bound and its unique minimizer.

worked_example.calculation: The census collision is exact over all binary assignments. At q=1/2, the first height separation equals (1/8)(1/2)(7/8)^2(15/16)^2=11025/262144. Support-three terms already cancel because they are binary; support-one terms cancel through the degree census, so the discrepancy comes from support two. For P₃, exact inversion gives diag K=(1/5,2/15,1/5). Forcing an endpoint to a under zero mean therefore costs 5a², while forcing the center costs 15a²/2. As a separate incidence example, the Fano matrix satisfies BBᵀ=2I+J, giving Heawood adjacency eigenvalues ±3 and ±√2, with the latter each sixfold.
worked_example.meaning: The same graph can support exact reconstruction obstructions, new distinguishing observations and sharp constrained energy calculations; each conclusion is tied to a particular observation map.

families.title: Incidence kernels, path differences and primal–dual graph witnesses
families.central_question: How do local incidence constraints produce global cycles, and when does a short witness prove an optimal graph action count?
families.synopsis: Incidence is the common finite language for conservation, cycle spaces, graph gauge classes and many covering arguments. An oriented edge is sent to the difference of its endpoint vertices; cancellation at internal vertices explains why a path has only source and sink boundary. Subtracting two paths therefore produces a circulation. The converse requires hypotheses: in a finite source-to-sink directed acyclic graph with every edge covered by a path, these differences span the entire real circulation space. Acyclic direction does not erase undirected cycles; a diamond already has a one-dimensional incidence kernel. The complementary optimization theme is that an admissible construction establishes an upper bound, while a matching or other dual witness establishes a lower bound. A support size or observed action count has no optimality meaning until the permitted action is stated. This family makes that action model and its certificate visible.
definitions: For an oriented graph with n vertices, m edges and c connected components, B is the vertex-by-edge matrix having −1 at a tail and +1 at a head.
The circulation space is ker B. Over any field its dimension is m−n+c; over the integers a spanning forest gives a fundamental cycle basis.
A vertex-call covers every edge incident to the chosen vertex. A matching consists of edges with disjoint endpoints, so any one vertex-call covers at most one matching edge.
For a graph regarded as a one-dimensional complex, H_1=ker B because there are no two-cells. Adding filled faces changes the quotient by their boundaries.

theorem.statement: The incidence rank is n−c, hence the circulation dimension is m−n+c. On a finite directed acyclic s-to-t graph with every edge on an s-to-t path, ker B is spanned over R by χ(p)−χ(p₀). In the vertex-call model on K_{a,b}, the exact minimum call count is min(a,b).
theorem.proof: On each connected component, incidence columns sum to zero and hence rank is at most n_component−1. A spanning tree contributes independent columns: remove a leaf and inspect its unique incident coefficient, inductively forcing every coefficient to zero. Summing components proves the rank formula. Every path difference has zero boundary. For the converse sum covering path indicators to obtain a strictly positive feasible flow f. For z∈ker B, both f and f+εz are nonnegative for small enough ε. A finite DAG permits a decomposition of each into nonnegative s-to-t path flows: follow positive flow, use conservation internally, and subtract the least path-edge value. At least one edge is removed at each stage. Their source divergence is the same, so subtracting the decompositions gives a combination of path differences. Finally assume a≤b. An a-edge matching demands at least a vertex-calls, and all a left vertices cover every edge. Matching lower bound and cover upper bound meet.

worked_example.setup: Use the diamond with edges (sa,at,sb,bt), then K_{3,3} and the call model K_{4,7}.

It is a DAG even though this undirected cycle survives. For K_{3,3}, m−n+1=9−6+1=4; a spanning tree and each of its four non-tree edges produce an integral fundamental cycle. For K_{4,7}, 28 edges are covered by four left-vertex calls. A four-edge matching proves that three calls cannot suffice. If a call instead selected one edge, the answer would be 28, demonstrating why action semantics changes the optimization problem.
