source.title: Separate the meanings of Q
source.status: Definitions resolved with a structural obstruction
source.summary: The original notation can be repaired completely at the level of objects. Robinson arithmetic Q is a first-order theory, Q_p is a valued field of characteristic zero, F_p[[q]] is a formal power-series ring of characteristic p, and D_q is an operator depending on a numerical or formal parameter. A proposed connection must name the relevant category and map; the shared letter Q supplies neither.
definitions: Robinson Q consists of axioms in the language of zero, successor, addition and multiplication; it is not a number field.
Q_p is the completion of Q for |x|_p=p^(−v_p(x)); Z_p is its valuation ring.
F_p[[q]] consists of formal series Σa_n q^n. Its q-adic topology measures vanishing order, not numerical size.
D_q f(x)=(f(qx)−f(x))/((q−1)x), initially for q≠1 and x≠0.

result.name: Characteristic obstructs a claimed field identification
result.statement: There is a canonical dense embedding Q→Q_p and a compatible reduction system Z_p→Z/p^nZ. There is no unital ring homomorphism Q_p→F_p[[q]], or in the reverse direction. In particular these objects cannot be identified by renaming their parameters.
result.proof: A unital homomorphism sends an integer n·1 to the same n·1. In characteristic p, p·1=0, whereas p is nonzero and invertible in Q_p. If φ:Q_p→F_p[[q]] were unital, then 1=φ(p p^(−1))=φ(p)φ(p^(−1))=0, a contradiction. In the reverse direction, applying φ to p·1=0 would give p·1=0 in Q_p, also impossible. The dense embedding Q→Q_p instead preserves characteristic and the field operations. The reductions from Z_p preserve ring operations but have nontrivial kernel p^nZ_p, so they are quotients rather than embeddings. This distinction already eliminates several possible informal identifications without requiring a difficult theorem.

example.setup: Compare a rational number, a p-adic approximation and a formal series.
example.calculation: The rational 1/3 maps into Q_7 and can be approximated by compatible residues modulo 7^n. The formal series (1−q)^(−1)=1+q+q²+⋯ belongs to F_7[[q]] because its coefficients satisfy a formal multiplication identity. Its formal variable q is not automatically the prime 7 or a neural-network parameter.
example.conclusion: A corrected dictionary gives legitimate arrows and a proof that one tempting arrow cannot exist.

source.limits: An arithmetic theory can be interpreted in structures, and equal-characteristic local fields can resemble mixed-characteristic fields in selected respects. The characteristic obstruction does not rule out every model-theoretic or categorical comparison; it rules out the specified unital ring identifications.
source.extension: For every later use of q or Q, record its type, admissible values and morphisms. A meaningful bridge should transport a named theorem, not merely an expression.

source.title: p-adic completion with certified digits
source.status: Simple-root lifting proved and calculated
source.summary: A useful p-adic computation is a compatible sequence of exact congruences with a precision guarantee. The essential advantage in this example is that a simple solution modulo p determines one branch at every higher precision; decimal proximity has no role in the argument.
definitions: v_p(x) is the exponent of p in a nonzero rational x, and |0|_p=0.
An approximation x_n modulo p^n certifies a p-adic ball x_n+p^nZ_p.
A simple root modulo p satisfies f(x_1)≡0 and f′(x_1) not≡0 modulo p.

result.name: Unique next digit in a Hensel lift
result.statement: For f∈Z_p[x], a simple root x_n modulo p^n has exactly one lift x_n+t p^n modulo p^(n+1), with t∈{0,…,p−1}. The compatible lifts converge to a unique root in x_1+pZ_p.
result.proof: Taylor expansion gives f(x_n+t p^n)≡f(x_n)+t p^n f′(x_n) modulo p^(n+1); all terms of degree at least two are divisible by p^(2n), hence by p^(n+1). Dividing by p^n reduces the lift equation to f(x_n)/p^n+t f′(x_n)≡0 modulo p. The derivative is a unit, so this linear equation has one digit t. Repeating constructs a compatible inverse-limit element. Completeness gives a limit α; polynomial continuity gives f(α)=0. If two roots share the residue x_1, the same unique-digit argument forces agreement modulo every p^n and therefore equality. A finite calculation consequently certifies a ball containing the unique branch, not an approximate real root.

example.setup: Lift x²−2 from the root 3 modulo 7.
example.calculation: At precision 7², write x=3+7t. Dividing f(x) by 7 gives 1+6t≡0 modulo 7, hence t=1 and x=10 modulo 49. Next x=10+49t gives 2+6t≡0, hence t=2 and x=108 modulo 343. Directly, 108²−2=34·343. The verifier continues the uniquely selected digits through precision 7^6.
example.conclusion: The result is a root α∈Z_7 with α≡108 modulo 343, with a proof that no other root in 3+7Z_7 has those initial conditions.

source.limits: If f′ vanishes modulo p, uniqueness and existence require a different argument; the simple-root calculation cannot be recycled unchanged. This example establishes an arithmetic algorithm, not a general computational speedup over real methods.
source.extension: Develop Newton lifting with precision doubling and an independent residual valuation; compare digit lifting and Newton lifting on the same branch.

source.title: Affine dynamics on Z_p
source.status: Complete fixed-point and attraction classification for the stated family
source.summary: The affine family can be settled exactly. The hypotheses a,b∈Z_p ensure that f(x)=ax+b maps Z_p into itself and never expands p-adic distance. Attracting, neutral and translational behavior can then be distinguished without metaphor.
definitions: A fixed point solves f(x*)=x*.
Attraction means f^n(x)→x* in the p-adic metric for nearby initial states.
Congruence modulo p^N means two states cannot be distinguished at N-digit precision.

result.name: Affine fixed points and orbit differences
result.statement: If a≠1, a fixed point in Z_p exists exactly when b/(1−a)∈Z_p, equivalently b=0 or v_p(b)≥v_p(1−a), and is then unique. If a=1, b=0 makes every point fixed and b≠0 gives none. For |a|_p<1 the unique point attracts every state; for |a|_p=1 no distinct state converges to a fixed point.
result.proof: The fixed-point equation is (1−a)x=b, which gives the classification because Q_p is a field and membership in Z_p is exactly nonnegative valuation. Subtract two trajectories: f^n(x)−f^n(y)=a^n(x−y). Taking norms gives |a|_p^n|x−y|_p. This converges to zero precisely in the nonunit case, while for a unit it remains constant whenever x≠y. When |a|_p<1, 1−a is a unit, so every b supplies an integral fixed point. For a≠1, direct induction gives f^n(x)=a^n x+b(1−a^n)/(1−a). Congruent initial states remain congruent at every step, since multiplication by a∈Z_p cannot lower their agreement precision.

example.setup: Take p=7, a=7 and b=1.
example.calculation: The fixed point is −1/6∈Z_7. Starting from x_0=0 gives x_n=1+7+⋯+7^(n−1), and x_n−x*=7^n/6. Its valuation is exactly n. Thus n iterations supply n correct base-seven digits. In contrast a=8,b=1 has no fixed point in Z_7 because (1−8)x=1 would require v_7(x)=−1.
example.conclusion: The same affine notation yields global contraction in one case and a provable integral fixed-point obstruction in the other.

source.limits: Neutral maps may have rich periodic structure modulo p^N; constant separation does not mean every orbit is constant. This classification is for affine maps on Z_p, not arbitrary nonlinear p-adic dynamics.
source.extension: Classify neutral affine cycles modulo p^N, then identify which cycle properties stabilize as N grows. Use gcd divisibility as an independent finite checker.

source.title: A valid probability model and identifiable parameters
source.status: Range failure proved and a finite-design model specified
source.summary: The original product can be analyzed before any modeling claim is made. A formula is a probability only on an admissible domain, and fitted coefficients are meaningful only when the observation design can distinguish them.
definitions: For the original expression P(x,y)=(1+x)(1−y), assume x,y∈[0,1].
For the alternative logistic model let z=(1,x,y), η=z·β and σ(η)=1/(1+e^(−η)).
A finite design matrix X has rows z_i and identifies β when distinct coefficients give distinct modeled probability vectors.

result.name: Exact admissible domain and logistic identifiability
result.statement: On [0,1]² the product lies in [0,1] exactly when y≥x/(1+x). A logistic model yields probabilities strictly between zero and one for every finite β. At a fixed design, its coefficient vector is identifiable exactly when X has full column rank.
result.proof: Nonnegativity of the product is automatic on the square. The upper bound is (1+x)(1−y)≤1, equivalent to y≥x/(1+x) because 1+x>0. The point (1,0) violates it with P=2. For the logistic family, σ is a strictly increasing bijection R→(0,1). Thus equal probability vectors are equivalent, after applying logit, to Xβ=Xβ′. Full column rank makes this imply β=β′; a nonzero null vector otherwise supplies indistinguishable coefficients. For independent Bernoulli observations the log likelihood is Σ[y_iη_i−log(1+e^η_i)]. Its Hessian is −XᵀWX with W diagonal and positive at finite β. Full rank gives strict concavity, but does not guarantee that a finite maximizer exists: complete separation can send the optimum to infinity.

example.setup: Use the three design points (0,0),(1,0),(0,1).
example.calculation: Their augmented rows form an invertible 3×3 matrix. β=(0,log3,−log3) gives probabilities (1/2,3/4,1/4). Taking logits yields (0,log3,−log3), from which β is uniquely recovered by solving the linear system. Repeating only the first point would identify β_0 but leave the other two coefficients free.
example.conclusion: The example separates probability range, structural identifiability and existence of an estimator—three questions the original toy formula left unresolved.

source.limits: Choosing a logistic family does not establish empirical truth, independence or adequate calibration. Identifiability is conditional on the design and model; it is not a performance guarantee.
source.extension: Add a specified observation model and investigate design conditioning or separation before optimizing the likelihood.

source.title: Specify a hard problem before using arithmetic complexity
source.status: A toy encryption proposal is explicitly broken
source.summary: Sophisticated number systems do not themselves supply one-wayness. A mathematically assessable proposal must say what an adversary receives, what recovery problem is being claimed difficult, and how problem instances are distributed.
definitions: A toy modular scheme publishes a prime p and nonzero multiplier a and maps a message x to y=ax modulo p.
Correctness of a private recovery algorithm is different from hardness of public recovery.
An instance distribution specifies which public parameters, secrets and observations occur; worst-case difficulty alone need not control that distribution.

result.name: Public linear arithmetic is publicly invertible
result.statement: For the stated toy map, every message is recovered from public data using x=a^(−1)y modulo p. Extended Euclid computes a^(−1), so adding large notation or expressing the same arithmetic p-adically cannot turn this construction into a secret inversion problem.
result.proof: Since p is prime and a is nonzero modulo p, gcd(a,p)=1. The extended Euclidean algorithm produces integers u,v with ua+vp=1. Reducing modulo p gives ua≡1, and multiplying y=ax by u recovers x≡uy. This is a deterministic polynomial-time attack in the bit length of p. More generally, a public invertible linear transformation over a field is inverted by linear algebra. If its matrix is hidden but an oracle permits arbitrary message queries, querying the coordinate basis recovers its columns. Neither attack needs to search the message space or exploit implementation defects. They attack the mathematical specification itself.

example.setup: Take p=101, a=7 and observed y=35.
example.calculation: Euclid gives 7^(−1)≡29 modulo 101, since 7·29=203≡1. Therefore x≡29·35≡5. The verifier recovers x using only these public quantities. A larger prime changes the input size but not the kind of attack.
example.conclusion: The construction is correct as a reversible encoding and fails as a claimed secret arithmetic trapdoor.

source.limits: This example does not establish security or insecurity of an unrelated fully specified cryptosystem. A different map might pose a genuinely different problem, but its hardness must be argued independently of the prestige of its geometric or arithmetic vocabulary.
source.extension: For any proposed replacement, give generation, evaluation, recovery, correctness and an explicit public attack model. Test algebraic simplifications on small instances before attaching a security claim.

source.title: Zeno through a convergent series and a time law
source.status: Convergence and endpoint behavior proved
source.summary: Infinitely many subdivisions do not determine elapsed time. Once both the distance increments and the time increments are stated, the mathematical ambiguity disappears: an infinite event sequence can accumulate at a finite time, or it can continue for an infinite duration.
definitions: Let distance increments be d_n=2^(−n), with milestones x_N=Σ_(n=1)^N d_n.
Let positive time increments be τ_n and milestone times t_N=Σ_(n=1)^N τ_n.
A finite accumulation time exists exactly when the positive time series converges.

result.name: Finite distance does not fix finite elapsed time
result.statement: The distances sum to one. Choosing τ_n=2^(−n) reaches milestones at t_N=1−2^(−N) and admits the continuous extension x(1)=1. Choosing τ_n=1/n instead takes infinite total time while approaching the same spatial limit.
result.proof: For the geometric sum, multiply S_N=1/2+⋯+2^(−N) by two and subtract to obtain S_N=1−2^(−N). Given ε>0, choose N>log₂(1/ε); then 0<1−S_N<ε, proving convergence. With equal distance and time increments, the piecewise linear motion is simply x(t)=t on [0,1), so continuity supplies the endpoint x(1)=1. In the harmonic-time model, the subsequence of times diverges because each block from 2^k+1 through 2^(k+1) contributes at least 1/2. A continuous piecewise linear interpolation still approaches spatial position one, but only as t→∞. The number of labeled milestones is identical in both descriptions; its cardinality does not decide the total time.

example.setup: Compare the first N milestones in the two parametrizations.
example.calculation: Both have spatial coordinate 1−2^(−N). In the first model the remaining time is 2^(−N). In the second, any finite milestone leaves an infinite tail Σ_(n>N)1/n. Their different conclusions follow from different time assignments, not from a contradiction in summing the same distances.
example.conclusion: The revised question separates convergence, continuity and parametrization, each of which can be proved with elementary estimates.

source.limits: A mathematical parametrization does not assert that a physical device can execute an unbounded rate of discrete operations. The continuous trajectory requires no such discrete mechanism; a physical implementation would add its own constraints.
source.extension: Study rectifiable curves with infinitely many segments and ask separately whether a chosen parametrization has bounded speed, finite length and a continuous endpoint.

source.title: Octonions with a declared multiplication convention
source.status: Nonassociativity exhibited and Moufang law certified by all coefficients
source.summary: An analogy involving octonions becomes mathematics once multiplication, regrouping and the surviving identities are explicit. The real octonions are a division algebra but not an associative algebra; consequently their nonzero elements form a Moufang loop rather than a group.
definitions: Represent an octonion as a pair (a,b) of quaternions with product (a,b)(c,d)=(ac−conj(d)b, da+b conj(c)).
Use the quaternion convention ij=k, jk=i, ki=j. Set e1=(i,0), e2=(j,0), e3=(k,0), e4=(0,1), e5=(0,i), e6=(0,j), e7=(0,k).
The associator is [a,b,c]=(ab)c−a(bc). The Euclidean norm on R⁸ is multiplicative.

result.name: A nonzero associator with an exact surviving identity
result.statement: Under this convention [e1,e2,e4]=2e7. Nevertheless the associator is alternating, and the Moufang identity (ab)(ca)=a((bc)a) holds for all real octonions. In particular any two elements generate an associative subalgebra, the classical alternative-algebra theorem.
result.proof: The displayed associator follows directly from e1e2=e3, e3e4=e7, e2e4=e6 and e1e6=−e7. For an independent finite certificate of alternation, expand the trilinear associator in the basis 1,e1,…,e7. The verifier checks all 512 triples and confirms [a,b,c]+[b,a,c]=0 and [a,b,c]+[a,c,b]=0 at every coefficient. Bilinearity of multiplication then proves alternation for arbitrary real coordinates. The Moufang residual is quadratic in a and linear in b and c. It is therefore enough to check a on each basis vector and each pairwise sum of basis vectors, with b and c on basis vectors: polarization recovers all squared and mixed coefficients. All 2304 evaluations vanish exactly. This finite coefficient certificate verifies the full identity, not merely a random sample.

example.setup: Regroup e1,e2,e4 and compare the two results.
example.calculation: The left grouping gives (e1e2)e4=e7 and the right gives e1(e2e4)=−e7. Their difference has norm two. If the third factor instead belongs to the associative quaternion algebra generated by e1,e2, regrouping makes no difference.
example.conclusion: The example demonstrates both a genuine failure and a precise replacement law. No philosophical interpretation is needed for either statement.

source.limits: Other octonion tables may change basis signs and the displayed associator sign. The convention must travel with every numerical example. Alternativity does not authorize arbitrary reassociation of three unrelated factors.
source.extension: Use the explicit coefficient tensor as an exact algebraic input when investigating invariant subalgebras, automorphisms or defect loci.

source.title: The sharp octonion regrouping bound
source.status: Sharp inequality proved with an equality example
source.summary: The earlier proposal to measure a regrouping defect can be carried to a sharp result. The defect is not just a qualitative marker: its exact universal scale follows from norm multiplicativity, and a basis triple attains that scale.
definitions: For octonions define d(a,b,c)=||(ab)c−a(bc)||.
Let n=||a||||b||||c||. Norm multiplicativity gives ||(ab)c||=||a(bc)||=n.
For unit factors the squared defect is 2−2⟨(ab)c,a(bc)⟩, using the Euclidean inner product.

result.name: Sharp norm bound and equality criterion
result.statement: For all real octonions, 0≤d(a,b,c)≤2||a||||b||||c||. If n>0, equality holds exactly when (ab)c=−a(bc). The constant two is optimal.
result.proof: Write u=(ab)c and v=a(bc). The triangle inequality gives ||u−v||≤||u||+||v||=2n. Alternatively, expand the squared norm: ||u−v||²=2n²−2⟨u,v⟩. Cauchy–Schwarz gives ⟨u,v⟩≥−n². Equality requires u and v to be oppositely directed; because their norms are equal and nonzero, this is exactly u=−v. The declared convention in M007 gives u=e7 and v=−e7 for a=e1,b=e2,c=e4, so the bound is attained at unit norm. Trilinearity also gives d(ra,sb,tc)=|rst|d(a,b,c) for real scalars. A norm-preserving algebra automorphism transports the associator and therefore preserves the defect.

example.setup: Evaluate the normalized defect on a maximally nonassociative basis triple and an associative quaternion triple.
example.calculation: For (e1,e2,e4), d=2. For (e1,e2,e3), both products equal −1, so d=0. The two calculations sit at opposite endpoints of the proved interval. The normalized quantity δ=d/(||a||||b||||c||) is consequently dimensionless on nonzero triples and ranges through values in [0,2].
example.conclusion: The revised concept now has a universal bound, a certified sharpness witness, scale behavior and an exact criterion for attaining the upper endpoint.

source.limits: This does not classify every zero-defect triple or every orbit of the automorphism group. A zero associator for one triple alone should not be promoted to a statement that an entire generated algebra is associative.

source.status: Exact derivative and travelling-wave calculation
source.summary: The corrected sech² identity supplies enough structure to verify a whole travelling-wave family. Instead of recognizing a familiar shape, we derive the amplitude-speed relation required by a specified nonlinear PDE.
definitions: Let T=tanh z and f(z)=sech²z=1−T².
The derivatives satisfy T′=f, f′=−2fT and d/dz=(1−T²)d/dT when applied to polynomials in T.
For a wave u(x,t)=A f(κ(x−ct−x0)), primes on u below denote spatial derivatives.

result.statement: For nonzero κ and the equation u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0, the sech² ansatz is a solution when A=2κ² and c=4κ². These constants are linked by the equation; they cannot be chosen independently.
result.proof: Differentiate f′=−2fT to obtain f″=−2f′T−2fT′=4fT²−2f²=4f−6f². Differentiating again gives f‴=(4−12f)f′. After rescaling, u_xxx=4κ²u_x−(12κ²/A)u u_x. The travelling-wave time derivative is u_t=−c u_x. The PDE residual is therefore (4κ²−c)u_x+(6−12κ²/A)u u_x. The stated amplitude and speed annihilate both coefficients. Conversely, for a nonconstant profile with A≠0, vanishing for the whole wave forces those coefficients to vanish because u takes a nontrivial interval of values wherever u_x is nonzero. The verifier independently represents u=2(1−T²) as a polynomial and obtains an identically zero residual using exact integer coefficients.

source.status: An exact coordinate transformation and endpoint asymptotic
source.summary: The Gudermannian is a genuine bridge between hyperbolic and circular expressions. Its advantage is algebraic simplification on a bounded angular interval; its cost is a singular inverse-coordinate derivative near that interval’s endpoints.
definitions: Set θ=gd(x)=arctan(sinh x), mapping R bijectively to (−π/2,π/2).
Then sinθ=tanh x, cosθ=sech x and θ′=cosθ.
The inverse is x=asinh(tanθ)=artanh(sinθ), with dx/dθ=secθ.

result.name: Transforming derivatives and integrals consistently
result.statement: For a smooth function F(θ), ∂_xF=cosθ F_θ and ∂_x²F=cos²θ F_θθ−sinθ cosθ F_θ. For an integrable profile u(x)=U(gd(x)), ∫_R u(x)dx=∫_(−π/2)^(π/2)U(θ)secθ dθ. The angular compression does not discard this Jacobian.
result.proof: Differentiate θ=arctan(sinh x): θ′=cosh x/(1+sinh²x)=sech x. Its range and monotonicity show it is a bijection. Since cosθ is positive in that range, the elementary identities follow by resolving a right triangle with tangent sinh x. The differential operator is ∂_x=cosθ∂_θ; applying it twice gives the stated second derivative. The ordinary change-of-variables theorem supplies dx=secθdθ. For x→+∞, π/2−gd(x)=2arctan(e^(−x))∼2e^(−x). Hence the inverse sensitivity secθ grows like 1/(π/2−θ). Bounded angular coordinates therefore do not guarantee bounded recovery error in x.

example.setup: Transform u(x)=Asech²x.
example.calculation: The angular profile is U(θ)=Acos²θ. Retaining the measure gives ∫u dx=A∫cosθdθ=2A, matching the direct calculation A[tanh x]_(−∞)^∞. If one integrated Acos²θ against dθ without the Jacobian, the answer would instead be Aπ/2 and would describe a different measure.
example.conclusion: The transformation simplifies a profile while preserving its integral only when the derivative and measure factors are carried along.

source.status: One-dimensional family and oblique KP line wave verified
source.summary: KdV is an evolution equation in one spatial coordinate. KP adds a second spatial coordinate and a sign that changes its transverse behavior. An exact KdV solution embeds in either stated KP sign when it is independent of the second coordinate, but this elementary inclusion does not solve the full two-dimensional problem.
definitions: Fix KdV as u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0.
Fix KP as (u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx)_x+3σu_yy=0 with σ=±1.
A line-wave phase is η=kx+ly−ωt+δ with real k≠0 and l,δ; set U(η)=(k²/2)sech²(η/2).

result.name: An explicit KP line-wave dispersion relation
result.statement: The profile u(x,y,t)=U(kx+ly−ωt+δ) solves the stated KP equation when ω=k³+3σl²/k. Taking l=0 recovers the KdV family of M009 after k=2κ.
result.proof: The travelling-wave derivative identity in the phase variable is U‴=U′−(6/k²)UU′. Thus the expression inside the outer x derivative is −ωU′+6kUU′+k³U‴=(k³−ω)U′. Its x derivative is k(k³−ω)U″, while u_yy=l²U″. The KP residual is [k(k³−ω)+3σl²]U″ and vanishes under the displayed relation. With l=0, η=2κ(x−4κ²t−x0), giving precisely 2κ²sech²(κ(x−4κ²t−x0)). This calculation fixes every coefficient and sign directly rather than inferring them from a remembered formula.

example.setup: Choose σ=+1, k=2, l=1 and δ=0.
example.calculation: Then ω=8+3/2=19/2, and u=2sech²((2x+y−(19/2)t)/2). The crest is the straight line 2x+y=(19/2)t. It is localized in the normal direction but extends along the line, so its total integral over the whole plane is not finite.
example.conclusion: The line wave is an exactly verified two-dimensional solution with a clear localization limitation.

source.summary: The interaction term can be determined rather than guessed. A positive tau-function supplies a nonsingular exact solution and gives a clean explanation of why the answer is not the sum of two single waves.
definitions: Take k1>k2>0, η_i=k_i x−k_i³t+δ_i and A=((k1−k2)/(k1+k2))².
Set τ=1+e^η1+e^η2+A e^(η1+η2), and u=2∂_x²logτ.
For exponentials, a Hirota bilinear operator acts by parameter differences; write P(k,ω)=kω+k⁴.

result.name: Interaction coefficient and asymptotic shifts
result.statement: This τ obeys (D_xD_t+D_x⁴)τ·τ=0 and u solves u_t+6uu_x+u_xxx=0. The fast wave’s spatial shift is −log(A)/k1>0 and the slow wave’s is log(A)/k2<0. The profile mass is 2(k1+k2).

These two polynomial values are 3k1k2(k1+k2)² and −3k1k2(k1−k2)², so their cancellation forces the stated A. Other coefficients reduce to the one-wave dispersion equations. Dividing the bilinear identity by τ² gives (logτ)_xt+(logτ)_xxxx+6((logτ)_xx)²=0; differentiating in x yields KdV for u. Because all four tau coefficients are positive, τ>0 for real x,t, eliminating zeros and singularities. In the fast moving frame, the effective one-wave factor changes from 1+e^η1 to 1+A e^η1 between early and late times, giving the fast shift. In the slow frame the factor changes in the reverse order, giving the slow shift. Finally ∫u dx=2[(logτ)_x]_(−∞)^∞=2(k1+k2).

source.title: Radial conservation and stereographic geometry
source.status: Two distinct inverse-power mechanisms calculated
source.summary: A coordinate projection and a conserved flux are mathematically different constructions. Each can generate a position-dependent factor, but the factors belong to different measures and have different meanings. Writing both down makes the proposed identification testable.
definitions: In Euclidean R^d with d≥2, a radial field has the form J(x)=F(r)e_r for r=||x||>0.
Conserved outward flux across a sphere means F(r) times its area is independent of r.
Stereographic coordinates (u,v) on the unit sphere use r²=u²+v² and X=(2u,2v,r²−1)/(1+r²).

result.name: Flux power law versus a projection Jacobian
result.statement: A rotationally symmetric conserved flux in dimension d has F(r)=C/r^(d−1), giving inverse-square magnitude in d=3. The unit-sphere stereographic metric is ds²=4(du²+dv²)/(1+u²+v²)² and its area measure is 4du dv/(1+u²+v²)². The latter is not a derivation of the former.
result.proof: The sphere of radius r has area ω_(d−1)r^(d−1). If its flux is Φ, then Φ=ω_(d−1)r^(d−1)F(r), yielding F(r)=Φ/(ω_(d−1)r^(d−1)). Equivalently, away from a source, the radial divergence is r^(1−d)∂_r(r^(d−1)F), which must vanish. For the projection, differentiate the displayed map X(u,v), take Euclidean inner products of its two coordinate derivatives and obtain a diagonal pullback metric with both diagonal entries 4/(1+r²)². Taking the square root of the determinant supplies the stated area factor. This second calculation concerns how one surface is charted, not how a physical flux changes across a family of spheres.

example.setup: Compare the large-distance factors in their own variables.
example.calculation: A three-dimensional radial flux decays as physical radius R^(−2). The stereographic area density decays as chart radius r^(−4). These statements do not contradict each other: R labels different spheres in a physical space, whereas r labels positions within a chart of one unit sphere. Identifying them would discard the very geometric distinction being calculated.
example.conclusion: The original question now has a derivation of each factor and a concrete reason the coordinate formula does not imply the conservation law.

source.limits: A projected representation of a conserved field can of course be constructed. It must transform the field and the integration measure together; conservation is then transported, not created by projection.

source.title: q-differentiation of the Gudermannian
source.status: An exact secant integral and uniform bounds
source.summary: There is a clean identity connecting q-differentiation and gd, but it is an instance of the fundamental theorem of calculus rather than evidence of a special learning mechanism. It allows the q-difference quotient to be bounded and its ordinary-derivative limit to be controlled.
definitions: For real q>0, q≠1 and x≠0, define D_qf(x)=(f(qx)−f(x))/((q−1)x).
Define D_qgd(0)=1 by continuous extension.
Let m=min(1,q) and M=max(1,q). On the interval between x and qx, the absolute coordinate lies between m|x| and M|x|.

result.name: Exact integral representation and bounds
result.statement: D_qgd(x)=∫_0^1 sech(x(1+s(q−1)))ds. Consequently sech(M|x|)≤D_qgd(x)≤sech(m|x|). As q→1 these quotients converge to sech x uniformly on compact x-intervals.
result.proof: Since gd′(t)=sech t, subtracting its values gives gd(qx)−gd(x)=∫_x^(qx)sech t dt. Substitute t=x+s(q−1)x; the oriented integral and denominator cancel even when q<1 or x<0, proving the formula. The function sech t is positive, even and decreasing as |t| increases, so its extrema on this same-sign interval give the bounds. For x in a compact interval and q in a sufficiently small neighborhood of one, all arguments remain in a common compact interval. Uniform continuity of sech there makes the integrand converge uniformly, hence the averaged quotients converge uniformly. At x=0 the integrand equals one, proving the claimed extension without division by zero.

example.setup: Compare q=1/2 and q=2 at x=2.
example.calculation: The first quotient averages sech between 1 and 2; the second averages it between 2 and 4. Both are positive, and the verifier checks their values against the exact endpoint bounds. These are secant averages over different intervals, not two names for the same local derivative.
example.conclusion: The relation is exact and has a precise limit. It distinguishes an honest q-difference calculation from a purely verbal association.

source.title: Quantitative Jacobian bounds for deep compositions
source.status: Vanishing demonstrated and a residual-depth bound derived
source.summary: A bounded activation does not protect its derivative from saturation. For gd the derivative is explicitly sech, so useful depth bounds can be derived without guessing from wave-propagation analogies. definitions: For scalar layers h_l=gd(w_l h_(l−1)+b_l), write z_l=w_l h_(l−1)+b_l.
The input derivative is J=∏_(l=1)^L w_l sech z_l.

For vector layers the Jacobian is D_lW_l with D_l diagonal and entries sech of the preactivations. For the residual construction take T>0 and K≥0. Singular-value bounds must use all relevant coordinates.

result.name: Saturation bound and a depth-scaled residual alternative
result.statement: If |w_l|≤W and every scalar |z_l|≥a>0, then |J|≤(W sech a)^L. For residual maps x_(l+1)=x_l+(T/L)F_l(x_l) with ||DF_l||₂≤K and L>TK, every total-Jacobian singular value lies between (1−TK/L)^L and (1+TK/L)^L. For L≥2TK, the bounds e^(−2TK) and e^(TK) are uniform in depth.
result.proof: The scalar chain rule gives the product, and monotonicity of sech on nonnegative arguments supplies the first estimate. In a residual layer, write its Jacobian I+E with ||E||≤TK/L. For every vector v, the triangle and reverse triangle inequalities give (1−||E||)||v||≤||(I+E)v||≤(1+||E||)||v||. Multiply the singular-value bounds across layers. The upper uniform estimate follows from log(1+s)≤s. For s≤1/2, log(1−s)≥−2s gives the lower estimate. These are worst-case deterministic bounds, conditional on a common derivative bound K; they make no distributional or performance claim.

example.setup: Use h_(l+1)=gd(h_l+2), h_0=0, with L=20.
example.calculation: Every preactivation is at least two. Therefore |J|≤sech(2)^20≈3.09865×10^(−12). Direct accumulation of logarithmic derivatives gives approximately 1.82740×10^(−24), far smaller still. The calculation avoids underflow and illustrates that the proved upper bound need not be sharp for a particular trajectory.
example.conclusion: The original concern is now expressed as a measurable derivative contraction, alongside a different architecture with an explicit conditional depth guarantee.

source.title: Minimal universal recurrences on an observable quotient
source.status: An exact annihilator theorem with a reduced example
source.summary: Cayley–Hamilton always gives a recurrence for a finite linear state, but the observable behavior may require a strictly smaller polynomial. The correct object is the induced operator after all permanently invisible directions have been quotiented out.
definitions: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field, A:V→V and C:V→Y linear, with outputs y_n=CA^n x.
Let N=∩_(k=0)^(n−1)ker(CA^k), where n=dimV. Cayley–Hamilton makes this the intersection over all k≥0.
A universal output recurrence with polynomial p means CA^k p(A)x=0 for every state x and every k≥0.

result.name: The observable quotient’s minimal polynomial is the universal recurrence
result.statement: N is A-invariant, so A induces A_bar on V/N. A polynomial p gives a universal output recurrence exactly when p(A_bar)=0. Thus the unique least-degree monic universal recurrence is the minimal polynomial of A_bar. Its degree is at most dim(V/N); for a scalar observable with an observable quotient it equals that quotient dimension.
result.proof: If v∈N, all outputs CA^kv vanish, hence CA^k(Av)=CA^(k+1)v=0 and Av∈N. Now a recurrence holds exactly when p(A)V⊂N, which is precisely p(A_bar)=0 after applying the quotient map. This proves both directions and minimality. The dimension bound is the standard minimal-polynomial bound. For scalar output, the row span of C,CA,… on the quotient has full dimension by observability. A polynomial of smaller degree would make every later row a combination of fewer initial rows, contradicting full dimension. This last equality need not hold for multiple outputs: A=I with C=I observes an n-dimensional state but has universal polynomial z−1.

example.setup: Take A=diag(1,2,3) and C=(1,1,0).
example.calculation: The invisible space is span(e3). On the two-dimensional quotient the minimal polynomial is (z−1)(z−2), so y_(n+2)−3y_(n+1)+2y_n=0 for every initial state. The full characteristic polynomial has a redundant factor z−3. If the particular initial state is e1, its individual sequence satisfies the shorter recurrence y_(n+1)=y_n.
example.conclusion: This distinguishes full-state, universal-observation and single-trajectory recurrences, rather than conflating their orders.

source.limits: A recurrence fitted to one finite prefix may be accidental. The quotient argument proves a recurrence for all times under the stated model; finite fitting alone does not.

source.title: The reachable and observable parts of a realization
source.status: Minimal zero-initial-state quotient constructed
source.summary: Reachability and observability answer different questions. Their intersection structure determines which internal modes affect driven input-output behavior from zero initial state. A mode can be unstable and entirely absent from the transfer function, making the initial-condition convention essential.
definitions: For a finite-dimensional real or complex system ẋ=Ax+Bu and y=Cx+Du with locally integrable inputs, define R=span{A^k imB:k≥0}, the reachable subspace.
Let N=∩_(k≥0)ker(CA^k), the unobservable subspace.
Both R and N are A-invariant, and the transfer function is H(s)=C(sI−A)^(−1)B+D where the resolvent exists.

result.name: The zero-initial input-output state lives on R/(R∩N)
result.statement: Restriction to R discards modes no input can excite from zero. Quotienting by R∩N then discards modes no output can detect. The resulting realization is reachable and observable and has the same zero-initial input-output map; its dimension is the standard minimal realization order.
result.proof: Starting at zero, the variation-of-constants formula x(t)=∫_0^t e^(A(t−s))Bu(s)ds lies in R because that subspace is A-invariant and contains imB. Adding a state in R∩N never changes any subsequent output, including under common future inputs, so the quotient preserves the response. Conversely, all reachable quotient states are generated by the projected input, and an invisible quotient class would have a representative in N, hence in R∩N, so it is zero. These properties characterize the usual minimal finite-dimensional realization. Replacing the zero initial condition by arbitrary initial states changes the target: visible but unreachable modes can now contribute.

example.calculation: R=span(e1,e3), while N=span(e3). The minimal driven state therefore has dimension one and transfer function 1/(s+1). The internally unstable e3 mode is reachable but invisible. The e2 mode is visible but unreachable; it matters for initial condition e2, producing e^(−2t), but not for zero-initial driven responses.
example.conclusion: The example has reachable rank two and observable rank two, yet minimal driven order one. Merely taking either rank misses the intersection.

source.limits: A stable transfer function does not establish internal stability when an unstable canceled mode remains. No empirical sensor claim follows without a correct state and observation model.

source.status: Invariant heat subspace and nonlinear no-go result proved
source.summary: A finite matrix can represent an infinite-dimensional evolution exactly on a proved invariant subspace. A truncation outside such a subspace instead produces an approximation. The distinction can be settled in examples, and a useful degree argument rules out a broad polynomial closure proposal.
definitions: A subspace W of observables is Koopman-invariant for a map f when p∈W implies p∘f∈W.
For the periodic heat equation u_t=u_xx, trigonometric modes are eigenfunctions of the generator ∂_xx.
For the obstruction, work with real polynomials as functions on an interval, and let f have degree d≥2.

result.name: No finite polynomial Koopman space can contain the state coordinate
result.statement: There is no finite-dimensional subspace W⊂R[x] that contains x and is invariant under p↦p∘f when degf=d≥2. In contrast, the heat equation exactly preserves every fixed finite span of Fourier modes.
result.proof: If W contains x and is invariant, it contains x∘f=f, then f∘f, and inductively every iterate f^(∘n). Their degrees are d^n because the nonzero leading coefficient of a composition cannot cancel. Polynomials with distinct degrees are linearly independent: in any finite linear combination the largest degree has a coefficient contributed by exactly one summand, so that coefficient must vanish, and descending induction eliminates the rest. Thus W would contain infinitely many independent vectors, a contradiction. For heat flow, ∂_xx sin(kx)=−k²sin(kx) and the same holds for cos(kx), while the constant mode has eigenvalue zero. This proves invariance of each chosen finite mode span and gives exact coefficient evolution a_k(t)=e^(−k²t)a_k(0).

example.setup: Compare the logistic map and a nonlinear PDE stencil.
example.calculation: For f(x)=2x(1−x), exact iterates have degrees 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 starting with x. No finite polynomial feature list containing x closes exactly on an interval. For Burgers-type nonlinearity u u_x, the initial mode sinx immediately generates sinx cosx=(1/2)sin2x, so the single-mode span is not invariant even though it is invariant for heat flow.
example.conclusion: Finite polynomial degree growth gives a proof of impossibility, while Fourier invariance gives a valid exact finite example. Neither conclusion rests on a numerical residual alone.

source.limits: The obstruction does not exclude nonpolynomial coordinate transformations, finite-state restrictions, approximate closures or special higher-dimensional nonlinear systems. On a finite orbit, polynomials are functions modulo additional relations and the interval argument no longer applies.
source.extension: Before applying Cayley–Hamilton to a nonlinear model, certify an invariant feature space or quantify the projection error. Investigate special model classes separately rather than assuming universal finite closure.

source.title: Hardy–BMO duality from atoms
source.status: Classical estimate proved; duality theorem identified
source.summary: The useful connection is a bounded pairing between a cancellation-sensitive signal space and a mean-oscillation space. This supplies an actual inequality; it does not make arbitrary behavior into a Hardy-space object.
definitions: A real H¹ atom a is supported in a finite interval I, satisfies ∫a=0 and ||a||∞≤1/|I|. Higher dimensions use cubes or balls.
The BMO seminorm is sup_I |I|⁻¹∫_I|b−b_I|, where b_I is the interval average. Constants have seminorm zero.
The atomic H¹ norm is the infimum of Σ|λ_j| over convergent atomic decompositions f=Σλ_j a_j. This is not the Sobolev H¹ norm.

result.name: Cancellation converts mean oscillation into a bounded functional
result.statement: For an atom a and b∈BMO, |∫ab|≤||b||_BMO. Consequently |⟨f,b⟩|≤||f||_H¹,atomic ||b||_BMO. The converse identification of every bounded H¹ functional with BMO modulo constants is the classical duality theorem, not a conclusion of the finite example alone.
result.proof: Subtract the constant b_I inside the pairing: ∫ab=∫_I a(b−b_I), because ∫a=0. The atom bound gives |∫ab|≤|I|⁻¹∫_I|b−b_I|≤||b||_BMO. For a finite atomic sum, apply the triangle inequality and sum the coefficient magnitudes. Completion gives the bounded functional on the atomic space. The quotient by constants is forced by cancellation: adding c to b leaves every atom pairing unchanged. The difficult converse is a representation theorem and requires the established Hardy-space theory; no finite rank calculation can replace it.

example.setup: Take I=[−1,1], a(x)=−1/2 on (−1,0), a(x)=1/2 on (0,1), and zero outside. Let b(x)=sign(x).
example.calculation: The atom has zero integral and supremum 1/2. For any interval containing positive fraction t and negative fraction 1−t, the mean oscillation of sign is 4t(1−t)≤1. Symmetric intervals achieve 1. The pairing is ∫ab=1, so the atomic estimate is sharp for this normalization.
example.conclusion: A normalization, a cancellation condition and a sharp example replace the earlier loose invocation of two named function spaces.

source.limits: Pairings of general distributions require the continuous extension, not an unjustified pointwise integral. Graph analogues need their own measure, Laplacian and atomic definitions; the Euclidean theorem is not automatically inherited.

source.status: Classical pair with exact finite certificate
source.summary: The 4×4 rook graph and the Shrikhande graph supply an exact obstruction to recovering a graph from its heat trace or diagonal heat signature. The full heat operator retains strictly more information.
definitions: Both graphs have vertex set Z₄×Z₄. Rook adjacency means sharing exactly one coordinate.
Shrikhande adjacency means the difference lies in {(±1,0),(0,±1),(1,1),(−1,−1)} modulo four.
For adjacency A, L=6I−A and K_t=exp(−tL). The heat trace is Tr K_t; the vertex signature is (K_t)_{vv}.

result.name: Identical spectra and vertex signatures do not force isomorphism
result.statement: Both graphs have Laplacian eigenvalues 0 once, 4 six times and 8 nine times, and every vertex in both has signature (1+6e^(−4t)+9e^(−8t))/16. Nevertheless their clique numbers are respectively four and three.
result.proof: The verifier constructs both integer adjacency matrices and checks A²=4I+2J. The all-ones vector has adjacency eigenvalue six. On its orthogonal complement J vanishes, so adjacency eigenvalues are ±2. Trace A=0 and dimension sixteen force multiplicities six and nine. Both graphs are connected because their Cayley generators span Z₄², hence eigenvalue six is simple. Their vertex translations act transitively, so all diagonal entries of any matrix function of A agree and equal its trace divided by sixteen. The verifier exhaustively checks four-vertex subsets: rook four-cliques exist, whereas Shrikhande has none, and Shrikhande has triangles. Clique number is invariant under isomorphism, proving the graphs differ.

example.setup: Use the two explicit sixteen-vertex adjacency matrices produced by rook_adjacency() and shrikhande_adjacency() in verify.py.
example.calculation: Exact matrix multiplication verifies the common-neighbor identity. Exhaustive enumeration of C(16,4)=1820 subsets per graph certifies the four-clique distinction. This does not rely on floating eigenvalue comparisons or a graph-isomorphism heuristic.
example.conclusion: Even the entire curve of diagonal heat signatures can lose structural information. This is a stronger failure than matching a handful of sampled times.

source.limits: The obstruction does not apply to the complete labeled K_t. For any fixed t>0, K_t is symmetric positive definite and its unique real symmetric logarithm gives L=−log(K_t)/t. source.title: Exact modularity phases on a four-cycle
source.status: Finite optimization solved exactly
source.summary: A small graph already exhibits resolution-dependent optima and nontrivial ties. Reporting one partition without its resolution parameter would conceal both effects.
definitions: The graph is C₄ with four edges, degree two at every vertex and total edge weight m=4.
For a vertex partition P and γ≥0, Q_γ(P)=Σ_{B∈P}[e(B)/4−γ(|B|/4)²], where e(B) counts internal undirected edges.
The feasible set contains all fifteen set partitions of four labeled vertices. Rotated partitions are distinct selections even when they have the same score.

result.name: The complete modularity phase diagram
result.statement: For 0≤γ<1 the all-in-one partition uniquely maximizes Q_γ=1−γ. For 1<γ<2 the two partitions into adjacent pairs maximize Q_γ=1/2−γ/2. For γ>2 the singleton partition uniquely maximizes Q_γ=−γ/4. At γ=1 there are three maximizers; at γ=2 there are seven.

Comparison of these finitely many affine functions gives the envelope above. The first two candidate lines meet at γ=1. The pair and singleton lines meet at γ=2, where the four adjacent-pair-plus-singletons partitions also tie. No discarded line is higher for γ≥0. The verifier independently enumerates the partitions and evaluates rational scores at interior and boundary values.

example.calculation: Their scores are −1/2, −1/4 and −3/8 respectively. Exactly two adjacent-pair partitions win. At γ=2 each has score −1/2, as do the four one-pair partitions and the all-singleton partition.

source.title: Ensemble assumptions determine the spectral baseline
source.status: Moment calculation proved
source.summary: A random-matrix comparison must preserve dependence, centering and normalization. A simple fourth-moment calculation shows why a sparse adjacency matrix cannot be treated as a dense Wigner matrix without qualification.
definitions: Let A be a simple random graph on n vertices with independent Bernoulli(p) upper-triangular entries and zero diagonal.
Set W_{ij}=(A_{ij}−p)/sqrt(np(1−p)) for i≠j and W_{ii}=0. Then E W_{ij}=0 and E W_{ij}²=1/n.
A sample covariance S=XᵀX/m is positive semidefinite and belongs to a different ensemble, even if X has independent entries.

result.name: Exact second and fourth normalized moments
result.statement: E[Tr(W²)/n]=(n−1)/n. Moreover E[Tr(W⁴)/n]=2(n−1)(n−2)/n²+(n−1)[1−3p(1−p)]/[n²p(1−p)]. Thus p=c/n with fixed c>0 yields fourth-moment limit 2+1/c, whereas np(1−p)→∞ removes this extra term.
result.proof: Expand the traces as sums over closed walks. For the second moment, each of n(n−1) directed edges contributes 1/n. For length four, centering kills walks containing an edge used only once. Two distinct edges traversed twice give two families of n(n−1)(n−2) walks, each with expectation 1/n². Alternating repeatedly on one edge gives n(n−1) walks with E W_{ij}⁴=[1−3p(1−p)]/[n²p(1−p)]. Divide by n to obtain the formula. This derivation depends on upper-triangular independence; it fails for matrices whose entries share hidden common factors.

example.setup: Compare dense p=1/2 with p=c/n and compare W with a covariance matrix.
example.calculation: The dense fourth-moment limit is two. The sparse fourth-moment limit retains 1/c. A covariance matrix satisfies xᵀSx=||Xx||²/m≥0, while centered symmetric adjacency matrices can have negative eigenvalues.
example.conclusion: One observed eigenvalue histogram cannot select its own null ensemble. The normalization and dependence structure must be specified before interpreting outliers.

source.limits: Two moments do not prove a complete limiting spectral law. The sparse calculation demonstrates a mismatch, not a universal law for every sparse network. No prediction about human behavior follows from these moment identities.

source.title: A reversible q-dependent chain with an exact gap
source.status: Finite family solved analytically
source.summary: Here q has one explicit meaning: the upward jump rate of a reflecting birth-death chain. This produces an actual probability model, stationary distribution and spectral answer.
definitions: The states are 0,…,N. From i<N the jump i→i+1 has rate q>0; from i>0 the jump i→i−1 has rate one.
The generator Q has diagonal entries equal to minus its outgoing rate and row sums zero. The process is irreducible on this finite state space.
Write Z=Σ_{i=0}^N qⁱ and π_i=qⁱ/Z. At q=1 this is uniform.

result.statement: Detailed balance holds, and the eigenvalues of −Q are zero and λ_k=q+1−2sqrt(q)cos(kπ/(N+1)), k=1,…,N. The spectral gap is λ_1>0.
result.proof: For each adjacent pair, π_i q=π_{i+1}; summing these balances proves πQ=0. Conjugate −Q by diag(sqrt(π_i)) to obtain a symmetric tridiagonal matrix S with off-diagonal −s, s=sqrt(q), interior diagonal q+1 and endpoint diagonals q and one. The interior eigenvalue recurrence has solutions v_i=sin((i+1)θ)−s⁻¹sin(iθ) for λ=q+1−2s cosθ. The left endpoint condition holds directly. The right endpoint reduces to (2cosθ−s−s⁻¹)sin((N+1)θ)=0. Taking θ=kπ/(N+1), 1≤k≤N, gives N independent nonzero eigenmodes; the stationary mode sqrt(π) supplies zero. These N+1 eigenvectors exhaust the dimension.

source.title: An independently replayable BCH certificate
source.status: Specified code completely enumerated
source.summary: The parameters are not merely a label: a generator polynomial, field convention and finite enumeration identify the exact code and establish the correction guarantee.
definitions: Work over F₂ and take α as a root of x⁴+x+1 in F₁₆. The verifier checks that α has multiplicative order fifteen.
Let g(x)=(x⁴+x+1)(x⁴+x³+x²+x+1)=x⁸+x⁷+x⁶+x⁴+1.
The cyclic code C consists of m(x)g(x) for deg m<7, represented as length-fifteen binary words. Hamming weight counts nonzero coordinates.

result.name: This standard narrow-sense BCH construction has parameters [15,7,5] and corrects any two errors
result.statement: The generator divides x¹⁵−1 and vanishes at α,α²,α³,α⁴. There are exactly 128 codewords and the least nonzero weight is five. Consequently distinct radius-two Hamming balls are disjoint.
result.proof: The root checks identify the designed-distance-five BCH construction. Polynomial division verifies cyclic divisibility. Multiplication by the nonzero monic g is injective on the 128 degree-below-seven messages, and the resulting degree is below fifteen; this establishes length and dimension. For a linear code, the distance between two codewords is the weight of their difference, another codeword, so minimum distance equals minimum nonzero weight. Exhaustive enumeration establishes that minimum as five. If a received word were within distance two of two codewords, the triangle inequality would put those codewords within distance four, a contradiction. Thus nearest-codeword decoding succeeds for every error pattern of weight at most two.

example.setup: Enumerate all messages and all error patterns of weights zero, one and two.
example.calculation: The exact weight enumerator is 1+18z⁵+30z⁶+15z⁷+15z⁸+30z⁹+18z¹⁰+z¹⁵. There are 1+15+C(15,2)=121 allowed error patterns per codeword, and the verifier obtains 128×121=15,488 distinct received words in the union of the decoding balls.
example.conclusion: The earlier one-error description understated the guarantee of this specified construction. The result is exhaustive for this finite code, including a reproducible generator and decoder-radius certificate.

source.limits: The code is not perfect: the 15,488 radius-two words do not exhaust all 32,768 binary words. The certificate says nothing about guaranteed correction of every three-error pattern. Other codes with the same length and dimension need not share the minimum distance.
source.extension: Publish syndrome calculation and a bounded-distance decoder, then compare decoder output against exhaustive nearest-codeword results on all received words. Treat larger parameters with algebraic decoding proofs rather than assuming enumeration remains cheap.

source.title: A finite Peter–Weyl calculation with an exact truncation error
source.status: Classical framework with worked cases proved here
source.summary: The useful question is which observables are retained by a representation cutoff. An expansion becomes operational once the group, normalized Haar measure and error norm are fixed. Both the circle and a noncommutative compact group admit short examples with an exactly known discarded component.
definitions: On U(1), write z=eⁱθ and use normalized measure dθ/(2π). The irreducible characters are zⁿ, n∈Z.
On SU(2), conjugacy classes have eigenvalues eⁱθ,e⁻ⁱθ, θ∈[0,π]. For class functions, normalized Haar integration is (2/π)∫₀^π f(θ)sin²θ dθ.

result.name: A finite Peter–Weyl calculation with an exact truncation error
result.statement: For f(θ)=3+2cosθ−sin2θ on U(1), projection to frequencies |n|≤1 has squared L² error 1/2. On SU(2), the square of the defining character decomposes as χ₁/₂²=χ₀+χ₁, and retaining only χ₀ has squared error 1.
result.proof: Orthogonality follows from integrating eⁱ(n−m)θ: the integral is zero unless n=m. Here the Fourier coefficients are c₀=3, c₁=c₋₁=1, c₂=i/2 and c₋₂=−i/2. The discarded orthogonal terms therefore contribute |i/2|²+|−i/2|²=1/2. For SU(2), χ₁/₂=2cosθ and χ₁=4cos²θ−1. Direct integration with the stated Haar density gives ∫χ₁=0 and ∫χ₁²=1, proving both the decomposition and the error claim without appealing to numerical fitting.

example.setup: Take the SU(2) class observable f(U)=(Tr U)². This is a function of the group element, not merely an arbitrary two-by-two mixing matrix.
example.calculation: The tensor product of two defining representations has characters χ₁/₂². Its invariant antisymmetric line gives χ₀=1; its symmetric three-dimensional summand gives χ₁. Thus f=1+χ₁, ∫f=1, ∫|f|²=2. Projection to constants has residual χ₁ with norm one, while retaining the spin-one character makes the residual exactly zero.
example.conclusion: A small representation cutoff can have a completely explicit observable loss. The calculation also shows why the group measure and the choice of function matter.

source.limits: This proves finite examples, not the full Peter–Weyl completeness theorem or a universal truncation rate. General noncentral functions require matrix coefficients rather than characters alone.

source.title: Rephasing invariance and a sharp three-flavor CP bound
source.status: Classical formula with an explicit sharpness derivation
source.summary: Complex entries are not themselves physical phase invariants: row and column conventions can change them. A four-entry product cancels those conventions, and in three dimensions its imaginary part admits a sharp elementary bound.
definitions: Let U be a three-by-three unitary mixing matrix. Row and column rephasings act by Uαi↦eⁱrα Uαi eⁱci.
For distinct rows and columns, define Jαβij=Im(Uαi Uβj U*αj U*βi). The sign depends on the ordered indices.

result.name: Rephasing invariance and a sharp three-flavor CP bound
result.statement: Each Jαβij is invariant under these rephasings. In the usual three-angle one-Dirac-phase parameterization, |J|≤1/(6√3), with equality attained by the normalized three-by-three discrete Fourier matrix.
result.proof: The phases in the four factors cancel pairwise: rα+rβ−rα−rβ and ci+cj−cj−ci both vanish. In the standard parameterization, J=c₁₂s₁₂c₂₃s₂₃c₁₃²s₁₃sinδ. The first two sine-cosine pairs have absolute value at most 1/2. With t=s₁₃∈[0,1], the remaining factor t(1−t²) has derivative 1−3t² and maximum 2/(3√3). Multiplication gives the bound. The Fourier example below attains it, so the bound is sharp rather than merely convenient.

example.setup: Set ω=exp(2πi/3) and Uab=ωᵃᵇ/√3 for a,b=0,1,2.
example.calculation: Geometric-series cancellation verifies U†U=I. The ordered quartet U₀₀U₁₁U*₀₁U*₁₀ equals ω/9, whose imaginary part is √3/18=1/(6√3). Complex conjugation changes its sign. In vacuum, an oscillation amplitude can be written Aαβ=Σi Uβi U*αi e⁻ⁱφi. Squaring shows directly that P(U)−P(U*)=4Σi>j Im(Zij)sin(φi−φj), where Zij=UβiU*αiU*βjUαj.
example.conclusion: A nonzero invariant is a mathematically meaningful obstruction to making the relevant matrix real by phase conventions; actual probability asymmetries also require nontrivial propagation phases.

source.limits: The calculation assumes the stated unitary three-flavor framework and says nothing about the experimentally fitted value of δ. Degenerate masses and inaccessible channels can suppress an observable asymmetry despite a formal matrix invariant. Column rephasings here concern oscillation equivalence; a Majorana mass term need not permit the same field rephasings in the full theory.

source.title: A complete small persistence calculation
source.status: Finite homology and barcode computed exactly
source.summary: Topology becomes a calculation only after a space and a filtration are specified. Three vertices provide a minimal example in which components merge, a loop is born and a filling destroys it. Every rank can be checked over the two-element field.
definitions: Let K₀ contain vertices 0,1,2; add edge 01 at time 1, edge 12 at time 2, edge 20 at time 3 and face 012 at time 4.
Use homology over F₂. For a finite chain complex, βk=dim Ck−rank ∂k−rank ∂k₊₁.

result.name: A complete small persistence calculation
result.statement: Across times 0,1,2,3,4, the pairs (β₀,β₁) are (3,0),(2,0),(1,0),(1,1),(1,0). The persistent barcode is H₀:[0,1),[0,2),[0,∞), and H₁:[3,4).
result.proof: The first two added edges each join different components and increase rank ∂₁ by one, from zero to two. The third edge has boundary equal to the sum of the first two boundaries, so rank ∂₁ stays two while dim C₁ becomes three; one cycle is born. The face boundary is 01+12+20, which is precisely the unique nonzero cycle up to scalar. Its addition raises rank ∂₂ from zero to one and kills H₁. The component survival convention can select any representative among equally old vertices, but the interval multiset does not depend on that tie-breaking.

example.setup: Compare the boundary of a triangle with the filled triangle on the same three vertices.
example.calculation: Both spaces have β₀=1. The boundary has C₂=0 and β₁=3−2=1. The filled triangle has one face with nonzero boundary and β₁=3−2−1=0. At time 4, the loop has not shrunk by geometric deformation; it becomes a boundary because the available chain complex changed.
example.conclusion: A Betti count is an invariant of the constructed space, while a barcode additionally records when a class appears and disappears in the chosen filtration.

source.limits: Different constructions from the same observations can yield different filtrations. Equal Betti numbers do not imply homeomorphism or homotopy equivalence. No universal data-to-topology interpretation is supplied by this example.

source.title: A two-level Berry holonomy with a gauge check
source.status: Classical holonomy evaluated explicitly
source.summary: The geometric object is an eigenline over a parameter loop. Choosing an eigenvector gives a connection formula, but the final phase must survive a change of that choice. A latitude on the Bloch sphere makes the distinction fully visible.
definitions: Take H=n·σ with n=(sinθ cosφ,sinθ sinφ,cosθ), fixed θ∈(0,π), and φ from 0 to 2π.

result.name: A two-level Berry holonomy with a gauge check
result.statement: The positive eigenline has γ=−π(1−cosθ). Under a periodic eigenvector gauge change, exp(iγ) is unchanged. At θ=π/3 the holonomy is −i; at the equator it is −1.
result.proof: Differentiation gives ⟨v,∂φv⟩=i sin²(θ/2), hence Aφ=−sin²(θ/2). Integrating yields −2πsin²(θ/2)=−π(1−cosθ). If v′=eⁱχ(φ)v, then A′=A−χ′. A single-valued gauge around the loop has χ(2π)−χ(0) an integer multiple of 2π, so exp(iγ′)=exp(iγ). This is a direct calculation of holonomy, independently of any physical interpretation of an adiabatic protocol.

Multiplying each sampled eigenvector by an arbitrary phase leaves the closed product unchanged because consecutive phase factors telescope. The verification program checks both convergence and exact cancellation of sampled gauge factors.

source.title: Crossing symmetry and an exactly opened spectral gap
source.status: Two-by-two spectral theorem proved directly
source.summary: A level crossing and an avoided crossing can be separated by a single parameter that either preserves or couples two invariant sectors. This gives an exact test of what a proposed symmetry protects.
definitions: Let H(t,ε)=[[t,ε],[ε,−t]] with real t and ε.
Write r=√(t²+ε²). For r>0, set P±=(I±H/r)/2.

result.name: Crossing symmetry and an exactly opened spectral gap
result.statement: The eigenvalues are ±r, the gap is 2r, and its minimum over t is 2|ε|. At ε=0, the diagonal sectors are uncoupled and the levels meet at t=0; ε≠0 removes that crossing.
result.proof: Direct multiplication gives H²=(t²+ε²)I. Therefore its minimal polynomial divides λ²−r² and, for r>0, P±²=P±, P+P−=0, P++P−=I and HP±=±rP±. The spectral gap formula follows. For ε=0, H commutes with σz, so each coordinate axis is an invariant symmetry sector. The εσx perturbation does not commute with σz and permits those sectors to mix. Thus protection is a statement about an operator relation, not a verbal appeal to symmetry.

example.setup: Set ε=1/5 and let t run through −1,0,1.
example.calculation: The gaps are 2√26/5, 2/5, 2√26/5. The trace remains zero and the determinant is −(t²+1/25), so an eigenvalue cannot pass through zero at any real t. At ε=0, the determinant at t=0 vanishes and both eigenvalues coincide. The projector formulas explicitly cease to apply at that degenerate point because r=0.
example.conclusion: A perturbation that changes a commutation relation can open a gap whose size is computed without approximation.

source.limits: This static spectral calculation does not determine transition probabilities during a time sweep. Those depend on a time law, an initial state and the dynamical equation; replacing the minimum gap by a guessed transition rate is unjustified.

source.title: A Moore spectrum as a precise chromatic example
source.status: Elementary cofiber consequence with general theory bounded explicitly
source.summary: Chromatic height refers to detection by homology theories at a fixed prime. It can already distinguish the sphere from a simple torsion object. This has no mathematical dependence on optical colors or on periodic measurements in an unrelated model.
definitions: Fix a prime p. Let M(p) be the cofiber of multiplication by p on the sphere spectrum: S→S→M(p).
Use K(0)=HQ. For n≥1, Morava K-theory has coefficient graded field K(n)*=F_p[v_n,v_n⁻¹], with |v_n|=2(pⁿ−1). A finite p-local spectrum has type t when K(n)* vanishes for n<t and is nonzero at n=t.

result.statement: The p-local sphere has type zero, while M(p) has type one. For each n≥1, the long exact sequence gives a short exact sequence 0→K(n)_q→K(n)_qM(p)→K(n)_(q−1)→0.

For K(n), n≥1, multiplication by p is zero because the coefficients have characteristic p. The cofiber long exact sequence therefore has zero connecting multiplication maps on both sides, yielding the displayed short exact sequence. It in particular contains a nonzero injected copy of K(n)*. Thus the first nonvanishing height is one. As a graded vector space over the coefficient graded field, the sequence can be split, though there is no need to claim a canonical splitting.

source.title: A conservative positive diffusion stencil with a sharp local condition
source.status: Discrete conservation positivity and energy estimate proved
source.summary: A numerical update should preserve the quantities its PDE is meant to preserve. On a periodic grid, the standard heat stencil admits exact mass, positivity and squared-norm statements before any simulation is run.
definitions: Let N≥3 periodic grid values be indexed modulo N. Set F_r(x)i=r x_(i−1)+(1−2r)x_i+r x_(i+1).
For heat diffusion, r=DΔt/Δx², D≥0. The grid mass is Σi x_i; the squared discrete norm is Σi x_i².

result.name: A conservative positive diffusion stencil with a sharp local condition
result.statement: For every r, the update preserves mass. It maps every nonnegative grid to a nonnegative grid exactly when 0≤r≤1/2. In that range it also contracts the squared norm.
result.proof: Summing the update cyclically makes each old value appear with coefficient r+(1−2r)+r=1, proving mass conservation. Nonnegative coefficients prove positivity. Conversely, a single nonzero grid basis vector detects a negative off-diagonal coefficient when r<0 or a negative central coefficient when r>1/2. For 0≤r≤1/2, convexity of z² gives F_r(x)i²≤r x_(i−1)²+(1−2r)x_i²+r x_(i+1)². Summing proves contraction. This proof is finite and exact, requiring no floating-point time stepping.

example.calculation: One step gives (1/2,1/4,0,0,1/4), preserving mass one and reducing the squared norm from one to 3/8. At r=3/4 the same initial condition produces a central value −1/2, immediately disproving positivity. Fourier modes e^(2πiki/N) have amplification factors 1−4r sin²(πk/N), providing a second independent stability calculation.
example.conclusion: The update is a well-defined averaging operator in the positive range. A nonlinear reaction term must be analyzed separately rather than multiplied into the diffusion formula without checking these properties.

source.status: Exact symmetry criterion proved for a stencil family
source.summary: Symbols for identity and reflection are meaningful only after their action on states has been defined. Commutation makes the claimed symmetry testable and exposes the effect of asymmetric coefficients or boundaries.
definitions: On a periodic N-grid, define (Rx)i=x_(−i mod N), so R²=I. Let S be the cyclic shift.
Consider F=aS⁻¹+bI+cS, and a pointwise reaction G(x)i=g(x_i). Reflection equivariance means F(Rx)=RF(x) for every x.

result.name: Reflection equivariance as an operator identity
result.statement: For N≥3, the three-point linear stencil commutes with reflection exactly when a=c. Any pointwise reaction using the same scalar function at every node commutes with reflection and every grid permutation.
result.proof: The identity RSR=S⁻¹ follows by applying both sides to an indexed coordinate. Conjugation gives RFR=aS+bI+cS⁻¹. For N≥3 the two shifts are distinct and linearly independent from each other in this coefficient comparison, so RFR=F exactly when a=c. For the nonlinear term, G(Rx)i=g(x_(−i))=(RG(x))i, proving equivariance directly. Consequently the composition of reflection-equivariant diffusion and reaction updates remains equivariant, whereas an asymmetric advection component generally does not.

The asymmetric stencil produces unequal neighboring weights and its reflected output differs. This single vector is a complete counterexample to the universal commutation claim. A spatially varying reaction g_i can fail similarly even when each g_i is smooth.
example.conclusion: Equivariance is a property of a typed update and group action. Writing an identity morphism or reflection symbol as an unexplained multiplicative factor does not supply it.

source.title: Affine coordinate changes and time evolution are different operations
source.status: Composition and transformed velocity derived
source.summary: An affine transformation changes a description of points; an evolution law describes a path. Their interaction is simple for constant frames and adds extra terms for moving frames. Mixing these roles can create a fictitious physical conclusion.
definitions: An affine map is T(x)=Mx+b. It is a coordinate isomorphism when M is invertible.
A path x(t) has velocity ẋ(t). A time-dependent frame is y(t)=M(t)x(t)+b(t).

result.name: Affine coordinate changes and time evolution are different operations
result.statement: Affine composition satisfies (M₂,b₂)∘(M₁,b₁)=(M₂M₁,M₂b₁+b₂). Under a moving frame, ẏ=Mẋ+Ṁx+ḃ, and ÿ=Mẍ+2Ṁẋ+M̈x+b̈.
result.proof: Substitute x into the second affine map and collect terms to obtain the composition law. Differentiate the frame relation using the product rule once and twice. The Ṁ and M̈ terms vanish only for a fixed linear frame; ḃ and b̈ vanish only for a fixed translation. Thus even a stationary world point may have nonzero coordinate velocity in a rotating or translating frame. This is a change in the description of motion, not a newly derived external force.

example.setup: Let R be rotation by 90 degrees in the plane and T translation by (1,0). Also take a free path x(t)=x₀+vt.
example.calculation: RT sends the origin to (0,1), whereas TR sends it to (1,0), exhibiting noncommutativity. In a constant affine frame, the free path becomes y(t)=Mx₀+b+(Mv)t, still affine in time. For a rotating frame M(t)=R(ωt), a stationary x=(1,0) is described by y=(cosωt,sinωt), with acceleration −ω²y. The derivative terms account for that coordinate acceleration exactly.
example.conclusion: The same geometric transformation may be used in a dynamical model, but its time dependence and reference-frame meaning must be stated.

source.limits: An arbitrary invertible linear map need not preserve Euclidean lengths or kinetic-energy expressions. Those require transforming the metric as well. Singular affine maps are projections rather than reversible coordinate changes.
source.extension: Carry a covariance or noise metric through the same coordinate change and verify which estimation errors are invariant; this prevents apparent gains caused solely by rescaling.

source.title: Mutual information detects dependence rather than a causal channel
source.status: Finite identities and data processing proved
source.summary: A dependence measure needs a joint distribution. Its nonzero value does not distinguish direct interaction from a shared source, while its change under a specified noisy channel can be calculated exactly.
definitions: For finite variables, I(X;Y)=Σx,y pxy log₂(pxy/(pxpy)); terms with zero mass contribute zero.
Let h₂(ε)=−εlog₂ε−(1−ε)log₂(1−ε). A binary symmetric channel flips an input bit independently with probability ε.

result.name: Mutual information detects dependence rather than a causal channel
result.statement: For a fair bit X and Y=X⊕E with E independent Bernoulli(ε), I(X;Y)=1−h₂(ε). For a Markov chain X→Y→Z, I(X;Z)≤I(X;Y). A common cause can give positive mutual information with no direct arrow between X and Y.
result.proof: The channel output is fair, so H(Y)=1, while conditioning on X leaves exactly the flip uncertainty H(Y|X)=h₂(ε). The entropy identity yields the formula. For data processing, expand the same quantity two ways: I(X;Y,Z)=I(X;Y)+I(X;Z|Y)=I(X;Z)+I(X;Y|Z). The Markov property makes the first conditional term zero and nonnegativity of conditional mutual information makes the second nonnegative.

example.setup: Cascade two independent binary symmetric channels with flip probability 0.1, and compare with X=Z, Y=Z for a fair common cause Z.
example.calculation: Two flips cancel, so the cascade error is 2ε(1−ε)=0.18. Thus information drops from 1−h₂(0.1)≈0.531004 bits to 1−h₂(0.18)≈0.319923 bits. In the common-cause example X and Y coincide, giving I=1 bit, although no direct causal channel X→Y has been specified. The identical joint table can arise from different causal descriptions.
example.conclusion: Information is a precisely calculable statistical quantity; assigning a mechanism requires additional assumptions or interventions.

source.limits: Plug-in estimates from finite samples are biased, and continuous differential entropies need separate treatment. The examples do not establish that a positive empirical estimate is significant or causally interpretable.
source.extension: Construct a sampling protocol and a null distribution for a chosen estimator, then quantify how much dependence remains after conditioning on measured common causes.

source.title: One measurement can miss coherence that another detects
source.status: Born-effect bounds and a two-observable example proved
source.summary: The same numerical overlap can represent different things depending on normalization and the measurement rule. An explicit qubit calculation shows why observable choice is also an identifiability choice.
definitions: A density matrix satisfies ρ≥0 and Trρ=1. A binary measurement effect satisfies 0≤E≤I, with probability p=Tr(ρE).
For a normalized pure state ψ and rank-one effect |φ⟩⟨φ| with normalized φ, the probability is |⟨φ,ψ⟩|².

result.name: One measurement can miss coherence that another detects
result.statement: Every valid effect gives 0≤Tr(ρE)≤1. The pure state ψ=(√3/2,1/2) and the mixed state diag(3/4,1/4) have identical probabilities in the coordinate-basis measurement but are separated by the plus-state effect.
result.proof: Diagonalize ρ=Σk wk|vk⟩⟨vk| with wk≥0 and Σwk=1. Then Tr(ρE)=Σwk⟨vk,Evk⟩ is a convex combination of numbers in [0,1], proving the bound. The pure density matrix is [[3/4,√3/4],[√3/4,1/4]], whereas the mixed matrix removes the off-diagonal terms. A diagonal effect only pairs with diagonal entries, so it cannot distinguish these states.

example.calculation: Both states give p(E₀)=3/4. The pure state gives p(E₊)=|(√3/2+1/2)/√2|²=(2+√3)/4≈0.933013, while the mixed state gives 1/2. The probability gap √3/4 is exactly the contribution from coherence in this basis. If an unnormalized vector is used instead, multiplying it by two multiplies an unnormalized squared overlap by four and can exceed one.
example.conclusion: A restricted observation panel defines equivalence classes of states. Adding a suitable observable can split those classes even when additional repeated measurements of the original observable cannot.

source.title: An observable timescale that saturates the energy–time bound
source.status: Mandelstam–Tamm observable inequality derived
source.summary: A time in an uncertainty relation must be defined operationally. For time-independent observables in a unitarily evolving state, the ratio between standard deviation and expectation-change rate yields a valid timescale. It is different from an arbitrary elapsed duration.
definitions: Let H and A be self-adjoint on a common suitable domain, with no explicit time dependence in A. Write ΔA²=⟨A²⟩−⟨A⟩² and likewise ΔH.
Where d⟨A⟩/dt≠0, define τ_A=ΔA/|d⟨A⟩/dt|.

result.name: An observable timescale that saturates the energy–time bound
result.statement: Under the usual finite-variance and domain assumptions, ΔH τ_A≥ℏ/2. A two-level precession example attains equality wherever the chosen observable has nonzero expectation derivative.
result.proof: The Robertson inequality gives ΔHΔA≥|⟨[H,A]⟩|/2. The Heisenberg expectation equation gives d⟨A⟩/dt=(i/ℏ)⟨[H,A]⟩. Substitute the latter into the former and divide by the nonzero derivative magnitude to obtain the result. No self-adjoint time operator was introduced, and nothing in this derivation permits replacing τ_A by an arbitrary measurement duration.

example.calculation: Unitary evolution gives ⟨A⟩=cosωt. Since A²=I, ΔA=|sinωt|, while |d⟨A⟩/dt|=ω|sinωt| and ΔH=ℏω/2. Whenever sinωt≠0, τ_A=1/ω and ΔHτ_A=ℏ/2. At the isolated zeros the ratio is 0/0 and is not defined by the formula; its limiting value exists. The state first becomes orthogonal to its initial state at π/ω, a separate timescale with a different constant.
example.conclusion: The inequality is exact once its time quantity and assumptions are specified. Saturation can be checked by elementary two-by-two dynamics.

source.status: Classical Eisenstein construction with explicit coefficient checks
source.summary: A q-series is not modular merely because it is written with q. The transformation law can be proved for an actual lattice sum, while low-order coefficients and forced special values provide useful checks of the implementation.
definitions: For Imτ>0 define G₄(τ)=Σ(m,n)≠(0,0)(m+nτ)⁻⁴, an absolutely convergent lattice sum.

result.statement: G₄((aτ+b)/(cτ+d))=(cτ+d)⁴G₄(τ) for matrices in SL₂(Z). E₄ begins 1+240q+2160q²+6720q³+17520q⁴. The weight-six transformation law forces E₆(i)=0.

Absolute convergence permits reindexing, proving weight four. The stated Fourier expansion supplies its holomorphic behavior at the cusp; coefficients follow by summing divisor cubes: σ₃(1),…,σ₃(4)=1,9,28,73. For E₆, the substitution τ↦−1/τ fixes i and multiplies its value by i⁶=−1, so its value must vanish.

The verification program checks these coefficients and the numerical special-value residual. A truncated series agreeing at one point still does not prove its global modularity; the reindexing argument or a theorem supplies that part.
