source.title: A classical abelian Chern–Simons calculation with its global boundary
source.status: Small-gauge invariance and a torus action evaluated
source.summary: The Chern–Simons integrand needs a geometric setting before it becomes an action. A globally defined abelian connection one-form on a closed manifold gives a tractable case in which gauge variation and an actual integral can be derived directly.
definitions: Let M be a closed oriented three-manifold and A a globally defined real one-form representing a connection on a trivial U(1) bundle.
Choose S_k(A)=(k/(4π))∫M A∧dA. A small gauge change is A↦A+dχ with χ a globally defined real scalar.

result.name: A classical abelian Chern–Simons calculation with its global boundary
result.statement: For this setting S_k is invariant under small gauge changes. Its first variation is δS_k=(k/(2π))∫δA∧dA. On the unit-period three-torus, A=a cos(2πz)dx+b sin(2πz)dy has S_k=−kab/2 for orientation dx∧dy∧dz.
result.proof: The gauge variation is (k/(4π))∫dχ∧dA=(k/(4π))∫d(χdA), which vanishes on a closed manifold by Stokes. For the first variation, expand the action to first order. Integration by parts makes the two terms δA∧dA and A∧dδA equal after integration, giving the factor two. For the torus example, differentiating A and expanding the wedge product yields A∧dA=−2πab(cos²(2πz)+sin²(2πz))dx∧dy∧dz; its integral is −2πab.

example.setup: Take a=b=1 and k=2 on the unit three-torus.
example.calculation: The classical action is −1. The form is globally periodic and smooth, but dA is nonzero, so it is not a stationary flat connection when k≠0. Varying a or b changes the action continuously. Thus even in this elementary example, quantization of a coupling level must not be confused with a claim that every classical action value is an integer.
example.conclusion: The calculation supplies an actual well-defined action and variation in a restricted setting, while identifying exactly where stronger global statements would enter.

source.limits: Nontrivial bundles and large gauge transformations require a globally consistent definition beyond a single one-form integral. Level quantization depends on the group, normalization, and often spin data; it is not proved by the small-gauge calculation.

source.title: Two-oscillator locking with stable and unstable branches
source.status: Exact phase reduction solved
source.summary: The missing time derivative in the old formula changes its mathematical type. Once the dynamics is restored, the smallest nontrivial network has a sharp synchronization threshold and an explicit stability classification.
definitions: Take θ̇₁=ω₁+Ksin(θ₂−θ₁) and θ̇₂=ω₂+Ksin(θ₁−θ₂), with K>0.
Let δ=θ₁−θ₂ and φ=(θ₁+θ₂)/2. Phases are taken modulo 2π.

result.name: Two-oscillator locking with stable and unstable branches
result.statement: The equations reduce to δ̇=Δω−2Ksinδ and φ̇=(ω₁+ω₂)/2. If |Δω|<2K there are two equilibrium phase differences: the branch with cosδ>0 is asymptotically stable, while the other is unstable. At equality they merge into a nonhyperbolic threshold.
result.proof: Subtract and add the two original equations; the sine terms cancel in the mean and reinforce in the difference. A locked difference requires sinδ=Δω/(2K), which has two solutions per period in the strict interior. The scalar linearization is −2Kcosδ. Negative derivative gives local asymptotic stability and positive derivative gives instability. At |Δω|=2K the derivative vanishes; a Taylor expansion gives a quadratic leading term and shows that the threshold equilibrium is not the same robust exponentially attracting situation as an interior stable branch.

example.setup: Let K=1 and Δω=1.
example.calculation: The stable difference is δ*=π/6 and the unstable one is 5π/6, with linearized rates −√3 and +√3. The common locked frequency is (ω₁+ω₂)/2. If instead Δω=3, then δ̇=3−2sinδ≥1, so the unwrapped phase difference increases forever and no phase lock is possible. A common shift θi↦θi+α changes neither difference dynamics nor locking.
example.conclusion: Synchronization here means a constant relative phase, not necessarily identical phases or a zero absolute frequency.

definitions: A gate q satisfies q̇=α(V)(1−q)−β(V)q, with nonnegative locally Lipschitz rates.

source.status: Finite models solved explicitly
source.summary: An uncertain state of nature does not automatically supply a second strategic player. The distinction can be made concrete by solving a one-agent decision and a separately defined coordination game.
definitions: In a decision model, nature selects state S with prior p and T with prior 1−p. Action B has payoffs M and −c, while action N has zero in either state, with M,c>0.
In a two-player coordination game, each chooses B or N. Payoffs are (2,2) at (B,B), (1,1) at (N,N), and (0,0) at mismatched choices.

result.name: Decision thresholds and genuine strategic equilibria
result.statement: In the decision problem B is optimal exactly when p≥c/(M+c), with indifference at equality. In the coordination game both (B,B) and (N,N) are Nash equilibria; there is also a mixed equilibrium where each chooses B with probability 1/3.
result.proof: Expected utility of B is pM−(1−p)c=p(M+c)−c, while N gives zero, yielding the threshold. In the game, a player facing B obtains 2 by B and 0 by N; facing N, the player obtains 1 by N and 0 by B. Thus both coordinated profiles resist unilateral deviation. If the opponent chooses B with probability q, the expected payoff from B is 2q and from N is 1−q. Equality gives q=1/3; this mutual indifference verifies the mixed equilibrium.

source.title: Infinite utilities through controlled finite limits
source.status: Limit-order obstruction exhibited
source.summary: Replacing very large payoffs by infinity can destroy the expectation being optimized. Finite truncations reveal when a conclusion is robust and when it depends on the order in which utility scales and probabilities approach their limits.
definitions: Take two states with probabilities p and 1−p. For truncation M>0, action A has payoffs (M,−M), action B has (−M,M) and action C has (0,0).
Expected utilities are UA=M(2p−1), UB=−UA and UC=0. Every finite model is well defined.

result.name: Infinite utilities through controlled finite limits
result.statement: At fixed p≠1/2 the better of A and B is determined by the sign of 2p−1. At p=1/2 all three actions tie for every M. But sequences of priors with the same limiting value 1/2 can produce opposite strict preferences that persist as M→∞.
result.proof: Choose p_M=1/2+a/M for fixed a and sufficiently large M so the prior is valid. Then UA=M(2a/M)=2a and UB=−2a. If a>0, A strictly wins; if a<0, B strictly wins; if a=0, all tie. All these priors converge to 1/2. Hence the limiting prior alone does not determine the limiting decision problem. Directly assigning payoffs +∞ and −∞ with both states of positive probability would require subtracting two infinite contributions, leaving an undefined expectation rather than a usable optimization objective.

example.setup: For M=100 take priors 0.51,0.49 and 0.50.
example.calculation: The respective expected payoffs of A are 2,−2 and 0, while B has the opposite values. Repeating with M=1000 and priors 0.501,0.499,0.500 gives exactly the same three outcomes. This is an exact algebraic example of a nonuniform limiting operation. The earlier finite wager threshold c/(M+c) instead tends to zero at fixed c, but that conclusion depends on its asymmetric payoff structure.
example.conclusion: A claim involving infinite utilities needs a declared finite approximation, probability assumptions and a limit argument; otherwise an asserted optimum may not exist as a defined mathematical object.

source.limits: This example shows sensitivity of one family of limits, not that every model with unbounded utility is inconsistent. Extended-valued expectations are legitimate when their positive and negative parts are not simultaneously infinite.
source.extension: Specify a utility function and a class of probability measures under which expectations are well defined, then use uniform-integrability conditions to justify exchanging limits and optimization.

source.title: A Cauchy model has no ordinary mean or variance
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: The useful revision is a complete separation between symmetry, existence of a mean, and concentration of an estimator. The Cauchy family gives an exact example in which averaging independent observations does not improve the distribution of the sample mean. This is a classical stability calculation, not a conclusion about any particular empirical dataset.
definitions: A Cauchy law with location μ and scale γ>0 has density γ/[π((x−μ)²+γ²)]. Its characteristic function is φ(t)=exp(iμt−γ|t|). Independence multiplies characteristic functions.

result.name: Exact failure of sample-mean concentration
result.statement: If X₁,…,Xₙ are independent Cauchy(μ,γ), then their arithmetic mean is again Cauchy(μ,γ), for every positive integer n. Neither E[X] nor Var(X) exists as an ordinary finite moment.
result.proof: The positive and negative parts of the centered first-moment integral each diverge logarithmically because x/(1+x²) has a logarithmic antiderivative. Symmetric truncation cancels these divergences, but that principal value is not a Lebesgue expectation. For the mean, independence gives E exp(itΣXⱼ/n)=φ(t/n)ⁿ=exp(iμt−γ|t|). Uniqueness of characteristic functions identifies the law. Thus no finite-variance central-limit estimate can be invoked. The same tail calculation gives a divergent second moment.

example.setup: Take standard Cauchy observations and ask whether the mean is within one unit of zero.
example.calculation: For every n, P(|X̄ₙ|≤1)=F(1)−F(−1)=1/2, using F(x)=1/2+arctan(x)/π. The probability remains one half even when n increases. In contrast, the population median is μ and independent sample quantiles can consistently estimate it because F is continuous and strictly increasing there.
example.conclusion: A stable distribution can make an apparently reasonable estimator permanently noisy. Quantile estimation and distribution fitting must be evaluated under their actual assumptions.

source.limits: This does not establish that observations are Cauchy, that every heavy-tailed law lacks a mean, or that all robust estimators have the same behavior. Dependence would also change the characteristic-function multiplication.
source.extension: For a specified tail exponent, determine which absolute moments exist, then compare mean, median and trimmed estimators using exact or justified asymptotic distributions.

source.title: Feedback instability is a mechanism to specify
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Feedback questions become testable once an update matrix and a measured norm are fixed. Eigenvalues determine asymptotic decay in finite dimension, but they do not bound all finite-time amplification. A two-dimensional Jordan block makes the distinction completely explicit.
definitions: A discrete linear system is xₙ₊₁=Axₙ. Spectral radius ρ(A) is the largest eigenvalue modulus. The Euclidean amplification at step n is the induced norm ||Aⁿ||₂. A real matrix is normal when AAᵀ=AᵀA.

result.name: Exact transient amplification in an asymptotically stable system
result.statement: For A=aI+bN with N=[[0,1],[0,0]], N²=0 and 0<a<1, Aⁿ=aⁿI+n aⁿ⁻¹bN. Although ρ(A)=a<1 and Aⁿ→0, intermediate norms can be arbitrarily large as |b| increases.
result.proof: The binomial theorem applies because I and N commute and every power Nᵏ with k≥2 vanishes. Only the terms k=0 and k=1 survive. The scalar sequences aⁿ and n aⁿ⁻¹ both tend to zero, proving asymptotic stability. Acting on e₂ yields Aⁿe₂=(n aⁿ⁻¹b,aⁿ), so its Euclidean norm supplies a lower bound on ||Aⁿ||₂. At a fixed step n this lower bound grows linearly in |b| without changing either eigenvalue.

example.setup: Choose A=[[1/2,4],[0,1/2]] and initial state e₂.
example.calculation: At one step the output is (4,1/2), with norm √65/2>4. At two steps the output is (4,1/4), although the eigenvalues remain 1/2. The exact formula predicts eventual decay after this transient. The corresponding continuous example A_c=[[-1,4],[0,−1]] has exp(tA_c)=e^(−t)[[1,4t],[0,1]].
example.conclusion: A stability statement and a peak-amplification statement answer different questions. A mechanism for a large transient can be proved without asserting any probability distribution for external shocks.

source.limits: The calculation assumes a fixed finite matrix. Nonlinear saturation, delayed feedback, time-varying matrices and stochastic inputs require additional models. A large matrix norm does not by itself imply a particular event occurs.
source.extension: Optimize supₙ||Aⁿ|| over a parameter family, then compare Euclidean bounds with a quadratic Lyapunov norm that contracts at every step.

source.title: Frobenius energy across disjoint blocks
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: A multiscale norm construction needs a bookkeeping theorem. The Frobenius norm behaves like a Euclidean norm on the list of matrix entries, so squared energies add over disjoint blocks. Overlapping descriptions need multiplicity corrections instead of an unqualified addition rule.
definitions: For a real or complex matrix A, ||A||_F²=Σᵢⱼ|aᵢⱼ|²=Tr(A* A). A block here means a subset of entry indices; blocks may have irregular shapes. A partition uses every entry exactly once.

result.name: Partition additivity and the overlap correction
result.statement: If entry blocks B₁,…,B_m partition the indices, then ||A||_F²=Σ_b||A|B_b||_F². If they cover entries with multiplicities cᵢⱼ, the uncorrected sum is Σᵢⱼcᵢⱼ|aᵢⱼ|².
result.proof: Expand every block norm as a sum of squared moduli and interchange two finite sums. The coefficient of a given entry is exactly the number of blocks containing it. For a partition that number is one. When every covered entry has positive multiplicity, assigning weight 1/cᵢⱼ to that entry within each occurrence restores the original energy. The argument needs no independence or probabilistic assumptions. An equivalent Hilbert-space statement uses orthogonal coordinate projections P_b and the identity ΣP_b=I.

example.setup: Let A=[[1,2],[3,4]]. Partition it by rows, then deliberately count its first row twice.
example.calculation: The complete squared Frobenius norm is 1+4+9+16=30. Row energies are 5 and 25, adding to 30. Repeating the first row gives 35, exposing five units of double counting. Dividing the two first-row occurrences by multiplicity two restores 30. By contrast, the unsquared norms √5+5 do not equal √30.
example.conclusion: Disjoint block decomposition preserves total squared energy. It does not automatically make values comparable across blocks of different cardinalities.

source.limits: When comparing differently sized systems, one must choose total energy, mean squared entry, an operator norm or a dimensionless normalization. Those choices encode different questions. Orthogonal-coordinate arguments also do not apply unchanged to arbitrary overlapping learned features.
source.extension: For nonorthogonal feature maps F_b, study frame bounds a||x||²≤Σ||F_bx||²≤b||x||² and determine whether a tight-frame normalization can preserve the intended energy.

source.title: Population weights versus amplitude weights
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: The distinction between probability weights and amplitude weights can be settled before any elaborate multiscale model is built. The former defines an expected square; the latter first attenuates the signal and then squares it. They agree only under special circumstances.
definitions: Let p_i≥0 with Σp_i=1 and let a_i be real or complex values. Expected square is E|A|²=Σp_i|a_i|². Entrywise amplitude weighting by p gives ||p⊙a||₂²=Σp_i²|a_i|².

result.name: Probabilistic weighting is implemented by square-root amplitudes
result.statement: The probability-weighted squared magnitude equals ||diag(√p_i)a||₂². Weighting the amplitudes by p_i instead yields a different quadratic form. Since 0≤p_i≤1, the second is no larger than the first.
result.proof: Expand the Euclidean norm after applying the diagonal matrix. Each squared coefficient is (√p_i)²=p_i. The ordinary amplitude weight p_i is squared by the norm, producing p_i². The inequality follows term by term from p_i²≤p_i. Equality requires p_i(1−p_i)|a_i|²=0 for every i: nonzero signals can occur only at weights zero or one, apart from degenerate cancellations that are impossible in this nonnegative sum.

example.setup: Use values a=(2,4) and probabilities p=(1/4,3/4).
example.calculation: Expected square is (1/4)4+(3/4)16=13. Squared probability-amplitude weighting gives (1/16)4+(9/16)16=37/4=9.25. The weighted mean is 7/2, so the variance is 13−(7/2)²=3/4. None of these three quantities is a substitute for the others.
example.conclusion: A correct implementation starts by deciding whether the data describe sampling frequencies, deliberate attenuation or an averaging measure. The square-root representation then supplies a precise matrix formula.

source.limits: If some weights vanish, the resulting quadratic form is only a seminorm on the full coordinate space. Importance weights need not sum to one, while signed weights need not produce a positive quadratic form at all.

source.title: Covariance inequalities with finite moments
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Covariance optimization is legitimate only after existence of the required moments is established. Once variables are square integrable, covariance becomes a positive semidefinite Gram matrix in an L² space, and the familiar bounds follow from one short argument.
definitions: For square-integrable X and Y, Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−EX)overline(Y−EY)]. For a real random vector Z, its covariance matrix Σ has entries Cov(Z_i,Z_j). Positive semidefinite means wᵀΣw≥0 for every w.

result.name: Covariance as a Gram matrix and its equality condition
result.statement: |Cov(X,Y)|²≤Var(X)Var(Y). For a finite square-integrable real vector, Var(wᵀZ)=wᵀΣw. If both variances are positive, equality in the scalar bound occurs precisely when the centered variables are proportional almost surely.
result.proof: Centered variables are elements of the Hilbert space L². Cauchy–Schwarz gives the bound. Alternatively, for real variables, nonnegativity of E[(X−EX−t(Y−EY))²] for every real t forces the discriminant of this quadratic in t to be nonpositive. Expanding the centered weighted sum proves the matrix identity and hence positive semidefiniteness. Equality in Cauchy–Schwarz identifies linear dependence in L², where two representatives differing only on a null set are equivalent.

example.setup: Let X be equally likely to be −1 or 1, and let Y=2X.
example.calculation: Both means vanish. Variances are 1 and 4, covariance is 2, and Σ=[[1,2],[2,4]] has determinant zero. The combination 2X−Y vanishes almost surely, so its variance is zero. This explains the singularity structurally rather than treating it as a numerical failure.
example.conclusion: A singular covariance matrix records an exact L² dependency. It can be essential information for a constrained quadratic calculation.

source.title: A quadratic program with singular cases included
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: The positive-definite inverse formula is only one branch of the quadratic-program problem. The singular case admits a clean complete classification, and inequality constraints can change the optimizer even when the matrix is nonsingular. These are mathematical statements about quadratic forms, not practical allocation recommendations.
definitions: Let Σ be a symmetric positive semidefinite real matrix and c≠0. Minimize wᵀΣw subject to cᵀw=1. Write Σ⁺ for its Moore–Penrose inverse and kerΣ for its nullspace.

result.name: Complete equality-constrained PSD classification
result.statement: If some z∈kerΣ has cᵀz≠0, the minimum is zero and all minimizers are the feasible null vectors. Otherwise c∈rangeΣ, q=cᵀΣ⁺c>0, the minimum is 1/q, and all minimizers are Σ⁺c/q+z with z∈kerΣ.
result.proof: In the first case, z/(cᵀz) is feasible and has zero objective; positive semidefiniteness rules out a lower value. In the second case, c is orthogonal to the nullspace and hence lies in the range. Set w₀=Σ⁺c/q. It is feasible and Σw₀=c/q. For any feasible w=w₀+h, cᵀh=0, so the cross term 2hᵀΣw₀ vanishes and the objective is 1/q+hᵀΣh. Equality holds exactly when h∈kerΣ. This also proves uniqueness precisely when the feasible tangent space contains no nonzero null vector.

example.setup: Compare a diagonal matrix, a rank-one matrix, and a nonnegative constraint.
example.calculation: For Σ=diag(1,4), c=(1,1), w*=(4/5,1/5) and the minimum is 4/5. For Σ=11ᵀ, every feasible w has objective one. For Σ=[[1,2],[2,9]], the unrestricted optimizer is (7/6,−1/6) with value 5/6; imposing w≥0 gives (1,0) with value one. Its KKT multiplier for the second coordinate is positive.
example.conclusion: Nullspaces, budgets and inequality constraints must be handled together; merely replacing an inverse by a pseudoinverse does not cover every singular case.

source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: An open-system equation must preserve the convex set of density operators, including when an auxiliary system is attached. An exactly solvable qubit channel provides a stronger check than inspection of trace alone. Its Kraus form supplies complete positivity directly.
definitions: A density operator is a positive semidefinite matrix ρ with trace one. A map is completely positive when its tensor product with the identity map on any finite auxiliary system preserves positivity. Set ℏ=1.

result.name: Exact amplitude-damping semigroup
result.statement: For H=0 and L=√γ |0⟩⟨1| with γ≥0, the Lindblad equation sends ρ=[[a,b],[b*,d]] to [[a+(1−q)d,√q b],[√q b*,qd]], where q=e^(−γt), t≥0. This defines a trace-preserving completely positive semigroup.

Their adjoint squares sum to I, and ΣK_jρK_j† reproduces the solution. Tensoring each K_j with an auxiliary identity shows complete positivity. Since q(t+s)=q(t)q(s), composition satisfies the semigroup law.

result.name: Energy dissipation and coordinate transport
result.statement: Every sufficiently differentiable solution satisfies dE/dt=−∇EᵀK∇E≤0. Under an invertible linear change y=Sx, the transported energy Ẽ(y)=E(S⁻¹y) and mobility K̃(y)=SK(S⁻¹y)Sᵀ preserve this dissipation identity.
result.proof: The chain rule gives Ė=∇Eᵀẋ, and positive semidefiniteness gives the sign. For the coordinate change, ∇_yẼ=S⁻ᵀ∇_xE and ẏ=Sẋ=−SKSᵀ∇_yẼ. Substitution recovers the same scalar energy derivative. This calculation explains why transforming only the state while keeping an arbitrary identity mobility generally changes the dynamics. The result requires neither thermodynamic terminology nor a claim that all dissipative systems are gradient flows.

example.setup: Take E(x)=xᵀAx/2 with symmetric A positive semidefinite, and K=I.
example.calculation: Then ẋ=−Ax and Ė=−xᵀA²x. A finite weighted-graph heat equation has this form with A equal to the graph Laplacian, while the scalar equation ẋ=−x is its one-dimensional instance. A constant component in the Laplacian nullspace is preserved rather than dissipated, which shows the difference between nonincrease and convergence to a unique state.
example.conclusion: The shared theorem is energy monotonicity under a specified positive mobility. A proof of equivalence requires an actual state-space map such as S and the correctly transported energy and mobility.

source.limits: Nonsymmetric transport, Hamiltonian components, constraints and nonlocal metrics require extensions. Energy decrease alone does not prove boundedness, uniqueness, convergence rate or identification from observations.

source.title: Bessel versus Parseval
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: The missing distinction in the original inequality list is completeness. Bessel’s inequality is an exact statement about projection error; Parseval’s equality appears when the chosen orthonormal family spans the relevant Hilbert space. A residual formula makes the practical meaning immediate.
definitions: Use an inner product linear in its first argument. For an orthonormal family e₁,…,e_m, define P_mx=Σ⟨x,e_j⟩e_j. Its span is a closed finite-dimensional subspace of the Hilbert space H.

result.name: Projection residual and completeness criterion
result.statement: For every x, ||x||²=Σ_{j=1}^m|⟨x,e_j⟩|²+||x−P_mx||². For a countable orthonormal family, the infinite coefficient sum is at most ||x||². Equality for every x holds exactly when its closed linear span is H.
result.proof: The residual is orthogonal to every e_j because taking its inner product with e_j subtracts the same coefficient. Pythagoras therefore splits the norm into projection and residual, and orthonormality gives the coefficient sum. Finite partial sums are increasing and bounded, so their limit exists. The partial projections form a Cauchy sequence, with squared differences equal to sums of omitted squared coefficients. Their limit projects onto the closed span. Equality means the residual projection onto the orthogonal complement vanishes. If equality holds for all x, that complement is zero and the span is dense.

example.setup: Take x=(2,3,6) in R³ and initially observe only e₁,e₂.
example.calculation: The observed squared coefficient sum is 4+9=13, total squared norm is 49, and residual squared norm is 36. Adding e₃ removes the residual exactly. Omitting e₃ never becomes harmless merely because the first two coefficients were calculated to high precision.
example.conclusion: This is both an approximation certificate and a statement of what the measurement family cannot see.

source.limits: An infinite orthonormal family need not be complete. For nonorthogonal features, coefficients from raw inner products are not automatically orthogonal projections, and frame or Gram-matrix analysis is needed.
source.extension: Develop a frame analogue with lower and upper frame bounds, or identify the cheapest observation family whose residual vanishes on a specified finite-dimensional model class.

source.title: Hölder and Young with equality cases
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Conjugate exponents and equality cases turn a generic inequality into a sharp tool. The proof below also states what must be checked before applying it: measurability, the relevant integrability and the distinction between the absolute-value bound and the signed integral.
definitions: Let 1<p<∞ and q=p/(p−1), so 1/p+1/q=1. Norms are ||f||_p=(∫|f|^p)^(1/p) and the analogous q-norm, on one fixed measure space.

result.name: Young and Hölder with sharp equality
result.statement: For a,b≥0, ab≤a^p/p+b^q/q, with equality exactly when a^p=b^q. Consequently ∫|fg|≤||f||_p||g||_q. For nonzero finite norms, equality holds exactly when |f|^p/||f||_p^p=|g|^q/||g||_q^q almost everywhere.
result.proof: Fix a and minimize h(b)=b^q/q−ab+a^p/p over b≥0. Its derivative is b^(q−1)−a, with its unique minimum at b=a^(p−1), and the minimum equals zero. Normalize nonzero f,g to unit p- and q-norms, apply the scalar inequality pointwise and integrate. Equality in the integrated nonnegative difference requires pointwise equality almost everywhere, which yields the normalized-power condition. To obtain equality for |∫fg| as well, the product must also have an almost-everywhere constant phase or sign.

example.setup: Choose p=3, q=3/2, a=2 and b=4.
example.calculation: Here a^p=b^q=8, so Young is exact: ab=8=8/3+8/(3/2). For a finite counting measure, proportional normalized powers supply equally explicit Hölder equality examples. Choosing disjointly supported nonzero functions makes the product integral zero while both norms are positive, showing a strict case.
example.conclusion: The equality condition identifies when a proposed estimate is sharp and which directions are responsible for slack.

source.limits: The endpoints p=1,q=∞ require essential-supremum language and a different equality statement. If either required norm is infinite, the finite useful estimate is unavailable even when a formal product expression can be written.
source.extension: Use the equality characterization to optimize a linear functional on an L^p unit ball and compare existence and uniqueness in endpoint versus strictly convex cases.

source.title: Matrix norms and the quantity being bounded
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Choosing a norm means choosing how input and output error are measured. A norm catalogue becomes useful only when attached to its induced error inequality. A two-dimensional example shows that several plausible norms report different numerical amplification.
definitions: The induced p-norm is ||A||_p=sup_{x≠0}||Ax||_p/||x||_p. The induced 1-norm is the largest absolute column sum, the induced infinity-norm is the largest absolute row sum, and the Frobenius norm is a Euclidean norm on entries.

result.name: Sharp induced bounds and singular-value comparisons
result.statement: For every vector x, ||Ax||_p≤||A||_p||x||_p. In Euclidean norm, ||A||₂ is the largest singular value, while ||A||_F² is the sum of squared singular values; hence ||A||₂≤||A||_F≤√r||A||₂ for rank r>0.
result.proof: The first inequality is the definition of the supremum. For p=1, triangle inequalities bound each output coordinate and collecting each |x_j| gives the maximum column sum; choosing a coordinate vector at a maximizing column attains it. The infinity case uses a maximizing row and matching signs. Orthogonal or unitary invariance reduces the Euclidean claims to a diagonal singular-value matrix, where the largest entry bounds their squared sum above and below. The rank-zero case has both norms zero.

example.calculation: Its induced 1- and infinity-norms are both three. Its Frobenius norm is √6. The eigenvalues of AᵀA=[[1,2],[2,5]] are 3±2√2, so ||A||₂=√(3+2√2)=1+√2. These are distinct measures of the same operator. A claim of amplification three is sharp for a 1-norm or infinity-norm question, but overestimates the sharp Euclidean factor.
example.conclusion: Reporting the input and output norms is part of stating the bound, not a cosmetic implementation detail.

source.limits: Condition numbers also depend on the norm and require invertibility or a specified pseudoinverse/restricted subspace. An entrywise norm cannot replace an induced one without tracking the comparison constants.
source.extension: For a chosen observation map, compute the restricted operator norm on the admissible state subspace and quantify how much a generic full-space bound overestimates the actual errors.

source.title: Lyapunov conditions in the right direction
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: A Lyapunov certificate is a sufficient argument tied to a chosen function. Failure of one function is not a system-instability certificate. The exact example below resolves that logical error and produces a contracting quadratic geometry for the same stable system.
definitions: For ẋ=Ax and symmetric P, define V(x)=xᵀPx. Positive definiteness P≻0 makes V comparable with ||x||². Along a trajectory, V̇=xᵀ(AᵀP+PA)x. A Hurwitz matrix has all eigenvalues in the open left half-plane.

result.name: Quadratic certificate and a counterexample to the failed converse
result.statement: If P≻0 and AᵀP+PA=−Q with Q≻0, then V(t)≤exp(−λ_min(Q)t/λ_max(P))V(0), proving exponential stability. A stable A can nevertheless make d||x||²/dt positive at some state.
result.proof: The derivative identity follows by the product rule. Since xᵀQx≥λ_min(Q)||x||² and V≤λ_max(P)||x||², V̇≤−[λ_min(Q)/λ_max(P)]V. Integration gives exponential decay of V; the lower eigenvalue bound on P translates this into a Euclidean state bound. The proof makes no assertion that every positive function has a negative derivative. For Hurwitz A, the integral P=∫₀∞exp(tAᵀ)Qexp(tA)dt provides the converse existence result, with convergence following from exponential matrix decay.

example.setup: Take A=[[-1,4],[0,−1]], whose eigenvalues are both −1.
example.calculation: At x=(1,1), Ax=(3,−1) and d(xᵀx)/dt=2xᵀAx=4>0. Yet P=[[1/2,1],[1,9/2]] has positive leading minor and determinant 5/4, and direct multiplication gives AᵀP+PA=−I. Thus the Euclidean norm can temporarily grow while the certified P-norm decreases.
example.conclusion: The apparent contradiction disappears once the certificate is interpreted in the right direction and its metric is stated.

source.limits: A certificate for one linearization is not automatically a global nonlinear proof. Semidefinite Q needs an invariance argument for asymptotic convergence, and strict inequalities matter near marginal modes.

source.title: Units of the Einstein equation
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Dimensional statements about tensor components must name the coordinate or frame convention. Using a local orthonormal frame and x⁰=ct makes the audit simple, while also explaining why coordinate components in other charts can carry different units.
definitions: Use metric signature (−,+,+,+), spacetime coordinates of length dimension, and a dimensionless orthonormal metric. Write G_N for Newton’s constant, c for speed, ε for energy density and G_μν for the Einstein tensor; the two symbols G have unrelated types.

result.name: A consistent dimensional audit of Einstein’s equation
result.statement: In this convention G_μν and Λg_μν have dimensions L⁻²; T_μν has dimensions ML⁻¹T⁻². Since [G_N]=L³M⁻¹T⁻² and [c⁴]=L⁴T⁻⁴, (G_N/c⁴)T_μν has dimension L⁻². The factor 8π is dimensionless and is not selected by dimensional analysis.
result.proof: A connection coefficient contains one derivative of a dimensionless metric, giving L⁻¹, and curvature has a derivative of the connection or a product of two connections, giving L⁻². Energy per volume is (ML²T⁻²)/L³=ML⁻¹T⁻². Multiplying exponents in G_N c⁻⁴T gives zero mass exponent, length exponent −2 and zero time exponent. The cosmological constant must have the same curvature dimension when it multiplies the dimensionless metric. All statements are frame and coordinate dependent at the component level, while the tensor equation is geometric.

example.setup: Consider a perfect-fluid stress tensor in its local rest frame.
example.calculation: T_00=ε and T_ii=p in the orthonormal convention, so pressure and energy density have matching units. If instead time is represented by t rather than ct, changing the coordinate basis introduces c factors into the time components; one must transform the tensor rather than recycle the orthonormal component units.
example.conclusion: The repaired equation is G_μν+Λg_μν=(8πG_N/c⁴)T_μν. It passes a dimensional audit without confusing Newton’s constant, curvature or matter units.

source.limits: The audit cannot fix signs, the numerical coupling or a curvature convention. Those require definitions and a limiting calculation. Natural units c=1 suppress dimensions in notation but do not remove the need to restore them consistently.

source.title: Why the coefficient is 8π
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: The coefficient 8π is determined by matching a conventioned relativistic field equation to Newtonian Poisson gravity. The trace reversal supplies a crucial factor one half. This is a derivation of the classical normalization, not a new gravitational law.
definitions: Set Λ=0 for the local weak-field limit. Use signature (−,+,+,+), x⁰=ct and R^ρ_{σμν}=∂_μΓ^ρ_{νσ}−∂_νΓ^ρ_{μσ}+Γ^ρ_{μα}Γ^α_{νσ}−Γ^ρ_{να}Γ^α_{μσ}, with R_σν=R^ρ_{σρν}. Let G_μν=κT_μν initially have an unknown κ.

result.name: Newtonian matching yields κ=8πG_N/c⁴
result.statement: For a static weak potential with g_00=−(1+2Φ/c²), slow matter and negligible pressure, R_00≈∇²Φ/c² and the trace-reversed source is T_00−g_00T/2≈ρc²/2. Matching ∇²Φ=4πG_Nρ therefore gives κ=8πG_N/c⁴.
result.proof: Contract the field equation in four dimensions: −R=κT. Substituting back gives R_μν=κ(T_μν−g_μνT/2). For dust at rest, T_00≈ρc², spatial diagonal stresses are negligible, and T≈−ρc²; with g_00≈−1 the displayed source becomes ρc²−ρc²/2. The weak, static connection is Γ^i_{00}≈∂_iΦ/c². In R_00, time derivatives vanish and connection products are higher order, leaving ∂_iΓ^i_{00}≈∇²Φ/c². Thus ∇²Φ=(κc⁴/2)ρ. Equating its coefficient with Poisson’s coefficient fixes κ.

example.setup: Track the factors before inserting the answer.
example.calculation: If one incorrectly equates R_00 with κρc² without trace reversal, the inferred coupling would differ by a factor of two. If one uses time rather than ct, the connection and stress components must both be rescaled. Either mistake can produce superficially plausible but inconsistent equations.
example.conclusion: The numerical factor and powers of c are fixed together once geometric, matter and Newtonian conventions are stated.

source.limits: This leading-order derivation assumes weak fields, slow motion, small stresses and a regime in which Λ is negligible. Reversing the Riemann-tensor sign requires changing the field-equation sign convention consistently. The result does not derive Einstein’s equation uniquely from Newtonian gravity.

source.title: Sixteen entries but ten independent components
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: There are several counts in general relativity, and conflating them produces incorrect conclusions. Matrix entries, independent tensor components, differential identities, initial-data constraints and physical propagating modes belong to different stages of the analysis.
definitions: Use indices μ,ν∈{0,1,2,3}. A symmetric covariant tensor satisfies S_μν=S_νμ. The Einstein tensor obeys four contracted Bianchi identities. In a 3+1 formulation, the spatial metric and its conjugate momentum have six components each.

result.name: Component count and local vacuum degree-of-freedom count
result.statement: A symmetric four-by-four tensor has ten independent components: four diagonal and six off-diagonal. The four contracted Bianchi identities are differential identities, not four duplicate entries. For regular vacuum general relativity, four first-class constraints acting on twelve spatial canonical variables leave four physical phase-space variables, or two configuration polarizations per spatial point.
result.proof: For an n-by-n symmetric matrix there are n diagonal entries and n(n−1)/2 unordered off-diagonal pairs, giving n(n+1)/2. At n=4 this is ten, although the full display contains sixteen slots. The Bianchi relations differentiate combinations of field-equation components; they do not identify any selected four slots algebraically. In the canonical count, a first-class constraint imposes one phase-space condition and generates one gauge direction. Four such constraints therefore remove eight of the twelve spatial canonical variables. Dividing the remaining four phase-space variables into coordinate-momentum pairs gives two local propagating degrees of freedom.

example.setup: Write the first row as S_00,S_01,S_02,S_03 and the remaining rows with S_10=S_01 and the corresponding symmetries.
example.calculation: There is no S_44 in the chosen zero-through-three convention. A one-through-four convention may use it, but mixing the two is invalid. In a linearized plane-wave gauge, the remaining transverse-traceless amplitudes can be represented by h_+ and h_×, illustrating rather than replacing the constrained Hamiltonian count.
example.conclusion: The repaired statement retains all ten independent equations while explaining their differential dependence and gauge structure.

source.limits: Boundary conditions, global moduli, matter fields and singular constraint surfaces can affect global degrees of freedom. Subtracting four identities from ten components is not on its own a derivation of two propagating modes.
source.extension: Perform an explicit linearized gauge reduction for a plane wave and compare it with the canonical count in a stated background and boundary setting.

source.title: Covariant conservation is a structural condition
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Covariant conservation is the compatibility condition supplied by the geometry of the field equation. It does not say that coordinate components are constant, or that a global conserved total energy exists in every spacetime. A homogeneous expanding metric gives an exact example of the distinction.
definitions: For the Levi-Civita connection, ∇g=0 and the contracted Bianchi identity is ∇^μG_μν=0. Let κ and Λ be constants. A perfect fluid has rest energy density ε, pressure p and four-velocity normalized by u·u=−1 in a c=1 convention.

result.name: Source conservation and the FLRW continuity equation
result.statement: The field equation G_μν+Λg_μν=κT_μν with κ≠0 implies ∇^μT_μν=0. In a homogeneous FLRW metric, this includes ε̇+3H(ε+p)=0, where H=ȧ/a. For constant equation-of-state parameter p=wε, εa^{3(1+w)} is constant.
result.proof: Apply the covariant divergence to the field equation. The geometric identity and metric compatibility eliminate the left side, and constant κ gives the conclusion. In comoving FLRW coordinates, expanding ∇_μT^{μ0}=0 combines the ordinary time derivative of ε with the connection terms associated with the changing spatial volume a³; isotropic pressure contributes three identical work terms. Substitution p=wε yields d logε/dt=−3(1+w)d loga/dt, whose integral gives the power law wherever ε and a are positive.

example.setup: Compare dust and radiation under a scale factor that doubles.
example.calculation: For dust w=0, energy density falls by 2³=8. For radiation w=1/3, it falls by 2⁴=16. Neither changing component violates covariant conservation. The additional radiation factor expresses the pressure-work or redshift contribution in this model.
example.conclusion: A conservation law can involve geometric transport and changing volume. Ordinary component constancy is not the right test.

source.limits: A global conserved charge generally needs an appropriate symmetry or boundary construction. If κ or Λ varies, additional derivative terms enter and the simple inference must be revised. Matter models must satisfy their own evolution equations consistently.

source.title: Grothendieck universes and their logical cost
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Universe language is a relative-size discipline backed by a set-theoretic assumption. It is not a mechanism for eliminating every paradox without cost. The useful mathematical task is to state the closure axioms and show exactly which categorical constructions they permit.
definitions: A Grothendieck universe U is a transitive set closed under pairing, power sets and unions indexed by a set belonging to U, with the family’s members in U. To support ordinary infinite mathematics one asks ω∈U. A U-small set is an element of U, which differs from merely being a subset of U.

result.name: The inaccessible-cardinal construction of a universe
result.statement: If κ is a strongly inaccessible cardinal, then V_κ is a Grothendieck universe containing ω. Consequently U-small sets, maps, finite products and function sets can be handled inside one fixed relative-size level. The existence of such an uncountable inaccessible cardinal is an additional assumption, not a theorem of bare ZFC.
result.proof: Transitivity of the cumulative hierarchy is immediate. If x,y∈V_κ, their ranks are below κ, so pairing and power sets still have rank below κ because κ is a limit ordinal. For an indexed family (x_i)_{i∈I} with I∈V_κ, strong inaccessibility ensures every set in V_κ has cardinality below κ. Regularity then bounds the supremum of the fewer-than-κ ranks of x_i below κ, so their union remains in V_κ. For function sets X→Y, their graphs are subsets of X×Y and are therefore contained in a suitable iterated power-set construction inside U.

example.setup: Take two U-small sets X and Y.
example.calculation: Ordered pairs can be constructed by the Kuratowski definition, yielding X×Y∈U. Every function graph lies in P(X×Y), and the collection of all such graphs is a subset of that power set, hence U-small under the closure axioms. By contrast, the entire collection of all U-small sets is U itself; asserting U∈U would contradict foundation. It belongs to a larger universe only when another size assumption is made.
example.conclusion: The construction makes size bookkeeping precise while retaining a visible logical boundary.

source.limits: This treatment proves the conditional construction, not consistency or existence of inaccessible cardinals. Degenerate finite universes and conventions excluding or including ω must be distinguished. Different foundational treatments can avoid universe axioms for specific constructions.
source.extension: Rebuild one category-of-structures construction using a fixed cardinal bound instead, then compare its smallness guarantees with the universe-based version.

result.statement: Arbitrary partitions satisfy S(N,k)=kS(N−1,k)+S(N−1,k−1); contiguous k-block partitions number C(N−1,k−1). For grid spacing h=L/N, E_N=(GJ/2)Σ_{i=0}^{N−1}[(θ_{i+1}−θ_i)/h]²h equals the continuum Dirichlet energy of the piecewise-linear interpolant.
result.proof: For Stirling’s recurrence, the last label either joins one of k existing blocks or forms a singleton. For contiguous partitions, choosing the cut gaps is a bijection. For energy, the interpolant derivative is constant on each grid interval and equals the difference quotient; integrating its squared derivative gives the formula exactly. Thus strong H¹ convergence of interpolants implies energy convergence. A bounded-energy sequence with a fixed endpoint has an H¹ bound; weak lower semicontinuity gives a lower energy bound at weak limits, while interpolating smooth functions supplies elementary recovery approximations. No set-partition count is needed for this argument.

example.setup: First take N=4,k=2, then a constant total twist Θ.
example.calculation: The partition counts are seven and three respectively. For θ_i=Θi/N, every difference quotient is Θ/L and E_N=GJΘ²/(2L) for every N. For L=GJ=1 and θ(x)=x², endpoint interpolation gives E_N=2/3−1/(6N²), converging to (1/2)∫₀¹4x²dx=2/3.

source.title: Vector motion and rotation conventions
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: Movement commands can be formulated without ambiguous appeals to trigonometry. Linear algebra combines the local commands; a rotation converts the resulting vector into another frame. Keeping magnitude conventions explicit resolves diagonal-speed discrepancies.
definitions: In a right-handed plane use column vectors and counterclockwise rotation R(θ)=[[cosθ,−sinθ],[sinθ,cosθ]]. Let a local command u=(u₁,u₂) specify components in orthonormal local axes. World velocity is v=su rotated by R, namely v=sR(θ)u.

result.name: Rotation preserves speed but raw diagonal input changes it
result.statement: Because RᵀR=I, ||v||₂=s||u||₂. A single unit-axis command has speed s, while raw input u=(1,1) has speed s√2. Normalizing nonzero input by its Euclidean norm produces constant speed s regardless of its direction.
result.proof: Multiply the displayed matrix by its transpose and use cos²θ+sin²θ=1 and cancellation of the cross terms. Taking squared norms then gives the identity. The difference between axis and diagonal commands follows from ||(1,0)||=1 and ||(1,1)||=√2. If the desired control preserves analog intensity below unit radius, the mapping u↦u/max(1,||u||) leaves small commands unchanged and caps only those outside the unit disk. This is a specified control law, not a consequence forced by coordinate geometry.

example.setup: Use the exact rotation with cosθ=3/5 and sinθ=4/5.
example.calculation: The unit forward command maps to (3/5,4/5), of squared norm one. The unnormalized diagonal maps to (−1/5,7/5), of squared norm two. Its normalized version divides both components by √2, returning squared norm one. These checks use exact rational arithmetic before the final normalization.
example.conclusion: Coordinate conversion and speed policy can be independently tested. This makes it possible to change a frame without silently changing the physical or numerical interpretation of commands.

source.title: A proposed analogy needs a dimensionless correspondence
source.status: Classical result developed and worked
source.summary: A spectral analogy becomes mathematical only when state spaces, operators, units and observables are related by an explicit map. A small periodic hopping model supplies a genuine Bloch calculation, while a similarity-transform example separates shared eigenvalues from shared dynamics.
definitions: Consider a two-site unit cell on an infinite one-dimensional lattice with real hoppings t₁,t₂. Its Hermitian Bloch matrix is H(k)=[[0,t₁+t₂e^(−ik)],[t₁+t₂e^(ik),0]], where k is a dimensionless crystal phase. Hopping parameters and eigenvalues have a common energy unit.

result.name: An explicit band gap and a warning about spectral equivalence
result.statement: The two bands are E_±(k)=±√(t₁²+t₂²+2t₁t₂cosk). Their minimum separation is 2||t₁|−|t₂||. Equality of eigenvalue sets in another model does not establish equivalence of observation maps or Euclidean amplification.
result.proof: The characteristic polynomial is E²−|t₁+t₂e^(−ik)|². Expanding the squared modulus gives the dispersion relation. Its minimum is (|t₁|−|t₂|)² because cosk ranges over [−1,1]. If B=SAS⁻¹, A and B share characteristic polynomials, but exp(tB)=S exp(tA)S⁻¹ and Euclidean norm bounds acquire the condition number of S. Only a unitary S preserves every Euclidean norm and the inner-product structure automatically. Observables must also transform, for example C_B=C_A S⁻¹, to preserve measured outputs.

example.setup: Take t₁=2,t₂=1 and compare an unrelated rescaled two-state model.
example.calculation: The bands at k=0 are ±3 and at k=π are ±1, so the gap is two. To transfer this statement, another model must supply a compatible periodic operator, an energy-scale conversion and a map respecting the relevant measurements. A match between an energy number and some unrelated flux number has no meaning until units and maps are supplied.
example.conclusion: This example yields an actual operator theorem and a precise test for proposed cross-domain correspondences.

source.limits: The toy model does not establish that another physical system has Bloch periodicity, the same Hilbert space or the same operator domain. Isospectral operators can remain distinguishable by eigenvectors, locality and response functions.
source.extension: Classify intertwiners BS=SA that also preserve a chosen observation map, and determine which spectral or transport identities survive after taking dimensionless variables.

source.title: Residual energy and exact Gaussian calibration
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: The original squared-deviation formula becomes useful once its units, reference model and covariance are specified. A squared residual is a geometric discrepancy. An entropy is a functional of a probability distribution. Neither name determines the other.
definitions: Let r=X−μ∈Rᵈ. The raw residual energy is E=rᵀr. If Σ is a specified positive-definite covariance, the whitened discrepancy is Q=rᵀΣ⁻¹r.
Here μ and Σ are known constants under the null model, rather than estimates obtained from the same observations.

result.name: Whitened Gaussian discrepancy
result.statement: If X has multivariate normal distribution N(μ,Σ) with Σ positive definite, then Q has the χ² distribution with d degrees of freedom. Consequently E[Q]=d and Var(Q)=2d. The unweighted E generally depends on the coordinate units.
result.proof: Factor Σ=LLᵀ with L invertible and put Z=L⁻¹r. The change-of-variables formula gives independent standard normal coordinates Z₁,…,Z_d. Then Q=ZᵀZ=ΣZᵢ². Its moment-generating function is the product (1−2t)^(−d/2), obtained by completing the square in each one-dimensional Gaussian integral. Differentiation at zero gives the stated moments. Changing the scale of one coordinate changes E but is canceled by the corresponding covariance transformation in Q.

example.setup: Take r=(1,2) and Σ=diag(1,4).
example.calculation: The raw residual is E=1+4=5. Whitening gives Z=(1,1), so Q=2. If both coordinates are expressed in ten times larger numerical units, r becomes (10,20) and Σ becomes diag(100,400); E becomes 500, whereas Q remains 2.
example.conclusion: The standardized discrepancy is dimensionless and has an exact reference distribution under the declared Gaussian null. It has not thereby become Shannon entropy.

source.limits: Estimating means, regression coefficients or covariance from the same sample changes the null distribution. In ordinary known-variance linear regression, orthogonal projection gives n−p residual degrees of freedom; estimated covariance can instead lead to F or other statistics. Nonnormal residuals need separate calibration.
source.extension: Study how Q changes under covariance uncertainty by bounding it between eigenvalue-controlled quadratic forms. This produces an honest robustness interval rather than assigning an entropy interpretation to a residual.

original.finish: Compute all three on a common example, specify the probability model and derive a calibration rather than assigning an entropy interpretation by name.

source.title: The chain rule as a statement about local linear maps
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: The derivative is the linear part of a local approximation. The chain rule composes these linear parts and tracks their domains; a secant slope or a scalar symbol does not replace a multivariable derivative.
definitions: For differentiable g:Rᵐ→Rⁿ and f:Rⁿ→Rᵏ, Dg(x):Rᵐ→Rⁿ and Df(g(x)):Rⁿ→Rᵏ are linear maps.
Differentiability means g(x+h)=g(x)+Dg(x)h+o(||h||), with the remainder small relative to ||h||.

result.name: Typed chain rule
result.statement: D(f∘g)(x)=Df(g(x))Dg(x). If a scalar F has Hessian operator norm at most M along the segment from x to x+h, its linearization remainder is at most M||h||²/2.
result.proof: Insert the differentiability expansion of g into the expansion of f at g(x). Since g(x+h)−g(x)=O(||h||), the outer remainder is o(||h||). The coefficient of h is exactly the displayed composition. For the second statement, integrate the directional derivative along the segment twice; the second integral is ∫₀¹(1−t)hᵀH_F(x+th)h dt, whose absolute value is bounded by M||h||²/2.

example.setup: Let g(u,v)=(u²+v,eᵘ) and f(a,b)=ab, so F(u,v)=(u²+v)eᵘ.
example.calculation: Dg=[[2u,1],[eᵘ,0]], while Df(g)=[eᵘ,u²+v]. Multiplication gives DF=[eᵘ(2u+u²+v),eᵘ]. At (1,2), DF=(5e,e). Direct differentiation of F gives the same row vector and therefore independently checks the composition order.
example.conclusion: A perturbation (h₁,h₂) changes F to first order by 5eh₁+eh₂. The two inputs have different sensitivities; one scalar slope would omit that distinction.

source.limits: The Hessian remainder bound requires a neighborhood with a uniform bound. A pointwise derivative alone supplies no global finite-step error estimate. Nondifferentiable coordinate changes need different calculus.
source.extension: For a long computation, propagate both Jacobians and explicit remainder bounds. This distinguishes a mathematically controlled sensitivity estimate from an uncalibrated finite-difference plot.

source.title: Graph heat flow and the stability of a discrete gradient step
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: Heat evolution and gradient descent share a variational structure after choosing a metric and boundary conditions. Their discrete stability restrictions come from the spectrum of the actual discretized operator.
definitions: Let L be a symmetric positive-semidefinite graph Laplacian and E(x)=xᵀLx/2.
Continuous heat evolution is ẋ=−Lx. A forward Euler step is x⁺=(I−ηL)x. The constant vector is in the kernel when L is an ordinary graph Laplacian.

result.name: Spectral energy decrease
result.statement: Continuous evolution satisfies dE/dt=−||Lx||². A discrete step is nonexpansive in Euclidean norm for every x exactly when 0≤η≤2/λ_max, assuming λ_max>0; the same interval makes E nonincreasing. Strict decay on every positive eigenspace holds for the explicit open interval 0<η<2/λ_max; η=0 produces no decay.
result.proof: Choose an orthonormal eigenbasis Lqᵢ=λᵢqᵢ and write x=Σcᵢqᵢ. Continuous coefficients are cᵢ(t)=e^(−λᵢt)cᵢ(0). For the step, cᵢ⁺=(1−ηλᵢ)cᵢ. Thus ||x⁺||²−||x||²=Σ[(1−ηλᵢ)²−1]cᵢ². This is nonpositive for every coefficient vector precisely when every factor has magnitude at most one. Multiplying each term by λᵢ/2 proves the energy version. Also 1ᵀx⁺=1ᵀx, so mass is preserved independently of decay.

example.setup: Use the four-cycle Laplacian with eigenvalues 0,2,2,4.
example.calculation: For η=0.4, the update factors are 1,0.2,0.2,−0.6, hence every nonconstant mode contracts. For η=0.6, the largest-frequency factor is −1.4 and that mode grows. The equilibrium constant mode remains unchanged in both cases.
example.conclusion: A large time step can turn a dissipative differential equation into an unstable numerical scheme. Continuous dissipation alone cannot certify the discretization.

source.limits: Energy monotonicity does not imply positivity of each coordinate. Positivity of forward Euler is governed by entrywise update weights and can require a smaller bound. Nonsymmetric operators require a different argument.
source.extension: Compare forward, backward and exponential steps for a common graph, recording preservation of mass, positivity and decay separately.

source.title: Exact exponent arithmetic before approximation
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: Very large magnitudes are best handled by separating an exact exponent from a modest mantissa. That separation avoids overflow and makes errors in scale immediately visible.
definitions: Scientific notation writes a positive number as a×10ᵏ with 1≤a<10.
Relative error for an approximation ỹ to y≠0 is |ỹ−y|/|y|. A decimal logarithm adds log₁₀a to the exponent.

result.name: Square-root normalization
result.statement: For an integer m and a>0, √(a×10^(2m))=√a×10ᵐ. For the recovered expression, √(5×10^54004)=√5×10^27002 exactly.
result.proof: Both factors on the right are positive, and squaring gives 5×10^(2×27002), which is the original radicand. Uniqueness of the positive square root completes the proof. If an exponent is odd, move one factor of 10 into the mantissa before taking the square root; there is no need to evaluate the enormous number itself.

example.setup: Approximate the exact answer by 10^27002, or instead retain eleven significant mantissa digits.
example.calculation: The exact logarithm is 27002+(log₁₀5)/2. Omitting √5 gives relative error 1−1/√5≈0.5527864045, over 55 percent. Keeping 2.2360679775 as mantissa gives a small rounding error whose size can be bounded by squaring rational decimal endpoints around √5. The old comparison with 25,000×10^50,000 differs by tens of thousands of decimal orders.
example.conclusion: An order-of-magnitude summary and a numerical approximation answer different questions. Stating the exact exponent costs essentially no extra computation.

source.limits: Exponent manipulations assume the usual positive real square root. Complex powers require a branch convention, and expressions with uncertain exponents need interval propagation rather than a single rounded exponent.
source.extension: Use rational interval endpoints for the mantissa and retain an integer exponent in all later products, quotients and roots. This gives a small certificate that can be replayed without arbitrary-precision libraries.

source.summary: A named empirical law is a family of fitted functions with a domain and an error model. A rigorous mathematical comparison first asks whether the parameters and competing shapes can be distinguished at all.
definitions: For x>0, a power response is y=axᵇ with a>0. Its logarithm is log y=α+b log x, α=log a.

result.name: Two-point identifiability in the noiseless power family

source.title: Tensor order and matrix rank are different invariants
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: A second-order tensor may be represented by a matrix, but its order is not the number of nonzero eigenvalues. A dyadic decomposition adds a third meaning of rank that needs a stated field and symmetry convention.
definitions: For a real matrix A, rank(A) is the dimension of its image. A rank-one dyad uvᵀ maps x to u(vᵀx).
For a real symmetric A, the spectral theorem gives an orthonormal eigenbasis and A=Σλᵢvᵢvᵢᵀ. Negative coefficients are permitted in this signed decomposition.

result.name: Minimal dyadic count for a symmetric matrix
result.statement: The minimum number of unrestricted real rank-one matrix summands is rank(A). A symmetric matrix has a signed symmetric dyadic representation with exactly that many nonzero terms. A decomposition into positive-weight vvᵀ terms exists only for positive-semidefinite A.
result.proof: The image of a sum of r rank-one maps is contained in the span of their r output vectors, so its rank is at most r. Therefore at least rank(A) summands are necessary. The spectral theorem supplies exactly rank(A) nonzero signed symmetric dyads. Finally every sum Σcᵢvᵢvᵢᵀ with cᵢ≥0 has nonnegative quadratic form, so an indefinite matrix cannot possess such a decomposition.

example.setup: Let A=diag(−2,0,3).
example.calculation: Its tensor order is two, its matrix rank is two, and its signed dyadic decomposition is −2e₁e₁ᵀ+3e₃e₃ᵀ. At e₁ the quadratic form equals −2, excluding any sum of positive dyads. Replacing the zero entry by ε≠0 changes rank to three even when ||A_ε−A||₂=|ε| is arbitrarily small.
example.conclusion: Exact rank is discontinuous at a rank-deficient matrix; numerical effective rank requires a declared threshold and noise scale.

source.limits: These conclusions concern matrices. Higher-order tensor rank, symmetric rank and border rank are different problems, and a matrix spectral decomposition does not solve them.
source.extension: Study a noisy matrix through singular-value intervals and separate exact algebraic rank from a tolerance-dependent approximation rank.

source.title: A fully normalized spin one-half Wigner representation
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: The spin phase space is a sphere, and its kernel and measure must be chosen together. For a qubit the complete reconstruction can be derived from elementary spherical moments, including the appearance of negative quasiprobabilities.
definitions: Write A=a₀I+a·σ, with Pauli matrices σ=(σ_x,σ_y,σ_z). For Hermitian A, the four coefficients are real.
Choose Δ(n)=(I+√3 n·σ)/2 for unit n∈S² and measure dμ=dΩ/(2π), whose total mass is two. Define W_A(n)=Tr(AΔ(n)).

result.name: Self-dual reconstruction and trace pairing
result.statement: W_A(n)=a₀+√3a·n, A=∫W_A(n)Δ(n)dμ and Tr(AB)=∫W_AW_Bdμ. For a density matrix ρ=(I+r·σ)/2, ∫W_ρdμ=1 even though W_ρ need not be nonnegative.
result.proof: Use Trσ_i=0 and Tr(σ_iσ_j)=2δ_ij. The spherical moments are ∫1dμ=2, ∫n_idμ=0 and ∫n_in_jdμ=(2/3)δ_ij. Substitution gives the symbol immediately. Expanding W_AΔ and integrating leaves a₀I+a·σ. Expanding W_AW_B gives 2a₀b₀+2a·b, exactly Tr(AB). source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: A rational cone contains enough combinatorial data to detect and resolve a simple affine toric singularity. The lattice, primitive generators and subdivision must be specified rather than inferred from a picture.
definitions: Use N=Z² and the cone σ generated by v₀=(1,0),v₂=(1,2). A full-dimensional two-dimensional cone is regular when its primitive ray generators form a lattice basis.

result.name: Regular subdivision of an index-two cone
result.statement: The original cone has determinant two and is singular. Adding the primitive ray v₁=(1,1) divides it into two determinant-one cones, giving a smooth toric surface mapping properly and birationally to the original affine surface.

The fan has the same support and agrees with the original torus, establishing properness and birationality by the standard toric fan criterion. The dual semigroup is generated by (0,1),(1,0),(2,−1), with the relation (0,1)+(2,−1)=2(1,0). Hence the original coordinate ring is C[u,v,w]/(uw−v²), whose gradient vanishes at the origin.

example.calculation: The defining polynomial F=uw−v² has gradient (w,−2v,u), so the only complex singular point is the origin. example.conclusion: This supplies a full combinatorial smoothness certificate for this fan and a concrete algebraic model of the singular target.

source.title: A rational parametrization and a nonexistence certificate
source.status: Developed classical result with worked example
source.summary: Finding many points and proving a point set complete are different achievements. Elementary conics already show how parametrization, integer constraints and local obstructions lead to distinct certificates.
definitions: For an equation X defined over Q, X(Q) is the rational point set, X(Z) the integral point set and X(F_p) a reduction over a finite field when defined.

result.name: Two conic certificates
result.statement: Every rational point of x²+y²=1 except (−1,0) is x=(1−t²)/(1+t²), y=2t/(1+t²) for t∈Q. The conic x²+y²=3 has no rational point.
result.proof: For the circle, draw the line y=t(x+1) through (−1,0). Substitution factors out the known intersection and yields the displayed second point. Conversely, for a rational circle point with x≠−1, t=y/(x+1) is rational and reconstructs the point, proving completeness. For x²+y²=3, a rational point would yield primitive integers a,b,c with a²+b²=3c². Modulo three, squares are zero or one; their sum can be zero only when a and b are divisible by three. Substituting a=3a₁,b=3b₁ gives c²=3(a₁²+b₁²), so c is also divisible by three, contradicting primitivity.

example.setup: Set t=2 for the parametrized circle.
example.calculation: This gives x=−3/5,y=4/5 and verifies the equation exactly. By contrast no finite search is needed for the second conic: the divisibility contradiction rules out every rational denominator at once. Its lack of integer points also follows from squares modulo four, but that easier integer argument alone would not automatically prove the rational statement.
example.conclusion: A complete parametrization and a nonexistence proof are both finite certificates, though of different kinds.

result.name: Type correctness and positivity are substantive conditions
result.statement: The matrix product rule requires the inner dimensions to match. A complex squared norm is z†z, not zᵀz. The latter can vanish for a nonzero vector, so substituting transpose for adjoint can invalidate a positivity argument.
result.proof: An m×n matrix represents a map from n-dimensional coordinate vectors to m-dimensional vectors. source.title: Bernstein–Sato certificates and a minimality proof
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The original broad application question becomes an exact operator identity with a lower-bound argument. A certificate proves that a polynomial works; minimality proves that it is the b-function. Both steps can be completed for monomials, and a linear coordinate change supplies a nonmonomial example.
definitions: Work over C in the Weyl algebra generated by x and ∂ with ∂x−x∂=1. The parameter s commutes with both generators.
A Bernstein–Sato relation is P(s)f^(s+1)=b(s)f^s in the formal localization module. The global b-function is the monic polynomial of least degree satisfying such a relation.

result.name: Exact monomial b-function
result.statement: For m≥1, b_(x^m)(s)=∏_(j=1)^m(s+j/m), with certificate P(s)=m^(−m)∂^m.
result.proof: Differentiate x^(m(s+1)) exactly m times. The coefficient is ∏_(k=0)^(m−1)(m(s+1)−k)=m^m∏_(j=1)^m(s+j/m), proving the certificate. To prove minimality, put an arbitrary polynomial-coefficient operator in normal order Σ a_ij(s)x^i∂^j. Its action contributes the Laurent monomial x^(ms+m+i−j). The coefficient of x^(ms) can only receive terms with j=m+i. Every such falling-factorial coefficient contains all m factors from the displayed certificate. The other Laurent powers are independent over C(s), so any possible b(s) is divisible by that monic product. Thus the candidate is minimal, not merely an annihilating multiple.

example.setup: Take f=x²y³ and then the nonmonomial f=x²+y².
example.calculation: For x²y³, P=(1/108)∂ₓ²∂ᵧ³ gives b(s)=(s+1/2)(s+1/3)(s+2/3)(s+1)². The same exponent-comparison argument in both variables proves minimality. Over C set u=x+iy and v=x−iy. Then x²+y²=uv and ∂ᵤ∂ᵥ=(1/4)(∂ₓ²+∂ᵧ²), so (1/4)Δf^(s+1)=(s+1)²f^s.
example.conclusion: A polynomial automorphism preserves the defining differential-operator problem, so the nonmonomial quadratic has b(s)=(s+1)². Repeated roots carry actual multiplicity; they must not be discarded.

source.limits: These are global polynomial examples in characteristic zero. General singularities may require local rather than global b-functions, elimination in a Weyl algebra, or additional singularity theory. The derivation does not establish that every proposed physical or statistical application admits a useful b-function.

source.title: Conic polarity as a typed point-to-line map
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The corrected construction identifies the quadratic form first, then derives polarity, the dual conic and coordinate covariance. It removes the undefined polar-line formula and the invented idea that one point dualizes to a conic.
definitions: Let Q be an invertible symmetric 3×3 matrix over a field of characteristic different from two. Points are nonzero column vectors modulo scale; lines are nonzero covectors modulo scale.
The nonsingular conic is C={x:xᵀQx=0}. The polar line of p has covector ℓ=Qp, because its equation is pᵀQx=0.

result.name: Polarity and the dual quadratic form
result.statement: The polarity p↦Qp is invertible, incidence is reciprocal, and the tangent-line locus in the dual projective plane is ℓᵀQ⁻¹ℓ=0.
result.proof: At a conic point a, differentiating xᵀQx gives tangent covector 2Qa, which defines the same projective line as Qa. Conversely any ℓ has pole p=Q⁻¹ℓ. That line is tangent precisely when its pole lies on C, which is exactly ℓᵀQ⁻¹ℓ=0. Reciprocity follows from pᵀQq=qᵀQp. Under x′=Mx, Q′=M⁻ᵀQM⁻¹ and ℓ′=M⁻ᵀℓ; hence Q′p′=M⁻ᵀQp. The construction therefore respects projective coordinate changes rather than depending on one affine drawing.

example.setup: Use the real unit-circle conic x²+y²−z²=0 and p=(2,0,1).
example.calculation: Here Q=diag(1,1,−1), so the polar is 2x−z=0. Its intersections with the conic are a±=(1/2,±√3/2,1). The tangents at these points have covectors (1/2,±√3/2,−1), and each contains p because their pairing with p is zero. The polar itself is not tangent: its dual quadratic value is 2²−1²=3.
example.conclusion: The polar joins the two contact points of tangents drawn from the exterior point. Applying Q⁻¹ to its covector returns p. This verifies the point-line correspondence and the dual-conic test separately.

source.limits: Invertibility of Q and the characteristic assumption matter. A degenerate quadratic form does not produce a global polarity. Real exterior/interior terminology has no direct analogue over every field; projective incidence survives, while real tangent counts may change.
source.extension: For higher-dimensional quadrics the same matrix argument defines polar hyperplanes. A useful further problem is to classify how the construction degenerates as det Q tends to zero and which incidence statements remain valid.

source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: Cross-ratio becomes a precise projective invariant once the four-point order and convention are fixed. Harmonicity is then a concrete value of that invariant, not an order-free label.
definitions: For distinct projective points a,b,c,d on P¹, choose nonzero representatives v_a,…,v_d and write [u,v]=det(u,v).
Use CR(a,b;c,d)=[v_a,v_c][v_b,v_d]/([v_b,v_c][v_a,v_d]). In an affine chart this is ((c−a)(d−b))/((c−b)(d−a)).

result.name: Projective invariance and harmonic ordering
result.statement: Every invertible 2×2 matrix preserves this ordered cross-ratio. Under permutations the possible values lie in {r,1/r,1−r,1/(1−r),r/(r−1),(r−1)/r}.
result.proof: Rescaling any representative multiplies one numerator factor and one denominator factor by the same scalar. Applying M multiplies each bracket by det M; the two determinant factors above and below cancel. Thus CR is both projectively well defined and invariant. The permutation formulas follow by swapping arguments in the affine expression. In particular r=−1 can become 2 or 1/2 after a different ordering, so a harmonic assertion must retain its convention. Homogeneous representatives make the point at infinity routine rather than an exception requiring an invented formula.

example.calculation: Using v∞=(1,0) gives CR=−1. The transformation has nonzero determinant one and sends the ordered tuple to (1,5/3;3/2,2). The transformed ratio is [(1/2)(1/3)]/[(-1/6)(1)]=−1, verified with rational arithmetic.
example.conclusion: The example simultaneously checks infinity, ordering and projective invariance. A dual statement for four concurrent lines follows only after identifying their pencil with P¹; duality is not a license to replace undefined point coordinates by arbitrary line expressions.

source.limits: The four points must be distinct for the displayed nondegenerate ratio. Coinciding points require a limiting or compactified configuration-space interpretation. Over a general field, the listed six values can coincide more than they do over the real numbers.

definitions: Let F=C[x₁,x₂,…], with each polynomial involving finitely many variables. Set a₋ₙ=xₙ by multiplication and aₙ=n∂/∂xₙ for n>0; let a₀ act as zero.

result.statement: [a_m,a_n]=mδ_(m+n,0)I. The singular contraction of J(z)J(w) is 1/(z−w)², in the formal expansion associated with |z|>|w|.

Splitting the field into annihilation and creation parts gives [J₊(z),J₋(w)]=Σ_(n≥1)n z^(−n−1)w^(n−1). Differentiating the formal geometric series Σ_(n≥0)wⁿz^(−n−1)=1/(z−w) produces the claimed double pole. The normally ordered remainder has no additional singular contraction. source.title: Four-site XXX spectrum and the regular one-magnon roots
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The corrected Bethe equations are tied to one Hamiltonian normalization and checked against a finite matrix. The resulting calculation verifies a sector, while keeping singular-root and completeness questions explicit.
definitions: Take N=4 periodic spin-1/2 sites and H=Σ_(j=0)^3(I−P_(j,j+1)), where P swaps adjacent spins and the last edge wraps around.
In the one-down-spin sector, |j⟩ denotes the down spin at site j. A plane wave has coefficients exp(ipj), with p=2πm/4.

result.name: Exact one-magnon diagonalization
result.statement: H|p⟩=(2−2cos p)|p⟩, so this four-dimensional sector has energies 0,2,4,2. The finite regular Bethe roots are λ=1/2,0,−1/2, giving energies 1/(λ²+1/4)=2,4,2.
result.proof: Only the two bonds incident on the down spin act nontrivially, giving H|j⟩=2|j⟩−|j−1⟩−|j+1⟩. Substitution of the plane wave yields the dispersion. In the periodic XXX convention the regular roots obey ((λ_j+i/2)/(λ_j−i/2))^N=∏_(k≠j)(λ_j−λ_k+i)/(λ_j−λ_k−i). For one root the right side is one. Writing exp(ip)=(λ+i/2)/(λ−i/2) gives λ=(1/2)cot(p/2), and the energy agrees with the plane-wave dispersion. The p=0 state corresponds to the infinite-root limit.

example.setup: Use real vectors in the ordered basis |0⟩,…,|3⟩.
example.calculation: The vectors (1,1,1,1), (1,0,−1,0), (0,1,0,−1) and (1,−1,1,−1) form a basis with eigenvalues 0,2,2,4. Exact integer matrix multiplication verifies all four. For λ=1/2,0,−1/2 the complex Bethe ratio is i,−1,−i respectively; its fourth power is one.
example.conclusion: This establishes agreement between a direct operator calculation and the regular Bethe description of the nonuniform one-magnon states. It also demonstrates why omitting the infinite-root state would lose an actual eigenvector.

source.limits: The calculation does not prove completeness in other magnetization sectors or for arbitrary N. Roots at ±i/2 and coincident roots need a regularization or a carefully specified admissibility convention. Including the self-index k=j would add a spurious factor and changes the equations.
