source.title: A complete two-site Gaudin to scalar-oper calculation
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: A concrete spectral bridge replaces the unsupported Fourier-to-automorphic-form slogan. In the smallest nontrivial sl₂ example, the Bethe vector, Hamiltonian eigenvalues, Miura potential and cancellation of the apparent singularity can all be computed exactly. A rational three-site continuation also gives a complete eight-dimensional joint eigenbasis and two additional scalar-oper certificates.
definitions: On each C² take h=diag(1,−1), e|↓⟩=|↑⟩, f|↑⟩=|↓⟩ and Ω=(1/2)h⊗h+e⊗f+f⊗e. Choose marked points z₁=0,z₂=1.
Let H₁=Ω/(z₁−z₂)=−Ω and H₂=Ω. For weights (1,1), one Bethe root obeys 1/w+1/(w−1)=0.

result.name: Singlet spectral data and apparent-pole cancellation
result.statement: The root w=1/2 yields a singlet with (H₁,H₂) eigenvalues (3/2,−3/2). Define u(x)=1/(2x)+1/(2(x−1))−1/(x−1/2). Then (∂−u)(∂+u)=∂²−V, where V=u²−u′=3/[4x²(x−1)²].
result.proof: The Bethe vector is w⁻¹|↓↑⟩+(w−1)⁻¹|↑↓⟩=2|↓↑⟩−2|↑↓⟩. Direct use of Ω gives eigenvalue −3/2, hence the Hamiltonian pair above. Near a root w, write u=−1/(x−w)+a₀+O(x−w). The double pole cancels in u²−u′, and its simple residue is −2a₀. Here a₀=(1/2)(1/w+1/(w−1))=0 precisely by the Bethe equation. Expanding at the physical points gives V=3/(4x²)+3/(4(x−1)²)+(3/2)/x−(3/2)/(x−1). Its simple residues match H₁ and H₂ in the declared normalization.

example.setup: Treat the scalar differential equation y″−V(x)y=0 on the punctured projective line.
example.calculation: The apparent point x=1/2 is absent from V. One solution is y₁=(x−1/2)/sqrt(x(x−1)). Reduction of order gives y₂=(x²−x/2+1/4)/sqrt(x(x−1)), with Wronskian one. Both are regular at x=1/2. Around x=0 or x=1 their common square-root factor changes sign, so monodromy is scalar and projectively trivial. The vacuum sector, with no root, instead has simple residues (−1/2,1/2), matching the triplet eigenvalues. For sites (0,1,8/3), the one-root equation reduces to 3w²−(22/3)w+8/3=0, with roots 2 and 4/9. Their eigenvalue triples are (−3/16,6/5,−81/80) and (25/16,−8/5,3/80). The highest vectors have one-down-spin coefficients (1/2,1,−3/2) and (9/4,−9/5,−9/20). Applying total lowering once to each gives two doublets; applying it zero through three times to the vacuum gives a quartet with eigenvalues (−11/16,1/5,39/80). All eight rational vectors are independent and satisfy all three full 8×8 Hamiltonians. For each regular root, with g=∏(x−z_i), u=g′/(2g)−1/(x−w) gives V=(3/4)Σ_i(x−z_i)^(−2)+Σ_iE_i/(x−z_i). Exact residual polynomials vanish. Since g′(w)=0, reduction of order has no logarithm: y₁=(x−w)/sqrt(g), y₂=[−g(w)+(g″(w)/2)(x−w)²+(x−w)³/2]/sqrt(g). Their Wronskian is one, and both ODE residuals vanish identically.
example.conclusion: The calculation supplies an actual rank-one instance of the Gaudin–oper relationship: eigenvalues are encoded in coefficients of a scalar differential operator. The simple finite example is classical; its explicit replay is an exposition and verification result. The three-site continuation settles this complete finite joint-spectrum example, including its scalar equations, rather than leaving it as a proposed computation.

source.limits: This is an sl₂ example, not a proof of the full Gaudin-algebra spectrum theorem, a global automorphic correspondence or arbitrary Bethe completeness. Oper terminology and Langlands duality must retain the relevant group, singularity and monodromy conditions.
source.extension: S010 develops the arbitrary-site one-magnon theorem, S013 completes the three-site exceptional-point analysis, and S014 classifies every distinct-complex-site one-magnon Jordan block with closed matrix and characteristic formulas. Remaining extensions concern multi-magnon sectors, higher representations or physical-site collisions; they require additional hypotheses and independent checks. This is separate from full Gaudin completeness.

source.title: Joint reliability is a dependence problem
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The arithmetic correction is only the first step. An all-success probability cannot be identified from marginal accuracies alone. Exact dependence constructions show the full gap between what the individual probabilities say and what independence adds.
definitions: Let A₁,…,A_n be success events with P(A_i)=p_i. The target is P(∩A_i), a joint probability.
Mutual independence means P(∩_(i∈S)A_i)=∏_(i∈S)p_i for every subset S. Pairwise independence checks only subsets of size two.

result.name: Fréchet bounds and an independence counterexample
result.statement: max(0,Σp_i−(n−1))≤P(∩A_i)≤min_i p_i. If all 104 marginals are 0.95, these bounds are 0 and 0.95, whereas independence gives 0.95^104≈0.00482230805327.
result.proof: The upper bound follows because the intersection is a subset of every A_i. For the lower bound apply the union bound to the failure events: P(∩A_i)=1−P(∪A_iᶜ)≥1−Σ(1−p_i). Probabilities are also nonnegative. The product formula follows only after imposing mutual independence. To see why pairwise independence is insufficient, let X,Y be independent fair bits and set Z=X xor Y. Any pair is independent, but P(X=Y=Z=1)=0 rather than 1/8.

example.setup: Construct joint laws for 104 events, each with success probability 0.95.
example.calculation: For the maximal case take every A_i={U≤0.95} for one uniform U; then all-success probability is 0.95. For a zero case let failures be arcs of length 0.05 on the unit circle, starting at i/104. Since adjacent starts are less than 0.05 apart, the arcs cover the circle, so at least one failure always occurs, although each event still succeeds with probability 0.95. Independent Bernoulli variables give the intermediate product.
example.conclusion: The same individual accuracy is compatible with no chance of complete correctness, a 95 percent chance, or the independent-model value. Replacing a dependency model by repeated multiplication can therefore be a major modeling error even after arithmetic is repaired.

source.limits: The numerical examples are abstract probability constructions, not estimated properties of a genealogy or any real audit. Real dependence requires observations or structural assumptions. Pairwise correlations alone generally do not determine the required high-order intersection.
source.extension: For a specified dependency graph, derive an interval using available joint moments or solve a finite linear program over atomic outcomes. Report the identified interval if the joint probability remains underdetermined.

source.title: Nonlinearity does not imply chaos or identifiability
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: A rigorous counterexample is more informative than another catalogue of nonlinear applications. A simple nonlinear ODE has a fully solvable, globally convergent flow and an observation that permanently hides the sign of its initial state.
definitions: Consider ẋ=−x³ on the real line for t≥0. The state is x, and first choose the observable y=x².
An observation model is identifiable on a set if no two admissible initial states generate exactly the same observed time history. This is distinct from state stability.

result.name: Global convergence with an exact observation collision
result.statement: For every initial x₀, x(t)=x₀/sqrt(1+2x₀²t). All trajectories converge to zero, while x₀ and −x₀ give identical y(t)=x₀²/(1+2x₀²t).
result.proof: For x₀≠0, differentiate x⁻² to obtain d(x⁻²)/dt=2 and solve; x₀=0 gives the equilibrium. The denominator stays positive, giving a global forward solution. With V=x²/2, V̇=−x⁴≤0, and the explicit solution proves convergence. Squaring removes the initial sign for all times. Equivalently y satisfies ẏ=−2y² with the same initial y₀ for both states. Thus the nonlinear system is elementary and convergent, while the chosen observation remains structurally ambiguous.

example.setup: Compare x₀=1 and x₀=−1, recording y=x² at any finite or infinite collection of times.
example.calculation: At t=0,1,2 the common observations are 1,1/3,1/5. No increase in temporal sampling resolves the sign because the entire continuous histories coincide. Adding the observable z=x distinguishes the two immediately. The exact rational y values and the observation evolution equation are checked by the verifier.
example.conclusion: Complexity of the evolution law, richness of sampling and distinguishability of states are separate questions. This example refutes a generic inference from nonlinear equations to chaos and a generic inference from many measurements to complete state reconstruction.

source.limits: This proof concerns one scalar system and one observation. It is not a general criterion for absence of chaos in higher dimensions. Nor does adding a sign-sensitive observation establish practical robustness when measurement noise is large.
source.extension: Classify observation collisions under a symmetry group: if both dynamics and output are sign-equivariant or sign-invariant in the appropriate way, determine whether the output can at best recover a symmetry orbit. Then quantify the additional measurement needed to break it.

source.title: The Klein–Gordon dispersion relation and its massless limit
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The mathematical comparison starts with two explicitly normalized differential operators. Their plane-wave dispersions, propagation equations and interpretation can then be compared without confusing a classical field equation with the procedure of quantization.
definitions: Use coordinates (t,x), speed c and □=c⁻²∂_t²−Δ. The free Klein–Gordon equation is (□+(mc/ℏ)²)φ=0.
A plane wave is exp(i(k·x−ωt)). Its wave vector k has inverse-length units, while ω has inverse-time units.

result.name: Massive and massless plane-wave dispersions
result.statement: Substitution gives ω²=c²|k|²+m²c⁴/ℏ². Setting m=0 gives the classical massless wave dispersion ω²=c²|k|².
result.proof: The second time derivative multiplies the wave by −ω² and the Laplacian by −|k|². The PDE therefore reduces to −ω²/c²+|k|²+(mc/ℏ)²=0. Multiplying by ℏ² and writing E=ℏω and p=ℏk gives E²=c²|p|²+m²c⁴. For m>0, differentiating the positive branch gives group velocity v_g=c²k/ω with magnitude below c; at high frequency it approaches c. These are consequences of the chosen PDE and Fourier ansatz, not additional quantum postulates.

example.setup: In units c=ℏ=1 take m=2 and spatial mode k=(3,0,0).
example.calculation: The frequencies are ω=±sqrt(13), and each wave has zero PDE residual because −13+9+4=0. The positive-branch group speed is 3/sqrt(13). On a periodic box of side L, allowed wave vectors are 2πn/L, producing a countable family of uncoupled harmonic oscillators at the classical level.
example.conclusion: Mass changes the relation between frequency and wave number. The periodic Fourier decomposition also identifies the finite-mode truncations that can be computed exactly; it does not by itself choose a Fock space or turn amplitudes into operators.

source.limits: Negative-frequency solutions do not by themselves establish a negative-probability theory. Quantization and the choice of conserved inner product require their own construction. Interactions, curved backgrounds and boundary conditions change the analysis.
source.extension: For a specified potential or curved metric, determine whether a positive self-adjoint spatial operator supplies a stable mode expansion. Retain the operator domain and boundary conditions rather than transferring the flat-space dispersion unchanged.

source.title: A controlled formal route from Dirac to Pauli
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The nonrelativistic limit must preserve spin and the magnetic coupling. Removing the rest-energy phase and eliminating the small spinor component gives the leading Pauli equation, together with an explicit statement of the scale assumptions.
definitions: Let π=p−qA with p=−iℏ∇ and B=∇×A. Use H_D=cα·π+βmc²+qΦ and a four-spinor ψ=e^(−imc²t/ℏ)(ϕ,χ)ᵀ.
The nonrelativistic regime requires typical |π|/(mc)≪1 and energies and time variation small compared with mc², together with fields smooth enough for the expansion.

result.name: Leading spin-sensitive Hamiltonian
result.statement: At leading order χ≈(σ·π)ϕ/(2mc), and iℏϕ̇=[π²/(2m)−(qℏ/(2m))σ·B+qΦ]ϕ.
result.proof: After extracting the rest-energy phase, the two components satisfy iℏϕ̇=qΦϕ+cσ·πχ and iℏχ̇=(qΦ−2mc²)χ+cσ·πϕ. The large 2mc² denominator permits the stated leading elimination of χ when the remaining terms are small. Pauli-matrix multiplication gives (σ·π)²=π²+(i/2)Σε_ijkσ_k[π_i,π_j]. Since [π_i,π_j]=iqℏε_ijkB_k, the second term is −qℏσ·B. Inserting this identity into the first equation produces the Hamiltonian and fixes the sign convention.

example.setup: First take A=Φ=0 and a plane wave of momentum magnitude p.
example.calculation: The exact positive relativistic energy is sqrt(m²c⁴+c²p²)=mc²+p²/(2m)−p⁴/(8m³c²)+O(p⁶/(m⁵c⁴)). Removing mc² leaves the Schrödinger kinetic term at leading order. For a magnetic field, the additional Pauli spin term survives at that same effective order; a scalar wave equation would miss it.
example.conclusion: The result specifies both the limiting equation and the leading neglected kinetic correction. Its small parameter is p/(mc), not simply the statement that an experiment looks classical.

source.limits: This is a formal asymptotic derivation for a prescribed background field. A uniform error theorem over long times needs operator estimates and additional regularity. Strong fields and pair-production regimes invalidate the elementary elimination.
source.extension: Choose a bounded momentum sector and smooth bounded fields, then derive a finite-time norm estimate comparing projected Dirac dynamics with the effective Pauli evolution. That is the appropriate next step toward a controlled approximation theorem.

source.title: Maxwell equations as field equations and identities
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: Differential forms separate what follows from a potential from what must be imposed as a sourced equation. Gauge redundancy becomes a precise kernel of the map from potentials to field strength, with topology supplying an important qualification.
definitions: On an oriented spacetime with a fixed metric, A is a one-form and F=dA is a two-form. The Hodge star depends on that metric and orientation.
Use normalization dF=0 and d⋆F=J, where J is a source three-form. Constants can be restored according to electromagnetic unit conventions.

result.name: Gauge invariance and current closure
result.statement: A↦A+dχ leaves F unchanged. Whenever d⋆F=J holds, dJ=0. Locally, every closed F is a potential field on a contractible coordinate patch.
result.proof: The identity d²=0 gives d(A+dχ)=dA. Applying d to the sourced equation gives dJ=d²⋆F=0, so source conservation is a compatibility condition. The local converse dF=0⇒F=dA is the Poincaré lemma under the contractibility assumption. It is not a global theorem on arbitrary manifolds: nontrivial degree-two cohomology can obstruct a single globally defined potential. The coordinate form of dF=0 is the homogeneous Maxwell system; the Hodge-star equation contains the metric-dependent dynamical content.

example.setup: On flat coordinates (t,x,y,z), choose A=a cos(kx−ωt)dy and use units c=1.
example.calculation: Then F=−ak sin(kx−ωt)dx∧dy+aω sin(kx−ωt)dt∧dy. Direct exterior differentiation gives dF=0 because the two mixed terms cancel. The vacuum sourced equation requires ω²=k². Adding dχ for χ=λtx changes components of A but contributes no change to F.
example.conclusion: The example distinguishes the automatic homogeneous identity, the dispersion imposed by the vacuum field equation and a gauge change of the potential. It also shows why covariant notation alone is not a quantization procedure.

source.limits: Global potentials, boundary conditions and gauge fixing require separate analysis. A flat connection can have nontrivial global holonomy while being locally pure gauge. A globally exact potential A=dχ with single-valued χ has no such loop holonomy; these cases must not be conflated.
source.extension: Develop the same problem on a torus or a punctured domain and calculate closed forms that are not exact. This makes the topology of gauge data explicit before introducing a quantum theory.

source.title: Ward–Takahashi constrains a vertex without determining it
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The identity is made concrete by verifying it at tree level, constructing a longitudinal vertex for a prescribed inverse propagator, and displaying the remaining transverse freedom. This explains both the power and the limitation of the constraint.
definitions: Factor the charge from the full electromagnetic vertex Γ^μ. With consistent momentum assignments, the identity is q_μΓ^μ(p+q,p)=S⁻¹(p+q)−S⁻¹(p).
A transverse addition T^μ satisfies q_μT^μ=0. Such an addition cannot be detected by this contracted identity alone.

result.name: An explicit longitudinal construction
result.statement: For a differentiable matrix-valued inverse propagator K(p)=S⁻¹(p), Γ_L^μ=∫₀¹(∂K/∂p_μ)(p+tq)dt satisfies the difference identity on any regular path. It is not the unique satisfying vertex.
result.proof: Contract with q and use the chain rule: q_μ∂K(p+tq)/∂p_μ=dK(p+tq)/dt. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives K(p+q)−K(p). Adding any transverse T preserves the contraction. At tree level K(p)=slash(p)−m and Γ^μ=γ^μ, reducing the identity to slash(q)=slash(p+q)−slash(p). These are direct algebraic checks of the kinematic relation; they do not assert that an arbitrarily chosen K and Γ arise from a complete interacting quantum field theory.

example.conclusion: The identity constrains differences of inverse propagators and the longitudinal vertex. It leaves dynamical transverse information undetermined. The polynomial example tests the logic without making a false renormalization claim.

source.title: A complete finite-dimensional perturbation calculation
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: A zero-dimensional quartic model permits an exact derivation of propagator contractions, vacuum normalization, connected coefficients and a rigorous asymptotic remainder. It supplies a fully checkable model of perturbative logic without claiming to construct a continuum field theory.
definitions: Let X be a real standard Gaussian and define Z(g)=E[exp(−gX⁴/24)] for g≥0. The normalized two-point function is G₂(g)=E[X²exp(−gX⁴/24)]/Z(g).
Gaussian moments are E[X^(2r)]=(2r−1)!! and odd moments vanish. Wick pairings count those double factorials.

result.name: Quartic coefficients and a controlled remainder
result.statement: Z(g)=1−g/8+35g²/384+O(g³), log Z(g)=−g/8+g²/12+O(g³), and G₂(g)=1−g/2+2g²/3+O(g³) as g↓0.
result.proof: Expand the interaction exponential to a fixed order and integrate each Gaussian moment. The nth coefficient of Z is a_n=(−1)^n(4n−1)!!/(24^n n!). Multiplying and dividing the resulting formal series gives the displayed connected and normalized coefficients. For g≥0, Taylor’s integral remainder for exp(−y) has magnitude at most y^(N+1)/(N+1)!; taking y=gX⁴/24 and integrating bounds the partition-function remainder by the next absolute coefficient times g^(N+1). This proves a finite-order asymptotic statement without exchanging an infinite series and the integral.

example.setup: Calculate through second order using integer Gaussian moments.
example.calculation: E[X⁴]=3, E[X⁸]=105 and E[X¹⁰]=945. Thus the numerator of G₂ is 1−5g/8+105g²/128+O(g³); division by Z gives 1−g/2+2g²/3. Meanwhile |a_(n+1)/a_n|=(4n+3)(4n+1)/(24(n+1)), which grows without bound.
example.conclusion: The perturbative series has zero radius of convergence although the original integral exists for every g≥0. Correct finite-order coefficients and an explicit asymptotic bound are therefore stronger and more honest deliverables than a claim that the infinite diagram sum converges.

source.limits: This toy integral has no spacetime ultraviolet divergences, locality or scattering theory. It does not replace renormalization of a continuum model. Its value is the exact separation of algebraic combinatorics, normalization and asymptotic control.

source.title: An exact RG toy flow and an invariant local exponent
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: The beta function must be specified before discussing running couplings. Simple autonomous flows can be solved exactly, and the derivative at a fixed point gives a local quantity that survives smooth invertible reparametrization of the coupling.
definitions: Write t=log(μ/μ₀) and dg/dt=β(g). A fixed point g* satisfies β(g*)=0.

A scheme coordinate change is a smooth locally invertible h=h(g). Its beta function is β_h(h(g))=h′(g)β(g). This is a coordinate statement for an exact flow, not a guarantee about truncated calculations. The nonzero-initial-condition formula below assumes g₀≠0; g₀=0 is the constant equilibrium.

result.name: Flow solutions and fixed-point linearization
result.statement: For β=bg², g(t)=g₀/(1−bg₀t). For β=−εg+bg² with ε,b>0 and g*=ε/b, g(t)=g*/[1+(g*/g₀−1)e^(εt)] wherever its denominator is nonzero. At a fixed point, dβ_h/dh=β′(g*).
result.proof: The first solution follows by differentiating 1/g. For the second, substitution or separation of variables verifies the displayed logistic-type formula. Linearization gives δġ=β′(g*)δg. Differentiating β_h=h′β with respect to h yields (h″β+h′β′)/h′. At a fixed point β=0, so the derivative equals β′. Thus the local exponent is invariant under the declared regular change of variable, although the numerical coordinate used to label the fixed point can change.

example.setup: Take ε=b=1 and g₀=1/2.

source.title: Moving level sets and the singularity of threshold coordinates
source.status: Classical result developed and example checked
source.summary: An implicit boundary can be differentiated only where its defining level is regular. The same calculation quantifies sensitivity and gives an exact example where a boundary is born and its graph velocity diverges.
definitions: Let f(x,t) be continuously differentiable and consider the level set f(x,t)=c. A regular spatial level has ∇ₓf≠0.
For a one-dimensional graph r(t), the condition is f_r(r(t),t)≠0. Choose the unit normal n=∇f/|∇f| when discussing normal velocity.

result.name: Implicit velocity and perturbation sensitivity
result.statement: Along a regular graph r′=−f_t/f_r. In several dimensions a moving level set has normal velocity v_n=−f_t/|∇f|. A small additive level perturbation δf produces first-order normal displacement −δf/|∇f|.
result.proof: Differentiate f(r(t),t)=c to obtain f_r r′+f_t=0. For a path X(t) on a spatial level, ∇f·X′+f_t=0; taking the normal component gives the velocity. For the perturbation, Taylor-expand f(X+δr n,t)+δf=c and use ∇f·n=|∇f|. The denominator therefore measures conditioning as well as existence of the local graph. Tangential motion is a parametrization choice and is not fixed by the level equation.

example.setup: Take f(x,y,t)=x²+y²−t and c=0.
example.calculation: For t>0 the boundary is a circle of radius sqrt(t), and its outward normal speed is 1/(2sqrt(t)). At t=0 the spatial gradient vanishes at the origin. For t<0 there is no real level set, at zero there is one point, and for t>0 there is a circle. The one-dimensional version r²−t=0 has two branches ±sqrt(t), neither a differentiable graph through the critical event.
example.conclusion: The diverging speed is not a contradiction in the implicit-function theorem; it occurs exactly where its nonzero-gradient hypothesis fails. The same inverse-gradient factor explains why threshold localization becomes unstable near a flat or critical level.

source.limits: These are local regularity and first-order sensitivity statements. They do not guarantee a global graph, a unique topology, or robustness under large perturbations. Nonsmooth defining functions need generalized notions of normal and solution.

source.status: Classical result or corrected formulation with a worked example
source.summary: On P¹×P¹, NS(X)=Pic(X)≅Z² with fiber-class intersection matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]. The class (a,b) has self-intersection 2ab. For a,b≥0, its space of sections has dimension (a+1)(b+1). definitions: For a smooth projective complex variety, Pic(X) is the abelian group of line bundles under tensor product. Pic⁰(X) denotes the subgroup algebraically equivalent to zero.
The Néron–Severi theorem makes NS(X) a finitely generated abelian group. Its real vector space has finite dimension ρ(X). This background theorem is not proved by a two-dimensional matrix check.
On X=P¹×P¹, write O(a,b) for the external tensor product of the two degree-a and degree-b bundles.

result.name: Picard classes and the Néron–Severi quotient
result.statement: On P¹×P¹, NS(X)=Pic(X)≅Z² with fiber-class intersection matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]. The class (a,b) has self-intersection 2ab. For a,b≥0, its space of sections has dimension (a+1)(b+1).
result.proof: The projective-bundle description of the product gives the two independent fiber classes and no Pic⁰ component. Two fibers of the same projection are disjoint and equivalent, so each fiber class squares to zero. A fiber of one projection meets a fiber of the other in one point; bilinearity gives (aF₁+bF₂)²=2ab. Sections of O(a,b) are bihomogeneous polynomials of bidegree (a,b). Their monomial basis consists of the (a+1) choices of first-factor exponent and (b+1) choices of second-factor exponent, proving the dimension formula directly. These explicit calculations use the product structure; they do not imply that Picard groups of arbitrary varieties are free of rank two.

example.setup: Take O(2,3) on the product and compare it with O(1,0).
example.calculation: The first class has twelve independent sections and self-intersection twelve. The second has two sections and self-intersection zero. Both are discrete divisor classes, whereas on an elliptic curve the degree-zero line bundles form a positive-dimensional Picard variety and cannot be replaced by a single rank count.
example.conclusion: The finite-rank divisor quotient is a well-defined geometric object. It is different from an unspecified real vector space obtained by tensoring every line bundle with R.

source.limits: Picard number does not classify a variety or its automorphism group. Torsion in NS and continuous Pic⁰ information can be lost after tensoring with R. Statements about singular or nonprojective spaces require different hypotheses.

source.title: The Schwarzian chain rule detects projective rather than affine structure
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: The Schwarzian involves third derivatives but has a particularly simple composition law. Specifying the order of composition matters: postcomposing by a Möbius map leaves it unchanged, whereas precomposition contributes a squared derivative. This entry derives the identities directly rather than relying on a memorized invariance slogan.
definitions: For a real C³ function f on an interval with f′≠0, define S(f)=f‴/f′−(3/2)(f″/f′)². The same formula applies to locally univalent holomorphic functions.
Write P(f)=f″/f′. Then S(f)=P(f)′−P(f)²/2, which makes cancellation in the composition rule visible.
A nonconstant Möbius map is M(x)=(ax+b)/(cx+d), with ad−bc≠0, restricted to an interval avoiding its pole.

result.name: A chain rule and the local zero-Schwarzian classification
result.statement: S(f∘g)=(S(f)∘g)(g′)²+S(g). Every Möbius map has zero Schwarzian, and locally every C³ map with nonzero derivative and zero Schwarzian is Möbius. Hence S(M∘f)=S(f), with the indicated domain restrictions.
result.proof: The ordinary chain rule gives P(f∘g)=(P(f)∘g)g′+P(g). Differentiate this identity, subtract half its square, and use g″=P(g)g′. The two mixed terms cancel, leaving exactly the displayed formula. To classify S(f)=0, put P=f″/f′; it satisfies P′=P²/2. Local uniqueness for this scalar ODE implies either P is identically zero or, after separating variables, P=−2/(x+c) on a suitable interval. The first case integrates to a nonconstant affine f. The second gives f′=A/(x+c)² and f=B−A/(x+c), again Möbius. Conversely direct differentiation of a Möbius map, or these forms, gives S=0. This is a local statement: poles and coordinate domains must still be tracked when joining intervals.

example.setup: Compare f(x)=eˣ, g(x)=x² on x>0, and their composite.
example.calculation: Since all derivatives of eˣ are eˣ, S(eˣ)=−1/2. For x², S(x²)=−3/(2x²). Thus S(e^(x²))=(−1/2)(2x)²−3/(2x²)=−2x²−3/(2x²), equal to −7/2 at x=1. Differentiating e^(x²) independently gives f′=2xe^(x²), f″=(2+4x²)e^(x²) and f‴=(12x+8x³)e^(x²), confirming the same rational expression. The verifier checks this at exact rational x after cancelling the common exponential factors.
example.conclusion: The third-derivative invariant has a short structural proof, and the example fixes both the sign and the placement of the derivative factor.

source.title: Euclidean certificates and a complete Pell example
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: These arithmetic concepts are connected by explicit certificates rather than a shared formula. The Euclidean algorithm produces a finite integer identity; Pell’s equation supplies an infinite family whose recurrence preserves a norm. A descent argument is included so that the chosen Pell example is more than a list of numerically observed solutions.
definitions: For integers a,b not both zero, gcd(a,b) is the positive generator of their common-divisor ideal. Bézout coefficients u,v satisfy ua+vb=gcd(a,b).
For the specific Pell equation x²−2y²=1 use integers x,y≥0. Multiplication in Z[√2] preserves the norm N(x+y√2)=x²−2y².
The unit 3+2√2 has norm one. Its powers define x₀=1,y₀=0 and xₙ₊₁=3xₙ+4yₙ, yₙ₊₁=2xₙ+3yₙ.

result.name: A terminating gcd algorithm and all nonnegative solutions for D=2
result.statement: Replacing (a,b) by (b,a−qb) preserves common divisors; choosing the remainder 0≤r<|b| ensures termination. For Pell D=2, every solution x,y≥0 is x+y√2=(3+2√2)ⁿ for a unique n≥0.
result.proof: For the gcd claim, any divisor of a,b divides b,a−qb, and conversely a=(a−qb)+qb. Positive remainders strictly decrease, so the last nonzero remainder is the gcd; back-substitution yields Bézout coefficients. For Pell, norm multiplication first proves that all stated powers are solutions. Conversely take any solution with y>0. If y=1, x²=3 is impossible. For y≥2, x/y=√(2+1/y²)≤3/2 and exceeds √2. Multiplying by 3−2√2 gives x′=3x−4y>0 and y′=3y−2x≥0. Moreover y′<y because x>y. The new pair remains integral with norm one, so this descent terminates at y=0, x=1. Reversing every step expresses the original pair as a power of 3+2√2. The exponent is unique because the positive real powers strictly increase. This proves the complete classification for this one value of D, without asserting a general fundamental-unit algorithm.

example.setup: Run Euclid on 240 and 46; then calculate the first four positive Pell pairs.
example.calculation: The remainders are 10,6,4,2,0, and back-substitution gives 2=−9·240+47·46. The Pell recurrence gives (3,2),(17,12),(99,70),(577,408); their norm-one identities are exact. For example 577²−2·408²=332929−332928=1. The verifier checks the Bézout identity, the recurrence and norm through twenty steps, and the descent for the same generated pairs.
example.conclusion: Finite integer arithmetic yields independently inspectable certificates. The written descent, rather than finite sampling, establishes that no nonnegative D=2 solutions are missing.

source.limits: The Pell classification is explicitly restricted to D=2 and nonnegative x,y; signs produce the other integer solutions. For square D the equation has a different character, and the general nonsquare case requires an additional existence and fundamental-unit argument.
source.extension: The error in xₙ/yₙ as an approximation to √2 is exactly 1/[yₙ²(xₙ/yₙ+√2)] for yₙ>0. Thus the same norm certificate gives a quantitative rational-approximation bound without subtracting nearly equal floating-point numbers.

source.title: Brouwer and hairy-ball obstructions require the right domain
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: These are global existence and obstruction theorems, not identities evaluated at a point. A closed ball and its boundary sphere behave differently, and even-dimensional spheres have a parity obstruction absent on S¹. The statements below make those distinctions explicit and identify the classical topological input used in each proof.
definitions: Brouwer: every continuous F:Bⁿ→Bⁿ on a closed Euclidean n-ball has a fixed point. Equivalently use the standard simplex Δⁿ={xᵢ≥0,Σxᵢ=1}.
For x∈S²⊂R³, a tangent vector v(x) satisfies x·v(x)=0. A tangent field is continuous when its three coordinate functions are continuous.
Use the classical degree facts deg(id:S²→S²)=1, deg(−id)=−1, and homotopy invariance of degree. These are explicit inputs to the hairy-ball proof.

result.name: A simplex limiting proof and a sphere-degree contradiction
result.statement: A continuous self-map of a closed ball has at least one fixed point. Every continuous tangent field on S² has at least one zero; neither assertion guarantees uniqueness, and the sphere itself is not the ball in Brouwer’s theorem.
result.proof: For Brouwer, use arbitrarily fine triangulations of Δⁿ and the classical Sperner lemma: if a vertex on a face receives a label belonging to that face, some small simplex has all n+1 labels. If F has no fixed vertex, label each vertex v by an i with vᵢ>Fᵢ(v); such an index exists because both coordinate sums are one, and vᵢ=0 prevents that label because Fᵢ≥0. A fully labeled small simplex therefore exists. Let its mesh tend to zero and choose a convergent subsequence of its vertices using compactness. Continuity gives xᵢ≥Fᵢ(x) for every i at the common limiting point. Equal coordinate sums force equality in all coordinates, giving a fixed point. This proof uses Sperner’s lemma as a stated classical combinatorial input. For hairy ball, suppose a nowhere-zero tangent field exists and normalize it to w(x). Then H(x,t)=cos(πt)x+sin(πt)w(x) stays on S² because x and w are orthogonal unit vectors. It is a homotopy from id to −id, contradicting their different degrees. This proves the obstruction using the stated degree facts.

example.setup: On [0,1]² take F(x,y)=(x/2+1/4,y/4+1/4). On S² project the fixed vector e₃ into each tangent plane.
example.calculation: The square map has fixed point (1/2,1/3), and each coordinate stays in [0,1]. The tangent field v(x,y,z)=e₃−z(x,y,z) has x·v=0 and ||v||²=1−z²; its zeros are exactly the north and south poles. In contrast w(x,y)=(−y,x) is a nonvanishing unit tangent field on S¹. The verifier checks these algebraic examples exactly. It does not pretend to verify a global topological theorem by sampling.
example.conclusion: Existence is supplied by compactness and topology, while the finite examples reveal the geometric content of the hypotheses.

source.limits: The proof explicitly imports Sperner’s lemma and basic degree theory rather than claiming a self-contained foundation of topology. Continuity, the closed-ball domain, and the even sphere dimension cannot simply be removed. A circle rotation has no fixed point despite being a continuous sphere self-map.
source.extension: In applications a stronger contraction estimate can additionally yield uniqueness and an iteration rate. For the square example the Euclidean Lipschitz constant is 1/2, a quantitative fact that Brouwer alone does not provide.

source.summary: A contour formula is incomplete without its enclosed point, orientation and analytic domain. With those specified, Cauchy’s formula turns a seemingly difficult complex integral into derivative evaluation. The formula also yields a useful derivative bound, so the same theorem supports both exact calculation and error control.
definitions: Let f be holomorphic on an open set containing the closed disk |z−a|≤r, with r>0. Let C be its counterclockwise circular boundary.
For an integer n≥0, Cauchy’s formula reads f^(n)(a)=n!/(2πi)∮_C f(z)/(z−a)^(n+1) dz. More general simple closed curves work when the same analyticity and interior conditions hold.
A line integral uses a parameterization z(t) and the factor z′(t)dt. Omitting that factor or reversing the orientation changes the calculation.

result.name: Boundary data recover derivatives and control their size
result.statement: Under the stated hypotheses, the derivative formula holds and |f^(n)(a)|≤n!M/rⁿ, where M=max_C|f|. In particular ∮_|z|=2 (z⁴+2z)/(z−1)³ dz=12πi and ∮_|z|=2 eᶻ/(z−1)³ dz=πie.
result.proof: For n=0, Cauchy’s theorem on the annulus between C and a small circle around a equates the two integrals of f(z)/(z−a). Parameterizing the small circle as a+εe^(it) makes its integral i∫₀^(2π)f(a+εe^(it))dt, which tends to 2πif(a) by uniform continuity. This proves the base formula using Cauchy’s theorem as the classical analytic input. For an interior variable a, differentiate under the boundary integral; the denominator stays uniformly separated from zero on a sufficiently small neighborhood. Repeating n times supplies n!/(z−a)^(n+1). The bound follows by taking absolute values, using contour length 2πr and denominator modulus r^(n+1). In the first example f″(1)=12, and the derivative formula multiplies this by 2πi/2!=πi. In the second f″(1)=e, giving πie. The pole at one is strictly inside |z|=2 and neither numerator has another singularity.

example.setup: Compute the two displayed integrals on z(t)=2e^(it), 0≤t≤2π.
example.calculation: For the polynomial, expanding z⁴+2z around z=1 gives coefficient six on (z−1)², so division by (z−1)³ has residue six and integral 12πi. For eᶻ, the corresponding coefficient is e/2 and integral πie. A periodic trapezoidal quadrature with 256 points independently approximates each integral and is compared with the analytic answers. That numerical agreement is a finite check; the coefficient and contour arguments give the proof.
example.conclusion: Both examples fix the factorial, orientation and 2πi normalization, while the bound shows what analyticity additionally controls.

source.limits: A contour passing through a singularity is outside these hypotheses. Merely having a real derivative on a curve does not imply complex analyticity inside it. The numerical quadrature is not used as a substitute for those conditions.

source.summary: A velocity component and a nonnegative speed have different distributions. The factor proportional to speed squared comes from three-dimensional volume, not an arbitrary correction. The derivation below identifies that Jacobian and calculates the distinct characteristic speeds from one normalized model.
definitions: Assume an equilibrium classical ideal-gas velocity vector V=(V₁,V₂,V₃) with independent centered Gaussian components of variance σ²=k_BT/m>0.
The vector density is (2πσ²)^(−3/2)exp(−|v|²/(2σ²)) on R³. The speed is R=|V|≥0.
The spherical volume element is r²sinθ drdθdφ. Integrating over directions contributes 4πr², so a speed density must include this factor.

result.name: Normalization, moments and three characteristic speeds
result.statement: The speed density is g(r)=√(2/π)r²σ^(−3)e^(−r²/(2σ²)) for r≥0. Its mode is √2σ, mean is √(8/π)σ, and root-mean-square speed is √3σ. More generally E[Rᵖ]=2^(p/2+1)Γ((p+3)/2)σᵖ/√π for p>−3.
result.proof: Integrate the vector density over each sphere of radius r to obtain g. The one-dimensional Gaussian integral can be normalized by squaring ∫e^(−x²/2)dx and changing to polar coordinates in R²; thus the joint Gaussian has total mass one, as does g. For the moments substitute u=r²/(2σ²) into ∫₀∞rᵖg(r)dr. The power of r and dr produce the stated gamma integral, finite near zero exactly when p>−3. Substituting p=1 and p=2 gives the mean and second moment. Alternatively E[R²]=ΣE[Vᵢ²]=3σ², an independent check. For the mode differentiate log g(r)=constant+2log r−r²/(2σ²) on r>0. Its derivative vanishes only at r=√2σ, changes from positive to negative, and the density vanishes at zero and infinity. This proves it is the unique positive maximum.

example.setup: Choose the nondimensional model σ=1, then compare the three speeds and the first two moments.
example.calculation: The mode is approximately 1.41421356, the mean 1.59576912 and the root-mean-square speed 1.73205081. The exact second moment is three and the variance is 3−8/π≈0.45352091. The verifier integrates g, rg and r²g over [0,10] with a declared composite Simpson rule, compares to 1,√(8/π),3 and reports the finite integration errors. The unintegrated tail is exponentially small; the proof of normalization and moments is the analytic gamma calculation, not the quadrature.
example.conclusion: The three commonly quoted speeds answer different mathematical questions, and their ordering is a consequence of the density rather than a convention.

source.limits: This is the explicitly assumed classical equilibrium Gaussian model, not a statement about every velocity sample or every interacting system. The scalar component density has its maximum at zero, while the speed density has its maximum away from zero; confusing them removes the radial Jacobian.

source.title: A catenary is fixed by force balance and an explicit length constraint
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: A catenary has a parameter with a physical and geometric meaning: horizontal tension divided by weight per unit arc length. Stating that meaning avoids confusing a chain under its own weight with a cable under a load uniform per horizontal distance, which instead gives a parabola.
definitions: Use a planar, perfectly flexible, inextensible chain in static equilibrium. Let w>0 be weight per unit arc length, H>0 the constant horizontal tension, and a=H/w.
Measure x horizontally and y upwards, with the lowest point at x=0. Let s(x) be signed arc length from that point, so s′=√(1+y′²).
For equal-height supports at x=±b, b>0, write the lowest height as y(0)=0. The total chain length is L>2b.

result.name: The catenary law and uniqueness of the length parameter
result.statement: Force balance gives y″=(1/a)√(1+y′²). With a horizontal tangent at the lowest point, y(x)=a(cosh(x/a)−1). Its length between ±b is L(a)=2a sinh(b/a). For each L>2b there is exactly one a>0 satisfying this equation.
result.proof: The vertical tension on the segment between the lowest point and x balances its weight ws. The tangent slope is vertical tension divided by horizontal tension, hence Hy′=ws. Differentiating and substituting s′ gives the stated ODE. Therefore d(arcsinh y′)/dx=1/a. With y′(0)=0, integration gives y′=sinh(x/a) and then the catenary expression. Its arc-length density is cosh(x/a), so integrating from −b to b gives L(a). To prove uniqueness, put z=b/a>0 and differentiate: L′(a)=2(sinh z−z cosh z). The expression in parentheses is zero at z=0 and has derivative −z sinh z<0 for z>0. Thus L′<0. As a→∞ the limit is 2b, while a→0⁺ sends L to infinity. Continuity and strict monotonicity give existence and uniqueness for every L>2b. The argument determines the one-parameter equilibrium graph in this model; it is not a claim about elastic or self-contacting chains.

example.setup: Take a=2 length units and b=2, so the supports are four units apart.
example.calculation: The endpoint sag above the lowest point is 2(cosh 1−1)≈1.08616126963. The length is 4sinh 1≈4.70080477458. At x=2 the slope is sinh 1 and the arc-length density is cosh 1. The ODE residual cancels because y″=(1/2)cosh(x/2) and √(1+y′²)=cosh(x/2). The verifier checks these identities numerically and brackets the unique inverse length parameter near a=2 using the proven monotonicity.
example.conclusion: The length condition fixes the scale and exposes exactly why a bare cosh formula has an undetermined parameter.

source.limits: Uniform weight here means uniform per actual arc length. A distributed horizontal load, bending stiffness, stretch, friction or unequal support heights changes the model or its boundary conditions. Finite numerical residuals confirm the chosen example; the differentiations and monotonicity argument provide the proof.
source.extension: For unequal support heights use y=a cosh((x−x₀)/a)+c and solve the endpoint and length constraints for a,x₀,c. Keeping the signed arc-length relation is often a cleaner route than squaring the equations and introducing spurious signs.

source.title: Navier plate modes and the Rayleigh quotient share a spectral calculation
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: A plate equation needs its boundary conditions before a Fourier formula is valid. A simply supported rectangle provides a case where each sine mode diagonalizes both the static equation and the vibration equation. The Rayleigh quotient is the corresponding energy ratio, with a small matrix example showing its algebra transparently.
definitions: In the linear isotropic Kirchhoff–Love model let D=Eh³/[12(1−ν²)]>0 be bending stiffness and μ=ρh>0 surface mass density. Use DΔ²w+μw_tt=p.

On a rectangle (0,a)×(0,b), Navier simply supported conditions are w=0 and Δw=0 on each straight edge. For a smooth solution they agree with zero normal bending moment because the tangential second derivative of the zero boundary trace vanishes.
For real symmetric A and nonzero v, define R_A(v)=vᵀAv/(vᵀv). For an admissible Navier plate mode the corresponding ratio is D∫(Δw)²/(μ∫w²).

result.name: Mode amplitudes, vibration frequencies and a residual bound
result.statement: Let φ_mn=sin(mπx/a)sin(nπy/b), λ_mn=(mπ/a)²+(nπ/b)². Then Δφ=−λφ and Δ²φ=λ²φ. A static load Pφ gives w=Pφ/(Dλ²), and a free vibration in this mode has ω²=Dλ²/μ. Also λ_min(A)≤R_A(v)≤λ_max(A) and dist(R_A(v),spectrum(A))≤||Av−R_A(v)v||/||v||.
result.proof: Differentiate each sine twice to obtain its Laplacian. Both φ and Δφ vanish on all four edges, so the mode satisfies the declared boundary conditions. Substitution reduces the static PDE to Dλ²W=P and the vibration PDE to μW″+Dλ²W=0. For the matrix statements, expand v=Σcⱼeⱼ in an orthonormal eigenbasis. Then R is the weighted average Σλⱼcⱼ²/Σcⱼ², proving the interval bound. The squared normalized residual is Σ(λⱼ−R)²cⱼ²/Σcⱼ², at least the square of the distance to the spectrum. This proves the residual estimate. Two integrations by parts under w=Δw=0 similarly turn ∫wΔ²w into ∫(Δw)², explaining the plate energy quotient. No unproved convergence assertion for an arbitrary Fourier load is needed for the single-mode example.

example.setup: Take a=b=π, m=n=1, D=3, μ=2 and load p=12sin x sin y. Separately take A=[[2,1],[1,2]], v=(1,2).
example.calculation: For the plate λ=2, so w=sin x sin y and ω²=6. The matrix has eigenvalues one and three, while R_A(v)=14/5. Its residual is (6/5,−3/5), giving normalized residual 3/5. The distance from 14/5 to the spectrum is 1/5, within that bound. The verifier checks all matrix identities exactly and checks the plate coefficients symbolically by integer arithmetic.
example.conclusion: Boundary conditions make the PDE mode legitimate, and the quotient supplies a concrete spectral bound rather than merely a suggestive analogy.

source.limits: This uses a thin, small-deflection, linear plate model. Clamped edges require different mode shapes, so the same sine formula cannot be transferred to them. A Rayleigh quotient is an estimate for a specified self-adjoint operator; it need not be an eigenvalue.
source.extension: For a finite span of admissible modes, form stiffness and mass matrices and solve Kc=ω²Mc. With positive definite M this becomes a symmetric matrix problem after conjugating by M^(−1/2), preserving the quotient interpretation.

source.title: Laplace tidal equations yield a local rotating-wave certificate
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: The tidal equations are a system for horizontal velocity and free-surface displacement. Their spherical geometry should not be silently replaced by a Cartesian formula. This treatment states the global coordinate model and then develops a precisely delimited local constant-depth calculation whose signs can be checked directly.
definitions: On a sphere of radius a use longitude λ, latitude φ, eastward velocity u, northward velocity v, constant mean depth H>0 and displacement η. Set f=2Ωsinφ and take g>0.
For a specified potential Φ, the spherical linear equations are u_t−fv=−(gη+Φ)_λ/(a cosφ), v_t+fu=−(gη+Φ)_φ/a, and η_t+H[ u_λ+(v cosφ)_φ ]/(a cosφ)=0, away from coordinate poles.
A small local patch freezes f and replaces metric derivatives by ∂x,∂y. With Φ=0 this gives u_t−fv=−gη_x, v_t+fu=−gη_y, η_t+H(u_x+v_y)=0. The calculation below is for this f-plane system.

result.name: Local energy balance and Poincaré-wave dispersion
result.statement: The local unforced system obeys ∂t[H(u²+v²)/2+gη²/2]+∇·[gHη(u,v)]=0. For a nonzero horizontal wavenumber k, a wave traveling along x has ω²=f²+gHk² and can be written η=Acosθ, u=ωAcosθ/(Hk), v=fAsinθ/(Hk), θ=kx−ωt.
result.proof: Multiply the first momentum equation by Hu and the second by Hv. Their Coriolis terms cancel exactly because −fuv+fvu=0. Multiply continuity by gη and add. The gradient products combine into the displayed divergence by the product rule. Thus integration over a periodic region or a region with zero normal velocity conserves the total positive quadratic energy. For the wave, continuity requires u to have amplitude ωA/(Hk). The second momentum equation then fixes the quadrature component v=fAsinθ/(Hk). Substitution in the first gives (ω²−f²)A/(Hk)=gkA, proving the dispersion relation for A≠0. This direct substitution also fixes the sign of the sine component. A stationary geostrophic component is possible in the full system and is not represented by this propagating branch.

example.setup: Use the constructed nondimensional coefficients H=1, g=16, f=3, k=1 and A=1/10.
example.calculation: Then ω=5, η=(1/10)cos(x−5t), u=(1/2)cos(x−5t), and v=(3/10)sin(x−5t). The momentum coefficient identities are 5·(1/2)−3·(3/10)=16/10 and −5·(3/10)+3·(1/2)=0. Continuity gives 5/10−1/2=0. The time period is 2π/5. These residuals and the dispersion equation 25=9+16 are checked exactly with rational coefficients.
example.conclusion: The example is a real solution certificate of the declared local system, while the global equations retain the geometry needed for an actual spherical tide model.

source.limits: The f-plane approximation is local, and the source’s catalog name alone supplies no coastline, depth map, forcing or dissipation data. The sinusoidal example is not an ocean prediction. Nonlinear advection, changing depth and friction require additional terms and may change the energy budget.
source.extension: Add Rayleigh friction −ru,−rv with r≥0. The energy law then has the nonpositive sink −rH(u²+v²). Including a specified potential contributes work −H(u,v)·∇Φ, which must be retained when comparing forcing and dissipation.

source.title: Hamilton, Hamilton–Jacobi and Riccati equations meet at a caustic
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: Three separately named catalog items can be made concrete with one harmonic oscillator. The Hamiltonian flow is a smooth rotation in phase space; a quadratic Hamilton–Jacobi function describes a graph inside it; a scalar Riccati equation controls that graph’s slope. The finite-time pole is therefore a coordinate failure of the graph description, not a singularity in the underlying oscillator.
definitions: For a C² Hamiltonian H(q,p,t), canonical equations are qdot=H_p, pdot=−H_q. Along a solution, dH/dt=H_t.
A C² Hamilton–Jacobi function S(q,t) solves S_t+H(q,S_q,t)=0. Its momentum graph is p=S_q, on a region where this is a valid smooth graph.
For H=(p²+q²)/2 and the quadratic ansatz S=A(t)q²/2, the PDE reduces to the scalar Riccati equation A′+A²+1=0.
More generally y′=a(t)+b(t)y+c(t)y² is Riccati. If c is C¹ and nowhere zero, y=−u′/(cu) transforms it, wherever u≠0, into u″−(b+c′/c)u′+acu=0.

result.name: Characteristic mechanics and an exactly solvable graph singularity
result.statement: For the unit oscillator, q(t)=q₀cos t+p₀sin t and p(t)=p₀cos t−q₀sin t solve Hamilton’s equations for all real t. With initial graph p₀=0, the Hamilton–Jacobi solution S(q,t)=−(tan t)q²/2 is valid for |t|<π/2, and A(t)=−tan t solves the associated Riccati equation.
result.proof: The oscillator expressions differentiate to qdot=p and pdot=−q. Their squared norm is q₀²+p₀², proving energy conservation directly, while the general chain rule gives H_qH_p−H_pH_q+H_t=H_t. For a general smooth S solving Hamilton–Jacobi, follow qdot=H_p(q,S_q,t). Differentiating p=S_q along that path gives pdot=S_qt+S_qqH_p. Differentiating the PDE in q gives S_qt+H_q+H_pS_qq=0, so pdot=−H_q: its characteristics obey Hamilton’s equations. In the quadratic oscillator ansatz, S_t=A′q²/2 and H(q,S_q)=(A²+1)q²/2, yielding Riccati. The initial value A(0)=0 has A=−tan t, or equivalently A=u′/u with u=cos t solving u″+u=0. For the general substitution write v=u′/u. Then v′+v²=u″/u; substituting y=−v/c yields precisely the displayed linear second-order equation. These transformations are valid only while their denominators do not vanish.

example.setup: Set q₀=2,p₀=0 and evaluate at t=π/4, then inspect the limit t→π/2.
example.calculation: At π/4 the trajectory has q=√2,p=−√2 and energy two. The phase coefficient is A=−1, so p=Aq and S=−q²/2 agree with the same graph. The Hamilton–Jacobi residual is [A′+A²+1]q²/2=0 because A′=−sec²t. At π/2 the trajectory is (0,−2), perfectly finite, but A=−tan t diverges. All starting q₀ with p₀=0 project to q=0 there, so one graph p(q) can no longer represent the family. The verifier checks the analytic coefficient identities numerically and uses exact rational values for the A=−1 residual.
example.conclusion: The shared example explains both the strength and the domain of the Riccati reduction, including a genuine geometric reason for its pole.

source.limits: This is the classical Hamilton–Jacobi equation, not automatically the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation of an optimal-control problem. A local smooth phase need not exist globally after characteristics cross. The written calculation does not claim global smooth solutions for an arbitrary Hamiltonian.
source.extension: For a quadratic multidimensional Hamiltonian, a matrix phase S=qᵀPq/2 produces a matrix Riccati equation. The graph remains meaningful only while the relevant position block of the linear symplectic flow is invertible; a singular block again indicates a projection caustic.

source.title: A cubic Routh–Hurwitz test with an exact stability boundary
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: The stability criterion is most useful when it gives a parameter certificate rather than a list of approximate roots. A cubic is small enough that the criterion can be proved directly from its possible real and complex factors. The equality boundary also reveals why strict inequalities are required.
definitions: A real polynomial is strictly Hurwitz when every complex root has negative real part. This is the spectral condition relevant to an autonomous linear ODE with that characteristic polynomial.
Write p(s)=s³+as²+bs+c with real a,b,c. Strict cubic Hurwitz conditions are a>0, b>0, c>0 and ab>c.
When a≠0, the cubic Routh first column is 1,a,(ab−c)/a,c. The proof below establishes the stable cubic case directly, without relying on a general root-count theorem.

result.name: Necessary and sufficient cubic inequalities
result.statement: The monic real cubic is strictly Hurwitz if and only if a,b,c>0 and ab>c. In the family p_K=s³+2s²+2s+K, this holds exactly for 0<K<4. At K=4 the factorization is (s+2)(s²+2), so the imaginary pair prevents strict stability.
result.proof: If all three roots are negative real numbers, write their negatives r₁,r₂,r₃>0. The elementary symmetric coefficient formulas make a,b,c positive, and expanding ab−c gives a sum of positive terms. If there is one negative real root −r and a conjugate pair −u±iv with r,u>0, factor p=(s+r)(s²+2us+u²+v²). Its coefficients are positive and direct expansion gives ab−c=2u[(r+u)²+v²]>0. This proves necessity. Conversely assume the inequalities. Positive coefficients imply p(s)>0 for all real s≥0, so no root is a nonnegative real number. If an unstable nonreal pair u±iv with u≥0 existed, the remaining real root would be −r with r>0, since c=r(u²+v²)>0. Factoring p=(s+r)(s²−2us+u²+v²) then gives ab−c=−2u[(r−u)²+v²]≤0, contradicting ab>c. All roots therefore lie strictly left of the imaginary axis. Applying the inequalities to a=b=2 gives K>0 and 4>K, as claimed.

example.setup: Compare K=2, K=4 and K=5 using exact coefficients.
example.calculation: For K=2 the Routh first column is (1,2,1,2), and the proved inequalities certify strict stability. For K=4 it is (1,2,0,4), signaling a boundary case; the exact factorization displays roots −2 and ±i√2. For K=5 the coefficient product ab−c is −1. Since all coefficients remain positive there is no nonnegative real root, and the failed strict criterion together with exclusion of an imaginary pair shows that the unstable roots are a conjugate pair with positive real part. The verifier checks the rational columns, inequalities and boundary product exactly.
example.conclusion: The parameter interval and its boundary are established without trusting floating-point root classifications near the imaginary axis.

source.limits: This proof is for a monic cubic with real coefficients. It is not a proof of the general Routh–Hurwitz theorem or its unstable-root counting rule. An imaginary-axis root means the strict criterion fails; any claim about bounded motion or nonlinear stability would need separate analysis.
source.extension: For a parameter-dependent polynomial, retaining symbolic Hurwitz determinants produces exact semialgebraic stability regions. A meaningful robustness certificate requires positive lower bounds on the relevant determinants throughout a stated parameter box.

source.title: A linear chirp has quadratic phase, with a precise sampling ambiguity
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: A time-dependent number placed directly into the argument of a cosine is not automatically its instantaneous frequency. Frequency is the derivative of phase divided by 2π. Starting from that definition fixes a common factor-of-two error and exposes an exact aliasing identity for sampled signals.
definitions: For the declared complex unit-amplitude signal z(t)=exp(iφ(t)) with differentiable unwrapped phase, define instantaneous frequency f(t)=φ′(t)/(2π), in cycles per unit time.
A linear chirp with starting frequency f₀ and rate κ is z(t)=exp(i[φ₀+2πf₀t+πκt²]). Its real part is the corresponding cosine.
Uniform samples have times tₙ=n/F_s. The phase must be interpreted as an unwrapped model; an isolated real cosine sample does not itself determine a unique phase.

result.name: Integrated frequency and an exact aliasing identity
result.statement: The stated chirp has f(t)=f₀+κt and net phase cycles N(T)=f₀T+κT²/2. Signals with f₀ replaced by f₀+ℓF_s, for any integer ℓ, have exactly the same complex samples. The discrete phase increment in cycles is [f₀+κ(n+1/2)/F_s]/F_s.
result.proof: Differentiate φ₀+2πf₀t+πκt² and divide by 2π to obtain the frequency. Integrating that frequency from zero to T gives the cycle count. In contrast, the tempting phase 2π(f₀+κt)t differentiates to frequency f₀+2κt, so it sweeps twice as fast. For sampled ambiguity, the extra starting frequency ℓF_s contributes phase 2πℓF_stₙ=2πℓn, whose complex exponential is one for every integer n. Thus no method using those samples alone can distinguish these models without a frequency prior. Finally subtract the quadratic phase at tₙ and tₙ₊₁; the difference of squares yields the displayed midpoint-frequency increment. If the modeled increment stays strictly between zero and half a cycle, the model’s successive phase steps are in the principal positive half-turn range. This condition describes the selected phase progression; it is not a proof that a finite-duration chirp is band limited.

example.setup: Take f₀=100Hz, κ=50Hz/s, T=2s and F_s=1000Hz.
example.calculation: The ending instantaneous frequency is 200Hz and the total net phase advance is 300 cycles. The naive unsafely substituted phase would end at 300Hz and accumulate 400 cycles. For n=0,…,1999 the correct sample increment ranges from 0.100025 to 0.199975 cycles. Increasing f₀ to 1100Hz gives the same 2001 complex samples at tₙ=n/1000 for n=0,…,2000, although its continuous frequencies differ by 1000Hz. The verifier proves the increment and cycle identities with rational arithmetic and checks a few exponential sample coincidences numerically.
example.conclusion: Integrating frequency gives the intended signal, and the exact sampling identity states a real nonidentifiability rather than an implementation defect.

source.limits: The instantaneous frequency of a real signal requires a chosen phase representation; zeros and multi-component mixtures can complicate that choice. A time-truncated chirp is not strictly band limited, so a Nyquist claim based solely on its endpoint instantaneous frequencies would overstate what was proved.
source.extension: For an arbitrary specified frequency law f(t), define φ(t)=φ₀+2π∫₀ᵗf(s)ds before sampling. An exponential frequency sweep then has exponential-integral phase rather than the quadratic phase of this linear model.

source.title: Stokes drag comes from a stress integral, not dimensional analysis alone
source.status: Classical mathematics newly developed from a recovered assistant-only catalog name
source.summary: Dimensions suggest drag proportional to viscosity, radius and speed, but cannot determine its numerical coefficient. That coefficient comes from the no-slip exterior Stokes solution and integration of its surface traction. A constructed settling example then checks whether the low-Reynolds-number hypothesis is internally consistent.
definitions: Assume a rigid sphere of radius a>0 in an unbounded incompressible Newtonian fluid of dynamic viscosity μ>0, with no slip and steady negligible inertia. The equations are ∇·u=0 and −∇p+μΔu=0.
In the sphere frame let the uniform far velocity be Ue_z. The standard Stokes solution is u_r=Ucosθ(1−3a/(2r)+a³/(2r³)), u_θ=−Usinθ(1−3a/(4r)−a³/(4r³)), p−p∞=−3μUa cosθ/(2r²).
Fluid stress is σ=−pI+μ(∇u+∇uᵀ). The traction integrated on the sphere gives the force exerted by the fluid. For a sphere translating at V relative to still fluid, set U=−V.

result.name: The surface integral and its low-Reynolds-number consequence
result.statement: The force on a translating sphere is F=−6πμaV. If its density exceeds the fluid density by Δρ>0 and gravity magnitude is g, the model terminal speed is V_t=2a²Δρg/(9μ). Its applicability must be checked using Re=2aρ_fV_t/μ≪1.
result.proof: Use the stated classical exterior solution as input; it satisfies no slip at r=a and tends to the chosen uniform flow at infinity. At the surface ∂_ru_r=0, so after subtracting the irrelevant constant pressure, σ_rr=(3μU/(2a))cosθ. The shear component is σ_rθ=μ(∂_ru_θ−u_θ/r+r^(−1)∂_θu_r)=−(3μU/(2a))sinθ there. The z component of traction is σ_rrcosθ−σ_rθsinθ=3μU/(2a), independent of θ. Integrating over area 4πa² gives 6πμaU. Equivalently the pressure contributes 2πμaU and shear contributes 4πμaU. Switching from incoming fluid velocity to body velocity reverses the sign. For settling, equate the magnitude 6πμaV_t to the net weight (4π/3)a³Δρg and cancel common factors to obtain the terminal formula. Thus the coefficient is derived from the explicit stress field, while the governing exterior solution itself is a stated classical input.

example.setup: Choose illustrative SI values a=10^(−5)m, μ=10^(−3)Pa·s, fluid density ρ_f=1000kg/m³, Δρ=1000kg/m³ and g=9.81m/s².
example.calculation: The formula gives V_t=0.000218m/s and Re=0.00436, small compared with one. Both expressions use exact terminating-decimal inputs, and the verifier evaluates them with rational arithmetic. It also checks the surface stress coefficients and the pressure/shear angular integrals exactly after dividing out πμaU. These calculations verify the chosen model; the parameters are not recovered historical measurements or a proposed experiment.
example.conclusion: The worked model explains the factor 6π, the direction of drag and the independent consistency check needed after calculating a speed.

source.limits: The derivation assumes an isolated sphere, no-slip boundary conditions and negligible inertia. Walls, finite Reynolds number, non-Newtonian rheology or slip change the problem. A small numerical Re supports this approximation within the declared model but is not a rigorous bound on every neglected physical correction.

source.title: Specify the clustering objective before adding weights
source.status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
source.summary: T=W+B. For nonnegative a,b with a+b>0, maximizing aB−bW over the same partitions gives exactly the minimizers of W. An added spatial or graph term can create a new tradeoff, but two copies of the same scatter information do not. The revised objective states what each term contributes and which weights are identifiable from the minimizers.
definitions: A partition consists of nonempty clusters C_j, sizes n_j and centroids μ_j. The global centroid is μ.
Define W=Σ_jΣ_{i∈C_j}||x_i−μ_j||², B=Σ_jn_j||μ_j−μ||² and T=Σ_i||x_i−μ||².
These definitions apply to a fixed dataset and fixed Euclidean metric. An objective also needs a direction of optimization, admissible partitions and explicit weights.

result.name: Specify the clustering objective before adding weights
result.statement: T=W+B. For nonnegative a,b with a+b>0, maximizing aB−bW over the same partitions gives exactly the minimizers of W. An added spatial or graph term can create a new tradeoff, but two copies of the same scatter information do not.
result.proof: Write x_i−μ=(x_i−μ_j)+(μ_j−μ) for i in cluster j. Expand its squared norm. The cross term sums to zero because Σ_{i∈C_j}(x_i−μ_j)=0. Summing proves the decomposition. Substituting B=T−W into aB−bW gives aT−(a+b)W. The first term is independent of the partition, which proves the optimizer statement, including all ties. This derivation prevents an apparently richer objective from concealing a redundant parameter. If cluster count is unrestricted, singleton clusters give W=0; a complexity penalty or fixed count is then necessary to obtain a meaningful grouping problem.

example.setup: Use four scalar observations 0,0,1,1 and compare two clusters {0,0},{1,1} with the crossed partition {0,1},{0,1}.
example.calculation: The global mean is one half and T=1. The first partition has W=0,B=1; the crossed partition has W=1,B=0. With a=2,b=3, the scores are two and negative three, exactly aT−5W. Repeating the data coordinates with a changed scale changes T,W,B quadratically, so unrelated penalties must be scaled or normalized deliberately.
example.conclusion: The revised objective states what each term contributes and which weights are identifiable from the minimizers.

source.limits: The scatter identity does not apply unchanged to arbitrary definitions of pairwise separation, nonsquared distances or kernel similarities. A source label such as synchronization does not define a function until its variables and symmetry are supplied.
source.extension: For any proposed extra term R, exhibit two partitions with the same W but different R. Such a pair proves that R supplies information not already contained in Euclidean scatter. Otherwise simplify the objective before tuning its parameters.

source.status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
source.summary: For γ≥0, the optimum is min(γ,1). The true split 00|11 is uniquely optimal as an unlabeled partition for γ<1; the one-cluster partition is uniquely optimal for γ>1; both tie at γ=1. Spatial regularization is a tunable mathematical preference with a measurable failure mode. It is not an automatic improvement independent of units or data contrast.
definitions: Take the path 1–2–3–4, scalar data (0,0,1,1), and partitions into at most two nonempty clusters.
W is within-cluster squared error using fitted centroids; cut is the number of path edges whose endpoints receive different labels.
Labels are immaterial: a binary labeling and its global complement encode the same partition. Use first label zero to enumerate eight cases exactly.

result.name: Spatial coherence gives an exact cut-versus-fit threshold
result.statement: For γ≥0, the optimum is min(γ,1). The true split 00|11 is uniquely optimal as an unlabeled partition for γ<1; the one-cluster partition is uniquely optimal for γ>1; both tie at γ=1.
result.proof: The all-equal partition has cut zero and W=1. Every nonconstant labeling on a connected path has at least one cut and W≥0, so its objective is at least γ. The labeling (0,0,1,1) has one cut and W=0, attaining that lower bound. For γ<1 it beats the constant partition. Equality in the nonconstant lower bound requires W=0, so no cluster can mix a zero and a one. With at most two clusters this forces exactly the split by value. For γ>1, every nonconstant partition has objective at least γ>1. The same argument gives only the two stated optima at equality; exhaustive enumeration independently checks the finite certificate.

example.setup: Compare γ=1/2, γ=1 and γ=2 without refitting or rescaling the data.
example.calculation: The split objectives are 1/2,1,2; the constant objective is always one. Thus increasing the spatial penalty crosses an exact boundary and eventually merges the two groups. Multiplying every observation by c multiplies W by c² but leaves cut unchanged, moving the threshold to γ=c².
example.conclusion: Spatial regularization is a tunable mathematical preference with a measurable failure mode. It is not an automatic improvement independent of units or data contrast.

source.limits: The proof uses this path, these observations and at most two clusters. More labels, normalized cuts, weighted edges or higher-dimensional data create different thresholds. A continuum perimeter limit needs additional scaling assumptions.
source.extension: On a larger finite graph, retain each partition’s pair (cut,W). Lower supporting lines of these points determine all parameter transitions. Dominated pairs can be discarded, yielding a compact exact certificate of the regularization path.

source.title: Three regularizers produce three different shrinkage rules
source.status: Corrected formulation or classical result with an explicit worked example
source.summary: The solutions are componentwise soft threshold x_i=sign(z_i)max(|z_i|−λ,0), radial shrink x=max(1−λ/||z||₂,0)z, and ridge x=z/(1+λ), respectively. Writing ||M||₂ without stating whether M is a vector or a matrix is incomplete: a matrix spectral norm, Frobenius norm and entrywise norm lead to different optimization problems.
definitions: Fix z∈Rⁿ and λ>0. Strict convexity of the quadratic term gives a unique minimizer for each convex penalty.
The ℓ₁ penalty is λΣ|x_i|. The unsquared ℓ₂ penalty is λ√Σx_i². Ridge uses λ||x||₂²/2.
A subgradient g of a convex function f at x satisfies f(y)≥f(x)+gᵀ(y−x) for every y.

result.name: Three regularizers produce three different shrinkage rules
result.statement: The solutions are componentwise soft threshold x_i=sign(z_i)max(|z_i|−λ,0), radial shrink x=max(1−λ/||z||₂,0)z, and ridge x=z/(1+λ), respectively.
result.proof: For ℓ₁ the coordinates separate. At a positive coordinate, optimality gives x_i−z_i+λ=0; at a negative one it gives x_i−z_i−λ=0. At zero, the subgradient interval [−λ,λ] contains z_i exactly when |z_i|≤λ. For the unsquared ℓ₂ norm and a nonzero solution, x−z+λx/||x||=0, so x points along z and its length is ||z||−λ. At zero, optimality requires z in the radius-λ Euclidean ball, giving the threshold case. Ridge is differentiable everywhere: x−z+λx=0. These conditions are sufficient by convexity and unique by strict convexity of the full objective.

example.setup: Use z=(3,4), λ=1, and then a small first coordinate z=(1/2,4).
example.calculation: For (3,4), soft threshold gives (2,3); radial shrink gives (12/5,16/5), since ||z||=5; ridge gives (3/2,2). For (1/2,4), ℓ₁ sets the first coordinate exactly to zero, while both other rules retain a nonzero first coordinate. Thus sparsity of individual coefficients follows from a specific corner geometry rather than from the generic word regularization.
example.conclusion: Writing ||M||₂ without stating whether M is a vector or a matrix is incomplete: a matrix spectral norm, Frobenius norm and entrywise norm lead to different optimization problems.

source.limits: The derivation concerns an identity quadratic data term. Replacing it with ||Ax−z||² generally destroys the coordinatewise closed form. It does not establish that any penalty identifies a scientifically correct model.
source.extension: For disjoint groups of coefficients, Σ_g||x_g||₂ yields one radial threshold per group. This keeps or removes entire groups and provides a precise intermediate choice between coordinate sparsity and uniform ridge shrinkage. Each of these proximal maps is nonexpansive: if outputs x,y correspond to inputs z,w, monotonicity of the convex subgradient gives〈(z−x)−(w−y),x−y〉≥0. Hence||x−y||²≤〈z−w,x−y〉≤||z−w||||x−y||, proving the unit Lipschitz bound.

result.name: An E² page is not already the homology of the total space
result.statement: For both fibrations over S² with fiber S¹, E² has one K in positions(0,0),(2,0),(0,1),(2,1). For the product the relevant differential is zero; for the Hopf fibration d₂:(2,0)→(0,1) is an isomorphism, leaving total degrees zero and three.
result.proof: The sphere and circle homology groups give the four nonzero terms directly. definitions: Assign F(U)=C⁰(U,R), with restriction maps that restrict functions. A sheaf requires locality and unique gluing for every open cover.

result.name: Sheaf notation needs a gluing rule and cohomology needs a complex
result.statement: Compatible continuous functions on an open cover glue uniquely to a continuous global function. On T² the classes[dx],[dy] have a nonzero product represented by dx∧dy, whose integral is one; each class squares to zero.
result.proof: Given f_i∈C⁰(U_i,R) agreeing on overlaps, set f(x)=f_i(x) for any i containing x. Agreement makes the definition independent of the choice. Continuity is local: every point has a neighborhood on which f equals a continuous f_i. Uniqueness follows because every point lies in some U_i. For the torus calculation, the integral of dx∧dy over a fundamental unit square is one. If this two-form were exact, Stokes’ theorem on the closed torus would make that integral zero. result.statement: Writingε=e+(trε)I/3 withtr(e)=0 gives energyμ||e||_F²+(μ/3+λ/2)(trε)². This is positive for every nonzero symmetric strain exactly under the stated two strict inequalities.

result.name: Conservation and first integrals distinguish two population models
result.statement: For SIR, S+I+R is constant and I+S−(γ/β)logS is constant whileS>0. For Lotka–Volterra, H=dx−clogx+by−αlogy is constant. Its nonminimal positive level sets are closed orbits.

Its Hessian isdiag(c/x²,α/y²), positive definite. It has a unique critical point(c/d,α/b), and diverges at the positive-quadrant boundary and at infinity. Every higher level is therefore a compact smooth strictly convex closed curve, and the vector field is nonzero there. Motion around such a curve is periodic because its speed has a positive minimum on that compact curve. This describes the ideal classical system, not generic interacting populations.

source.status: Classical or elementary result developed here with explicit scope
source.summary: The recovered contour expression becomes a topological invariant only for a closed nonvanishing loop with enough regularity to integrate. Its integer value comes from the endpoint change of a lifted angle, not from a numerical convention for complex logarithms.
definitions: Let z:[0,1]→C∖{0} be a piecewise continuously differentiable closed loop.

result.name: Winding number from a lifted angle
result.statement: The integral equals [α(1)−α(0)]/(2π), an integer. Winding adds under concatenation and is unchanged under a continuous homotopy through loops avoiding zero.
result.proof: On each smooth segment, z′/z=r′/r+iα′. The real contribution is log r(1)−log r(0)=0 because the loop closes. The remaining term is the argument difference divided by 2π. Equal endpoints imply exp(i(α(1)−α(0)))=1, so the difference is an integer multiple of 2π. Concatenation joins lifts after adding a constant multiple of 2π and therefore adds endpoint differences. During a homotopy avoiding zero, lifted endpoint differences vary continuously but remain integer multiples of 2π; their integer cannot change. This proof also identifies the precise excluded event: crossing zero destroys the nonvanishing lift.

example.setup: For integer k consider z_k(t)=2exp(2πikt). Contrast it with a loop translated through the origin.
example.calculation: Here z′_k/z_k=2πik, so w(z_k)=k exactly. A reverse traversal changes k to −k. The circles z_a(t)=a+exp(2πit), for real a, have winding one when |a|<1 and zero when |a|>1; at a=±1 the curve passes through zero and the integral is undefined. Consequently no invariant-preserving homotopy through nonvanishing loops can connect the k=1 and k=0 cases. For two nonvanishing differentiable loops z and u, the logarithmic derivative of their pointwise product is (zu)′/(zu)=z′/z+u′/u. Integration therefore proves w(zu)=w(z)+w(u). result.statement: Any weak solution is the unique global minimizer. For every admissible perturbation v, J(u+v)−J(u)=(1/2)∫[(v′)²+v²]dx≥0, with equality only for v=0.
result.proof: Expand J(u+εv). Differentiating at ε=0 gives the weak equation. For the exact difference formula, expand J(u+v) and use the weak equation to cancel its cross term ∫(u′v′+uv−fv).
