definitions: Let ẋ=−a x+b y+u and ẏ=c x−d y+v, with a,d>0 and real b,c,u,v.
Set A=[[-a,b],[c,−d]], D=ad−bc and forcing h=(u,v). A fixed point solves A z+h=0.

result.name: Coupled equilibria with a complete two-variable stability test
result.statement: If D≠0 the fixed point is unique. It is exponentially stable exactly when D>0, because the trace is −(a+d)<0. If D<0 it is a saddle. At D=0, equilibrium existence and nonuniqueness depend on forcing compatibility.
result.proof: The characteristic polynomial is λ²+(a+d)λ+D. For a real two-by-two matrix, both roots have negative real part precisely when their sum is negative and product positive. Here the sum is always −(a+d), so positivity of D is the remaining condition. If D<0, the real roots have opposite signs. At D=0 one eigenvalue is zero, and solving the singular linear equations requires h to lie in the image of −A; if it does, adding any null vector gives another fixed point. These statements follow directly from the quadratic polynomial and linear algebra, not from the word equilibrium.

example.setup: Take a=d=1 and b=c=r with forcing u=1,v=0.
example.calculation: For |r|<1, D=1−r²>0 and the fixed point is (1/(1−r²),r/(1−r²)); the eigenvalues are −1±r. At r=1 the equations require −x+y+1=0 and x−y=0, which are inconsistent, so no fixed point exists. With zero forcing instead, r=1 has the entire line x=y of equilibria. For r>1, the unique forced fixed point is unstable even though its algebraic formula still exists. The stable fixed point also becomes sensitive near the boundary. As r approaches1 from below, both coordinates grow like1/[2(1−r)]. The slow eigenvalue−1+r tends to zero at the same time. Algebraic solvability away from the singular value therefore supplies neither a uniform response bound nor a uniform decay rate.
example.conclusion: A static equation, a unique solution and an attracting state are three distinct claims with separate conditions.

definitions: Let dX_t=−aX_tdt+σdW_t, where a>0, σ≥0 and W is standard Brownian motion. Assume X₀ is independent of future Brownian increments and has finite second moment.

result.statement: The solution is X_t=e^(−at)X₀+σ∫₀^t e^(−a(t−s))dW_s. Its mean is e^(−at)EX₀ and its variance is e^(−2at)Var(X₀)+(σ²/(2a))(1−e^(−2at)). The centered Gaussian N(0,σ²/(2a)) is invariant.
result.proof: Multiply the SDE by the deterministic integrating factor e^(at); the product rule has no quadratic-variation cross term with that factor, giving the explicit solution. Independence and zero mean of the stochastic integral give the mean formula and eliminate the covariance cross term. Itô isometry evaluates the noise variance as σ²∫₀^t e^(−2a(t−s))ds. A deterministic initial state leads to a Gaussian integral, and starting with the stated independent Gaussian makes the displayed variance constant. source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
source.summary: The historical answer invoked circle coordinate rings, prime ideals and scaling. A point prime is not the same thing as an irreducible component, and a map of spaces acts in the opposite direction on coordinate functions. Both distinctions can be checked in this small example.
definitions: Let A=R[x,y]/(x²+y²−1) and B=R[u,v]/(u²+v²−4).
A geometric scaling φ:(x,y)↦(2x,2y) induces φ*:B→A by substituting u↦2x and v↦2y.

result.name: The circle is irreducible and its radius scaling has a contravariant map
result.statement: The defining polynomial is irreducible over R and generates a prime ideal, so A is a domain. The scaling φ is an algebraic isomorphism with inverse division by two, and its pullback is well defined. The point ideal (x−1,y) in A is maximal but does not define an extra irreducible component.
result.proof: If x²+y²−1 factored nontrivially over R, its degree two would force two affine-linear factors. Their highest homogeneous parts would multiply to x²+y², which has no real linear factor: a nonzero real direction cannot make a sum of two squares vanish identically along a line. Thus the polynomial is irreducible. R[x,y] is a unique factorization domain, where irreducibles are prime, proving the domain assertion. Substituting into B’s relation gives 4x²+4y²−4=0 in A; substituting x↦u/2,y↦v/2 gives the inverse homomorphism. The quotient of A by (x−1,y) is R, proving maximality.

example.setup: Evaluate a coordinate function f(u,v)=u+v on the radius-two point φ(3/5,4/5).
example.calculation: The geometric point is (6/5,8/5) and f takes value14/5. The pulled-back function φ*f=2x+2y takes the same value14/5 at (3/5,4/5). This illustrates the reversed arrow B→A. Meanwhile the zero ideal of the domain A describes its single generic irreducible component; individual point ideals provide locations within that component. Evaluation at a real circle point is a surjective algebra map to R whose kernel is the ideal of coordinate functions vanishing there. The quotient is R, hence that ideal is maximal. This is why a point ideal and the zero ideal describing the irreducible component carry different information.
example.conclusion: Coordinate rings make maps and component claims exact when the relevant ideal and arrow direction are stated.

source.limits: Over another field, irreducibility and point interpretation must be reconsidered. Even over R, not every maximal ideal of a finitely generated algebra need have real residue field, so this example is not a classification of every prime.

definitions: Cover S¹ by connected contractible arcs U,V whose intersection has two connected components. Let R_const be the sheaf of locally constant real functions.

Its image is the diagonal line, and quotienting R² by that line leaves one dimension, detected by the difference of the two coordinates. definitions: Let H={x+iy:y>0} with metric ds²=(dx²+dy²)/y². Use the Levi-Civita connection of this metric.

result.name: Hyperbolic curvature and geodesics in a declared metric
result.statement: For the stated metric, the only nonzero Christoffel symbols are Γˣ_xy=Γˣ_yx=−1/y, Γʸ_xx=1/y and Γʸ_yy=−1/y. Its curvature is −1. Vertical lines x=x₀, y=y₀e^t are unit-speed geodesics. The Cayley map w=(z−i)/(z+i) identifies this metric with 4|dw|²/(1−|w|²)² on the unit disk.
result.proof: The Christoffel formula Γᵏ_ij=(1/2)g^(kℓ)(∂ig_jℓ+∂jg_iℓ−∂ℓg_ij) uses g_xx=g_yy=y⁻² and inverse y²I. Differentiating yields the displayed coefficients. source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
source.summary: The Virasoro and Ward-identity fragment invokes an infinite-dimensional algebra. Its concrete content can be developed without claiming a full conformal field theory: compute the vector-field bracket, specify the central cocycle, and prove the Jacobi identity for that extension.
definitions: On Laurent polynomials let ℓ_m=−z^(m+1)d/dz for m∈Z. The Witt bracket is the commutator of derivations.
Introduce a central symbol C, with [C,L_m]=0, and set [L_m,L_n]=(m−n)L_(m+n)+((m³−m)/12)δ_(m+n,0)C. In a representation C may act by a scalar c.

result.name: Witt brackets and the Virasoro central term
result.statement: These brackets define the Virasoro Lie algebra. The span of L_−1,L_0,L_1 is an sl₂ subalgebra with no central contribution, and the noncentral quotient is the Witt algebra.
result.proof: Apply the commutator of ℓ_m and ℓ_n to z^r. The two second-derivative contributions cancel, leaving (m−n)ℓ_(m+n)z^r. This proves the Witt bracket and Jacobi follows from the commutator algebra of linear operators. For the central extension it remains to check the central part of Jacobi. It vanishes unless m+n+p=0. When that sum is zero, its coefficient, up to the factor1/12, is the cyclic sum of (m−n)((m+n)³−(m+n)). Substitute p=−m−n and expand: the cubic and linear terms cancel separately. Antisymmetry follows because m³−m is odd when n=−m. Thus the displayed extension is a Lie algebra. For m=−1,0,1 the polynomial m³−m is zero, so their brackets close without C.

example.calculation: [L₁,L_−1]=2L₀, while [L₂,L_−2]=4L₀+C/2. Choosing E=L₁, F=−L_−1 and H=−2L₀ gives [H,E]=2E, [H,F]=−2F and [E,F]=H. Thus a finite sl₂ subalgebra is visible, but it does not remove the independent central direction detected by modes±2. The verifier checks the cocycle cancellation on a finite range as an arithmetic check; the polynomial calculation supplies the general proof.

For the torus, the loop t↦(2t,3t) modZ² has class(2,3); it is noncontractible despite ending where it starts. source.summary: The recovered exterior-calculus passages mixed antisymmetry, volume, differential forms and topology. The key distinctions are degree, closure and exactness. definitions: For a p-form α and q-form β, α∧β=(−1)^(pq)β∧α. Thus two one-forms anticommute, but two two-forms commute.
On oriented Euclidean R³ use dx∧dy∧dz as volume and the Hodge star defined by α∧*β=⟨α,β⟩vol. In particular *(dx∧dy)=dz.

result.name: Wedge products, Hodge duality and a genuine closed-form obstruction
result.statement: On the plane, η=(−y dx+x dy)/2 satisfies dη=dx∧dy and ∮_(unit circle)η=π. On the punctured plane, ω=(−y dx+x dy)/(x²+y²) is closed but not exact; its circle integral is2π. This is a well-defined topological obstruction to one global potential.
result.proof: Differentiate η term by term: d(−y dx)=−dy∧dx=dx∧dy and d(x dy)=dx∧dy, giving dη=dx∧dy. Parameterize the circle by x=cos t,y=sin t to obtain η=dt/2 and integralπ, equal to the disk area. For ω, the coordinate calculation ∂x[x/(x²+y²)]−∂y[−y/(x²+y²)]=0 gives dω=0 wherever the denominator is nonzero. On the unit circle ω=dt and its integral is2π. If ω=df globally, the integral along any closed parametrized path would equal f at the endpoint minus f at the start, hence zero. The nonzero period disproves exactness. Locally one can use an angle branch, but no single-valued angle exists on the full punctured plane.

example.setup: Express area and volume using coordinate differentials rather than informal antisymmetric symbols.
example.calculation: (a dx+b dy)∧(c dx+d dy)=(ad−bc)dx∧dy, so the coefficient is the oriented parallelogram area. In R³, (dx∧dy)∧dz is the volume form and its coefficient changes sign when orientation reverses. A scalar density ρ becomes a mass three-form ρ dx∧dy∧dz; multiplying scalar functions alone does not create a three-form. The Hodge star additionally depends on the metric, whereas wedge multiplication does not.
example.conclusion: The local operations and the global obstruction are now separate statements with direct calculations.

source.limits: The closed-not-exact example concerns the punctured domain; including the origin makes ω undefined. Hodge theory on general manifolds requires boundary conditions and analytic hypotheses not supplied by these identities.

source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored derivation or finite example and explicit scope
source.summary: The recovered density, implicit-surface and finite-element discussion becomes concrete on one tetrahedron. Barycentric coordinates give an exact mass formula and an explicit positivity criterion; the regular-value test prevents a singular point from being mislabeled a smooth surface.
definitions: Let T be the tetrahedron with vertices v₀=(0,0,0), v₁=(1,0,0), v₂=(0,1,0), v₃=(0,0,1). Its barycentric coordinates are λ₀=1−x−y−z, λ₁=x, λ₂=y, λ₃=z.
An affine density is ρ=Σ_(i=0)^3 ρ_i λ_i. A level set F=0 is regular at a point when ∇F is nonzero there.

result.name: Affine density integrates exactly on a simplex
result.statement: For every affine density on a nondegenerate tetrahedron, ∫_Tρ dV=Vol(T)(ρ₀+ρ₁+ρ₂+ρ₃)/4. It is nonnegative everywhere if and only if every vertex value is nonnegative. For F=x²+y²+z²−r², the zero set is a regular two-dimensional surface when r>0, but at r=0 it is one singular point.
result.proof: Affine permutations of the four vertices preserve the tetrahedron and its volume measure. They permute the barycentric functions, so all four integrals ∫λ_i are equal. Since Σλ_i=1, each is Vol(T)/4. Integrating the linear combination proves the mass formula. Since λ_i≥0 and sum to one, ρ is a convex combination of its vertex values; their nonnegativity implies pointwise nonnegativity. The converse follows by evaluating at a vertex. For the implicit surface, ∇F=2(x,y,z). On F=0 with r>0 its norm is2r, nonzero, so the implicit-function theorem gives a local surface chart. With r=0 the only real solution is the origin, where the gradient vanishes and there is no two-dimensional neighborhood.

example.setup: Integrate ρ=1+x+y+z on the standard tetrahedron.
example.calculation: The volume is1/6, and the four vertex values are1,2,2,2. Consequently mass=(1/6)(7/4)=7/24. Direct integration gives the same answer: ∫1=1/6 and ∫x=∫y=∫z=1/24. The mean density is7/4, equal to the value at the centroid(1/4,1/4,1/4). Nonnegative nodal coefficients preserve positivity for this affine basis, a property that need not survive an arbitrary oscillatory higher-order basis.
example.conclusion: The density representation now yields a finite exact calculation rather than an unspecified numerical pipeline.

result.proof: For x=(x₁,x₂,x₃), xᵀAx=x₁²+(x₂−x₁)²+(x₃−x₂)²+x₃². This is positive for every nonzero vector, proving SPD without numerical eigenvalue tolerances. Standard CG orthogonalizes residuals in the appropriate Krylov space; in exact arithmetic it terminates within the number of distinct eigenvalues, but a nonsymmetric or varying preconditioner invalidates this particular argument.

definitions: Let R_y(w)=[[cos(w/2),−sin(w/2)],[sin(w/2),cos(w/2)]] act on |0⟩. Measure |1⟩ with probability p(w)=sin²(w/2).

result.statement: The exact derivatives are p′(w)=(1/2)sin w and L′(w)=(p(w)−t)(1/2)sin w. The parameter-shift identity is p′(w)=[p(w+π/2)−p(w−π/2)]/2. Replacing this derivative by a general f does not guarantee descent.

result.proof: The periodic rectangular quotient is a torus: gluing opposite sides of a rectangle gives the standard surface, and the chosen diagonal triangulates it. source.summary: A genuine categorical transport can preserve every composition law while changing the usual Hamming distance of a code. source.summary: A precise generating-function calculation is a much stronger result than a broad application list. definitions: Work in the formal ring Z[[q]], where each coefficient of an infinite product depends on finitely many factors. Let p(n) count unrestricted partitions, with p(0)=1 and p(n)=0 for n<0. Its generating series is P(q)=∏_{m≥1}(1−q^m)⁻¹.

result.name: Pentagonal recurrence with formal-series scope
result.statement: Euler’s classical identity ∏_{m≥1}(1−q^m)=Σ_{k∈Z}(−1)^kq^{k(3k−1)/2} implies p(n)=Σ_{k≥1}(−1)^(k−1)[p(n−k(3k−1)/2)+p(n−k(3k+1)/2)]. Each coefficient equation is finite.

Multiply Euler’s identity by P to obtain one. For n>0, its nth coefficient is zero; isolate the k=0 term p(n), pair positive and negative k, and move the remaining terms to the other side. Formal finiteness follows because the pentagonal exponents grow quadratically. This argument derives the recurrence from the stated classical theorem, rather than pretending a finite coefficient test proves the entire Euler identity.

source.title: A tangent deformation can exist while its next lift is obstructed
source.status: Revised classical development with scoped worked result
source.summary: A finite-group character gives a complete toy deformation problem. It makes the difference between a nonzero tangent space and a smooth deformation space explicit, without pretending to reconstruct an absent Galois representation or Eisenstein ideal. The group is deliberately small so that the full relation can be checked by polynomial arithmetic.
definitions: Let G be cyclic of order two, generated by g. Over a field k, take the trivial one-dimensional residual character. A deformation over a local Artinian k-algebra sends g to a unit u≡1 modulo its maximal ideal and must satisfy u²=1. Conjugation is trivial in dimension one.

result.name: Characteristic two supplies a nontrivial obstructed tangent direction
result.statement: Over k[ε]/(ε²), write u=1+aε. The character relation is2a=0. For characteristic different from two, the tangent space is zero. In characteristic two it is one-dimensional, represented by arbitrary a. The tangent u=1+ε does not lift to u=1+η+bη² over k[η]/(η³) for any b.
result.proof: Expand(1+aε)²=1+2aε because ε²=0. In characteristic two the linear relation disappears. For a prospective second-order lift, square1+η+bη² moduloη³: all doubled terms vanish and η² survives, yielding1+η² rather than1. Thus no choice of b solves the relation. The complete fixed-characteristic local relation can be represented by k[[t]]/(t²), since u=1+t and u²=1 is exactly t²=0 in characteristic two.

example.setup: Compare the number of first-order characters over F₂ and F₃.
example.calculation: Over F₂ there are two, with a=0 or1; over F₃ only a=0 works. The nontrivial F₂ tangent direction is obstructed at the next order. A one-dimensional tangent space therefore does not imply a one-dimensional smooth formal family.
example.conclusion: The deformation functor, its coefficient category and its relation determine what the tangent calculation means.

source.title: Finite zero checks and an arbitrary spectral gap cannot prove a Riemann hypothesis
source.status: Revised classical development with scoped worked result
source.summary: A rigorous revision identifies the specific analytic function and the missing all-zero theorem. Functional symmetry, entire continuation and a finite verified zero list are valuable information, but do not force every future zero onto a line in a broad class of analytic functions. definitions: For the Riemann zeta function define ξ(s)=s(s−1)π^(−s/2)Γ(s/2)ζ(s)/2, with its analytic continuation. It is entire and satisfiesξ(s)=ξ(1−s), together with conjugation symmetry. result.name: Symmetry alone does not force the critical line
result.statement: The real polynomial P(s)=[(s−1/4)²+1][(s−3/4)²+1] satisfiesP(1−s)=P(s) and has zeros1/4±i,3/4±i. Multiplying an entire symmetric function by P preserves those elementary symmetries while adding off-line zeros.
result.proof: The substitution s↦1−s exchanges the two quadratic factors, so their product is invariant. Real coefficients give conjugation symmetry, and factoring each positive quadratic over C gives its declared roots. Thus the example refutes only an inference from these insufficient analytic conditions, not RH itself. An operator proof would additionally need a rigorous bijection covering every zero, with the correct multiplicities and domain conditions.

source.title: A finite-field zeta example gives a genuine cohomological counting bridge
source.status: Revised classical development with scoped worked result
source.summary: The projective line over a finite field supplies a complete classical example of arithmetic counting and a rational zeta function. It illustrates an actual bridge between algebraic geometry and an analytic-looking generating series. It does not identify this finite-field theorem with a number-field Riemann hypothesis or with an unspecified physical operator.
definitions: For a finite-type variety X over F_q define its formal zeta series Z(X,t)=exp(Σ_{n≥1}#X(F_{q^n})t^n/n). The exponential and logarithm are formal power series over Q, so every finite coefficient calculation is well defined.

result.name: Exact zeta function of the projective line
result.statement: For X=P¹ over F_q, #X(F_{q^n})=q^n+1 and Z(X,t)=1/[(1−t)(1−qt)]. Its two elementary factors record the constant and degree-two cohomological contributions in the standard Frobenius interpretation.
result.proof: Every F_{q^n}-point of P¹ is either an affine coordinate in F_{q^n} or the single point at infinity, giving the count. Substitute it into the logarithm of Z. The formal identity−log(1−at)=Σ_{n≥1}a^nt^n/n gives−log(1−qt)−log(1−t); exponentiating yields the rational expression. Coefficients can be checked independently by multiplying the two geometric series: the coefficient of t^m is1+q+⋯+q^m. This establishes the complete rational formula without a numerical approximation.

example.setup: Choose q=2 and calculate the first three extension-field counts and series coefficients.
example.calculation: The counts for n=1,2,3 are3,5,9. The series coefficients through degree three are1,3,7,15. The count at n=2 is five, not the series coefficient seven: logarithmic point-count data and ordinary generating coefficients are different sequences. source.title: Formal, rigid and Berkovich disks are related constructions with different data
source.status: Revised classical development with scoped worked result
source.summary: The closed unit disk over a nonarchimedean field gives a concrete way to distinguish formal models, analytic functions and seminorm points. The Gauss norm can be proved multiplicative, and a simple polynomial shows that the resulting Berkovich point is not evaluation at a single ordinary field-valued point.
definitions: Let K=Q_p with its usual nonarchimedean absolute value. The Tate algebra K⟨T⟩ consists of seriesΣa_nT^n with a_n→0, endowed with Gauss norm max_n|a_n|. A standard integral formal model uses Z_p⟨T⟩. A Berkovich point is an appropriate bounded multiplicative seminorm extending the absolute value on K.

result.name: The Gauss norm is multiplicative and differs from point evaluation
result.statement: For polynomials f,g over K, ||fg||_G=||f||_G||g||_G. Evaluation at any a with|a|≤1 satisfies|f(a)|≤||f||_G. The Gauss seminorm is not evaluation at any single such a∈K.
result.proof: The coefficient triangle inequality gives the upper bound. Rescale each nonzero polynomial by a coefficient of maximal absolute value, so both have integral coefficients and a nonzero reduction in F_p[T]. Their reductions have a nonzero product because that polynomial ring is a domain. Some coefficient of the product is therefore a unit, proving the lower bound after restoring the scales. The evaluation inequality follows termwise from the ultrametric inequality and|a|≤1. For any proposed evaluation point a, the polynomial T−a has Gauss norm one but evaluates to zero at a, disproving equality of these seminorms.

example.setup: Use p=3, f=1+3T and g=1+T.
example.calculation: Both Gauss norms are one, and fg=1+4T+3T² still has norm one. Their reductions are1 and1+T, whose product is nonzero. The formal reduction of the integral model records a special fiber over F₃, whereas the generic analytic disk concerns a K-algebra. The Gauss point records the whole unit-disk norm rather than choosing one residue or evaluation coordinate.
example.conclusion: The constructions are related by precise model and analytification procedures, not by interchangeable terminology.

source.limits: This polynomial proof is not a construction of all rigid or Berkovich geometry. Extensions to convergent series use completion, and generic-fiber conventions depend on the formal topology. No operadic correction is supplied by the mere existence of these spaces.

source.summary: A one-even-variable, one-odd-variable algebra gives an explicit model in which square-zero and bracket calculations can be completed. result.statement: Δ²=0 and Δ has differential order at most two. For polynomials f,g, {f,g}=0, {f,gθ}=f′g, {fθ,g}=−fg′ and{fθ,gθ}=(f′g−fg′)θ. In particular{x,θ}=1 and{θ,x}=−1.

source.summary: The source gap is preserved: no exact Hardy–BMO modification or date within the two-day cluster is invented. definitions: For a locally integrable real b and bounded interval I, let b_I be its average and osc_I(b)=|I|⁻¹∫_I|b−b_I|. The classical BMO seminorm is the supremum over intervals. An H¹ atom on I has mean zero, support in I and L∞ norm at most1/|I|.

result.statement: |∫ab|≤osc_I(b) for an atom a supported on I. If b∈BMO and||e||∞≤ε, then b+e∈BMO and||b+e||_BMO≤||b||_BMO+2ε. Applying the same bound to−e gives the finite two-sided seminorm difference bound.
result.proof: Because the atom has mean zero, ∫ab=∫a(b−b_I). Bounding|a| by1/|I| gives the first inequality. result.statement: The discriminant of E is37. Its point counts at p=2,3,5,7 are5,7,8,9, giving traces −2,−3,−2,−1 respectively.

source.title: A rational point of infinite order without assuming BSD
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: A numerical deformation of Frobenius traces is not a rank theorem. For the same curve, a short exact argument proves a genuine rank lower bound by identifying a non-torsion rational point. This separates an established statement from the much stronger BSD claim.
definitions: The rational points of an elliptic curve form an abelian group with identity O, the point at infinity.
At a good prime p, reduction is injective on rational torsion whose order is prime to p. This classical reduction theorem is the only structural input used here.

result.name: A certified non-torsion point
result.statement: For E:y²+y=x³−x, the torsion subgroup E(Q)_tors is trivial. Consequently P=(0,0) has infinite order and rank E(Q)≥1.
result.proof: The preceding exact counts give #E(F5)=8 and #E(F7)=9. Suppose E(Q) contains torsion of prime order ℓ. If ℓ≠5, injectivity of ℓ-torsion under reduction at5 forces ℓ|8, so ℓ=2. But reduction at7, where ℓ≠7, then forces2|9, impossible. If ℓ=5, reduction at7 forces5|9, also impossible. Every nontrivial finite abelian group has an element of prime order, so rational torsion is trivial. The point(0,0) lies on the curve and differs from O; it is therefore non-torsion. A non-torsion element supplies a copy of Z inside E(Q), proving the rank lower bound. This does not require knowing the analytic order of vanishing of L(E,s). The two reduction primes are used asymmetrically only to respect the prime-to-p restriction. In general, gcd(#E(Fp),#E(Fq))=1 at distinct good primes does not justify simply quoting an unrestricted injection twice; the proof must separately exclude possible p-primary and q-primary torsion. Those exclusions are explicit here.

example.setup: Check several multiples of P by the generalized Weierstrass group law.
example.calculation: Negation is(x,y)↦(x,−y−1). The tangent at P has slope−1, giving2P=(1,0). Adding P gives3P=(−1,−1). Further exact rational additions yield7P=(−5/9,8/27); substitution gives y²+y=280/729 and x³−x=280/729. The non-torsion conclusion itself comes from the reduction argument, not from merely observing several nonzero multiples.
example.conclusion: An exact arithmetic certificate proves rank at least1 while leaving rank upper bounds and BSD outside its scope.

source.limits: The injectivity theorem is stated with its prime-to-p restriction; ignoring that restriction would invalidate many reduction arguments. This proof does not establish rank exactly1, finiteness of the Tate–Shafarevich group or the BSD leading coefficient.

definitions: For good primes set t_p=a_p/(2√p)∈[−1,1] and θ_p=arccos t_p∈[0,π].

result.name: Normalization and elementary moments
result.statement: The Sato–Tate probability law has E[t]=0 and E[t²]=1/4; equivalently for u=2t=a_p/√p it has E[u²]=1. If g is measurable, a transformed variable g(t) follows the pushforward law, not automatically the original law.

For the second moment, write t=sinφ and integrate: ∫_(−1)^1t²√(1−t²)dt=π/8. Multiplication by2/π gives1/4. More directly the beta integral gives the same value. The density integrates to1 because the upper semicircle has areaπ/2. For a transformed variable, probabilities satisfy P(g(t)∈B)=μ(g⁻¹(B)); unless g preserves μ, the law changes. For example g(t)=ct with |c|≠1 changes the second moment to c²/4 and its support to[−|c|,|c|]. Hasse’s bound is what keeps the classical t_p inside[−1,1]. source.title: A Benford law needs logarithmic equidistribution
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The September 10 assistant claim gives no usable definition or asymptotic proof of a deformed Benford law for elliptic coefficients. A sound formulation reduces leading digits to fractional logarithms and proves an exact model where equidistribution is available.
definitions: For x>0, its base10 leading digit is d when the fractional part of log10x lies in[log10d,log10(d+1)).
For signed coefficients use |a_n|; zero coefficients must be excluded or counted in a separately specified category.

result.name: A sufficient criterion and a proved model
result.statement: If the fractional parts of log10x_n are uniformly distributed on[0,1), then digit d has limiting frequency log10(1+1/d). For x_n=10^(nθ), every irrational θ satisfies this criterion.
result.proof: The digit event is precisely the interval in the definition, whose length is log10(d+1)−log10d. Uniform distribution gives its limiting frequency. For the model sequence and every nonzero integer k, the exponential average is N⁻¹Σ_(n=1)^N exp(2πiknθ). It is a geometric sum with ratio q=exp(2πikθ)≠1. Its magnitude is at most2/(N|1−q|), which tends to zero. Weyl’s criterion therefore yields uniform distribution. The nonvanishing denominator is where irrationality is used. In contrast, x_n=10^n always begins with1; rapid growth alone is insufficient. A nonlinear change of the index or coefficients needs a new equidistribution argument, because it changes the logarithmic sequence. The exponential-sum estimate depends onk through|1−exp(2πikθ)|. It proves convergence for every fixed nonzerok but does not give a uniform discrepancy bound over allk. A quantitative digit error estimate needs additional Diophantine control or an explicit finite-frequency approximation of the interval indicator.

example.setup: Take θ=√2 and compare x_n=10^(n√2) with y_n=10^n. No huge numbers need be formed.
example.calculation: For x_n compute only {n√2}; the limiting probability of first digit1 is log10 2≈0.30103 and of digit9 is log10(10/9)≈0.04576. For y_n every fractional logarithm is0, so digit1 has frequency1. A finite program can count the first10000 logarithmic fractions reproducibly, but the geometric-sum proof supplies the actual limiting conclusion.
example.conclusion: Benford behavior is an equidistribution theorem, not a generic consequence of attaching an exponent or a star to an arithmetic sequence.

result.name: Two-point identifiability
result.statement: Two exact positive correction measurements d1=d(x1), d2=d(x2), with x1≠x2, determine β=log(d2/d1)/log(x2/x1) and α=d1/x1^β uniquely.

Conversely, the resulting pair satisfies both observations, so existence and uniqueness hold. With noisy observations, the same transformation becomes linear regression, but its errors are logarithmic errors, not necessarily additive errors in the original units. One observation gives the entire curve α=d1x1^(−β), so it cannot distinguish exponents. A short input range makes log(x2/x1) small and amplifies measurement errors. This is a conditioning issue that extra printed decimal places do not resolve.

source.title: A Toeplitz eigenvalue law with a complete elementary proof
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered spectral-limit expression needs a symbol, matrix convention and test-function class. The tridiagonal Toeplitz family gives a complete exact calculation and makes the limiting measure visible without relying on a general theorem whose hypotheses were omitted.
definitions: Let T_n have diagonal entries a and adjacent off-diagonal entries b, with real a,b. Its symbol is f(θ)=a+2b cosθ.
The empirical spectral average is n⁻¹Σ_(k=1)^nF(λ_k(T_n)).

result.name: An exact Toeplitz spectral limit
result.statement: The eigenvalues are λ_k=a+2b cos(kπ/(n+1)). For every continuous F on[a−2|b|,a+2|b|], the empirical average tends toπ⁻¹∫₀πF(a+2b cosθ)dθ, equivalently the normalized circle integral.
result.proof: For k=1,…,n set v_j=sin(jkπ/(n+1)), with boundary values v_0=v_(n+1)=0. The identity v_(j−1)+v_(j+1)=2cos(kπ/(n+1))v_j shows T_nv=λ_kv. The sine vectors are an orthogonal basis, so these are all eigenvalues, including multiplicities. The average of F at the equally spaced interior angles is a Riemann sum for the continuous integrand. Replacing n by n+1 in the normalization changes the limit by a factor tending to1, and the endpoints contribute vanishing weight. Reflection of cosine extends the half-circle integral to the full-circle expression. When b=0 the measure is the point mass at a, covered by the same formula. For b≠0, changing variablesx=a+2b cosθ gives limiting density1/[π√(4b²−(x−a)²)] on the interior of the spectral interval. Its integrable endpoint singularities explain why a uniform angular mesh does not produce a uniform eigenvalue density. This density is derived from the same cosine map, not separately fitted.

example.setup: Choose a=3,b=1 and F(t)=t².
example.calculation: Tr(T_n²)=n a²+2(n−1)b²=11n−2, so the empirical second moment is11−2/n. The integral gives the same limit because the cosine mean is0 and cosine-square mean is1/2: a²+4b²(1/2)=11. At n=3, the eigenvalues are3+√2,3,3−√2, with squares totaling31=11·3−2.
example.conclusion: The recovered limit is valid here with explicit finite-size error for the quadratic test function.

source.limits: This proof is for a scalar real tridiagonal symbol and continuous F. General symbols, discontinuous tests, nonnormal Toeplitz matrices or logarithms near zero require additional theorems. A spectral average alone does not establish a proposed decay-rate formula.
source.extension: For polynomial symbols, compare normalized traces of powers and control boundary terms. Then extend from polynomial to continuous test functions by uniform approximation.

source.title: A Toeplitz log determinant needs positivity
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The historical use of an integral of log f resembles a Toeplitz determinant theorem, but it was inserted into an undefined decay model. A positive tridiagonal family gives an exact determinant recurrence and an independently derived limiting logarithm.
definitions: Let T_n=tridiag(b,a,b) with a>2|b| and D_n=detT_n; set D_0=1.
Define r_±=(a±√(a²−4b²))/2. For b≠0, 0<r_-<r_+; b=0 is immediate.

result.name: Exact determinant and limiting geometric mean
result.statement: D_n=(r_+^(n+1)−r_-^(n+1))/(r_+−r_-), and lim n⁻¹logD_n=logr_+=π⁻¹∫₀πlog(a+2b cosθ)dθ.
result.proof: Expansion along the last row gives D_n=aD_(n−1)−b²D_(n−2), with D_0=1,D_1=a. Solving this second-order recurrence yields the formula, as its two characteristic roots are r_±. Factor r_+^(n+1) to obtain logD_n=(n+1)logr_++log[1−(r_-/r_+)^(n+1)]−log(r_+−r_-). Division by n gives the limit. Independently, the preceding eigenvalue formula and the positivity bound λ_k≥a−2|b|>0 permit the continuous test F=log, so the same limit is the symbol integral. This proves the integral identity without importing a decay interpretation. Positivity supplies a consistent real logarithm and bounds it on the entire spectral interval. Positive definiteness can also be verified without eigenvectors: the quadratic form is aΣu_j²+2bΣu_ju_(j+1), bounded below by(a−2|b|)Σu_j² using2|uv|≤u²+v². Thus every finite determinant is positive under the same hypothesis, independently confirming that its real logarithm is legitimate.

example.setup: Take a=3,b=1.
example.calculation: D_0=1,D_1=3,D_2=8,D_3=21,D_4=55. The limiting geometric mean isr_+=(3+√5)/2≈2.61803. For n=4, D_4^(1/4)=55^(1/4), still above that limit. The recurrence gives every finite determinant exactly and a transparent exponential correction through(r_-/r_+)^(n+1).
example.conclusion: The logarithmic integral computes a normalized determinant in this model. Calling its exponential a decay rate requires a separate, defined dynamical equation.

source.limits: At a=2|b| the symbol touches zero and the continuity argument for log fails, although some limits can still exist after extra work. With a sign-changing or complex symbol, branches, zeros and possible winding become substantive issues.
source.extension: If a proposed Γ uses this determinant, state the finite-n formula relating Γ_n to D_n, check its units and derive its limit. Do not identify a geometric mean with a physical or arithmetic observable by notation alone.

source.title: The atomic Hardy-space inequality requires cancellation
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered inequality is a standard atomic estimate once the function has mean zero. Omitting cancellation materially changes the theorem. The normalization can be proved in one line, but specifying the ambient real Hardy space and the atom conditions is essential.
definitions: On R^d, an L² Hardy atom supported in a ball B has integral0 and L² norm at most |B|^(−1/2).
The atomic H¹ norm is the infimum of Σ|λ_j| over representations g=Σλ_ja_j by such atoms. This chooses an equivalent Hardy norm convention.

result.name: A correctly normalized one-atom estimate
result.statement: If g∈L² is supported in B and ∫g=0, then ||g||_(H¹,atomic)≤|B|^(1/2)||g||₂. The zero function is included.
result.proof: For g≠0 put λ=|B|^(1/2)||g||₂ and a=g/λ. The support and mean-zero conditions are preserved. Moreover ||a||₂=|B|^(−1/2), so a is an atom. The single-term representation g=λa gives the stated upper bound by the infimum definition. Also Cauchy–Schwarz gives ||a||₁≤1, so atomic convergence in coefficient sum entails L¹ convergence and preserves zero integral. Consequently every function represented by these global atoms has integral0. A nonnegative nonzero compactly supported bump has positive integral and cannot satisfy this global atomic H¹ condition, even though it has finite support and finite L² norm. This is a direct obstruction to dropping the cancellation hypothesis.

example.setup: Let B=[−1,1] in R and g=1_[−1,0]−1_[0,1], with endpoints irrelevant in L².
example.calculation: The support has measure2, the integral is0 and ||g||₂=√2. Hence the coefficient bound is2. Indeed a=g/2 has L² norm1/√2 and is an atom, while ||g||₁=2 forces every atomic coefficient sum to be at least2. Thus its atomic H¹ norm is exactly2 in this convention.
example.conclusion: The example both proves the bound can be sharp and identifies the missing mean-zero assumption.

source.limits: Local Hardy spaces, Hardy spaces on compact groups and analytic Hardy spaces use related but different atom conventions. The constant changes under equivalent norm definitions. The historical notation did not specify which setting was intended.
source.extension: For a supported function with nonzero mean, split it into a canceled part plus its average times a fixed bump. Analyze the second part in an appropriate local Hardy space rather than applying the global estimate.

source.title: A6 automorphisms must preserve element orders and class structure
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered passage names A6 outer automorphisms without specifying an actual map. Before proposing such a map, one can compute conjugacy classes and enforce automorphism invariants. This prevents an informal relabeling of cycle types from masquerading as an automorphism.
definitions: A6 consists of the360 even permutations of six symbols. An automorphism is a bijective homomorphism A6→A6.
An inner automorphism is conjugation by a group element. Outer means its class modulo inner automorphisms is nontrivial.

result.name: Necessary invariants and an exact class inventory
result.statement: Every automorphism preserves element order, centralizer size and conjugacy-class size. A6 has class sizes1,45,40,40,90,72,72, corresponding to types1,(2,2),(3),(3,3),(4,2) and two split5-cycle classes.
result.proof: For an automorphism φ, φ(g^m)=φ(g)^m, and applying φ⁻¹ gives equality of orders. The map x↦φ(x) bijects C(g) with C(φ(g)), because commuting equations are preserved in both directions. Orbit–stabilizer then preserves class size. Count double transpositions by choosing their four symbols and one of three pairings:15·3=45. Three-cycles number C(6,3)·2=40. Products of two disjoint three-cycles number(1/2)C(6,3)·2²=40. Type(4,2) has C(6,4)·6=90. There are6·24=144 five-cycles. Their S6 class splits in A6: the centralizer of a five-cycle is its cyclic order5 subgroup and contains no odd permutation, so each A6 orbit has360/5=72 elements. The sizes total360 and exhaust the group.

example.setup: Consider a proposed map taking a3-cycle to a5-cycle, and another merely exchanging the two order3 cycle types.
example.calculation: The first proposal fails immediately because orders3 and5 differ. The second passes these necessary tests: both relevant classes have size40 and centralizer order9. Passing does not prove that an extension to all360 elements is a homomorphism. A full certificate must verify products, or provide a structural construction such as the exceptional S6 action and its restriction.
example.conclusion: The exceptional phenomenon can be discussed precisely without inventing a map from matching labels alone.

source.limits: The full classification Out(A6)≅C2×C2 is a classical theorem requiring additional construction and proof; it is not derived by this inventory. The cited primary work constructs the exceptional S6 automorphism, a related ingredient. The executable check verifies the inventory, not the full automorphism classification.

source.title: Weight38 modular forms: specify the group, then compute the space
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The historical mention of weight38 does not specify level or character. The level-one case is a precise starting point with an exact basis. Weight alone would not determine a space at arbitrary level.
definitions: Let M_k denote holomorphic modular forms of weight k for SL2(Z), and S_k its cusp subspace.

result.name: An exact level-one basis
result.statement: M_38 has basis E4^8E6, E4^5E6³, E4²E6⁵ and dimension3. Its cusp subspace has dimension2 and equals ΔM_26, with basis ΔE4^5E6 and ΔE4²E6³.
result.proof: The classical level-one structure theorem says the graded ring is C[E4,E6], with weights4 and6, and its cusp ideal is generated by Δ of weight12. These structural theorems are the stated external input; the remaining computation is elementary. Solving4a+6b=38 means2a+3b=19. Nonnegative solutions are(a,b)=(8,1),(5,3),(2,5). Algebraic independence supplies the displayed basis. Similarly4a+6b=26 gives(a,b)=(5,1),(2,3), proving the cusp dimension and basis after multiplication by Δ. Each weight38 monomial has constant term1, so the cusp condition on a linear combination is exactly that its three coefficients sum to zero; this independently identifies a two-dimensional kernel. For example E4^8E6−E4^5E6³=1728ΔE4^5E6 by the defining relation for Δ. Multiplication byΔ is injective because a holomorphic form whose product with the nonzero holomorphic functionΔ vanishes must itself vanish on a nonempty open set and hence everywhere. This justifies the dimension transfer S38=ΔM26 once the classical cusp-ideal theorem is supplied. A Fourier truncation is a check, not a replacement for the structure theorem.

example.setup: Compute the first Fourier coefficient of the first two monomials.
example.calculation: For E4^8E6 it is8·240−504=1416. For E4^5E6³ it is5·240−3·504=−312. Their difference has q-coefficient1728, agreeing with1728ΔE4^5E6 because Δ begins q and the remaining factor has constant term1. The third monomial has q-coefficient2·240−5·504=−2040.
example.conclusion: The weight38 reference becomes a finite exact vector-space calculation with a clear cusp test.

source.limits: This does not determine a level-N space, Hecke eigenbasis, coefficient field or attached Galois representation. Those depend on additional data. The ring theorem is cited, while the basis enumeration and Fourier checks are reproduced exactly.

source.title: A sublinear signed deformation is a homeomorphism, with a cusp at zero
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The historical radial correction becomes a precise real-variable map once its sign and parameter range are fixed. It is invertible for every α>0 and 0<β<1, but its derivative is unbounded near zero. This distinction matters whenever the map is inserted into a differential equation or metric.
definitions: Let φ(x)=x+α sign(x)|x|^β and φ(0)=0.
A map is inverse 1-Lipschitz when |φ⁻¹(u)−φ⁻¹(v)|≤|u−v| for all u,v.

result.name: Global inversion and regularity
result.statement: For α>0 and 0<β<1, φ is an increasing homeomorphism R→R. Its inverse is 1-Lipschitz. The map φ is smooth off zero and fails to have a finite derivative at zero.
result.proof: The signed power s(x)=sign(x)|x|^β is continuous and strictly increasing. Thus for y>x, φ(y)−φ(x)=(y−x)+α[s(y)−s(x)]≥y−x>0. This proves injectivity and the inverse Lipschitz inequality. The limits at positive and negative infinity are respectively positive and negative infinity; continuity and the intermediate value theorem give surjectivity. A continuous strictly monotone bijection has a continuous inverse. For x≠0, φ′(x)=1+αβ|x|^(β−1)>1. At zero, φ(h)/h=1+α|h|^(β−1), which diverges as h→0. Consequently a smooth change-of-variables theorem requiring a finite nonzero derivative cannot be invoked at zero. There is a useful local Hölder estimate as well: for0<β<1, the signed power is β-Hölder with constant at most2^(1−β). On a bounded interval, φ therefore has a quantitative modulus of continuity even though it is not Lipschitz at zero. This separates continuity, differentiability and inverse stability.

example.setup: Take α=1/3 and β=2/3. Evaluate at x=−8,0,8 and examine the inverse close to zero.
example.calculation: φ(8)=8+4/3=28/3 and φ(−8)=−28/3. For small y, y≈α sign(x)|x|^β, hence φ⁻¹(y)≈sign(y)(|y|/α)^(1/β)=sign(y)(3|y|)^(3/2). The exact inverse inequality bounds any recovered-input error by the output error.
example.conclusion: The transformation is globally well behaved for inversion, while differentiating it at its cusp requires separate treatment. These are compatible facts.

source.limits: The later logistic-factor formula X+α|X|^βF(X/X_P) is a different function and has not been substituted into this proof. Its negative-input behavior and monotonicity require their own analysis.

source.title: An irrational angular frequency does not define a closed polar curve
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered “irrational monogon” series must first pass a periodicity test. A formula on the real angular line is not automatically a function on the quotient circle R/(2πZ). Without that descent, closing the curve and assigning its homology are extra operations.
definitions: A function r:R→R descends to S¹ precisely when r(θ+2π)=r(θ) for all θ.
For positive continuous periodic r, the map θ↦r(θ)(cosθ,sinθ) is a polar graph.

result.name: A one-mode obstruction
result.statement: For a≠0 and ξ>0, r(θ)=1+a cos(ξθ) is 2π-periodic if and only if ξ is an integer. For irrational ξ, the endpoints of its restriction to [0,2π] have different radial distances.
result.proof: If r is periodic, evaluate at θ=0 to obtain cos(2πξ)=1, hence ξ is an integer. Conversely an integer frequency is periodic by the cosine addition formula. For irrational ξ, cos(2πξ)≠1, so r(2π)−r(0)=a[cos(2πξ)−1]≠0. The same polar direction at the two endpoints therefore has different radii. This proof does not automatically classify infinite sums: different frequencies can cancel, and their coefficients must be examined. It does show that irrationality by itself is not a mechanism producing a closed “one-sided” polygon. One may instead study an almost-periodic function on R, or add a closing segment, but those choices define different spaces. If a closing segment is explicitly added, the resulting loop can be studied, but its geometry depends on that segment. An endpoint identification in the parameter interval is a quotient construction instead and may fail to give a continuous planar map when the two endpoints have different images. These are distinct repairs.

example.setup: Take r(θ)=1+(1/4)cos(√2θ). It stays between3/4 and5/4, so the issue is not passage through the origin.
example.calculation: r(0)=5/4, while r(2π)=1+(1/4)cos(2π√2)≠5/4. The polar arc therefore has a nonzero endpoint gap of magnitude (1/4)|1−cos(2π√2)|. Replacing √2 by3 makes the endpoint gap zero and produces a threefold periodic radial graph.
example.conclusion: A continuous nonclosed arc and a simple closed curve have different topological models. The model must be chosen before computing homology.

source.limits: This is a necessary-definition correction, not a proof that every irrational-frequency infinite series is nonperiodic. Nor does it preclude studying nonperiodic angular curves as legitimate objects.
source.extension: For a finite trigonometric sum with distinct positive frequencies, prove linear independence of exponentials to determine exactly which coefficients can survive a prescribed period. Then specify whether the domain is R, an interval or S¹.

source.title: Regularity of the recovered lacunary angular series
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: A meaningful infinite angular construction needs a convergence theorem. The same coefficients that control its size do not necessarily control its slopes: each differentiation multiplies the nth oscillation by ξ^n. This gives an explicit hierarchy of sufficient conditions.
definitions: Let ξ>1 and r(θ)=1+Σ_{n≥0}a_n cos(ξ^nθ).
For k≥0, put M_k=Σ_{n≥0}|a_n|ξ^(kn), allowing the value infinity.

result.name: A sufficient regularity criterion
result.statement: If M_k is finite for an integer k≥0, the series defines a C^k function on R. Every derivative of order j≤k is obtained term by term and is uniformly bounded by M_j.
result.proof: The jth derivative of a_n cos(ξ^nθ) has absolute value at most |a_n|ξ^(jn). Since ξ>1 and j≤k, finiteness of M_k implies finiteness of M_j. The Weierstrass uniform convergence test therefore applies to every derivative series through order k. To justify differentiation, fix a base point and integrate the uniformly convergent first derivative series: the fundamental theorem of calculus identifies its integral with the uniform limit of the original partial sums. Repeating this argument proves the result through order k. The criterion is sufficient only. Failure of absolute summability of derivative bounds does not by itself prove nondifferentiability, because cancellation can matter. For k=0 the uniform tail bound is sup|Σ_(n>N)a_n cos(ξ^nθ)|≤Σ_(n>N)|a_n|. In the first geometric example this equals(1/16)(1/8)^(N+1)/(1−1/8). Thus every plotted truncation has a certified amplitude error, independently of sampling density on the angular line.

example.setup: Choose a_n=2^(−3n−4), ξ=2, and n starting at0. Compare it with a_n=2^(−n−4).
example.calculation: For the first choice, M_0=(1/16)/(1−1/8)=1/14 and M_2=(1/16)/(1−1/2)=1/8. Hence r≥13/14 and r is C² with |r″|≤1/8. For the second, M_0=1/8 but the first derivative majorant is Σ1/16, which diverges; the theorem guarantees continuity but supplies no C¹ conclusion.
example.conclusion: The first series is a quantitatively controlled positive radial function. The second needs additional analysis before slopes or curvature can be used.

source.limits: For noninteger ξ the resulting function still need not descend to S¹. Positivity and regularity do not repair missing periodicity. No fractal dimension is inferred from the divergence of a sufficient derivative bound.

source.title: Homology follows from a specified space, not a deformation name
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The historical rank formula needs a definition of κ and a construction of the underlying space. Two elementary models expose the issue: a finite graph has computable cycle rank, whereas every positive continuous periodic radial graph is a single topological circle.
definitions: A finite graph has V vertices, E edges and C connected components; homology here uses integer coefficients.
A positive radial graph is Γ={r(θ)(cosθ,sinθ):θ∈S¹} with continuous r>0.

result.name: Two exact homology models
result.statement: For a finite graph, H0≅Z^C, H1≅Z^(E−V+C), and higher homology vanishes. A positive continuous radial graph has H0≅Z and H1≅Z.
result.proof: Orient the graph edges. Its boundary map ∂1:Z^E→Z^V sends an oriented edge to head minus tail. On each connected component, a spanning tree supplies V_component−1 independent boundary columns; all columns lie in the subgroup whose coordinate sum on that component is zero. Thus rank ∂1=V−C. There are no 2-cells, so H1=ker∂1, a free group of rank E−V+C; H0 is the component group. For Γ, the polar parameterization is a continuous bijection from compact S¹ to a Hausdorff space: positivity makes its inverse the angular projection. It is therefore a homeomorphism, and the usual circle homology applies. Subdividing a graph edge increases both E and V by one and leaves E−V+C unchanged. This is an elementary consistency check for the claimed invariant: changing the mesh of a polygonal approximation should not create a new cycle merely by inserting vertices. Adding an actual closing edge can change the rank.

example.setup: Compare a circle with a connected graph consisting of two circles meeting at one vertex.

source.title: A complete small sheaf calculation before spectral-sequence claims
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered passage names sheaf spectral sequences without specifying a sheaf or cover. A two-set calculation gives the missing data and shows exactly where first cohomology comes from. The example uses the constant real sheaf on a circle.
definitions: Cover S¹ by two connected proper open arcs U,V whose intersection has two connected components.

result.name: The circle Čech calculation
result.statement: For this cover and the constant real sheaf, the Čech complex is R²→R², (a,b)↦(b−a,b−a), in degrees0 and1. Its cohomology is R in each of degrees0 and1, and zero above1.
result.proof: A section on each connected arc is a single number, so degree0 is R⊕R. A section on U∩V can take independent values on its two components, so degree1 is R⊕R. Restriction subtracts the U-value from the V-value on both components, producing the displayed differential. Its kernel is the diagonal line a=b, and its image is the diagonal line in degree1. Thus H0 has dimension1 and H1 is R² modulo a one-dimensional diagonal, also dimension1. There are no triple intersections of distinct cover members, so higher Čech groups vanish. Because the arcs and their intersection components are contractible and acyclic for this sheaf, this cover computes the sheaf cohomology. The acyclicity is part of why this particular cover is useful.

example.setup: Take the degree1 cochain c=(1,0). Determine whether it is a coboundary.
example.calculation: Every coboundary has equal coordinates, so c cannot equal(b−a,b−a). Its class is nonzero. The quotient can be identified with R by the difference map (u,v)↦u−v; c maps to1. A class represented by(5,4) is the same class because their difference(4,4) is a coboundary.
example.conclusion: The nontrivial class records incompatibility between the two overlap components. There is no need to infer it from an undefined “deformed” spectral sequence.

source.title: Hochschild homology and K-theory detect different data
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: Naming several invariants does not make them interchangeable. An exact matrix example supplies two computable definitions and shows why a topological-cycle rank cannot simply be reused as a Hochschild or K-theory rank.
definitions: For a complex algebra A, HH0(A)=A/[A,A], where [A,A] is the linear span of commutators xy−yx.
For a unital C*-algebra, K0 is the group completion of stable projection classes. For complex matrix algebras these classes are classified by ordinary rank after stabilization.

result.name: An explicit matrix calculation
result.statement: HH0(M₂(C))≅C via trace, whereas K0(M₂(C))≅Z via stable rank. With the rank-one projection as generator, the unit matrix has K0-class2.
result.proof: Trace annihilates every commutator, since Tr(XY)=Tr(YX). Conversely, write Eij for matrix units. The off-diagonal units satisfy E12=[E11,E12] and E21=[E22,E21], while E11−E22=[E12,E21]. These three matrices span the traceless subspace. Hence the commutator span is exactly the kernel of trace, so the quotient is one-dimensional and trace identifies it with C. For K0, a complex projection is unitarily diagonalizable with diagonal entries0 or1. Under direct sum, ranks add. Every nonnegative rank occurs among matrix algebras over M₂(C), and equality of rank gives stable equivalence. The resulting monoid is N and its group completion is Z. The identity in M₂(C) has rank2, explaining the normalization of its class. The trace used in the Hochschild quotient is unnormalized, so the identity matrix maps to2. A normalized trace would send it to1 and change the numerical comparison with K0, without changing either invariant group. This small normalization choice is another reason to state a proposed comparison map explicitly.

example.setup: Consider P=diag(1,0) and Q=diag(0,1).
example.calculation: P−Q=[E12,E21] vanishes in HH0. In K0 the projections P and Q are equivalent via the matrix unit E21, so [P]−[Q]=0 as well. However Tr(P)=1 is a complex scalar while [P] is an integer class; these live in different coefficient groups. The trace induces a particular map between them after choosing the normalization.
example.conclusion: Explicit definitions explain both agreements and distinctions. A common symbol or shared rank does not identify the theories.

source.limits: This proves only degree-zero Hochschild homology and K0 for this matrix algebra. Higher Hochschild/cyclic groups, topological K-theory of spaces and algebraic K-theory require their own definitions. No general deformation-invariance theorem is asserted.

source.title: A genuine deformed algebra requires transported operations
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered framework applies a common deformation to many algebraic objects. A rigorous interpretation is transport of structure: a bijection can re-express a known algebra without changing its identities. Merely replacing symbols by starred symbols does not determine a new multiplication.
definitions: Let φ:R→R be a bijection. Define x⊕y=φ⁻¹(φ(x)+φ(y)) and x⊙y=φ⁻¹(φ(x)φ(y)).
The transported zero is z=φ⁻¹(0), and the transported unit is e=φ⁻¹(1). Scalar coordinates are part of the definition.

result.name: Transport gives an isomorphic field
result.statement: The operations ⊕ and ⊙ make R into a field isomorphic to the ordinary real field by φ. In particular, associativity and distributivity are exact, irrespective of whether φ is linear.
result.proof: Apply φ to (x⊕y)⊕w. The result is (φ(x)+φ(y))+φ(w), which equals φ(x)+(φ(y)+φ(w)); injectivity of φ proves associativity. Similarly φ(x⊙(y⊕w))=φ(x)(φ(y)+φ(w))=φ(x)φ(y)+φ(x)φ(w)=φ((x⊙y)⊕(x⊙w)). The remaining field axioms follow by the same argument, with additive inverse φ⁻¹(−φ(x)) and multiplicative inverse φ⁻¹(1/φ(x)) when x≠z. This proof also explains its limit: no new intrinsic field invariant appears, because φ is an explicit isomorphism. Geometry, norms or differentiation added afterward may change, but they need independent definitions. For the cubic example the transported additive inverse remains−x, but the transported sum is not ordinary addition. Its scalar action must likewise be transported: c acting onx becomesφ⁻¹(cφ(x)) if the scalar field itself is left in ordinary coordinates. Mixing these two scalar conventions would create a different structure.

example.setup: Use φ(x)=x³, a simple exact bijection that avoids numerical inversion.
example.calculation: x⊕y=(x³+y³)^(1/3), whereas x⊙y=xy. Thus 1⊕1=2^(1/3). Both (1⊕1)⊕(−1) and 1⊕(1⊕(−1)) equal1. Ordinary addition combined with an arbitrary corrected product would not be covered by this calculation.
example.conclusion: The example supplies an exact associative deformation, with a completely explicit explanation of what has and has not changed.

source.limits: Transport through a coordinate bijection is not a proof that a proposed starred Lie algebra, magic square or mass formula has new representation theory. For vector spaces or noncommutative algebras, one must specify a bijection on the entire underlying set and transport all relevant operations.

result.proof: The vector z determines a line ℓ=Cz in C^m. The covector w vanishes on ℓ, and the rank-one tensor z⊗w defines a linear map C^m/ℓ→ℓ. Under(z,w)↦(tz,t⁻¹w) this map is unchanged. Other charts glue by the usual cotangent transition law, so this local calculation is compatible with the global bundle description rather than merely an informal equation count.

result.statement: The initial-value problem D_C^γg=ag, g(0)=g0 has solution g(t)=g0E_γ(at^γ). Equivalently, g=g0+(a/Γ(γ))∫₀ᵗ(t−s)^(γ−1)g(s)ds.
result.proof: For a monomial with exponent q>0, the beta-integral substitution s=tu gives D_C^γt^q=Γ(q+1)t^(q−γ)/Γ(q+1−γ); a constant has Caputo derivative zero. Integrating the Caputo equation by the fractional integral yields the Volterra equation; conversely that equation can be differentiated fractionally under standard local regularity. Uniqueness on compact time intervals follows by iterating the Volterra bound: a difference is bounded by C|a|^nt^(nγ)/Γ(nγ+1) for all n, whose right side tends to zero. At γ=1 the Mittag-Leffler series becomes the ordinary exponential becauseΓ(n+1)=n!, so the model continuously connects to the familiar linear flow in that parameter limit. source.summary: The historical formula becomes rigorous when local outcomes are specified as signs on a common probability space. The same expression can then be evaluated for a singlet state and explicit spin observables. The two calculations use different mathematical models.
definitions: Let A,A′,B,B′ be random variables taking values±1 on one probability space.

result.name: Local bound and exact quantum example
result.statement: The displayed sum is at most2 in the common-probability-space model. The singlet with a=z,a′=x,b=(x+z)/√2,b′=(x−z)/√2 gives2√2.
result.proof: Write E(AB)−E(AB′)=E[A(B−B′)] and E(A′B)+E(A′B′)=E[A′(B+B′)]. By the triangle inequality their absolute values sum to at most E[|B−B′|+|B+B′|]. For signs B,B′, exactly one of the two inner quantities is2 and the other is0, so the expectation is2. The singlet correlation identity follows from its density matrix or by evaluating the Pauli tensor products: equal-axis correlations are−1 and cross-axis correlations vanish. For the chosen unit directions, E(a,b)=−1/√2, E(a,b′)=+1/√2, and both E(a′,b),E(a′,b′)=−1/√2. Substitution gives√2+√2. source.title: Unitary evolution does not make neighboring states orthogonal
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered discussion mentions temporal orthogonality but the relevant formula is truncated. A two-dimensional example settles the basic issue: unitarity preserves inner products between jointly evolved states, but does not make a trajectory orthogonal to itself at every later time.
definitions: For a self-adjoint finite-dimensional Hamiltonian H and ℏ=1, U(t)=e^(−itH).
The survival amplitude of a unit initial vector ψ is c(t)=〈ψ,U(t)ψ〉; orthogonality means c(t)=0.

result.name: An exact two-level orthogonality criterion
result.statement: For H=diag(1,−1) and ψ=(1,1)/√2, c(t)=cos t. Orthogonality occurs exactly at t=π/2+kπ, not at arbitrary nonzero time steps.
result.proof: Diagonal exponentiation gives U(t)=diag(e^(−it),e^(it)). Therefore c(t)=(e^(−it)+e^(it))/2=cos t. Its zeros are precisely the stated times. More generally, if ψ=Σ_jc_j e_j in an orthonormal eigenbasis, then c(t)=Σ_j|c_j|²e^(−itE_j). Thus the overlap is the Fourier transform of a probability measure on energies. If ψ is an eigenstate, the amplitude has modulus1 for every time and never vanishes. Also c(0)=1 and continuity ensures that every fixed finite-dimensional state has a nonzero overlap with itself for all sufficiently small time increments. A global phase multiplying a state changes its vector representative but not its ray or the modulus of its overlap. The eigenstate example makes this distinction exact: the vector rotates by e^(−it), yet its survival probability remains1. Orthogonality is invariant under those phase choices.

example.setup: Compare the equal superposition ψ above with the eigenstate e1.
example.calculation: For ψ, |c(π/4)|²=1/2 and |c(π/2)|²=0. For e1, c(t)=e^(−it) and |c(t)|²=1. The difference is entirely determined by the energy distribution, even though both evolutions are unitary under the same H.
example.conclusion: Orthogonality is a special cancellation condition in the energy phases. It cannot be imposed as a universal property of continuous unitary evolution.

source.limits: This example does not derive a general quantum speed-limit theorem. Unbounded operators require a self-adjoint domain and additional moment assumptions if derivatives of c(t) are used. The truncated historical source cannot support a more specific original theorem.

source.summary: The recovered scripts compare finite eigenvalues with a short list of zeta-zero ordinates. A residual is a useful certificate when the operator is self-adjoint and its domain is controlled. Without those hypotheses even a very small residual may not place an eigenvalue nearby.
definitions: For a unit vector v in the domain of A and a real candidate λ, the residual is r=Av−λv.

result.name: A self-adjoint residual bound
result.statement: If A is self-adjoint, dist(λ,σ(A))≤||r||. For a nonnormal matrix this conclusion can fail by an arbitrarily large factor.
result.proof: By the spectral theorem, ||(A−λ)v||²=∫|t−λ|²dμ_v(t). The probability measure μ_v is supported on σ(A), so the integral is at least dist(λ,σ(A))²∫dμ_v=dist(λ,σ(A))². Taking square roots gives the bound. This asserts proximity to some spectral point; it does not identify which eigenvalue, prove multiplicity or exclude missing eigenvalues. For a nonnormal counterexample let A=[[0,M],[0,0]] and w=(1,1/M), with λ=1. Then (A−I)w=(0,−1/M), so the normalized residual is1/√(M²+1), while the spectrum is{0} and the spectral distance is1. A certified residual interval may contain several eigenvalues. If the operator has a known isolated spectral cluster and a gap separating it from the rest, stronger subspace-angle estimates become possible. Such a gap must be established independently; choosing the nearest target ordinate afterward does not provide it.

example.setup: Use M=100 and compare with a diagonal self-adjoint matrix B=diag(1,4).

If a candidate is put into the matrix by construction, a small residual establishes only that construction, not correspondence with an independently defined arithmetic operator.
example.conclusion: Operator structure turns a residual into a precise spectral statement. Matching finitely many target numbers is a different validation question.

source.title: The GUE Wigner surmise has exact normalization, but is a model
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered formula is the GUE Wigner surmise. It is an exact elementary density with unit mean and a useful model for unfolded spacings, rather than the exact universal nearest-neighbor law of large GUE matrices. This distinction prevents an approximate diagnostic from becoming a theorem about zeros.
definitions: Let p(s)=(32/π²)s²e^(−4s²/π) for s≥0 and p(s)=0 otherwise.
An unfolded spacing compares neighboring levels after a declared transformation that makes their mean local density approximately1.

result.name: Normalization and first two moments
result.statement: The density p integrates to1, E[s]=1 and E[s²]=3π/8. Its variance is3π/8−1.
result.proof: For a>0, ∫₀∞s^m e^(−as²)ds=(1/2)a^(−(m+1)/2)Γ((m+1)/2), by u=as². Set a=4/π. For m=2 the integral is√π/(4a^(3/2))=π²/32, canceling the prefactor. For m=3 it is1/(2a²)=π²/32, so the mean is1. For m=4 it is3√π/(8a^(5/2)); multiplication gives3π/8. These identities certify the density, not a fit to a particular finite sequence. For zeta ordinates, the mean density varies with height, so raw gaps should not be pooled across very different heights without an explicit unfolding convention. The surmise has quadratic repulsion near zero because p(s)/s² tends to32/π². Its tail is Gaussian in s, unlike an exponential spacing law. These local and tail features are separate testable properties; imposing sample mean1 alone cannot enforce either of them on a finite dataset.

example.setup: Use the five recovered approximate ordinates14.134725,21.022039,25.010857,30.424876,32.935061.
example.calculation: The four gaps are6.887314,3.988818,5.414019,2.510185. Dividing by their sample mean4.700084 gives spacings with sample mean exactly1 by construction. That normalization consumes a degree of freedom and leaves only four observations; resemblance to a smooth density has no strong asymptotic content. The values were recovered as approximations, so no certified zero enclosure is claimed.
example.conclusion: The formula itself is precisely checkable. A four-spacing comparison is a small descriptive experiment with no implication of an exact spectral correspondence.

source.limits: Neither agreement with a random-matrix model nor disagreement in a tiny sample proves or refutes RH. The infinite GUE spacing law is more complicated than this surmise.
source.extension: Use a fixed smooth zero-counting approximation for unfolding, predeclare a large height window and examine several independent statistics. Keep sampling uncertainty separate from numerical error in the ordinates.

source.title: Euler products require a convergence domain and controlled tails
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered moment formula is nonstandard and its quantities, factors, branches and error term were not defined adequately. A rigorous replacement starts with a classical Euler product in its absolute-convergence domain and derives an explicit truncation error. A Hadamard product over zeros is a separate analytic construction.
definitions: For real σ>1 let Z_P(σ)=∏_{p≤P}(1−p^(−σ))⁻¹.
Absolute convergence permits expanding geometric series and reordering positive terms; for complex s one needs the corresponding absolute-value argument.

result.name: A reproducible Euler-product tail bound
result.statement: For σ>1 and integer P≥2, 0≤logζ(σ)−logZ_P(σ)≤P^(1−σ)/[(σ−1)(1−2^(−σ))].
result.proof: Unique factorization shows a finite product expands as the sum of n^(−σ) over integers whose prime factors are at mostP. Increasing P exhausts all integers, and monotone convergence yields ζ(σ). Next, −log(1−u)=Σ_{m≥1}u^m/m≤u/(1−u) for0≤u<1. Therefore the missing logarithm is at mostΣ_{p>P}p^(−σ)/(1−p^(−σ))≤(1−2^(−σ))⁻¹Σ_{n>P}n^(−σ). Since the summand decreases, the last tail is bounded by∫_P∞x^(−σ)dx=P^(1−σ)/(σ−1). This proves both convergence and the displayed certified inequality. It does not continue the product into the critical strip. The logarithmic enclosure can be exponentiated because all factors in the realσ>1 model are positive. For complexs, a chosen analytic logarithm is available through the absolutely convergent series, but an argument based only on positive inequalities no longer applies directly. The absolute-value majorant remains the appropriate starting point.

example.setup: Take σ=2 and P=100.
example.calculation: The logarithmic tail is at most1/[100(1−1/4)]=1/75. Thus Z_100(2)≤ζ(2)≤e^(1/75)Z_100(2), an explicit relative enclosure obtainable from finitely many primes. The bound is deliberately elementary and can be sharpened with arithmetic information.
example.conclusion: A product formula needs definitions, a region and a truncation theorem. These are missing from the historical mixed moment/zero expression.

source.limits: The proposed exponent involving λ(1−λ) has ambiguous grouping in the retrieved text and may require complex branch choices. No claimed O(T^(−1/2+ε)) estimate is accepted. The proof above concerns only the classical zeta Euler product for σ>1.

definitions: For a positive discrete operator L, N_L(Λ) counts eigenvalues at mostΛ, with multiplicity.
The zeta-zero count is N_ζ(T)=T/(2π)log(T/(2π))−T/(2π)+O(logT), counting zeros in the critical strip with positive ordinate.

result.name: A concrete density mismatch
result.statement: If L=−d²/dx²+B on(0,π) with Dirichlet conditions and bounded self-adjoint B, then N_L(Λ)=√Λ+O(1). It cannot equal the multiset {γ_n²} of ordinates of all nontrivial zeta zeros.

result.statement: For t>−minλ_j, d(logD(t))/dt=Tr((L+tI)⁻¹)=Σ_j1/(λ_j+t), and logD(0)=−ζ_L′(0).

definitions: Let A=−d²/dx² on L²(0,π), with domain H²(0,π)∩H₀¹(0,π).
Assume W is a bounded real multiplication operator, T_p are bounded self-adjoint operators on this same Hilbert space, and Σ_p|R_p| ||T_p||<∞.

result.name: A bounded self-adjoint perturbation theorem
result.statement: For real λ_R,R_p, the operator L=A+λ_R W+Σ_pR_pT_p is self-adjoint on D(A), bounded below and has compact resolvent.
result.proof: The coefficient condition makes the prime sum Cauchy in operator norm; its limit B is bounded and self-adjoint because taking adjoints is norm-continuous. Including λ_RW preserves these properties. The adjoint identity (A+B)*=A*+B* on D(A*) holds for bounded B, so L is self-adjoint on D(A). The form inequality 〈u,Lu〉≥(1−||B||)||u||² follows from the first Dirichlet eigenvalue1. For a sufficiently large negative real z, ||B(A−z)⁻¹||<1; a Neumann series makes I+B(A−z)⁻¹ invertible. The resolvent factorization (L−z)⁻¹=(A−z)⁻¹[I+B(A−z)⁻¹]⁻¹ is compact because the Laplacian resolvent is compact. Compactness then holds at all resolvent points by the resolvent identity.

definitions: A towera^(b^c) means exponentiateb byc first. The parenthesized expression(a^b)^c is a different binary-operation tree.

result.statement: For positivea,(a^b)^c=a^(bc), whereas a^(b^c) generally differs. Ifa≠1, equality holds exactly whenbc=b^c.

A parser records exponentiation as a node with left and right children; choosing right association createsa^(b^c), while left association creates(a^b)^c. definitions: For a unit vectorψ and HermitianA,B, seta=〈A〉,b=〈B〉 andΔA=||(A−aI)ψ||.

result.statement: ΔAΔB≥(1/2)|〈ψ,[A,B]ψ〉|. For positionX and momentumP=−iℏd/dx on a suitable Schwartz state, this givesΔXΔP≥ℏ/2.
result.proof: Letu=(A−aI)ψ andv=(B−bI)ψ. Cauchy–Schwarz gives||u||||v||≥|〈u,v〉|≥|Im〈u,v〉|. Hermiticity implies〈ψ,[A,B]ψ〉=2iIm〈u,v〉, proving the bound. source.title: Least action reduces to a first variation with fixed endpoints
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered flashcards include least action and Newton’s law. Their mathematical core is a stationary-action calculation, with an important distinction between stationarity and a genuine minimum. An elementary quadratic action permits both to be checked exactly.
definitions: For a C² pathx:[0,T]→R with fixed endpoint values, takeS[x]=∫₀ᵀ[(m/2)(x′)²−V(x)]dt, withm>0.
An admissible variationη is smooth and vanishes at0 andT. Stationarity means the derivative ofS[x+εη] atε=0 vanishes for everyη.

result.name: First and second variation
result.statement: Stationarity impliesmx″+V′(x)=0. ForV(x)=kx²/2 and zero-endpoint variations, the second variation is∫[m(η′)²−kη²]dt and is positive whenk<mπ²/T².
result.proof: Differentiate under the integral to getδS=∫[mx′η′−V′(x)η]dt. Integration by parts removes the endpoint term becauseη vanishes there, leaving−∫[mx″+V′(x)]ηdt. The fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations forces the continuous bracket to vanish. For the quadraticV, differentiating a second time gives the stated form exactly. The Dirichlet Poincaré inequality∫η²≤(T/π)²∫(η′)² then bounds it below by[m−kT²/π²]∫(η′)². Strict positivity proves a strict minimum for this quadratic functional under fixed endpoints. Ifk>mπ²/T², takeη=sin(πt/T); the second variation is negative, so a stationary path need not minimize the action.

example.setup: Choosem=1,k=1 andT=π versusT=2π.
example.calculation: AtT=π, the variationη=sin t has zero second variation. AtT=2π,η=sin(t/2) gives∫η′²=π/4 and∫η²=π, soδ²S=−3π/4. The same stationary zero path is therefore not an action minimum on the longer interval.
example.conclusion: “Least” action requires an actual second-variation argument. The Euler–Lagrange equation alone proves stationarity.

source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The recovered list names entropy without specifying a probability space or convention. On a finite alphabet, Shannon entropy is a concrete concave function and its maximum has a short complete proof. This supplies mathematical content without importing thermodynamic interpretations.
definitions: For probabilitiesp_i≥0 withΣp_i=1, defineH(p)=−Σp_i logp_i, with0log0=0 and natural logarithms.

result.name: Exact upper bound and equality case
result.statement: For a distribution onm outcomes,0≤H(p)≤logm. The maximum occurs exactly at the uniform distribution; the minimum0 occurs exactly at point masses.
result.proof: The elementary inequalitylogu≤u−1 gives−log(q_i/p_i)≥1−q_i/p_i forp_i>0. Multiplying byp_i and summing provesD(p||q)≥1−Σ_(p_i>0)q_i≥0. Withuniformq_i=1/m, D(p||q)=logm−H(p), soH≤logm. Equality inlogu≤u−1 requiresu=1 on the support and no missing positiveq mass, forcingp uniform. Nonnegativity follows termwise from−p_i logp_i≥0. A term vanishes only atp_i=0 or1, soH=0 forces a point mass. On the interior, the Hessian ofH isdiag(−1/p_i); restricting to the probability simplex shows strict concavity, consistent with uniqueness of the maximum.

example.setup: Comparep=(1/2,1/4,1/4) with the uniform distribution on three outcomes.
example.calculation: H(p)=(1/2)log2+2(1/4)log4=(3/2)log2≈1.03972. The maximum islog3≈1.09861, so the deficit isD(p||uniform)=log3−(3/2)log2≈0.05889. These exact expressions specify the logarithm base; base2 would divide every value bylog2.
example.conclusion: Entropy is a defined functional whose inequality and equality cases can be proved, rather than a universal synonym for disorder.

result.name: A convergent local sum need not have compact resolvent
result.statement: B=Σ_(k≥1)2^(−k)P_k converges in operator norm and is bounded self-adjoint. In the reference-sector binary tensor model it has infinitely many orthogonal eigenvectors with eigenvalues2^(−k), so it has no compact resolvent.
result.proof: The tail norm is bounded byΣ_(k>N)2^(−k)=2^(−N), proving norm convergence and self-adjointness. Choose each local space C² with reference vector e0, and P_ke1=e1,P_ke0=0. If(B+iI)⁻¹ were compact, its images of this bounded orthonormal sequence would have a convergent subsequence. But the images are(2^(−k)+i)⁻¹v_k, whose norms tend to1 and whose pairwise distances stay bounded away from zero. Compactness is impossible.
