source.title: Adding time as an operator changes the spectral problem
source.status: Classical result; recovered proposal repaired
source.summary: The historical advanced sum includes iℏ∂t+H(t). Even when this is self-adjoint, it is an operator on a time-function space, not merely an additional spatial potential. Its basic periodic spectrum is unbounded in both directions.
definitions: Work on L²(R/TZ)⊗C^d with periodic H¹ domain, letω=2π/T andℏ>0.
Take a constant Hermitian matrix H0 with eigenvectors u_j and eigenvaluesμ_j.

result.name: Exact periodic-time spectrum
result.statement: K=iℏ∂t+H0 is self-adjoint and has eigenvectors e^(inωt)u_j with eigenvaluesμ_j−ℏnω, n∈Z. Its heat traceΣe^(−βλ) diverges for everyβ>0.
result.proof: The periodic Fourier basis diagonalizes i∂t: differentiation of e^(inωt) gives inω times the function, so multiplication by i yields−nω. The self-adjoint diagonal operator has domain characterized by square-summability of n times the Fourier coefficients, which is the periodic H¹ domain. The bounded Hermitian term H0 commutes with this Fourier decomposition and preserves self-adjointness. The displayed tensor products form a complete orthogonal basis. For n→+∞, μ_j−ℏnω→−∞; consequently e^(−β(μ_j−ℏnω)) tends to infinity rather than zero. The positive heat-trace sum cannot converge. Quasienergy is often considered moduloℏω in Floquet theory, but that quotient is a separate spectral interpretation, not a convergent Gibbs trace of K.

example.calculation: The eigenvalues are1/3−n, so n=−1,0,1 give4/3,1/3,−2/3. The same physical quasienergy class has infinitely many translated representatives. Inserting these raw eigenvalues into a positive-temperature partition sum makes it diverge.
example.conclusion: The time term is mathematically meaningful on a defined domain, but it changes boundedness and multiplicity properties that a spatial heat-trace argument may have relied on.

source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The recovered experiment evaluated ordinary partial Euler products on the critical line and interpreted small values as evidence for zeros. The product’s justified domain and its exact factor sensitivity resolve the issue before any high-precision computation.
definitions: For Re(s)=σ>1 define Z_P(s)=∏_{p<P}(1−p^(−s))^(−1).

result.name: Absolute convergence and a finite-factor perturbation identity
result.statement: For σ>1 the infinite Euler product converges to ζ(s) and is nonzero. Replacing one factor z=p^(−s) by (1+δ)z changes the finite product by the exact ratio (1−z)/(1−(1+δ)z)=1/[1−δz/(1−z)], whenever the denominator is nonzero.
result.proof: Expand each factor as its absolutely convergent geometric series. Unique factorization identifies the resulting sum with Σn^(−s), and absolute convergence justifies rearrangement. Alternatively Σ_pΣ_k|p^(−ks)|/k is finite because it is bounded by a constant times Σ_{n≥2}n^(−σ); its exponential gives a nonzero product. The perturbation formula follows by cancelling every unchanged factor, then algebraically factoring the denominator. Its derivative at δ=0 is z/(1−z), so the conditioning depends on the complex phase as well as the size of p. These arguments do not extend absolute Euler-product convergence to σ=1/2. Analytic continuation of ζ is a different construction.

example.setup: At s=2 perturb the p=2 factor and compare with the full product. Then examine any finite product at s=1/2+it.
example.calculation: Here z=1/4 and the ratio is 1/(1−δ/3); the first-order relative change is δ/3. At any point with Re(s)>0 every |p^(−s)|<1, so each finite factor is finite and nonzero and consequently the finite product cannot be a zero of ζ. A numerical value near zero is not a zero certificate.
example.conclusion: The original critical-line experiment had no established convergence argument and cannot prove the Riemann hypothesis or even locate a zero reliably by ordinary Euler products.

source.limits: This does not rule out suitably regularized products, explicit formulas, or Euler–Hadamard hybrid approximations; each needs its own theorem and error bounds.

If a band has zero rate, its component is preserved, so asymptotic convergence to zero cannot be concluded. For a forward Euler update I−hA, the multiplier in band j is 1−ha_j. Contractivity is equivalent to |1−ha_j|≤1, hence 0≤ha_j≤2 for every band; continuous stability alone does not justify an arbitrary step size.

source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The historical claim that differing degrees of a property force a maximum is false without restrictions. Compactness, continuity, and the distinction between closed and constructible images give a precise replacement for the suggested Chevalley-based argument.
definitions: A supremum is a least upper bound, which need not be a value of the function.

result.name: Attainment under compactness; an algebraic projection counterexample
result.statement: A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact space attains both extrema. However the projection of a closed affine algebraic set need not be closed: the image of xy=1 under (x,y)↦x is A¹ minus {0}.
result.proof: For the analytic assertion, the continuous image of a compact space is compact in R and therefore closed and bounded. Its supremum belongs to that closed image, hence is attained. The hypotheses are essential: f(x)=x on (0,1) has supremum one but never reaches it, and f(x)=x on R is unbounded. For the algebraic assertion, every nonzero x has y=1/x and zero has none, proving the exact image. It is open and constructible but not Zariski closed. Chevalley’s theorem predicts constructibility for finite-type morphisms, not universal closedness. Proper morphisms, including projections with a projective factor, provide stronger closed-image statements.

example.setup: Compare f(x)=x/(1+x) on [0,∞) with the same f on [0,M], and compare the affine hyperbola projection with a projective parameter space.
example.calculation: On the half-line, f increases toward one, so sup f=1 but there is no maximizing point. On [0,M], the maximum is M/(1+M). The derivative 1/(1+x)² is never zero, so solving ∇f=0 would find neither the boundary maximizer nor the unattained limit. Algebraic rational functions also require their denominator-nonzero domain to be stated.
example.conclusion: A degree comparison alone proves neither boundedness nor attainment. The required hypotheses can be checked explicitly.

result.statement: A homomorphism φ:A→B satisfying φ(r)=0 for all r∈R factors uniquely through A/⟨R⟩. A proposed affine-to-finite quotient therefore requires explicit generator images that satisfy every affine relation.

source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The recovered symbolic example is correct once the two-sided shift topology is specified. It supplies a complete model calculation; applications to a flow require a separate conjugacy or hyperbolic return-map argument.
definitions: Let Σ={0,1}^Z with d(x,y)=Σ_{k∈Z}2^(−|k|)|x_k−y_k|.

result.name: Finite-support homoclinic characterization
result.statement: A binary sequence is homoclinic to zero, meaning d(σ^n x,0)→0 as n→±∞, if and only if it has only finitely many nonzero coordinates. The full two-shift has topological entropy log 2.
result.proof: If x is supported in [−M,M], then σ^n x is supported in [−M−n,M−n]. As |n| grows this interval leaves every fixed coordinate window. The metric tail outside a large window is arbitrarily small, proving convergence in both directions. Conversely d(σ^n x,0)≥|(σ^n x)_0|=x_n. Since this is zero or one, convergence as n→+∞ forces x_n=0 for every sufficiently large positive n; convergence as n→−∞ forces the same in the negative tail. Only a finite window remains. For entropy, every length-N binary word occurs and two differing words can be distinguished at some one of the first N iterates, yielding 2^N separated orbit patterns. Conversely there are only 2^N such central words up to fixed finite-window boundary factors, giving entropy log 2.

example.setup: Let x have ones at −2,0,3 and zero elsewhere. Track the support under σ^n.
example.calculation: The support becomes {−2−n,−n,3−n}. The convergence is thus explicitly exponential for this finite pattern.

source.title: Cylindrical Gaussian data versus a Radon Gaussian on Hilbert space
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: Consistent finite-dimensional Gaussian distributions need not live in the proposed infinite-dimensional space. On a separable Hilbert space, a positive trace-class covariance gives a direct construction, while identity covariance supplies the decisive counterexample.
definitions: Take H=ℓ² with orthonormal basis e_n and eigenvalues q_n≥0.
Let Z_n be independent standard real normal random variables.

result.name: Trace-class diagonal Gaussian construction
result.statement: If Σq_n<∞, then X=Σ√q_n Z_ne_n converges in H almost surely and in mean square, with characteristic function E exp(i⟨h,X⟩)=exp(−Σq_n h_n²/2). Identity covariance does not define an ℓ²-valued Gaussian.
result.proof: The nonnegative random variable S=Σq_nZ_n² has expectation Σq_n by monotone convergence. Finite expectation implies S<∞ almost surely, proving that the coordinate series is square-summable almost surely. The tail mean square is Σ_{n>N}q_n→0, proving L² convergence. Finite-dimensional normal characteristic functions multiply, and dominated convergence passes to the limit, giving the displayed formula. Since ℓ² is a separable complete metric space, its Borel probability law is Radon. In contrast, for q_n=1, the strong law gives N^(−1)Σ_{n≤N}Z_n²→1 almost surely, so the squared norm diverges. The consistent cylinder marginals still exist as a product measure on R^N, but that measure gives ℓ² probability zero.

example.setup: Choose q_n=2^(−n), n≥1, and compare with q_n=1.
example.calculation: The trace is Σ2^(−n)=1, so E||X||²=1, and truncating after N coordinates has squared mean error 2^(−N). The identity-covariance truncation instead has expected squared norm N and no tight ℓ² limit. For any fixed radius R, the strong law shows its probability of lying in that radius tends to zero.
example.conclusion: The missing issue is support and tightness, not merely consistency of finite-dimensional marginals.

source.limits: This proves the diagonal Hilbert-space Gaussian case; general Sazonov extension theorems use an appropriate topology on the dual and require their own hypotheses. A pushforward also requires a specified measurable map and target space.

definitions: Let a finite group G act unitarily through U_g on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space V.

result.name: Reynolds projection and equivariant block decomposition

source.summary: A Reynolds number summarizes competing terms after nondimensionalization, while an energy identity gives a proved inequality under boundary and regularity assumptions. These statements are mathematical; neither imports finite-group character heights into a fluid model.

definitions: On ℓ²(Z), define (H_{α,θ}u)_n=u_{n+1}+u_{n−1}+2cos(2παn+θ)u_n.
At α=P/Q in lowest terms, the coefficients are Q-periodic and a Bloch fiber satisfies u_{n+Q}=e^(ik)u_n.

result.name: Spectral bound and flux symmetry
result.statement: H is bounded self-adjoint with ||H||≤4, so its spectrum lies in [−4,4]. H_{α+1,θ}=H_{α,θ}; H_{−α,θ}=H_{α,−θ}. The union over θ is symmetric under E↦−E.
result.proof: The forward and backward shifts each have norm one and are adjoints; the real diagonal cosine operator has norm at most two. The triangle inequality gives the norm bound and self-adjointness. Periodicity in α follows because 2πn is an integer multiple of 2π. The reflection identity follows from cosine’s evenness. Let (Ju)_n=(−1)^nu_n; conjugating the shifts changes their signs, whereas the diagonal potential is unchanged. Therefore JH_{α,θ}J=−H_{α,θ+π}, proving energy reflection for the phase-union spectrum. source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The integrated density of states counts states below an energy per lattice site. In a spectral gap it can have arithmetic labels. The label constrains a gap value, not an arbitrary eigenvalue, and its topological interpretation requires a specified two-parameter family.
definitions: For a rational flux P/Q, a gap above r of the Q band branches has normalized IDS r/Q.

result.name: Rational label congruence and ambiguity
result.statement: If gcd(P,Q)=1, the equation r=QS+PT has integer solutions and determines T modulo Q. It does not determine a unique integer T without an additional selection rule or a Chern-number calculation.
result.proof: Bézout’s identity supplies integers a,b with aP+bQ=1. Multiplying by r gives T=ar,S=br as one solution. If (S,T) and (S′,T′) are solutions, Q(S−S′)=−P(T−T′). Coprimality forces T−T′ to be a multiple of Q and S−S′ the opposite multiple of P. Conversely every such pair solves the equation. Thus the label is a congruence class. For an actual isolated Bloch spectral projection over a two-torus, its first Chern number can select the Hall integer, but one must prove the projection is smooth and the gap stays open. An arithmetic equation alone neither proves existence of the gap nor chooses its orientation convention.

example.calculation: 1=5S+2T has solution S=1,T=−2, and all solutions are S=1−2k,T=−2+5k. A conventional representative |T|≤5/2 gives T=−2. For r=2, T=1,S=0 is a representative. If those gaps close, the equations remain soluble but no isolated spectral projection exists there; the labels do not create missing gaps.
example.conclusion: The old Wannier formula becomes an exact solvable arithmetic condition, with its spectral and topological assumptions separated.

source.title: Frenet frames, Darboux rotation, and covariant differentiation
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The historical Beta-frame equations reproduce the Frenet–Serret system under an arc-length and positive-curvature hypothesis. They describe local rotation of an orthonormal moving frame; their coefficients are not automatically new physical tensor components.
definitions: Let γ(s) be a C³ unit-speed curve in oriented Euclidean three-space with curvature κ=||γ″||>0.
Set T=γ′, N=T′/κ, B=T×N, and τ=−B′·N.

result.name: Frenet–Serret equations and the Darboux vector
result.statement: T′=κN, N′=−κT+τB, B′=−τN. The vector Ω=τT+κB satisfies E′=Ω×E for E=T,N,B.
result.proof: Because the frame is orthonormal, differentiating its pairwise dot products makes its derivative matrix skew-symmetric. The definition gives T′=κN and therefore N′·T=−κ. Since T′·B=0 and B′·T=−B·T′=0, B′ lies along N; its coefficient is −τ. Orthogonality then gives N′·B=τ and no N-component, proving all three equations. Cross products T×N=B, B×T=N and T×B=−N verify the Darboux expression. On an oriented Riemannian three-manifold, replace ordinary derivatives by ∇_T and use the metric-compatible cross product; covariant frame equations still describe motion along the curve. Ambient curvature enters comparisons around loops and commutators of covariant derivatives, not an arbitrary extra term in each Euclidean formula.

example.setup: Take γ(s)=(a cos(s/c),a sin(s/c),bs/c) with c=√(a²+b²) and a>0.
example.calculation: Its speed is one, κ=a/(a²+b²), and τ=b/(a²+b²). For a=b=1 these are both 1/2. A planar circle has b=0, hence τ=0 and a fixed binormal; a straight line has κ=0 and the Frenet normal is undefined, requiring a different frame such as a parallel-transport frame.
example.conclusion: The equations have exact hypotheses, a geometric derivation, and a worked nonplanar example.

source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; historical claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The recovered catalogue mentioned Pontryagin terms alongside curvature actions. Chern–Weil theory gives precise invariant integrals; their local variations are boundary terms under the appropriate hypotheses. This is a different role from an Einstein–Hilbert kinetic term.
definitions: For a connection A on a complex bundle, F=dA+A∧A and D_AF=0 is the Bianchi identity.

definitions: On L²([0,L]), let A_θ=−d²/dx² with domain {f∈H²: f(L)=e^(iθ)f(0), f′(L)=e^(iθ)f′(0)}.

result.name: Self-adjoint twisted Laplacian and shifted Fourier modes
result.statement: A_θ is self-adjoint and has orthonormal eigenbasis L^(−1/2)exp(i(2πn+θ)x/L), n∈Z, with eigenvalues ((2πn+θ)/L)².
result.proof: Integration by parts gives the boundary form [−overline f g′+overline f′g]_0^L. The equal phase factors in function and derivative values cancel, so the form vanishes on the domain. To establish self-adjointness, multiply by exp(−iθx/L), a unitary map to periodic functions. Under this gauge transformation A_θ becomes (−i∂_x+θ/L)² on the periodic H² domain. Its action on the complete periodic Fourier basis is multiplication by real numbers ((2πn+θ)/L)² with the usual square-summability domain, which is self-adjoint. This also proves completeness, not merely a list of candidate eigenfunctions. If only the function boundary condition were imposed, the boundary form would retain uncontrolled derivative terms and symmetry could fail.

example.setup: Take L=2π and compare θ=0 with θ=π.

source.summary: The historical claim of going beyond toric code needs a baseline with a defined lattice, code space, and error model. The square torus code has exact commuting stabilizers and nonlocal logical operators; these properties can be proved at the Pauli-algebra level.
definitions: Place one qubit on every edge of an L×L square lattice with periodic boundaries,L≥3.
For a vertexv setA_v=∏_{e incident v}X_e; for a plaquettep setB_p=∏_{e∈∂p}Z_e.

result.name: Commuting stabilizers and distanceL
result.statement: AllA_v andB_p commute. Their common+1eigenspace encodes two qubits, and a shortest noncontractible Pauli loop has lengthL, giving code distanceL.
result.proof: X andZ anticommute on one edge. A star and plaquette share either zero or two edges, so their commutation sign is(+1)or(−1)²=+1. Products of all stars and all plaquettes each equalI because every edge occurs twice. On the connected torus these are the only independent relations of each type; thus the stabilizer rank is2L²−2 among2L²qubits and the code dimension is2². AZ string anticommutes with stars at its endpoints, detecting open-string errors; a closed string commutes with all stars. Contractible loops are products of plaquettes and act trivially on the code. A noncontractible loop cannot be such a boundary and acts logically. The shortest noncontractible direct or dual cycle hasLedges, yielding the minimum nontrivial logical Pauli weightL.

example.setup: TakeL=3 and follow a Z string along one periodic row.
example.calculation: There are18edge qubits,9stars,and9plaquettes,with16independent stabilizers and a four-dimensional code space. A one-edgeZerror creates two violated star syndromes; a length-three wrappedZloop has no syndrome but changes a logical state. Thus local detectability and logical vulnerability coexist exactly as the distance statement predicts.
example.conclusion: The baseline protection is a precise code-space statement against bounded-weight Pauli errors, not an unrestricted immunity claim.

source.summary: CNOT is an exact permutation unitary and creates an entangled state from a separable input. A telescoping estimate bounds accumulated implementation error, but unitarity alone does not prove fault tolerance.
definitions: DefineCNOT|a,b⟩=|a,b⊕a⟩ for binary labels. The Hadamard gate sends|0⟩ to(|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2.

Protection is a statement about specified errors, encoding, correction and a performance bound, not merely a name for the intended gate.

result.statement: CNOT²=I andCNOT is unitary. CNOT(H⊗I)|00⟩=(|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, whose one-qubit marginal isI/2. The two circuit products differ by at mostΣ_jε_j.
result.proof: CNOT permutes the four orthonormal basis states and is its own inverse, proving unitarity. Applying it to(|00⟩+|10⟩)/√2 gives the displayed Bell state. Taking a partial trace eliminates the two off-diagonal cross terms and leaves equal populations, so the pure joint state is not a product. For the error bound, subtractV_m⋯V₁−U_m⋯U₁ and insert mixed products one gate at a time. The resulting sum has termsV_m⋯V_{j+1}(V_j−U_j)U_{j−1}⋯U₁. Unitary factors have norm one, so submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality giveΣ ε_j. This is a worst-case coherent-error estimate and requires no stochastic independence.

source.summary: On the symplectic plane one can write the prequantum connection and verify its curvature directly. The constant-Poisson Moyal product and a normalized Gaussian then give exact, separately checkable quantization statements.
definitions: Use coordinates(q,p),ω=dq∧dp,H=(q²+p²)/2 andħ>0. DefineX_H byι_Xω=dH, givingX_H=p∂q−q∂p.

ForH⋆H the first Poisson term is zero; the second derivative combination isH_qqH_pp+H_ppH_qq=2, so its coefficient is−ħ²/8 times two. Higher derivatives vanish. source.status: Developed mathematical result with explicit hypotheses and checked example; historical claims repaired where necessary
source.summary: On a two-point space the bounded derived category can be classified completely. Equivalences permute the two simple objects and shift them; a shift-and-swap gives an exact involution.
definitions: Letk be a field andD=Dᵇ(Vec_k×Vec_k), represented by pairs of bounded finite-dimensional complexes.
Write[1] for the cohomological shift. Each complex over a field is isomorphic in the derived category to the direct sum of its cohomology spaces placed in their degrees.

result.statement: Everyk-linear triangulated equivalence ofD permutesS₁,S₂ and assigns an integer shift to each. In particularF(V,W)=(W[1],V[−1]) is an equivalence withF²≅Id.
result.proof: Split every differential into its image, a complement in its kernel and a remaining complement; the image/complement pairs form contractible two-term summands. This leaves precisely the graded cohomology, proving the decomposition. An equivalence preserves indecomposability and all graded morphism spaces. It therefore sends eachS_i to a shifted simple. The two images cannot be shifts of the same simple, since then some shifted morphism between them would be nonzero although everyHom(S₁,S₂[n]) vanishes. Essential surjectivity forces both simple types to occur. Conversely a permutation with prescribed shifts has an inverse permutation with the opposite shifts and acts componentwise on morphisms, so it is an equivalence. source.title: A weight filtration need not split canonically
source.status: Developed mathematical result with explicit hypotheses and checked example; historical claims repaired where necessary
source.summary: A two-step filtered vector space admits many splittings, none invariant under all filtration-preserving automorphisms. This elementary example identifies the extra choice suppressed by writing a weight filtration as a direct sum.
definitions: LetV=ke₁⊕ke₂,W₀=ke₁,W₁=W₀,W₂=V, with the evident zero and full extensions outside this range.
The associated graded isGr⁰_W=ke₁ andGr²_W=V/ke₁. A splitting selects a lift of each quotient vector and identifiesV with their direct sum.
A canonical splitting would have to be preserved by every automorphism of the given filtered object.

result.name: No functorial splitting for this filtered object
result.statement: Every complement ofW₀ has the formk(e₂+ce₁). The filtered automorphismsT_a(e₁)=e₁,T_a(e₂)=e₂+ae₁ act transitively on these complements. No complement is fixed by allT_a.
result.proof: A line complementary toke₁ has a vector with nonzeroe₂ coordinate; rescaling it gives e₂+ce₁, proving the classification. ApplyingT_a sends this line to the line with parameterc+a. Choosing any nonzeroa changes it, so no complement can be invariant under the whole automorphism group. EachT_a induces the identity on both graded quotients, showing that the associated graded forgets genuine extension automorphisms. The equality of graded dimensions withdimV therefore does not provide a distinguished decomposition. In mixed Hodge theory additional structures constrain the extensions, and certain splittings may exist after changing scalars or adding hypotheses; those theorems must be stated rather than replacingW_k by an unexplained Hodge-index sum.

example.setup: Compare the complementske₂ andk(e₂+3e₁).
example.calculation: Both project isomorphically toGr²_W and yield identical graded dimensions(1,1). T₃ exchanges the first with the second while acting trivially onGr_W. A numerical routine that returns one complement has selected coordinates, not found an invariant hidden direct-sum decomposition.
example.conclusion: The finite calculation explains exactly why filtrations and decompositions encode different information.

source.limits: This is a filtered-vector-space theorem, not a classification of mixed Hodge extensions. A pure Hodge decomposition is a different structure and can be canonical under its own hypotheses. The historical formulaW_k=⊕_{p+q=k}H_M^{p,q} conflates indices unless its objects are redefined.
source.extension: Add a specified nondegenerate inner product and take the orthogonal complement. Then identify the smaller symmetry group preserving that metric and show the splitting is natural only for that smaller category. This exposes the cost of the additional choice.

source.status: Developed mathematical result with explicit hypotheses and checked example; historical claims repaired where necessary
source.summary: The projective line minus two points gives a fully specified localization example. It has classL−1 and compactly supported cohomology in degrees one and two; no undefined infinite motivic series is needed.
definitions: In the Grothendieck ring of varieties,[X]=[Z]+[X∖Z] for a closed subvarietyZ. SetL=[A¹].
LetX=P¹_C,Z={0,∞},U=C*. The open/closed trianglej_!k_U→k_X→i_*k_Z produces a long exact compact-support cohomology sequence.
The existence of this sheaf-theoretic localization sequence is standard background; its maps and dimensions are computed below.

result.name: Exact class and compact-support cohomology ofC*
result.statement: [C*]=L−1. Over a fieldk,H_c¹(C*;k)=k,H_c²(C*;k)=k and the other compact-support groups vanish. Its compact-support Euler characteristic is zero.
result.proof: DecomposeP¹ intoA¹ and the point at infinity to obtain[P¹]=L+1. Removing two points givesL−1. In the long exact sequence, H⁰(P¹)=k maps toH⁰(Z)=k² by the diagonal mapc↦(c,c). Its kernel is zero and cokernel is one-dimensional, soH_c⁰(U)=0 andH_c¹(U)=k. SinceH¹(P¹)=0,H¹(Z)=0,H²(P¹)=k andH²(Z)=0, exactness givesH_c²(U)=k. Hence the Euler characteristic is−1+1=0. The cohomological subtraction includes connecting maps and degrees; it is not literal subtraction of ordinary vector spaces. Its numerical Euler realization agrees with evaluatingL at one in the classL−1.

example.setup: Write the finite matrix for the only nontrivial map in low degrees.
example.calculation: The column(1,1)ᵀ has rank one. The quotientk²/diag(k) is detected by(a,b)↦b−a. Thus two removed points create one compact-support degree-one class, even thoughC* itself has no compact connected component.
example.conclusion: This is a constructive interpretation of additivity, six-operation notation and a motivic class in one exact example.

source.limits: A motivic integral over arcs additionally needs a measure, cylinder normalization and a completed coefficient ring. The recovered sumΣ[X_n]L^−n does not automatically converge or define that measure. No quantum volume is inferred.
source.extension: ForP¹ withr punctures, repeat the same diagonal-map calculation to obtainH_c¹ dimensionr−1 andH_c² dimension one, and verify the classL+1−r. Then state what additional completion would be needed for an actual arc-space sum. Over field coefficients, the compact-support Künneth theorem gives dimensions 1,2,1 in degrees two, three and four for (C*)². Its class is (L−1)² and its Euler characteristic is again zero. source.status: Developed mathematical result with explicit hypotheses and checked example; historical claims repaired where necessary
source.summary: Associative commutators satisfy Jacobi by cancellation. An explicit octonion triple has a nonzero Jacobiator, furnishing a concrete nonassociative example without identifying it with a physicalR-flux.
definitions: For a bilinear multiplication define[a,b]=ab−ba andJ(a,b,c)=[a,[b,c]]+[b,[c,a]]+[c,[a,b]].
Use octonion unitse₁,…,e₇ with squares−1 and oriented Fano triples(123),(145),(176),(246),(257),(347),(365); reversing an ordered pair changes sign.
The associator is(a,b,c)=(ab)c−a(bc). Parentheses cannot be omitted in a nonassociative product.

result.name: An exact nonzero Jacobiator
result.statement: For(a,b,c)=(e₁,e₂,e₄), the associator is2e₇ andJ=−12e₇. In every associative algebra the same commutator formula hasJ=0.
result.proof: In an associative algebra expand the three nested commutators. Each of the six ordered triple products occurs twice with opposite signs, giving zero. In the specified octonion table,e₂e₄=e₆,e₁e₆=−e₇, so[e₁,[e₂,e₄]]=−4e₇. Alsoe₄e₁=−e₅,e₂e₅=e₇, giving the second term−4e₇. Finallye₁e₂=e₃,e₄e₃=−e₇ gives the third−4e₇. Their sum is−12e₇. Separately(e₁e₂)e₄=e₃e₄=e₇, wherease₁(e₂e₄)=e₁e₆=−e₇, giving associator2e₇. This verifies the sign convention rather than appealing to a generic nonassociative slogan. Left multiplication still represents every octonion as a linear map, but it is not a product-preserving representation: L_{e₁}L_{e₂}e₄=−e₇ whereas L_{e₁e₂}e₄=e₇. Commutators of the linear maps satisfy Jacobi, while the octonion commutators need not. This prevents confusing an operator embedding with an associative algebra embedding.

example.setup: Compare this triple with the quaternionic subalgebra spanned by1,e₁,e₂,e₃.
example.calculation: Within that four-dimensional subalgebra multiplication is associative and every commutator Jacobiator vanishes. The chosen triple involvinge₄ leaves that subalgebra and gives the nonzero value above. Thus a large algebra can contain associative sectors without being associative globally.
example.conclusion: A nonzero Jacobiator is now attached to a declared multiplication table and a checked triple.

source.status: Developed mathematical result with explicit hypotheses and checked example; historical claims repaired where necessary
source.summary: A finite nonnegative input network has a convergent response series when its spectral radius is below one. A two-sector example yields an exact multiplier, showing why a universal scalar such as2.68 needs a declared model.
definitions: Letx=Ax+d, whereA has nonnegative entries andd is an external input. All coordinates use compatible units.
Assume spectral radiusρ(A)<1. Then(I−A)⁻¹=Σ_{n≥0}Aⁿ and the response to a shockδd isδx=(I−A)⁻¹δd.
A scalar multiplier also needs an aggregation rowwᵀ; it iswᵀδx divided by a stated input normalization.

result.name: Exact two-sector propagation
result.statement: ForA=[[0,1/4],[1/2,0]],(I−A)⁻¹=[[8/7,2/7],[4/7,8/7]]. A unit shock in sector one gives total output12/7; a unit shock in sector two gives10/7.
result.proof: A²=I/8, so even and odd powers form two geometric series andρ(A)=1/√8<1. Their sum is(I+A)/(1−1/8), giving the inverse directly. Multiplication byI−A independently verifies the identity. The two different column sums demonstrate that even one fixed network need not have a single shock-independent scalar multiplier. For a general finite matrix the Neumann series follows by Jordan form or an equivalent norm in which high powers decay; the spectral-radius hypothesis is essential to that series interpretation.

example.setup: Useδd=(1,0) and compare the first three response rounds.
example.calculation: The direct response is(1,0), the first spillover(0,1/2), and the next(1/8,0). Summing all rounds gives(8/7,4/7). Counting the direct input once and then adding the full inverse response again would double count the zeroth round.
example.conclusion: The mathematical multiplier is computable, directional and conditional on a network that must be independently justified.

If||B||||E||<1, derive||B′−B||≤||B||²||E||/(1−||B||||E||), quantifying how uncertain links can amplify multiplier uncertainty. For the concrete network, the sum of all response rounds after round m is bounded by a geometric tail because A²=I/8. source.summary: A quotient of capacity by demand is not itself an allocation theorem. A concave two-recipient model yields a unique feasible optimum and an exact water-filling rule.
definitions: Letx_i≥0 be allocated units withΣx_i≤C,C>0. Let benefit beΣa_i log(1+x_i), witha_i>0.

result.statement: The log-utility problem has a unique optimumx_i=max(a_i/λ−1,0), withλ>0 chosen soΣx_i=C. For(a₁,a₂)=(2,1),C=2, the allocation is(5/3,1/3).
result.proof: The compact feasible simplex gives existence. The Hessian is diagonal with strictly negative entries−a_i/(1+x_i)², so the objective is strictly concave and has at most one maximizer. Each benefit increases, so capacity is exhausted. Lagrange optimality givesa_i/(1+x_i)=λ on positive coordinates and a_i≤λ on zero coordinates. These conditions yield the formula and are sufficient by concavity. For the example both coordinates are positive, so2/λ−1+1/λ−1=2 givesλ=3/4 and the displayed allocation.

example.setup: Compare the optimum with equal allocation(1,1) and concentrated allocation(2,0).

Equal allocation has marginal benefits one and one half, so moving a small unit from the second to the first improves the objective. Concentration at(2,0) has first marginal2/3 and second marginal one, so it is also improvable. The certificate uses exact marginal comparisons rather than promotional ranking.
example.conclusion: A feasible allocation and an aggregate index have explicit but different mathematical contracts.

source.limits: No choice of utility or normalization is scientifically or socially compelled by this calculation. Zero demand makes the quoted ratio undefined, and unbounded capacity claims cannot be repaired by optimization alone.

definitions: Let S be a compact oriented piecewise smooth surface in R³ with oriented boundary C. Let F be C¹ on a neighborhood of S.

result.statement: Φ_F(S)=∮_C F·dr. Consequently two admissible surfaces with the same oriented boundary give the same integral for the same field. The value can nevertheless vary continuously under changes of F while the surface topology stays fixed.

Applying it to S₁ and S₂ with the same C gives equal values, provided F is defined smoothly on both. definitions: A primitive positive solution of a⁴+b⁴+c⁴=d⁴ has gcd(a,b,c,d)=1. Euler’s classical exclusion of three fourth powers is false.

result.name: An exact primitive counterexample and a local parity restriction
result.statement: 95800⁴+217519⁴+414560⁴=422481⁴ and the four integers have gcd one. Also φ(1680)=384. The latter number does not imply the absence of the former solution. Any primitive solution has exactly one odd number among a,b,c and has d odd.
result.proof: The fourth-power equality and gcd are finite integer certificates, checked without rounding by the verifier. For the parity statement, every fourth power is zero or one modulo sixteen. Thus the number of odd summands on the left, an integer from zero through three, must equal zero or one modulo sixteen according to the parity of d. It is therefore zero or one exactly. If all three left entries were even, d would also be even, violating primitivity. Exactly one must be odd and d must be odd. For the totient, factor 1680=2⁴·3·5·7 and multiply 1680(1/2)(2/3)(4/5)(6/7)=384. The angle π/840 is indeed 2π/1680, compatible with a primitive 1680th root. source.summary: The exact periodic operator is one of the grounded parts of the May14 framework. Its sign must be fixed before writing a heat semigroup or a spectral gap. Primality of p is unnecessary for the diagonalization: the same calculation works for every integer p≥3.
definitions: On G=(Z/pZ)³ let (Lu)(x)=Σ_{j=1}³[u(x+e_j)+u(x−e_j)−2u(x)]. Define the positive operator A=−L.
For k∈G use normalized Fourier characters χ_k(x)=p^(−3/2)exp(2πik·x/p). Orthogonality is with the finite counting inner product.

result.statement: Lχ_k=−4Σ_j sin²(πk_j/p)χ_k, so A is positive semidefinite with a one-dimensional constant kernel. Its smallest positive eigenvalue is γ_p=4sin²(π/p)∼4π²/p². The contractive heat evolution is e^(−tA)=e^(tL), not e^(−tL).
result.proof: A shift by ±e_j multiplies χ_k by e^(±2πik_j/p). Adding the two shifts and subtracting two gives 2cos(2πk_j/p)−2=−4sin²(πk_j/p). Summing proves the eigenvalue formula. The character inner products are products of geometric sums, zero unless the indices agree, so these p³ characters form a full orthonormal basis. Every eigenvalue of A is nonnegative, and it vanishes only when all k_j=0 modulo p. The least positive sine square occurs at k_j=±1 in one coordinate with the other coordinates zero. The limit sin z/z→1 proves the asymptotic. In this eigenbasis the norm of e^(−tA) is one, while its restriction to mean-zero functions has norm e^(−tγ_p). The opposite sign e^(−tL) amplifies nonconstant modes and is not a dissipative heat operator.

example.calculation: Each one-coordinate contribution to A is 0,2,4,2. Thus the three-dimensional eigenvalues are sums of three such entries, the kernel is constants and the gap is two. Two modest exact statements replace that missing certificate: a spectral maximum bound and a local Newton remainder estimate. Neither relies on an unrecorded Zolotarev constant.
definitions: Let A be real symmetric with spectrum in [a,b]. Let r be a rational function with no pole on that interval and f continuous there.
For Newton’s method let F be C² near a root α, assume |F′|≥m>0 and |F″|≤M on an interval containing α and the current iterate, and assume the next iterates remain in that interval.

result.name: Spectral error transfer and a local quadratic recurrence
result.statement: ||f(A)−r(A)||₂=max_{λ∈spectrum(A)}|f(λ)−r(λ)|≤sup_[a,b]|f−r|. Newton’s update x⁺=x−F(x)/F′(x) satisfies |x⁺−α|≤[M/(2m)]|x−α|² under the stated local bounds.
result.proof: An orthogonal diagonalization A=Udiag(λ_i)Uᵀ makes f(A)−r(A) orthogonally similar to the diagonal matrix of scalar errors; its Euclidean operator norm is the largest absolute diagonal entry. The pole exclusion makes r(A) well defined. For Newton, Taylor-expand F(α)=F(x)+F′(x)(α−x)+F″(ξ)(α−x)²/2 for some intermediate ξ. Rearranging and using F(α)=0 gives x⁺−α=F″(ξ)(x−α)²/[2F′(x)], up to an irrelevant sign, proving the absolute bound. Remaining inside the interval is a real hypothesis: a local error estimate is not global convergence from every initial point.

example.setup: Use A=diag(1,2), f(λ)=1/λ and r(λ)=3/2−λ/2. Separately use F(x)=x²−2 and x₀=3/2.
example.calculation: The polynomial r is exact at both eigenvalues, so r(A)=A^(−1), although it is not exact throughout [1,2]. Newton gives x₁=17/12 and x₂=577/408. The exact residuals are x₁²−2=1/144 and x₂²−2=1/166464. These are also Pell-type rational certificates, computed without floating-point cancellation.
example.conclusion: A finite spectrum can make a simple approximation exact, while iteration convergence requires a separate nonlinear argument.

For a pure state of exactly three parties, the quantity vanishes identically. This is a structural obstruction to using it as the proposed transition marker, independent of numerical precision.
definitions: For a density matrix ρ define S(ρ)=−tr(ρlog₂ρ), with 0log0=0. For a pure state on A⊗B⊗C define I₃=S_A+S_B+S_C−S_AB−S_AC−S_BC+S_ABC.
GHZ=(|000⟩+|111⟩)/√2 and W=(|001⟩+|010⟩+|100⟩)/√3. The retrieved parameterized state ψ(g) was not supplied.

result.name: Pure-state cancellation and unequal entanglement spectra
result.statement: Every finite-dimensional pure three-party state has I₃=0. GHZ has all nontrivial one-party and two-party entropies equal to one; W has them equal to h₂(1/3)≈0.9182958341. The two states therefore share I₃ despite different reduced spectra.
result.proof: The Schmidt decomposition across A versus BC gives identical nonzero eigenvalues for ρ_A and ρ_BC, so S_A=S_BC. The other two bipartitions give S_B=S_AC and S_C=S_AB. Purity gives S_ABC=0. Substituting cancels every term. For GHZ, tracing two qubits leaves diag(1/2,1/2). For W it leaves diag(2/3,1/3); permutation symmetry makes this true for each party. The two-party entropies follow from the same Schmidt argument, avoiding a larger eigenproblem. This proves exact zero rather than an approximately small or slightly negative value.

example.setup: As a declared new comparison family take ψ(θ)=cosθ|000⟩+sinθ|111⟩ for 0≤θ≤π/2.
example.calculation: Every one-party entropy is h₂(sin²θ), every two-party entropy is the same, and I₃=0 throughout. At θ=0 it is a product; at θ=π/4 it is GHZ. The entropy changes continuously, while I₃ contains no information about this change. The verifier checks the reduced diagonal eigenvalues for GHZ/W and the exact entropy cancellations numerically.
example.conclusion: A vanishing summary statistic does not imply absent entanglement and cannot locate the claimed g=1 or1.67 transitions without a specified state and observable.

result.proof: Use the augmented complex …→A→A→A→k→0, with every positive-degree differential multiplication by ε and the final map the quotient. Consecutive differentials compose to multiplication by ε²=0. In A, an element is a+bε; multiplying by ε gives aε, so the kernel and image of multiplication by ε are both the one-dimensional ideal εA. The kernel of A→k is also εA. Hence the complex is an exact free resolution. Tensoring with k sends ε to zero, so all resulting differentials vanish and each chain group is k. Its homology is therefore k in every nonnegative degree. This is a complete calculation rather than an invocation of derived language alone.

source.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
source.summary: A fitted score and a theorem about unseen samples are different mathematical objects. The source’s spectral PAC–Bayes claim does not provide its prior, posterior, sample law or loss bound. A standard finite-hypothesis theorem can be derived transparently and shows exactly where those assumptions enter.
definitions: Let H be finite, P a strictly positive prior fixed independently of an iid sample of size m, and ℓ(h,z)∈[0,1]. Define population loss L(h), empirical loss Lhat(h), and KL(Q||P)=ΣQ(h)log[Q(h)/P(h)].
Fix λ>0 andδ∈(0,1) before seeing the sample. Write L(Q),Lhat(Q) for posterior averages.

result.name: A fixed-parameter PAC–Bayes–Hoeffding bound
result.statement: With probability at least1−δ, simultaneously for every posterior Q, L(Q)≤Lhat(Q)+[KL(Q||P)+log(1/δ)]/λ+λ/(8m). This is a theorem under the declared iid bounded-loss model, not a consequence of R² or a spectral fit.
result.proof: Hoeffding’s bounded-variable lemma gives E_sample exp(λ[L(h)−Lhat(h)])≤exp(λ²/(8m)) for each h. Average over the fixed prior and apply Markov: with probability at least1−δ, log E_P exp(λ[L−Lhat])≤λ²/(8m)+log(1/δ). For any finite probability Q, Jensen’s inequality applied after writing the prior sum using Q gives λE_Q(L−Lhat)≤KL(Q||P)+log E_P exp(λ[L−Lhat]). Combining proves the bound uniformly in Q on that one event. Zero posterior masses are handled by continuity. Optimizing λ after observing Q requires a separate uniformization or parameter grid; the fixed-λ theorem does not silently supply it.

example.setup: Choose two hypotheses with uniform prior, a point-mass posterior, m=100,δ=.05,λ=20 and empirical loss.1.
example.calculation: Then KL=log2 and the penalty is log40/20+20/800≈.2094439727, giving L(Q)≤.3094439727 on the stated event. Separately R²=1−SSE/SST only describes squared errors on its evaluated response set; the number.847 omits the response normalization, split and dependency assumptions needed to connect it with this theorem.

source.summary: The historical report’s multiplicative-function approximation and inversion claims lack their actual kernel and norms. definitions: For arithmetic functions f,g:N→C, define(f*g)(n)=Σ_{d|n}f(d)g(n/d). Let1(n)=1 and ε(1)=1, ε(n)=0 for n>1.
A function is multiplicative if f(mn)=f(m)f(n) for coprime m,n and f(1)=1. Its Dirichlet series is D_f(s)=Σf(n)n^(−s) where absolutely convergent.

result.name: Convolution, inversion and a transform product
result.statement: Dirichlet convolution is associative and commutative with identity ε. The Möbius function satisfies μ*1=ε. Whenever D_f,D_g converge absolutely, D_(f*g)(s)=D_f(s)D_g(s). Multiplicative inputs give a multiplicative convolution.
result.proof: Associativity follows by writing either parenthesization as the finite sum overabc=n of f(a)g(b)h(c); commutativity swaps complementary divisors. For μ, summing μ(d) over divisors of n factors as∏_{p|n}(1−1), zero unless n=1. The Dirichlet-series product is the absolutely convergent double sumΣ_{a,b}f(a)g(b)(ab)^(−s); group terms by n=ab to obtain the formula. For coprime m,n, each divisor of mn decomposes uniquely into a divisor of m times a divisor of n, so the convolution sum factors. These are concrete algebraic and analytic hypotheses, not consequences of a neural architecture name.

example.setup: Take f=g=1, then invert the divisor-count function τ=1*1 by μ.
example.calculation: τ(12)=6 from divisors1,2,3,4,6,12. The identity μ*τ=1 gives at12 the sum τ(12)−τ(6)−τ(4)+τ(2)=6−4−3+2=1. Consequently the absolutely convergent series of τ is ζ(s)² for Re(s)>1. The verifier checks the convolution and inversion on every integer through120.

source.title: A fibre functor reconstructs a finite group only with its whole category
source.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
source.summary: Grothendieck’s Galois theory is a substantial theorem about categories and fibre functors. A finite group version admits a short complete proof and identifies the essential naturality requirement. It does not assert that the historical modal implementation exists.
definitions: Let G be a finite group, FinGSet its category of finite left G-sets and equivariant maps, and F its forgetful functor to finite sets.
A natural automorphismη of F is a family of bijectionsη_X:F(X)→F(X) commuting with every equivariant map. Its components are not required to be equivariant themselves.

result.name: Aut(F) is canonically G
result.statement: The map a∈G↦[η_X(x)=ax] is a group isomorphism G→Aut(F). Natural automorphisms are determined by their action on the identity element of the regular G-set.
result.proof: For any a, equivariance of a map f gives f(ax)=af(x), so the family is natural; the inverse family uses a^(−1). Conversely letη be natural and let a=η_G(1), where G carries its left regular action. For any G-set X and x∈X, the map f_x:G→X, g↦gx, is equivariant. Naturality givesη_X(x)=η_X(f_x(1))=f_x(η_G(1))=ax. Thus every natural family has the displayed form and its a is unique. Composition of families corresponds to multiplication ab, proving the group law. The proof uses all these maps f_x; isolated orbit sizes or a single matrix do not supply the reconstruction.

example.setup: Take G=C₃ acting regularly on{0,1,2} by cyclic addition.
example.calculation: The three possible natural families restrict to the three cyclic shifts on the regular set. A transposition fails to commute with its equivariant right translations and therefore cannot be a natural automorphism. The verifier enumerates all six permutations and retains exactly three.
example.conclusion: The finite model shows what is reconstructed and why categorical compatibility is mathematical data rather than a label.

source.status: Developed mathematical repair or classical result; speculative source claims delimited
source.summary: The historical correction marked the étale modality and implementation incomplete. An elementary representation example supplies genuine unit, idempotence and adjunction data. definitions: Work over R with a finite-dimensional representation of C₂, specified by S²=I. Let V_+=ker(S−I) and V_−=ker(S+I), with projections P_±=(I±S)/2.

result.name: A concrete reflector and a tensor obstruction
result.statement: R is left adjoint to I through Hom(V_+,W)≅Hom_C₂(V,IW). The induced idempotent monad IR projects to the trivial summand and is exact. But R(V)⊗R(W)→R(V⊗W) need not be an isomorphism.
result.proof: P_+²=P_+ follows from S²=I, and P_++P_−=I with P_+P_−=0 splits V into the two eigenspaces. If fS=f, then fP_+=f and f kills V_−, so f factors uniquely through V_+. This gives the adjunction and its naturality directly. An equivariant exact sequence splits into independent plus and minus sequences by these natural projections, proving exactness of R. For the tensor claim, take both V and W to be the one-dimensional sign representation. Each invariant subspace is zero, so R(V)⊗R(W)=0. Their tensor has action(−1)(−1)=+1, so R(V⊗W)=R, disproving strong tensor preservation.

example.setup: Use S=diag(1,−1) and compare its plus projection with two sign factors.
example.calculation: P_+=diag(1,0), with rank one and P_+²=P_+. A sign vector has zero plus projection, but the tensor of two sign vectors is invariant and nonzero. The verifier checks the matrices and tensor signs exactly. No postulate is counted as an implementation proof.
example.conclusion: The example distinguishes categorical idempotence, exactness and monoidal compatibility, each of which has different obligations.

source.summary: Several retrieved rules attempted to compute all motivic cohomology from a small inequality in p,q,n. definitions: For a field k and standard integral motivic cohomology of smooth schemes, use H^{p,q}(X,Z)=CH^q(X,2q−p).

result.name: Correct projective decomposition and the Chow diagonal
result.statement: H^{p,q}(P^n_k,Z)≅⊕_{i=0}^n H^{p−2i,q−i}(Spec k,Z). In particular CH^*(P^n_k)=Z[h]/(h^{n+1}); hence H^{2q,q}=Z for0≤q≤n and zero outside that Chow range. Other bidegrees are not specified by that diagonal rule.
result.proof: The projective-bundle theorem states thatΣh^iπ^* gives the displayed isomorphism, withπ:P^n→Spec k. The shifts follow from deg(h^i)=(2i,i). On the diagonal, H^{2r,r}(k)=CH^r(Spec k), which is Z for r=0 and zero for r>0 because a point has no positive-codimension cycles. Thus only i=q survives, yielding the polynomial Chow ring and the relation h^{n+1}=0. Off the diagonal, H^{1,1}(k)=k× is generally nonzero, so a computer rule returning merely zero or one Tate symbol loses genuine base-field data. The general projective-bundle theorem is cited rather than claimed as proved by finite tests; the diagonal and grading consequences are derived explicitly.

example.calculation: The groups in bidegrees(0,0),(2,1),(4,2) are each Z, h² is the point class, and h³=0. For P¹, H^{1,1} contains k× even though its Chow ranks are only one in codimensions zero and one. The verifier implements only the declared truncated polynomial ring and checks degree shifts and products; it does not pretend to compute arbitrary field K-theory.
example.conclusion: A symbolic Tate-basis engine can be correct on a specified cellular Chow subtheory without being a universal motivic-cohomology algorithm.

source.summary: The early July project proposed a homological complexity hierarchy. Its simplicial construction can be made coherent, but its asserted topological classification needs independent proof. Even the empty2-CNF formula provides a decisive counterexample to universal contractibility.
definitions: For n Boolean variables use vertices x_i,¬x_i. A face contains no opposite pair and no set consisting of all negated literals of a clause. Termwise integration is justified by absolute exponential convergence on t>=A and gives the stated series. The coefficient bound yields |a_n/n|<=2, so a geometric series bounds the omitted tail. source.title: Consistent Gaussian coordinates need not live in the Hilbert space
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The August9 synthesis invoked Sazonov and Minlos. A diagonal Hilbert-space construction proves a concrete sufficient condition and exhibits the failure of identity covariance. This keeps a genuine measure theorem separate from formal consistency or category names.
definitions: Let H=ℓ² with basis e_n and independent standard normals Z_n. For q_n≥0 consider X=Σ√q_nZ_ne_n. The covariance has diagonal entries q_n.

result.name: Trace-summable construction and identity-covariance failure
result.statement: IfΣq_n<∞, X converges almost surely in H and in mean square, with characteristic function exp(−Σq_nh_n²/2). For q_n=1 the coordinate law givesℓ² probability zero.
result.proof: The nonnegative random sum S=Σq_nZ_n² has expectationΣq_n by monotone convergence. Finite expectation implies S<∞ almost surely, which is exactly square summability of the coordinates. The tail mean-square error equalsΣ_{n>N}q_n, proving L² convergence. Finite Gaussian characteristic functions multiply, and dominated convergence yields the displayed limit. The resulting Borel probability on the Polish spaceℓ² is Radon. By contrast the strong law gives N⁻¹Σ_{n≤N}Z_n²→1 almost surely when q_n=1, forcing divergence of the squared norm. Consistency of all finite marginals remains true, but their product measure is supported outsideℓ².

example.setup: Choose q_n=2^(−n),n≥1.
example.calculation: The covariance trace and E||X||² are one. Truncation after N has squared mean error2^(−N). Identity-covariance truncations have expected squared norm N and their probability of lying in any fixed-radius ball tends to zero.
example.conclusion: Support and tightness, not just finite consistency, are the decisive missing hypotheses.

source.summary: The geometric τ-clock was eventually described as a sampling cadence rather than a PDE mechanism. That modest interpretation still has a complete mathematical development: exponential decay can be recovered from unequally spaced samples, and a geometric schedule has a transparent resolution-versus-horizon tradeoff.
definitions: Choose times t_k=t₀q^k with t₀>0,q>1, and a positive signal E(t)=C exp(−αt), C>0.
For consecutive samples define α_hat_k=−[log E(t_k)−log E(t_(k−1))]/[t_k−t_(k−1)].

result.name: A geometric checkpoint clock estimates a decay rate without being a soliton
result.statement: For exact exponential data α_hat_k=α for every k, regardless of q. The number of positive checkpoints through horizon T≥t₀ is1+floor(log(T/t₀)/logq). If each log measurement has absolute error at mostδ, then |α_hat_k−α|≤2δ/(t_k−t_(k−1)).
result.proof: Take logarithms: logE(t)=logC−αt. Subtracting two samples cancels logC and gives−α times their time difference, proving the rate identity. The checkpoint count follows by solving t₀q^k≤T for integers k≥0. If the measured logarithms are logE(t_k)+e_k with |e_k|≤δ, the estimated slope differs by−(e_k−e_(k−1))/(t_k−t_(k−1)); the triangle inequality gives the error bound. Thus larger gaps reduce this particular absolute log-noise amplification, while they also discard information about changes within those gaps.

example.setup: Let t₀=1,q=2,C=3,α=1/2 and T=16.
example.calculation: The checkpoints are1,2,4,8,16, exactly five. Their log values are log3−1/2,log3−1,log3−2,log3−4,log3−8. Every consecutive secant gives1/2. With log-error boundδ=1/100, the first rate uncertainty is at most1/50, and the last is at most1/400. A nonexponential signal could share all five values yet differ between them, so this schedule alone does not identify a differential equation. A dimensionless geometric ratio controls the schedule; the decay rate still has reciprocal-time units. Rescaling time by a positive constant rescales the estimated rate inversely, while leaving the geometric checkpoint count through a similarly rescaled horizon unchanged.
example.conclusion: The clock has an exact estimation law and an explicit sampling cost, without importing unsupported soliton terminology.

definitions: Use arithmetic parameters α,β satisfying α+β=a and αβ=p. On the symmetric square, the eigenvalues areα²,αβ,β².

Expanding the three linear factors proves the cubic formula without choosing roots numerically. For p=2,a=−2, the roots of X²+2X+2 are−1±i, whose squares are∓2i. source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
source.summary: The historical pipeline proposed DFT derivatives for a critical-line zero hunt. Fourier differentiation can be exact and useful, provided its object is identified: it differentiates the trigonometric interpolant selected by the sample grid. Finite samples alone cannot bound derivatives of an unrestricted analytic function.
definitions: Sample a2π-periodic function at x_j=2πj/N, j=0,…,N−1. The DFT assigns coefficients to one representative of each frequency class modulo N.
A band-limited trigonometric polynomial with frequencies |k|<N/2 has derivative coefficients ikc_k. Modes k and k+N have identical samples.

result.name: FFT derivatives are exact for an interpolant, not for an unknown function
result.statement: DFT differentiation exactly recovers derivatives of the declared band-limited polynomial. Without a frequency or analytic-tail bound, no finite sample grid gives a uniform derivative-error bound: h(x)=cos(Nx)−1 vanishes on the grid but h″(0)=−N².
result.proof: Discrete orthogonality gives N⁻¹Σ_jexp(i(k−ℓ)x_j)=1 when N divides k−ℓ and0 otherwise, by the finite geometric-sum formula. If all frequencies lie in a single nonaliasing band, this recovers each coefficient exactly. Differentiating the finite Fourier expansion multiplies its coefficient by ik, so the derivative is exact for that expansion. For the counterexample, Nx_j=2πj makes every value of h zero, while differentiating twice gives h″(x)=−N²cos(Nx). Multiplying h by any positive constant enlarges the derivative discrepancy without changing any sample. Analyticity alone therefore does not remove finite-grid nonidentifiability.

example.setup: Use N=8 and the known polynomial f(x)=sin x+2cos2x.
example.calculation: Its nonzero frequencies are±1,±2, all inside the nonaliasing band. The DFT differentiates it to cos x−4sin2x and gives f′(0)=1 exactly in symbolic arithmetic. Adding3(cos8x−1) changes none of the eight samples or the first derivative at zero, but changes the second derivative at zero by−192. A double-zero diagnostic relying on both numerical derivatives needs an error estimate that excludes precisely this kind of invisible high-frequency component.
example.conclusion: The Fourier method becomes a rigorous tool when accompanied by its bandwidth or tail certificate.

source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
source.summary: The double-zero search correctly described its status as heuristic. The distinction can be made mathematically sharp: a contour comparison robustly certifies a total count, whereas a double zero requires exact vanishing of the value and first derivative at the same point.
definitions: A holomorphic function has a zero of multiplicity two at z₀ exactly when f(z₀)=f′(z₀)=0 and f″(z₀)≠0.
Rouché’s theorem says that |h|<|g| on a simple closed contour implies g and g+h have the same total zero count inside, including multiplicities, provided they are holomorphic on the enclosed region.

result.name: A contour count can certify two zeros without certifying a double zero
result.statement: For f_ε(z)=(z−1)²+ε and0<|ε|<r², the circle |z−1|=r encloses exactly two zeros, but both are simple. Its midpoint has f′_ε(1)=0 and f″_ε(1)=2, although it is not a zero.
result.proof: On the contour, |(z−1)²|=r²>|ε|, so Rouché compares f_ε with(z−1)² and gives total count two. Alternatively its roots are1±√(−ε), both strictly inside the circle. When ε≠0 they are distinct, and the derivative2(z−1) is nonzero at either root, proving simplicity. At ε=0 the roots merge and the first two vanishing equations hold exactly. The strict contour gap r²−|ε| is robust under additional perturbations smaller than that gap, while exact equality f(1)=0 is not stable under arbitrary small constant perturbations.

example.setup: Take ε=1/100 and r=1/2.
example.calculation: The roots are1±i/10. On the contour the unperturbed modulus is1/4 and the perturbation is1/100, leaving margin6/25. A certified evaluation error below that margin preserves the total count, but not a claim that either root is repeated. The midpoint values are f(1)=1/100,f′(1)=0,f″(1)=2. A tolerance treating the first value as zero can therefore misclassify two nearby simple zeros as one double zero.
example.conclusion: A useful certificate states exactly whether it establishes existence, total multiplicity, isolation or an exact repeated root.

source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
source.summary: The September sampler used cosine aggregates and bootstrap intervals under an Iwasawa label. A genuine elementary analogue starts with a power series over Z_p. Its invariants come from coefficient valuations and reduction modulo p, and can be proved invariant under multiplication by a unit.
definitions: For nonzero F(T)=Σa_nTⁿ∈Z_p[[T]], define μ(F)=min_n v_p(a_n) and λ(F)=min{n:v_p(a_n)=μ(F)}.
Write F=p^μF₀, where at least one coefficient of F₀ is a unit. A power-series unit U has constant coefficient in Z_p×.

result.name: A μ-invariant is a valuation, not a real-valued twist statistic
result.statement: For nonzero F,G, μ(FG)=μ(F)+μ(G) and λ(FG)=λ(F)+λ(G). In particular multiplication by a unit preserves both invariants. These statements follow directly from the integral-domain property of F_p[[T]].
result.proof: Divide F and G by their lowest p-powers, obtaining primitive series F₀,G₀ whose reductions modulo p are nonzero. Their product remains nonzero because a formal series ring over a field is a domain: the first nonzero coefficients multiply to the first nonzero coefficient of the product. Thus no extra p divides every coefficient of F₀G₀, proving the μ identity. The orders in T of the two nonzero reductions are λ(F),λ(G); their product has the sum of those orders. A unit has μ=λ=0, so multiplication by it preserves both values. The argument uses the complete power series, not a real distributional interpretation.

example.setup: Use p=3 and F(T)=9(3+T²+3T³).
example.calculation: The coefficient valuations are at least two, with the first valuation-two coefficient at degree two; hence μ=2 and λ=2. Multiplying by1+T gives9(3+3T+T²+4T³+3T⁴). After division by9 and reduction modulo3 this is T²+T³=T²(1+T), retaining the same invariants. Conversely, a finite truncation before degree two would incorrectly suggest all known coefficients have valuation at least three; unseen coefficients must be controlled before certifying the infinite-series minimum.
example.conclusion: The arithmetic meaning is now explicit and supplies exact certificates for a declared algebraic object.

source.limits: This elementary definition does not prove that a sampled series is the characteristic series of an Iwasawa module or a p-adic L-function. Real cosine twists, confidence intervals and numerical regularity alone do not establish that connection.

definitions: Let resource shares be rationals q∈[0,1]. Define q⊕r=q+r only when q+r≤1; zero is the identity.

result.name: Fractional ownership is a partial algebra, not duplicable permission
result.statement: This operation is a partial commutative monoid with cancellation. A full share has no compatible positive remainder and cannot be composed with a second full share. Any positive rational share can be split into smaller compatible rational shares.
result.proof: Commutativity and the zero law follow from rational addition. If q⊕r=q⊕s, cancellation in Q gives r=s. If1⊕r is defined with r≥0, the defining inequality1+r≤1 forces r=0. Thus1⊕1 is undefined. source.summary: The free-abelian formalization naturally leads to integer cokernels. Their torsion is a concrete and computable obstruction. Passing to real vectors can erase it entirely, so an approximate linear solve is not a replacement for the integral certificate.
definitions: For an integer matrix F:Zⁿ→Zᵐ, its cokernel is Zᵐ/imF. Smith normal form uses unimodular integer row and column changes to diagonal entries d₁|d₂|⋯.

result.statement: coker diag(2,3) is Z/2⊕Z/3≅Z/6. Its order is six although F is invertible over Q and R. Every homomorphism from this finite cokernel to the additive group Z is zero.

source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
source.summary: The index tables have a rigorous finite analogue that explains the mechanism behind protection: a differential pairs nonzero even and odd modes, so their heat contributions cancel. An ordinary heat trace does not have this cancellation.
definitions: Take a two-term finite-dimensional real or complex Hilbert complex C⁰→ᵈC¹. Let D=d+d* on C⁰⊕C¹, graded even/odd.

result.statement: For every t≥0 in this finite-dimensional complex, Str(e^(−tD²))=dimkerd−dimcokerd=dimC⁰−dimC¹. More generally a finite complex has heat supertrace equal to its alternating cohomology dimension.
result.proof: The positive spectra of d*d and dd* agree including multiplicities: if d*d v=λv with λ>0, then dv≠0 and dd*(dv)=λdv, with inverse correspondence λ⁻¹d* on the eigenspaces. Hence e^(−tλ) cancels between the two graded traces. The remaining zero modes are kerd in degree zero and ker d*=cokerd in degree one. Rank-nullity gives their dimension difference dimC⁰−dimC¹. The same pairing on each degree proves the finite-complex statement, equivalently by decomposing into harmonic spaces and two-term exact pairs.

Their supertrace is zero for every t. The cohomology dimensions are one in each degree, also giving1−1=0. This explicitly demonstrates why the grading and the differential identity are part of the index theorem’s mechanism.
example.conclusion: A protected quantity can be constructed and checked, but its protection comes from a proved pairing of modes.

source.status: Classical mathematics with newly authored proof or worked finite certificate
source.summary: The October audit correctly questioned using positive-degree Ext in a semisimple setting. The exact reason is elementary: every short exact sequence splits, and every object is projective. A deformation theory must therefore identify another complex or weaken semisimplicity.
definitions: An abelian category is semisimple here when every short exact sequence splits. In finite-dimensional vector spaces, every subspace has a complement.

result.name: Semisimplicity kills ordinary extension classes
result.statement: In a semisimple abelian category with the usual Ext construction, Extⁿ(C,A)=0 for n>0. For finite-dimensional vector spaces, a split extension is explicitly B≅A⊕C.
result.proof: Choose a section s:C→B of the surjection p:B→C. Then(a,c)↦i(a)+s(c) is an isomorphism A⊕C→B: injectivity follows after applying p, and surjectivity follows by subtracting s(p(b)) from b. Hence every extension represents the zero class in Ext¹. More generally, given an epimorphism and a map from any object, a splitting of the epimorphism lifts that map; therefore every object is projective. A resolution concentrated in degree zero computes all higher Ext as zero. This is a theorem about this specific derived functor, not every cohomology assigned to a tensor category.

A hypothetical lift of1 from the quotient would be1+cε, but multiplication by ε sends it to ε≠0, whereas ε acts as zero on k. Thus nontrivial extensions arise once the semisimple hypothesis is removed.

source.summary: The recovered integral was described as lacking an elementary closed form. Its asymmetry disappears under x↦−x, leaving the classical Fourier transform of a quartic rational function. The resulting formula is exact for every real modulation parameter.
definitions: Let a∈R and I(a)=∫R cos²(ax)/[(1+ix²)(1+4^x)(1−ix²)]dx.
Write w(x)=1/(1+4^x); then w(x)+w(−x)=1.

result.name: Parity reduction and quartic transform
result.proof: The conjugate factors multiply to1+x⁴. The remaining factor f(x)=cos²(ax)/(1+x⁴) is even and integrable. Substitution x↦−x gives I=∫f(x)w(−x)dx, so adding yields2I=∫f. Now cos²(ax)=(1+cos2ax)/2. For b>0 close the contour for e^(ibz)/(1+z⁴) in the upper half-plane; the poles are e^(i π/4) and e^(3i π/4), with residues e^(ibz)/(4z³). Their sum, multiplied by2π i, is F(b)=π e^(−b/√2)[cos(b/√2)+sin(b/√2)]/√2. The large arc vanishes by the exponential factor and quartic denominator; b=0 follows directly or by dominated convergence. Evenness supplies F(−b)=F(b). Therefore I=(F(0)+F(2a))/4, proving the formula. Every exchange is justified by domination with1/(1+x⁴).

example.setup: Evaluate a=0, compare large|a|, and check local curvature at the origin.
example.calculation: I(0)=π/(2√2), while I(a)→π/(4√2) as|a|→∞. Differentiating under the integral twice is allowed since x²/(1+x⁴) is integrable, giving I″(0)=−π/√2. The third derivative cannot be justified by the same absolute-moment argument; the closed form indeed has an|a|³ term near zero.
example.conclusion: The recovered prototype is solved exactly, and its smoothness is linked to the decay of the quartic weight.

source.limits: This identity proves no eigenvalue law for an unspecified integral operator and no physical realization. A finite precision plot should be checked against this formula rather than treated as evidence for a new constant.
source.extension: Replace4^x by any positive-base exponential c^x with c>0, c≠1: the same symmetry gives exactly the same integral for every even integrable numerator.

source.title: Exact forms have zero periods; winding and entropy need different data
source.status: Classical or newly chosen explicit model developed with proof; historical conjectures delimited
source.summary: The recovered model simultaneously declared Jconstant, defined χ=(e/N)d J, and assigned nonzero quantized integrals. These statements are incompatible. A genuine circle one-form gives a constructive replacement and makes clear what hash entropy would mean mathematically.
definitions: Let N>0 and J be a single-valued smooth real function; χ=(e/N)d J is exact.
On S¹ the angular differentiald θ is a global closed one-form even though θ is only locally a single-valued real function.

result.name: Period obstruction and a correct circle model
result.statement: Every closed-loop integral of χ is zero. In contrast η=(N/(2π e))d θ has period∫_γη=n N/e for a loop of windingn. The expressionlog(N/e)=1 holds only when N=e², not for arbitrary N.
result.proof: For a parametrized closed loop γ, the chain rule gives∫_γ d J=J(γ(1))−J(γ(0))=0. If Jis constant, χ vanishes pointwise, making the contradiction stronger. For the circle model lift γ to an angle Θ(t) on an interval. Its endpoint difference is2π n, so the integral of η is Nn/e. There is no globally single-valued real Jwithd J=d θ, because such a function would force the nonzero circle period to vanish. Finallylog(N/e)=log N−1, so setting it equal toone fixes N=e². If N denotes the number of independent uniform hash bits, Shannon entropy is Nlog2 nats, whereaslog N is the entropy of N equiprobable outcomes; these are different sample spaces.

example.setup: Take N=320 and a once-around circle loop.
example.calculation: The exact-form model gives zero regardless of N. The corrected angular form gives320/e. The claimed entropy becomeslog320−1≈4.76832nats, while320uniform bits have320log2≈221.807nats. Merely rescaling384to320 cannot preserve an equation asserting the same fixed entropy.
example.conclusion: Winding can be modeled consistently, but it requires a non-exact cohomology class and a clearly specified probability space.

source.limits: No cryptographic deck transformation or physical energy quantization follows from these definitions. A hash digest is finite discrete data and does not automatically define a smooth covering-space action.
source.extension: Specify a principal U(1)bundle and connection, then compare gauge-invariant holonomy with integral cohomology and a separately defined entropy model.

source.title: A positive kernel is not necessarily positive definite
source.status: Classical or newly chosen explicit model developed with proof; historical conjectures delimited
source.summary: The recovered kernel discussion moved from positive integrands to kernel methods and a conjectured spectral decay. A covariance or reproducing kernel must satisfy all finite Gram-matrix inequalities, a much stronger condition than having positive values.
definitions: A Hermitian kernel k(x, y) is positive definite if Σ overline c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j)≥0 for every finite point set and coefficients.
For a real translation kernel k(x, y)=f(x−y), Hermitian symmetry requires f(−t)=f(t).

result.name: An exact quartic Gram counterexample
result.statement: The pointwise positive even function f(t)=1/(1+t⁴) is not positive definite on R. Its Gram matrix at points−1/2,0,1/2 has negative determinant−157/1156.
result.proof: At adjacent separation1/2, f=16/17; at separation1, f=1/2. The Gram matrix is[[1, a, b],[a,1, a],[b, a,1]] witha=16/17, b=1/2. Expanding its determinant gives(1−b)(1+b−2a²). Here1+b−2a²=3/2−512/289=−157/578, so the determinant is−157/1156. A positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix has nonnegative determinant, proving failure. An even more immediate obstruction affects the original real asymmetric logistic factor: a translation kernel using it is not even, hence not Hermitian. On the other hand the quartic Fourier transform F(b)=∫e^(ibx)/(1+x⁴)dx is positive definite as a function of b: the Gram quadratic form equals∫|Σ c_j e^(ib_jx)|²/(1+x⁴)dx≥0. The response and its Fourier transform therefore play different roles.

example.setup: Compare f itself with F(b)=π e^(−|b|/√2)[cos(|b|/√2)+sin(|b|/√2)]/√2.
example.calculation: F can take negative values, yet its Gram forms remain nonnegative by the integral-square representation. Thus pointwise nonnegativity is neither necessary nor sufficient for positive definiteness. A valid covariance can have negative correlations, whereas a positive-valued response can fail the covariance test.
example.conclusion: The exact three-point certificate distinguishes two often-confused meanings of “positive kernel.”

source.limits: No spectrum λ_n can be assigned until an operator, domain, measure and boundary conditions are supplied. In particular the recovered(n logn)^(−4/3) claim is not certified by a scalar formula.
source.extension: Define an integral operator on a compact measured domain, prove self-adjointness and compactness, and derive its eigenvalue asymptotics from regularity and geometry rather than from a numerical fit.

source.title: A bridge functional with an exact variance
source.status: Classical or newly chosen explicit model developed with proof; historical conjectures delimited
source.summary: The recovered stochastic calibration used a kernel inside an OU/Wiener functional without a complete process specification. A Brownian bridge example gives an exact definition and reveals the covariance correction that is lost if a bridge is treated as an unconstrained Wiener process.
definitions: Let W_t be standard Brownian motion on[0, T] and B_t=W_t−(t/T)W_T.
For deterministicf∈L²(0, T), define its bridge functional J_f=∫₀ᵀf(t)d W_t−(W_T/T)∫₀ᵀf(t)dt.

result.name: Gaussian bridge-functional variance
result.statement: J_f is centered Gaussian and Var(J_f)=∫f²dt−T^(−1)(∫fdt)². Consequently a constantf produces zero, rather than Wiener variance T f².
result.proof: Approximatef by step functions to define the Wiener integral in mean square. Its mean is zero, its variance is∫f² by the Itô isometry, and its covariance with W_T=∫1d W is∫f. Expanding the variance of the displayed linear combination gives∫f²−2T^(−1)(∫f)²+T^(−1)(∫f)², proving the formula. It is nonnegative by Cauchy–Schwarz and vanishes exactly for almost-everywhere constantf. Gaussianity follows because the approximating functionals are finite linear combinations of a jointly Gaussian process and converge in L². This definition also avoids incorrectly using the original Brownian filtration to treat the anticipative representation of B as an ordinary Itô integrator.

example.setup: Take T=1 andf(t)=t, then comparef(t)=1.
example.calculation: Forf=t the variance is1/3−(1/2)²=1/12. Forf=1, J_f=W_1−W_1=0. An unconstrained Wiener functional∫₀¹td W has variance1/3, so conditioning removes a substantial component. For an OU bridge the same Gaussian conditional-covariance rule is C_br(s, t)=C(s, t)−C(s, T)C(T, t)/C(T, T), with the OU covariance explicitly supplied first.
example.conclusion: The stochastic object has a complete probability model, a proved variance, and an exact nontrivial example.

source.limits: Random or adapted kernel parameters require separate integrability and filtration conditions. A complex-valued kernel needs its Hermitian covariance convention. This finite-time construction does not validate a device or an unspecified stochastic calibration.
source.extension: For a deterministic observation kernel and a specified OU covariance, evaluate the double covariance integral and compare bridge and unconditioned uncertainties with rigorous quadrature errors.

definitions: On[0, L], imposew(0)=w(L)=w″(0)=w″(L)=0 and let A=D∂ₓ⁴+P∂ₓ², with D>0.
For a damped equationmw_tt+η w_t+Aw=0 use the time convention e^(−i ω t), withm, η≥0.

result.name: Hinged spectrum and positive-form threshold
result.statement: The sine modes have eigenvalues D(n π/L)⁴−P(n π/L)². The form⟨w, Aw⟩=D||w″||²−P||w′||² is positive if P<D π²/L². The Fourier response denominator is Dk⁴−Pk²−m ω²−i ηω under the stated convention.
result.proof: Integrating the fourth derivative twice and using both hinged endpoint conditions removes boundary terms. Integrating the second derivative once gives the negative gradient norm, proving the form. The sine basis satisfies both endpoint conditions and differentiates to the displayed eigenvalues. Since||w″||²≥(π/L)²||w′||² by sine expansion, the threshold gives a strictly positive form. Conversely the first sine mode has zero form at P=D π²/L² and negative form above it, so the threshold is sharp. Finally substitutinge^(ikx−i ω t) gives∂ₓ⁴=k⁴,∂ₓ²=−k²,∂_t²=−ω²,∂_t=−i ω. A plusi ηω term would correspond to the opposite time convention, not a different damping law.

example.setup: Take D=1, L=π, m=1 and P=1/2.
example.calculation: The first two stiffness eigenvalues are1−1/2=1/2 and16−2=14. At P=1 the first mode becomes neutral. With η>0 and positive stiffness, each modal energy E_n=(|a_n′|²+λ_n|a_n|²)/2 satisfies E_n′=−η|a_n′|²≤0.
example.conclusion: The boundary domain, stiffness spectrum, threshold and damping sign are all fixed by the equation rather than an analogy.
