source.title: Contraction yields finite-resolution stabilization only with a compatible observation
source.status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
source.summary: A geometric error bound gives an explicit resolution time. Exact digit stabilization additionally requires the fixed point to lie inside an observation cell; convergence in an ordinary metric alone cannot rule out endless crossings of a cell boundary.
definitions: Let R be a q-contraction on a complete metric space, 0<q<1, with fixed point x_*. Then d(R^nx,x_*)≤q^n d(x,x_*).
Let O_k be a finite-resolution observation and assume O_k is constant on the open ball B(x_*,δ_k), with δ_k>0.
For a binary prefix metric, q=2^{−a} and initial depth ℓ₀ give depth at least ℓ₀+an when the metric contraction and encoding are genuinely compatible.

result.name: Explicit resolution bound and a boundary counterexample
result.statement: If q^n d(x,x_*)<δ_k, then O_k(R^nx)=O_k(x_*). Thus any integer n>log(d(x,x_*)/δ_k)/log(1/q) suffices. With a non-strict cell convention this becomes the familiar ceiling formula after checking equality cases.
result.proof: Iterate the contraction inequality and compare its right side with the stated observation radius. The radius assumption then gives exact equality of the finite observations; no limit interchange is needed. For binary depth, taking base-two logarithms of d_n≤2^{−ℓ₀}q^n gives the linear-depth lower bound and the source’s N_lin expression with the appropriate strictness convention. To see the missing hypothesis in Euclidean space, use R(x)=−x/2 and O(x)=1_{x≥0}. The fixed point zero lies on the observation boundary. Starting at any positive x, the iterates alternate sign forever while their distance to zero contracts by one half.

example.setup: Let q=1/2, initial distance one and δ_k=2^{−k}.
example.calculation: For the open-ball criterion, n=k+1 always suffices, while n=k only reaches the boundary. At k=12 a certified interior observation stabilizes by step13. The sign observation in the preceding counterexample never stabilizes at any step, despite exactly the same numerical contraction factor.
example.conclusion: Approximate convergence and exact stabilization become equivalent only after the observation topology is controlled.

source.limits: Stabilization of one orbit is not automatically the Mittag–Leffler stabilization of all tower images. A proof requires a uniform bound over each declared domain and compatible bonding maps; vanishing lim¹ alone does not imply contraction.
source.extension: For a concrete truncation tower, prove a uniform image-diameter bound and cell-interior condition at every level. Distinguish monotonicity of every register from an aggregate score, and include periodic-map analysis when the derivative has modulus one or greater.

source.title: A semigroup contraction is exactly a generator inequality in the same metric
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; recovered claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The recovered contraction equivalence is correct after specifying its metric and the generator domain. It is a theorem about one chosen quadratic energy; existence of some equivalent contractive metric is a separate question. The proof works without assuming a bounded generator.
definitions: Let T(t) be a strongly continuous semigroup on a real or complex Hilbert space with generator A and dense domain D(A). Let P be bounded self-adjoint with mI≤P≤MI for constants 0<m≤M.
Write V(x)=⟨Px,x⟩. The expression A*P+PA is interpreted as the quadratic form 2 Re⟨PAx,x⟩ on D(A), without assuming P maps D(A) into D(A*).

result.name: Generator–energy equivalence
result.statement: For α real, V(T(t)x)≤e^(−2αt)V(x) for all x and t≥0 if and only if 2 Re⟨PAx,x⟩≤−2αV(x) for all x∈D(A). Consequently ||T(t)||≤√(M/m)e^(−αt).
result.proof: For x∈D(A), semigroup invariance of D(A) gives a differentiable trajectory and dV(T(t)x)/dt=2 Re⟨PAT(t)x,T(t)x⟩. Multiplying by e^(2αt) makes the derivative nonpositive. Integrating proves decay on D(A), and density plus boundedness of T(t) and P extends it to every x. Conversely, divide the energy inequality by t after subtracting V(x), and take t↓0 for x∈D(A). The two norm bounds m||x||²≤V(x)≤M||x||² yield the asserted ordinary-norm estimate. This establishes both directions in exactly the declared metric, including α=0.

example.setup: Use A=diag(−1,−3), P=diag(2,1), α=1.
example.calculation: AᵀP+PA=diag(−4,−6)≤−2P=diag(−4,−2). The trajectory has V(T(t)x)=2e^(−2t)x₁²+e^(−6t)x₂²≤e^(−2t)V(x). The metric condition ratio is M/m=2.
example.conclusion: The rate and the norm-equivalence prefactor are explicit and independently checkable.

source.limits: If P is merely positive and not coercive in infinite dimension, this energy may fail to control the original norm. The form statement avoids an unjustified operator-domain identity.
source.extension: For a PDE, specify D(A), prove the integration-by-parts boundary terms have the required sign, and establish uniform coercivity under discretization.

source.title: A vanishing gap produces inverse time scales only for the modes it controls
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; recovered claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The recovered learning program proposes several co-closing gaps and inverse-gap laws. A diagonal gradient-flow model proves the mechanism while showing exactly what the spectrum and the forcing must contribute. Co-closing distinct gaps remains an additional hypothesis.
definitions: Let H be symmetric positive definite and consider x′=−Hx+b. Its gap is Δ=λ_min(H). The equilibrium is H⁻¹b.
For a spectral density cλ^(ν−1) on [0,1] with ν>0, consider the mode average C(t)=c∫₀¹e^(−tλ)λ^(ν−1)dλ.

result.name: Gap, susceptibility and near-zero tails
result.statement: The worst-case decay time is 1/Δ and ||H⁻¹||=1/Δ. If a continuous spectral measure has the stated density, C(t)∼cΓ(ν)t^(−ν), despite the absence of a positive gap.
result.proof: Diagonalize H in an orthonormal basis. Each error coordinate evolves as e^(−λ_jt), and the slowest allowed eigenvector attains the rate Δ. The equilibrium derivative with respect to b is H⁻¹, whose largest singular value is 1/Δ. In the integral set u=tλ, obtaining C(t)=ct^(−ν)∫₀^t e^(−u)u^(ν−1)du. The integral tends to Γ(ν) by monotone convergence. A spectral density alone does not specify an observed correlation unless the observable has that spectral measure; an observable orthogonal to slow modes can decay faster. Finally, independent diagonal blocks H₁=diag(ε,1) and H₂=I show one gap can close while another stays one.

example.calculation: The slow time is 10 and equilibrium is (10,0), with sensitivity 10 in the first direction. The continuum average is C(t)=(1−e^(−t))/t, so tC(t)→1. Replacing b by (0,1) removes the slow equilibrium response.
example.conclusion: Inverse-gap and power-law claims become testable statements about named modes and spectral weights.

source.title: The Lyapunov Gramian certifies stability and exposes nonnormal amplification
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; recovered claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The March resolvent program contains a valid finite-dimensional core. A positive Gramian turns asymptotic eigenvalue stability into an energy identity, while a triangular example shows why stable eigenvalues alone do not control transient gain.
definitions: Let A be a real Hurwitz matrix, meaning every eigenvalue has negative real part, and let Q be symmetric positive definite.
Define P=∫₀^∞e^(Aᵀt)Qe^(At)dt. Finite dimension ensures exponential integrability, even for Jordan blocks.

result.name: Continuous Lyapunov construction
result.statement: The integral is positive definite, satisfies AᵀP+PA=−Q, and is the unique symmetric solution. Conversely, P>0 and Q>0 in this equation imply A is Hurwitz.
result.proof: Differentiate e^(Aᵀt)Qe^(At) and integrate from zero to infinity; the boundary values are zero and Q. Positivity follows because the integrand at t=0 is positive on each nonzero vector and is continuous. If AᵀX+XA=0, the function e^(Aᵀt)Xe^(At) is constant and tends to zero, so X=0. For the converse, if Av=λv for a complex nonzero eigenvector, then 2 Re(λ)v*Pv=−v*Qv<0, forcing Re λ<0. These arguments also distinguish solving the equation from merely observing a small numerical residual: coercivity must be checked.

example.calculation: e^(At)=e^(−t)[[1,2t],[0,1]]. Integrating its Gram product gives P=[[1/2,1/2],[1/2,3/2]], with determinant 1/2>0. Direct multiplication gives AᵀP+PA=−I. Starting from (0,1), the first coordinate is 2te^(−t), which initially grows despite both eigenvalues being −1.
example.conclusion: The Gramian supplies a rigorous metric; it does not remove amplification in the original Euclidean metric.

source.limits: An infinite-dimensional integral Gramian may be bounded and injective without being coercive. The converse then needs additional observability or energy hypotheses.
source.extension: For a family of matrices, certify lower and upper Gramian eigenvalue bounds uniformly and compare the resulting energy bound with direct resolvent estimates.

source.title: A resolvent measures gain; it does not determine arbitrary parameter curvature
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; recovered claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The source asserts a proportionality involving a Hessian condition number, directional resolvent gain and metric eigenvalues. Such a universal identity is unsupported without defining the objective and its parameterization. A precise derivative formula gives a useful replacement.
definitions: For an invertible matrix M(θ), define R(θ)=M(θ)⁻¹ and use the Euclidean operator norm. Assume M is twice differentiable in θ.
A stable system can use M=iωI−A(θ). The Hessian of a separate scalar objective additionally depends on its output map and second derivatives.

result.name: Inverse derivative and a sharp limitation
result.statement: DR[H]=−RHR when H is the perturbation of M; hence ||DR[H]||≤||R||²||H||. No Hessian-condition identity depending on R alone holds for arbitrary scalar objectives.
result.proof: Differentiate MR=I to obtain H R+M DR[H]=0, and multiply by R on the left. Differentiating again along affine M gives D²R[H,K]=RHRKR+RKRHR, bounded by 2||R||³||H||||K||. For the limitation, hold A=−I fixed, so the resolvent at ω=0 is I. Choose a parameter objective f_c(θ)=θ₁²/2+cθ₂²/2 for any c≥1. Its Hessian has condition number c, while every system resolvent remains unchanged. Even for a fixed objective, changing parameter units rescales its Hessian by a congruence. An invariant comparison therefore requires an explicitly transported parameter metric.

example.setup: Perturb the scalar matrix M=2 by h.
example.calculation: R(h)=1/(2+h), R′(0)=−1/4 and R″(0)=1/4. The derivative bound ||R||²=1/4 is attained for H=1. The independently chosen f_100 has Hessian condition 100 although the unperturbed resolvent is 1/2.
example.conclusion: A valid gain-to-sensitivity estimate emerges, with a transparent counterexample to universal curvature identification.

source.title: Discrete stability has its own Gramian and a unit-circle resolvent
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; recovered claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The source correctly distinguishes AᵀP+PA from the discrete Stein equation. The distinction matters because a discretization may destroy stability even when its underlying continuous generator is stable. Exact scalar calculations show the admissible step range.
definitions: Let F be a real matrix with spectral radius less than one and Q>0. Define P=Σ_(k≥0)(Fᵀ)^kQF^k.
For x_(n+1)=Fx_n, the energy change is x_nᵀ(FᵀPF−P)x_n. Frequency response is evaluated at z=e^(iω) on the unit circle.

result.name: Discrete Lyapunov identity
result.statement: The convergent series is positive definite and satisfies FᵀPF−P=−Q. Conversely, a positive solution with Q>0 forces every eigenvalue of F to have modulus less than one.
result.proof: Shift the summation index in FᵀPF; all terms cancel except the k=0 term, yielding −Q. Positivity follows from the first summand. For an eigenvector Fv=λv, the equation gives (|λ|²−1)v*Pv=−v*Qv, hence |λ|<1. A forced harmonic trajectory x_n=z^n u with input z^n b satisfies (zI−F)u=b. Thus the harmonic gain is controlled by ||(zI−F)⁻¹||, rather than by the continuous resolvent with an unchanged frequency variable. The proof makes no claim that the numerical time step has a negligible effect on the spectrum.

example.setup: Apply explicit Euler with step h to x′=−2x, giving F=1−2h and Q=1.
example.calculation: Stability is |1−2h|<1, exactly 0<h<1. At h=1/4, F=1/2 and P=Σ4^(−k)=4/3, so F²P−P=−1. At h=3/2, F=−2 and trajectories diverge although the original ODE decays.
example.conclusion: The energy certificate must be recomputed or preserved by the chosen discretization.

source.limits: Finite-dimensional spectral radius suffices for the series, whereas an infinite-dimensional bounded operator can require stronger power bounds. Sampling aliasing also changes frequency interpretation.
source.extension: Compare implicit Euler, exact sampling and a structure-preserving scheme through a uniform discrete coercivity estimate on a declared step interval.

definitions: A three-partite three-uniform hypergraph has vertex classes X,Y,Z and edges containing one vertex from each class. A matching has pairwise vertex-disjoint edges.
Let m be the number of edges and Δ the maximum vertex degree. An induced matching additionally forbids every other edge among the chosen vertex sets.

result.name: Greedy matching certificate and induced obstruction
result.statement: Every such hypergraph has an ordinary matching of size at least m/(3Δ−2), rounded upward. The largest possible size is at most min(|X|,|Y|,|Z|). Neither bound alone controls induced matching size.
result.proof: Choose an edge and delete every edge sharing one of its vertices. At most 1+3(Δ−1)=3Δ−2 edges disappear in a step, because counting overlaps multiple times only enlarges this upper bound. Repeating until no edge remains gives m≤(3Δ−2)|M|. The upper bound follows because each matching edge consumes one vertex from each class. For the induced limitation, take the complete three-partite hypergraph with each class of size n≥2. It has an ordinary perfect matching of size n. Any two selected edges already create cross edges using vertices from their six endpoints, so no induced matching has size two. Regularity and perfectly balanced projection sizes therefore do not remove the obstruction.

example.calculation: There are m=8 edges and Δ=4. The greedy bound is ceil(8/10)=1, the ordinary optimum is 2, and the induced optimum is 1. All three vertex projections have size 2, yet their logarithmic sizes do not determine the induced optimum.

source.title: The logarithmic-cosine integral has an exact evaluation on its convergence strip
source.status: Developed classical result with a checked example; recovered claims corrected where needed
source.summary: The source integral admits a classical analytic proof. The endpoint at zero is essential: an unrestricted Laplace–Fubini argument fails above one half even though the complex integral itself remains integrable up to exponent one.
definitions: For 0<x<π/2 set L(x)=−log cos x, W(x)=L(x)+ix, and use the principal complex power W^(−α). Let I(α)=∫₀^(π/2)Re W(x)^(−α)dx for real α.
Near zero, W=ix+O(x²); near π/2, Re W tends to infinity. The holomorphic complex integral J(α)=∫W^(−α)dx exists for 0<Re α<1.

result.name: Exact integral identity
result.statement: For real 0<α<1, I(α)=π/[2(log 2)^α]. The proof first uses absolute Fubini on 0<Re α<1/2 and then analytic continuation inside the convergence strip.
result.proof: For t>0, set z=e^(2ix) on the upper unit semicircle. The integrand (cos x)^t e^(−itx) equals ((1+z⁻¹)/2)^t. Equivalently conjugating uses ((1+z)/2)^t; integrate dz/(2iz), and close by the real diameter with a small indentation at zero. The diameter contribution has real part zero except the indentation, whose contribution is π/2 times the value at zero, 2^(−t). Thus ∫cos^t x cos(tx)dx=π/2^(t+1). The Laplace formula W^(−α)=Γ(α)⁻¹∫₀^∞t^(α−1)e^(−tW)dt is absolutely integrable jointly when Re α<1/2 because L∼x²/2. Taking the symmetric combination W^(−α)+conj(W)^(−α) gives the cosine identity and π/[2(log2)^α]. Both sides are holomorphic for 0<Re α<1, using local domination x^(−Re α), so the identity theorem extends the result throughout that strip.

example.setup: Take α=1/2.
example.calculation: The result is I(1/2)=π/(2√log2), approximately 1.8867186678. At the recovered α≈0.7418045150878947 the expression is approximately 2.0615613748; this is a fresh evaluation, not an endorsement of the source’s separate repeated-value claim.
example.conclusion: The evaluation is rigorous within the stated strip and has a clear endpoint restriction.

definitions: Let a be the positive real fourth root of two. The roots of x⁴−2 are a,ia,−a,−ia, and the splitting field is K=Q(a,i).

result.statement: [K:Q]=8 and Gal(K/Q)=⟨ρ,τ:ρ⁴=τ²=1,τρτ=ρ⁻¹⟩≅D₄.
result.proof: Eisenstein at two makes x⁴−2 irreducible over Q, so [Q(a):Q]=4. The field Q(a) is real and does not contain i; adjoining i doubles the degree, giving eight. Conjugation τ has order two and sends ia to −ia; checking on the generators a and i gives τρτ=ρ⁻¹. The eight maps ρ^j and τρ^j are distinct: the first four fix i while the other four conjugate it, and their images of a distinguish j. A degree-eight splitting field has exactly these eight automorphisms.

example.calculation: ρ acts by the four-cycle (1 2 3 4). τ fixes roots one and three and swaps two and four. Composing τρτ sends a to −ia, matching ρ⁻¹(a).

definitions: On the disk |z|<1 use ds=2|dz|/(1−|z|²). For real t≥0, distance from zero to r∈[0,1) is 2artanh r.
For M∈SL₂(R), its projective action on the upper half-plane is hyperbolic when |trM|>2, parabolic when |trM|=2 with nontrivial projective action, and elliptic when |trM|<2.

result.name: The Poincaré disk distance and hyperbolic generator gate have exact formulas
result.statement: The disk distance is d(z,w)=2artanh|(z−w)/(1−conj(w)z)|. A hyperbolic M has translation length ℓ=2arcosh(|trM|/2); parabolic or elliptic generators do not have this positive hyperbolic translation length.
result.proof: The disk automorphism φ_w(z)=(z−w)/(1−conj(w)z) sends w to zero. Direct differentiation gives |φ_w′(z)|/(1−|φ_w(z)|²)=1/(1−|z|²), so it preserves the line element. Integrating the radial line gives ∫₀^r2du/(1−u²)=2artanh r. A radial line is shortest: for any path, radial variation gives the same integral as a lower bound on its length, with equality for the radial path. For the matrix formula, hyperbolicity gives real eigenvalues of absolute values λ,λ^{−1} with λ>1, so |trM|=λ+λ^{−1}=2cosh(logλ). The conjugated dilation calculation yields length 2logλ and hence the formula. At trace magnitude two the length degenerates to zero and a cusp orbit has different growth geometry.

source.status: Classical result or newly stipulated finite model; historical claims explicitly delimited
source.summary: The HED audit correctly separates asymptotic information about a spectral diagnostic from an operator-ideal assertion. A diagonal heat semigroup makes the distinction precise. It also supplies error bounds that can replace an unreachable absolute threshold.
definitions: On ℓ²(N₀), let A have diagonal eigenvalues n, n≥0. The heat operator H_t=e^{−tA} has eigenvalues e^{−tn}, t>0.
A positive diagonal operator is trace class exactly when its diagonal entries have a finite sum. Small-time heat behavior concerns t→0 rather than a fixed t.

result.name: A heat-trace asymptotic is different from a trace-class statement at a fixed time
result.statement: H_t is trace class for every t>0, with TrH_t=1/(1−e^{−t})=t^{−1}+1/2+O(t) as t→0. Its trace diverges as t→0, and H_t converges strongly to the noncompact identity. The trace-norm truncation tail after n=N is e^{−t(N+1)}/(1−e^{−t}).
result.proof: The geometric series gives the trace and exact tail, all terms being nonnegative. Taylor expansion 1−e^{−t}=t−t²/2+O(t³) and division give the small-time expansion. For a fixed vector x∈ℓ², ||(H_t−I)x||²=Σ_n|e^{−tn}−1|²|x_n|² tends to zero by dominated convergence, since the multiplier is bounded by one. Identity is not compact because the standard basis has no norm-convergent subsequence. Thus trace-class operators can converge strongly to a noncompact operator while their trace norms diverge. This does not contradict trace-norm closedness because convergence is only strong. For a trace difference, a cancellation of leading asymptotic coefficients likewise says nothing by itself about whether the corresponding operator difference is trace class at a fixed parameter.

example.calculation: The full trace is two. Keeping indices n=0,…,9 gives trace 2−2^{−9}, and the exact positive tail is 2^{−9}=1/512. At t=log2/2 the trace is 1/(1−1/√2)=2+√2, showing sensitivity to the time scale without any failure of trace class.
example.conclusion: The model gives separately a summability theorem, an asymptotic formula and an explicit numerical cutoff certificate.

definitions: On R² use ω=dq∧dp and define X_H by ι_{X_H}ω=dH. Then X_H=H_p∂_q−H_q∂_p. Define {f,H}=f_qH_p−f_pH_q.

Standard trigonometric half-angle identities give sinq=2sech t tanh t, while p′=−2sech t tanh t, proving p′=−sinq. Also cosq=2sech²t−1, so p²/2+1−cosq=2sech²t+2−2sech²t=2. example.calculation: The energy is 2. The stable equilibrium q=p=0 instead has energy zero and quadratic Hessian diag(1,1); at q=π,p=0 the Hessian is diag(−1,1), giving a saddle. source.title: Symplectic reduction removes a cyclic coordinate only after fixing momentum
source.status: Classical result or newly stipulated finite model; historical claims explicitly delimited
source.summary: The source names canonical transformations, quotienting and Marsden–Weinstein reduction. A two-pair translation example provides a fully explicit model of the reduction mechanism, without assuming that an arbitrary quotient inherits a nondegenerate two-form.
definitions: On T*R² use coordinates (q₁,q₂,p₁,p₂) and ω=dq₁∧dp₁+dq₂∧dp₂. The additive group R translates q₂. Its momentum is J=p₂ under the convention ι_Xω=dJ.
Fix J=μ and quotient its level set by translations of q₂. The quotient is identified with (q₁,p₁). Let H=(p₁²+p₂²)/2+V(q₁), which is translation invariant.

result.name: Symplectic reduction removes a cyclic coordinate only after fixing momentum
result.statement: The level-set pullback of ω is dq₁∧dp₁; its null direction is precisely ∂_{q₂}. It descends to a nondegenerate reduced symplectic form, and the reduced Hamiltonian is H_μ=p₁²/2+V(q₁)+μ²/2. Projected full trajectories agree with its Hamiltonian flow.
result.proof: On the level p₂=μ, tangent vectors satisfy dp₂=0. Hence the pullback of the second wedge term vanishes. The remaining form pairs only q₁ and p₁, and its kernel within the three-dimensional level set is the one-dimensional translation direction. Because it is invariant and annihilates vertical vectors, it descends to the quotient; in the quotient coordinates its matrix is the standard invertible two-dimensional symplectic matrix. Full Hamilton equations are q₁′=p₁,p₁′=−V′(q₁), q₂′=p₂ and p₂′=0. Fixing p₂=μ and forgetting q₂ leaves exactly the equations of H_μ. The additive constant μ²/2 changes energy values but not the reduced vector field. This is the simplest complete reduction theorem, with regularity and freeness visible in coordinates.

example.setup: Let V(q₁)=q₁²/2 and μ=3.
example.calculation: The reduced flow is the unit harmonic oscillator. Starting at q₁=1,p₁=0 gives q₁=cost,p₁=−sint, with reduced energy five. The full trajectory also has q₂(t)=q₂(0)+3t and p₂=3. Quotienting removes this drift while preserving the physical equations in the remaining pair.
example.conclusion: The quotient has a proved descended form and an exact dynamical interpretation.

source.limits: If the group action is not free, the momentum value is singular or the Hamiltonian is not invariant, this coordinate proof does not apply. A generic structured-object quotient is not automatically a symplectic reduction.

definitions: For x′=Ax with real A, take a symmetric positive-definite P and define ||x||_P²=xᵀPx. A certificate with rate α>0 is AᵀP+PA≼−2αP.

For the perturbed generator, 2xᵀPEx is at most 2||x||_P||Ex||_P≤2δ||x||_P², giving the new rate. If Av=0 for a nonzero real or complex vector, the left quadratic form at v is zero while the strict right side is negative, a contradiction. definitions: For symmetric matrices use ⟨A,X⟩=tr(AX). Consider the primal minimum ⟨C,X⟩ subject to ⟨A_i,X⟩=b_i and X≽0.

result.name: An SDP primal-dual pair gives an exact certificate and a traceable gap
result.statement: Every primal/dual feasible pair has gap ⟨C,X⟩−bᵀy=tr(SX)≥0. A zero-gap pair proves global optimality without an appeal to strong duality or numerical convergence.
result.proof: Substitute the slack expression and use the primal equalities: tr(SX)=tr(CX)−Σ_i y_i tr(A_iX)=tr(CX)−bᵀy. To prove nonnegativity, write X=RRᵀ by the spectral theorem. Then tr(SX)=tr(RᵀSR), a sum of nonnegative diagonal quadratic forms. If the gap is zero, weak duality sandwiches every feasible primal value above the dual value and every feasible dual value below the primal one, so the pair is optimal. This argument requires only exact feasibility and positivity. Approximate residuals can also be handled, but then the result needs bounds on the unknown multipliers or variable size; a tiny objective gap alone cannot repair unbounded feasibility error.

example.setup: Minimize X₁₁+2X₂₂ subject to trX=1 and X≽0 in dimension two.

An off-diagonal perturbation of the optimal X is not automatically feasible: [[1,t],[t,0]] has determinant −t² and is positive semidefinite only for t=0.

For the graph limitation, take three Boolean constraints x=0, y=0 and x∨y=1. source.summary: The May artifact calculus proposed a six-coordinate authority profile. A precise finite poset model makes the intended monotonicity rule executable, while retaining the distinction between an order-theoretic accounting theorem and the truth of any mathematical assertion entered into the system.
definitions: Let A={0,1,2}⁶ with coordinatewise order and meet a∧b given by coordinatewise minimum. A dependency graph is a finite directed acyclic graph; every node has a local authority cap c(v).

result.name: Authority composition is a meet calculation with an explicit proof dependency graph
result.statement: For every node v, a(v) is the meet of c(w) over all ancestors w of v, including v. It is the largest profile simultaneously bounded by all those caps. Adding an additional dependency can only decrease or preserve the profile.
result.proof: Order the graph topologically. The claim is immediate for a source. If it holds for the predecessors of v, substituting their ancestor meets into the defining equation gives exactly the union of their ancestor sets together with v; repeated factors do not matter because meet is idempotent. This proves the formula by induction. Any other profile bounded by every ancestor cap is bounded by their meet, so the formula is the greatest admissible profile. Enlarging the ancestor set introduces further meet factors and cannot raise any coordinate. None of these steps supplies a proof that an individual premise is true: that requires a separately checked derivation. A soundness statement is conditional: if the local inference rules preserve truth and the source propositions are true, induction through the same graph proves every output proposition true.

example.setup: Use two premises with profiles a=(2,2,1,2,1,2) and b=(2,1,2,2,2,1), and a local cap c=(2,2,2,1,2,2).
example.calculation: The output meet is (2,1,1,1,1,1). A later node whose only extra cap is (1,2,2,2,2,2) receives (1,1,1,1,1,1). Swapping premise order or duplicating a premise changes neither result. A forgotten dependency with first coordinate zero would reduce that coordinate to zero, exposing why the dependency set itself must be complete.
example.conclusion: The calculus now has a small genuine theorem: maximal admissible authority propagates by a meet, with a transparent dependency invariant.

result.name: A chain contraction proves homology equivalence and survives a controlled elementary perturbation
result.statement: These contraction equations imply that i and p induce inverse homology isomorphisms. In the displayed complex, choose p(u)=0,p(v)=v, i(v)=v and h(u)=−e,h(v)=0. If d(e) changes to (1+ε)u with ε≠−1, replacing h(u) by −e/(1+ε) preserves every contraction identity.
result.proof: For any cycle z, the equation ipz−z=dhz+hdz=dhz says that ipz and z differ by a boundary. Thus H(i)H(p)=I; the identity pi=I gives the other composite. In the example, on e the map hd is −I, while on u the map dh is −I and on v both sides vanish. Therefore ip−I=dh+hd in every degree. Changing the nonzero coefficient simply rescales the inverse on the contractible summand. The equation at ε=−1 is exceptional: d becomes zero, so both e and u become new homology classes and no reduction to the old one-dimensional H can exist. Formally 1/(1+ε)=Σ_{j≥0}(−ε)^j when |ε|<1; in a nilpotent filtered coefficient ring the same series terminates and gives an exact algebraic inverse. result.name: The RG characteristic-function map has explicit stable fixed points and a finite-variance Gaussian obstruction

Iterate the fixed equation to obtain φ(t)=φ(t/√(2^n))^{2^n}. The factors approach one, so use the continuous logarithm near one: 2^n logφ(t/√(2^n))→−σ²t²/2. source.summary: The homological followup contains the Maurer–Cartan equation and the class of one-half the bracket square. definitions: Work over Q in a differential graded Lie algebra (L,d,[,]) with d of degree+1. For a degree-one formal series α=t a+t²b+O(t³), the equation is dα+[α,α]/2=0.

result.proof: Expand the formal equation. The t coefficient is da. The t² coefficient is db+[a,a]/2, so b exists exactly when the bracket square is the negative of a boundary. Its differential vanishes because da=0 and the derivation identity gives d[a,a]=[da,a]−[a,da]=0. Thus it defines a cohomology class, not merely a vector norm. In the displayed algebra take every bracket involving b or c to be zero; all Jacobi identities then vanish because the only nonzero bracket lands in central c. The derivation identity also holds, including d[a,b]=0 and its right side−[a,c]=0. For α=t a−t²b, dα=−t²c and [α,α]/2=t²c, cancelling at every order. If instead db=0, c is a nonzero cohomology class and no coefficient can cancel it.

example.calculation: With db=c the second-order correction is−b and the exact deformation is polynomial in t. With d=0 the same [a,a]/2=c is nonzero in H², so even an arbitrarily small nonzero t cannot solve the formal equation beginning with a. Its norm can be made small by t, but the obstruction class remains algebraically nonzero.
example.conclusion: The obstruction criterion is exact and its solvable and obstructed cases are explicit.

definitions: Let f(T)=T³+T+1 over F₂ and F=F₂[T]/(f), with α the residue of T. Represent every element uniquely by a binary polynomial of degree at most two.

result.statement: f is irreducible, F has eight elements, α has multiplicative order seven, and Frobenius cubed is the identity. The three conjugates of α are α,α²,α⁴, and all satisfy f.
result.proof: A cubic over a field is reducible if and only if it has a linear factor. Here f(0)=f(1)=1, proving irreducibility and hence that the quotient is a field. Its nonzero multiplicative group has seven elements; α is neither zero nor one, and Lagrange implies its order is seven because seven is prime. Direct reduction with α³=α+1 also verifies α⁷=1. In any field of characteristic two, squaring respects sums and products, so Frobenius is a homomorphism. It is injective and hence surjective on a finite field. Every nonzero element has seventh power one, so x⁸=x for every element; thus the third iterate is identity. Applying Frobenius to f(α)=0 proves the conjugate equations. The three conjugates are distinct because α has order seven and the exponents1,2,4 differ modulo seven. An embedding is therefore a concrete substitution map, not merely an equality of field sizes.

example.calculation: They are1,α,α²,α+1,α²+α,α²+α+1,α²+1,then1. None of the first seven nonzero powers repeats. The map α↦α² is an automorphism; the map α↦1 is not a field homomorphism from this presentation because f(1)=1≠0. A primitive-root test must actually exclude the identity element, especially when the group order is prime.

source.status: Classical result or newly stipulated finite model; historical claims explicitly delimited
source.summary: The SIT fragment specifies species (3,2,1), least representative360 and arithmetic invariants. We formulate the underlying optimization exactly and prove its general rearrangement rule. This is independent of whether the historical Lean tranche compiled.
definitions: A species is a finite nonincreasing list a₁≥⋯≥a_r≥1 of prime exponents. Its representatives are positive integers with that multiset of nonzero exponents. Let p_i denote the i-th prime.
Define the least candidate m(a)=∏_{i=1}^r p_i^{a_i}. Arithmetic invariants are Ω=Σa_i, ω=r and τ=∏(a_i+1).

result.name: An exponent species has a unique least integer representative
result.statement: m(a) is the unique least positive integer in its species. Its divisor-count, total-prime-factor and distinct-prime-factor invariants are exactly the stated product and sums.
result.proof: First any chosen r distinct primes q₁<⋯<q_r satisfy q_i≥p_i. Replacing them by the first r primes without changing exponent assignments cannot increase the product and strictly decreases it if any chosen prime differs. Next if p<q but exponents a<b are assigned in the wrong order, compare p^a q^b with p^b q^a: their ratio is (q/p)^{b−a}>1. Swapping the exponents strictly decreases the number. Repeated exchanges put the exponents in descending order on ascending primes. Equality permits only swaps among equal exponents, which do not change the integer, proving uniqueness of the numerical minimizer. Every divisor independently chooses an exponent between zero and a_i, yielding τ; counting factors with and without multiplicity gives Ω and ω.

example.calculation: The least integer is2³·3²·5=360. Its τ is4·3·2=24, Ω=6 and ω=3. Swapping the first two unequal exponents gives2²·3³·5=540, larger by3/2. Using primes2,3,7 instead gives504, larger by7/5. Exhaustively assigning these exponents to the first few primes verifies the exchange proof’s finite predictions.
example.conclusion: The least-representative theorem gives SIT a concrete arithmetic object and an exact comparison principle.

Let R_n(t)=Σ_{d|n}t^{ρ(d)} and Ω(n)=Σa_i. A chain C_{a_i+1} is the totally ordered set {0,…,a_i}.

result.name: The divisor lattice is a product of chains with a symmetric rank polynomial
result.statement: D(n)≅∏C_{a_i+1} as lattices, with meet and join given by coordinate minima and maxima. R_n(t)=∏(1+t+⋯+t^{a_i}); R_n(1)=τ(n), its degree is Ω(n), and t^{Ω(n)}R_n(t^{−1})=R_n(t).
result.proof: Unique factorization makes the divisor-vector correspondence bijective. Divisibility is coordinatewise inequality, so greatest lower and least upper bounds are coordinatewise minimum and maximum, proving the lattice isomorphism. Multiplying the finite geometric polynomials records every independent choice of b_i once, proving the rank formula. Substitution t=1 counts all choices and hence all divisors. The top vector has rank Σa_i, and every saturated chain from bottom to top increments one exponent at a time, giving that height in edges. The involution d↦n/d replaces each b_i by a_i−b_i and reverses rank, proving coefficient symmetry and the reciprocal polynomial identity. Thus not only τ and Ω, but the full rank distribution, is determined by the species.

example.setup: For n=360 use exponents3,2,1.
example.calculation: R(t)=(1+t+t²+t³)(1+t+t²)(1+t)=1+3t+5t²+6t³+5t⁴+3t⁵+t⁶. The coefficients sum to24, and the longest chain has six edges. Complementary ranks zero/six, one/five and two/four have matching counts. The rank-three divisors are the six choices of exponent sum three inside the box.
example.conclusion: The product-of-chains description yields exact combinatorics and a canonical duality.

source.limits: Lattice isomorphism forgets actual prime values. Different integers of the same species have the same divisor lattice but can differ radically in size and arithmetic congruences.

source.title: Quadratic polarization is symmetric and cannot equal an alternating form at odd order
source.status: Classical theorem or newly stipulated exact model; speculative source assertions delimited
source.summary: The source writes q(x+y)−q(x)−q(y)=ω(x, y) for a finite phase module. The left side is symmetric in x and y. At odd order it therefore cannot be a nonzero alternating form. This elementary obstruction is foundational for choosing consistent Weil and Heisenberg data.
definitions: Let A be an abelian group and Q:A→Q/Z with Q(0)=0. Define b_Q(x, y)=Q(x+y)−Q(x)−Q(y). A quadratic form additionally has bilinear b_Q and Q(nx)=n²Q(x).
An alternating form ω has ω(x, x)=0 and ω(y, x)=−ω(x, y). The Heisenberg commutator form and a quadratic module’s symmetric bilinear form play different roles.

result.name: Quadratic polarization is symmetric and cannot equal an alternating form at odd order
result.statement: b_Q is always symmetric. If b_Q is also alternating and A has odd order, then b_Q=0. For A=Z/pZ with odd prime p, Q_a(x)=ax²/p mod1 has b_Q(x, y)=2axy/p and is nondegenerate exactly when p∤a.
result.proof: Symmetry follows immediately from commutativity of x+y. If a form is symmetric and skew-symmetric, then2b(x, y)=0. For finite odd-order A, each b(x, y) has odd order dividing the order of x, so it cannot have order two unless it is zero. This proves the obstruction. The cyclic example is well defined because replacing x by x+p changes ax²/p by2ax+ap, an integer. Expansion gives the displayed polarization. If p∤a and b_Q(x, y)=0 for every y, choose y=1; then p divides2ax, and oddness implies x=0. If p|a the form is zero. The same calculation shows why Q(x)=x²/(2L) must be assigned a correct underlying cyclic group and parity condition rather than copied to any Z/LZ: changing x by L contributes x+L/2, which is integral only when L is even.

example.setup: Use A=Z/3Z and Q(x)=x²/3.
example.calculation: Its values are0,1/3,1/3, and b(1,1)=2/3≠0, so it is nondegenerate symmetric but not alternating. In contrast the standard form on F₃², ω((x, y),(x′, y′))=(xy′−yx′)/3, is alternating and nonzero; it cannot be the polarization of an ordinary scalar quadratic Q on that group.
example.conclusion: The source’s two structures are separated by an exact impossibility result and a valid replacement.

source.limits: Characteristic two and groups with two-torsion require different quadratic-refinement conventions. This theorem does not deny those theories; it states why the odd-order identification fails.

result.statement: The composed branches have Kraus operators L_{bs|a}K_{ar}. Summing all branches is trace preserving. Ignoring or renormalizing away failed branches changes the process and can conceal arbitrarily small success probability.
result.proof: Complete positivity of each branch follows directly from the Kraus form, including after adjoining any untouched auxiliary system. For completeness, sum(LK)†(LK) over b, s first; the conditional later identity collapses that sum to K†K. Summing a, r then gives I. Cyclicity of trace proves total output trace equals input trace. source.title: Two-sector failure has a correlation parameter and a rigorous confidence envelope
source.status: Classical theorem or newly stipulated exact model; speculative source assertions delimited
source.summary: The source gives a two-sector failure product and fitted threshold candidates. We replace an implicit independence assumption with an exact joint-probability formula, then add a finite confidence calculation. Threshold fitting is kept distinct from a theorem about arbitrarily large devices.
definitions: Let X and Z be failure events with probabilities p_X, p_Z and intersection r. Their combined failure is the union. Feasibility requires max(0, p_X+p_Z−1)≤r≤min(p_X, p_Z).

If n independent identically distributed trials each have failure probability p, the probability of zero observed failures is(1−p)^n. Independence of trials is separate from independence of sectors within one trial.

result.name: Two-sector failure has a correlation parameter and a rigorous confidence envelope
result.statement: P(X∪Z)=p_X+p_Z−r, hence max(p_X, p_Z)≤P(X∪Z)≤min(1, p_X+p_Z). The product formula1−(1−p_X)(1−p_Z) holds exactly when r=p_Xp_Z. After zero failures in n trials, the one-sided level1−δ upper confidence bound is p≤1−δ^{1/n}.
result.proof: The union identity follows by partitioning into the three disjoint regions X\Z, Z\X and X∩Z. The intersection bounds follow from nonnegative probabilities of all four cells; conversely those bounds make the four cell probabilities r, p_X−r, p_Z−r,1−p_X−p_Z+r nonnegative and summing to one, so the bounds are sharp. Sector independence is exactly the additional equality r=p_Xp_Z. For the zero-failure bound, a candidate p above1−δ^{1/n} makes the zero-count event have probability belowδ. Inverting this binomial test gives the stated confidence procedure; it is a coverage statement about repeated sampling, not a posterior probability that the fixed parameter lies in the interval.

example.setup: Take p_X=p_Z=1/10 and n=100 independent trials with zero observed combined failures.
example.calculation: Independent sectors give combined failure19/100. Perfectly coincident sectors give1/10, and disjoint sectors give1/5. At δ=1/20 the zero-failure confidence upper bound is1−(1/20)^{1/100}≈0.029513. A point estimate zero is therefore not a proof of zero failure probability.
example.conclusion: The reported sector model can now state exactly where correlations and finite evidence enter.

definitions: Let B be a finite nonnegative transition matrix on directed edge states, chosen so that every allowed nonbacktracking fault walk is represented. Let its maximum row sum be r<1.

result.statement: Finite invertible solutions force q^d=1. For q of order L, the displayed L-dimensional unitary pair satisfies the relation and generates all L-by-L matrices; its commutant is the scalars and its representation is irreducible.

source.summary: The late-June closure calculus includes projection commutators and a convergence table. A two-dimensional model proves both constants exactly and shows that commutation defect and iterative contraction measure different features.
definitions: Let Pproject orthogonally ontoe₁inR² andQonto v=(cosθ, sinθ), with0<θ<π/2. Setc=cosθ, s=sinθ.
One cycle acting on the P line isPQP. The commutator is[P, Q]=PQ−QP, measured in Euclidean operator norm.

result.statement: On imP, the cycle PQP contracts by ρ=c². Its n-th iterate is ρ^nP. The commutator norm is |cs|=|sin2θ|/2. To reach ρ^n≤ε with 0<ε<1 requires n≥ceil(logε/logρ).
result.proof: The matrices are P=[[1,0],[0,0]] and Q=[[c², cs],[cs, s²]]. Multiplication gives PQP=c²P, proving the iterate by induction. Their commutator is[[0, cs],[−cs,0]]. Its transpose times itself is c²s²I, so both singular values are |cs| and the norm formula follows. Since 0<ρ<1, taking logarithms of ρ^n≤ε and dividing by negative logρ reverses the inequality, giving the exact ceiling. As θ→0 the commutator tends to zero but ρ→1 and convergence becomes slow. As θ→π/2 the commutator again tends to zero but ρ→0 and one cycle annihilates the P line. Thus small commutator alone cannot distinguish near-coincident from near-orthogonal subspaces or predict a unique convergence rate.

example.calculation: ρ=1/4 and||[P, Q]||=√3/4. Three cycles leave 1/64>1/100, while four leave 1/256<1/100, so the exact count is four. Atθ=π/6 the commutator norm is the same, but ρ=3/4 and the required count is seventeen, demonstrating nonidentifiability from the commutator norm alone. There is also a distinction between the norm of PQ and the eigenvalue of the cycle on the first line: ||PQ||=|cosθ|, while PQP restricted to that line is multiplication by cos²θ. A convergence table must specify which operation counts as one step. Squaring the wrong quantity changes its inferred exponent by a factor two.

source.summary: The external June file asserts a quartic uniqueness theorem involving enumeration, a probabilistic middle range and large bounds. We do not promote that claim. Instead we prove the concrete quartic’s irreducibility, discriminant and signature and construct explicit exceptional units.
definitions: Let f(x)=x⁴−x−1 and K=Q(α) for a root α. Its polynomial discriminant is the resultant Res(f, f′), since the quartic sign factor is positive.
An exceptional unit is an algebraic integer z for which both z and1−z are units. The field signature(r₁, r₂) records real embeddings and conjugate pairs of complex embeddings.

result.name: The quartic discriminant−283 is exact, but its claimed global uniqueness is not established
result.statement: f is irreducible over Q, has discriminant−283 and signature(2,1). Both α and1−α are units, so α is an exceptional unit. The polynomial order Z[α] is maximal because its squarefree discriminant leaves no nontrivial square index.
result.proof: Modulo two the polynomial is x⁴+x+1. It has no root in F₂. The only monic irreducible quadratic is x²+x+1; reducing x⁴+x+1 modulo that polynomial gives one, so there is no quadratic factor. Hence it is irreducible over F₂ and therefore over Q by Gauss’s lemma. The depressed-quartic formula for x⁴+bx+c gives discriminant256c³−27b⁴; substituting b=c=−1 yields−256−27=−283. This can also be checked as the determinant of the7-by7 Sylvester matrix, which the verifier does exactly. The derivative4x³−1 has one real root, so f decreases then increases and has at most two real zeros. Since f(−1)=1, f(0)=−1, f(2)=13, there are two, leaving one complex pair. Normα=f(0)=−1 and Norm(1−α)=f(1)=−1, proving both are units. Finally discZ[α]=[O_K:Z[α]]²discK; squarefreeness forces index one.

source.status: Classical theorem or newly stipulated exact model; speculative source assertions delimited
source.summary: The external research program proposes corner equations and several variants. We give a useful elementary arithmetic theorem valid for positive exponents. It yields a finite orbit of exceptional units but avoids assuming that six written formulas produce six distinct field elements.
definitions: Let z be an algebraic integer and suppose (1−z)^a=εz^b, where a, b are positive integers and ε is an algebraic unit.
The anharmonic transforms are z,1−z,1/z,1/(1−z), z/(z−1),(z−1)/z, defined for z≠0,1.

result.name: Corner pins generate exceptional units and a finite anharmonic orbit
result.statement: z and1−z are units. Every anharmonic transform is also an exceptional unit and lies in the same number field. The orbit has at most six elements and can be smaller at special values.
result.proof: The principal ideals(z) and(1−z) are coprime because their sum contains z+(1−z)=1. The corner equation says(1−z)^a=(z)^b as ideals, since ε is a unit. If a nonzero prime ideal divided(z), it would divide the right side and hence(1−z), contradicting coprimality. Thus(z) is the unit ideal, and similarly for1−z. This proves both are units. Their inverses and quotients are therefore algebraic integers and units. For each anharmonic transform w, its complement1−w is again a signed quotient or inverse of z and1−z; for example1−1/z=(z−1)/z and1−z/(z−1)=−1/(z−1), so it too is a unit. The transformations are generated by z↦1−z and z↦1/z; their elementary composition table has at most six forms, all rationally invertible, proving the same-field and orbit statements. The argument requires positive exponents and integrality, not merely a complex numerical solution.

example.setup: Take the golden-ratio unit z=φ satisfying(1−z)²=z^{−2}.
example.calculation: This written relation uses a negative exponent, but multiplication gives z²(1−z)²=1, directly proving both factors are units. Its six transforms reduce to φ,1−φ,φ^{−1},−φ,φ²,φ^{−2}, with possible equality checked algebraically. By contrast z=1/2 has an anharmonic orbit of only three values and is not an algebraic integer unit, showing why the unit hypotheses matter.
example.conclusion: The corner program gains a rigorous bridge to exceptional-unit arithmetic and an exact finite symmetry.

result.statement: If p(T)=0, then E_λ=e_λ(T) are pairwise disjoint idempotents, sum to I and satisfy T=ΣλE_λ. The spectrum equals S exactly when every E_λ is nonzero; one vector with E_λv≠0 certifies each nonzero projector.

definitions: Let k be any field and λ∈k. In k[a,b] set Q=(a²−λ²b²,ab−λb²). Let m=(a,b),u=a−λb and v=b. The coordinate change is invertible with a=u+λv.

source.summary: The July29 source reports multiples, a 2-descent and rank-one conclusions for the conductor37 curve. Exact group arithmetic and reductions modulo small primes give a self-contained rank lower bound. The stronger Selmer and Tate–Shafarevich claims remain conditional on an unavailable descent certificate.
definitions: Let E/Q be y²+y=x³−x with identity O at infinity and P=(0,0). Negation is−(x,y)=(x,−1−y). The discriminant is Δ=37. A prime is good when it does not divideΔ.

result.name: Infinite order without adopting the reported descent
result.statement: E(Q) has trivial torsion and P has infinite order; consequently its rank is at least one. The displayed calculation alone does not prove rank exactly one.
result.proof: For distinct points use slopeλ=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁); doubling uses λ=(3x₁²−1)/(2y₁+1). Then x₃=λ²−x₁−x₂ and y₃=−y₁−1+λ(x₁−x₃). These formulas give exact rational multiples. Counting solutions over F₃ and F₅ gives group orders7 and8, respectively. Good reduction injects the prime-to-p rational torsion into E(F_p). Any torsion prime other than3,5 would therefore divide gcd(7,8)=1. A 3-primary torsion point would inject at5 and require3|8; a 5-primary one would inject at3 and require5|7. Neither is possible, so the torsion subgroup is trivial. P is a finite point and hence nonzero, proving infinite order. This argument supplies no upper rank bound. A certified 2-Selmer calculation of dimension one, together with the found point and no rational2-torsion, would supply that missing bound.

example.setup: Compute P through6P, and transform the equation for a 2-division check.
example.calculation: The multiples are2P=(1,0),3P=(−1,−1),4P=(2,−3),5P=(1/4,−5/8),6P=(6,14). With X=4x,Y=8y+4 the equation becomes Y²=X³−16X+16. Its cubic has no rational root, consistently with no rational2-torsion; the exact torsion argument above is stronger.
example.conclusion: The visible orbit is an exact constructive result, while descent claims are kept distinct from it.

source.limits: No covering curves, local-solubility witnesses or Selmer basis were recovered. The source’s exact rank and Sha[2] assertions are not certified here.
source.extension: Return a complete2-descent packet with étale-algebra representatives, local tests and covering maps, then combine its upper bound with the explicit infinite-order point.

source.title: Riemann–Roch proves a code bound, not an unexhibited minimum-weight word
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The July31 assistant source gives a genus-three curve over F₄₉,92 rational points and a code[91,37,52]. The curve equation, point list and decoder were not recovered. A conditional theorem proves the guaranteed dimension and distance bound without promoting an asserted exact distance into a demonstrated one.
definitions: Let X/F_q be a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g. Choose distinct rational points P₁,…,P_n and a divisor G disjoint from them. The evaluation code is C_L(D,G)={ (f(P₁),…,f(P_n)):f∈L(G)}, with D=ΣP_i.

result.name: One-point Goppa parameter certificate
result.statement: If2g−2<degG<n, then dimC_L=degG+1−g and its minimum distance is at least n−degG. Thus a genus-three curve with92 rational points yields a one-point code[91,37,d≥52] usingG=39P_∞ and the other91 points.
result.proof: The kernel of evaluation is L(G−D). Its divisor degree is negative, so only zero belongs to that space: a nonzero function has principal divisor degree zero and cannot satisfy a negative-degree effectivity condition. Evaluation is therefore injective. Riemann–Roch and degG>2g−2 giveℓ(G)=degG+1−g. A nonzero f∈L(G) has at mostdegG zeros among the evaluation points, since its zero divisor and pole divisor have the same degree and its poles are bounded byG. Its evaluation has weight at least n−degG. These arguments prove a lower bound; equality additionally needs an f attaining exactlydegG evaluation zeros. The Hasse–Weil upper bound atq49,g3 is49+1+2·3·7=92, so the reported count would indeed be maximal, provided the actual curve and count are verified.

example.setup: Work conditionally with q=49,g=3,N=92,n=91 and degG=39.
example.calculation: The dimension is39+1−3=37 and the designed distance is91−39=52. A nearest-codeword decoder is uniquely defined for every received word within⌊(52−1)/2⌋=25 errors of a codeword. An algorithm reported only through24 errors may have a weaker guarantee; that does not contradict the distance bound. It does not establish an efficient25-error algorithm either.
example.conclusion: The construction separates existence, parameter bounds, exact distance and algorithmic decoding into independent mathematical obligations.

source.limits: The actual curve and decoder remain unavailable. Larger reported tower-code tuples likewise need explicit function fields, evaluation divisors and certificates.
source.extension: Publish the curve over F₇[u]/(u²+1), its92 points and an evaluation basis, then exhibit a weight52 codeword or prove the true distance is larger.

source.title: Base twelve changes representation while preserving exact arithmetic
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The July31 language discussion includes base twelve and symbolic representation. Its mathematical core is a division algorithm, not a change in the underlying rational numbers. Exact remainder orbits give terminating and repeating expansions with unambiguous conventions.
definitions: Use digits0,…,9,A,B for values0,…,11. For a rational0≤a/b<1 in lowest terms, long division sets r₀=a,12r_j=b d_{j+1}+r_{j+1}, with0≤r_{j+1}<b. A bar denotes infinite repetition.

result.name: Termination and periodicity criterion
result.statement: The base-twelve expansion of a/b terminates exactly when b divides12^N for some N, equivalently b has no prime factors except2 and3. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion; after removing the2- and3-parts of the denominator, the period divides the multiplicative order of12 modulo its remaining part.
result.proof: AfterN steps the division identities telescope to a/b=Σ_{j=1}^N d_j12^{-j}+r_N/(b12^N). Termination is equivalent to r_N=0 and hence to b|12^N because gcd(a,b)=1. Conversely that divisibility forces zero remainder. Only finitely many remainders occur, so a nonzero remainder must eventually repeat and the deterministic update then repeats forever. When the denominator is coprime to12, the remainder is12^j a modb and the first return occurs at the multiplicative order of12. Powers of2 and3 contribute only a finite preperiod. An expansion ending in infinitely manyB digits is the familiar alternate representation of a terminating number; choosing the non-B-tail convention restores uniqueness. The same remainder identity certifies truncation error without a decimal approximation: afterN digits the omitted fraction is exactlyr_N/(b12^N), betweenzero and12^{-N}. For a repeating block oflengthh, multiplying by12^h and subtracting yields a rational denominator12^h−1. These two identities provide exact conversion in both directions.

example.setup: Represent2026,1/8 and1/5 in base twelve.
example.calculation: 2026=1·12³+2·12²+0·12+10, so it is120A₁₂. Also.16₁₂=1/12+6/144=1/8. For1/5 the remainders follow1→2→4→3→1 and the digits are2,4,9,7. Thus1/5=.overline{2497}₁₂; equivalently(2·12³+4·12²+9·12+7)/(12⁴−1)=4147/20735=1/5.
example.conclusion: Each symbolic statement reduces to an integer identity and a finite remainder certificate.

source.limits: This does not support claims that a base or symbolic language changes numerical truth or objectively improves perception. Those would require separately defined criteria.
source.extension: Specify a concrete coding cost for a symbolic arithmetic language and compare bases by provable representation length and exact arithmetic complexity rather than aesthetic analogy.

source.title: A root atlas combines Rouché counts with explicit root squaring
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The July31 source proposes square-free reduction, Pellet/Graeffe filters and a universal polynomial-solving atlas. A useful classical atlas certifies where roots are and how many occur. It does not bypass the obstruction to general radical formulas.
definitions: For p(c+rw)=Σ_{j=0}^n b_jw^j, a disk means|z−c|<r and roots are counted with multiplicity. Write p(z)=E(z²)+zO(z²), with even and odd parts separated.

result.name: Dominant-term disk count and Graeffe identity
result.statement: If|b_k|>Σ_{j≠k}|b_j|, then p has exactly k roots in the disk. For leading coefficienta and rootsr_i counted with multiplicity, G(y)=E(y)²−yO(y)²=(−1)^n a²∏(y−r_i²). Thus its roots are the squares of those ofp, with multiplicities.
result.proof: On|w|=1 the non-k terms have magnitude at mostΣ_{j≠k}|b_j|, strictly below|b_kw^k|. Rouché’s theorem therefore gives the same zero count as the monomial b_kw^k, namelyk. Strictness also proves the boundary is root-free. For the second statement, p(z)p(−z)=E(z²)²−z²O(z²)². Factoring p(z)=a∏(z−r_i) gives p(z)p(−z)=(−1)^n a²∏(z²−r_i²). Substituting y=z² proves the claim and the sign. Root squaring separates distinct root moduli, but may merge roots of opposite signs and amplify coefficient ranges. It is a filtering tool; square-free factorization and subsequent certified isolation remain necessary. The boundary inequalities also distinguish open disks from uncertain boundary roots. Equality in a coefficient comparison is not a validRouché certificate; it may place a root directly on the circle. For p(z)=z−1 at radiusone, the two coefficient magnitudes tie and the root lies on the boundary, exactly the situation strict dominance excludes.

example.setup: Use p(z)=z³−4z+1 for disk counts and q(z)=z²−3z+2 for root squaring.
example.calculation: On|z|=1,4>1+1 proves one root inside. On|z|=3,27>12+1 proves all three inside; hence exactly two lie in1<|z|<3. Forq, E(y)=y+2 and O(y)=−3, soG(y)=(y+2)²−9y=y²−5y+4, with roots1 and4, the squares of1 and2.
example.conclusion: The output is a finite exact counting certificate with stated disks and multiplicities.

source.limits: No original all-degree solver or test corpus was recovered. These sufficient tests can be inconclusive, especially near equal-modulus clusters; inconclusive does not mean root-free.
source.extension: Combine exact square-free factorization, adaptive rational disks, Graeffe filters and certified local Newton steps, returning an independently checkable disjoint root cover.

source.title: A contraction certificate gives a genuinely guaranteed Newton enclosure
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The late-July universal-solving discussion is made constructive by replacing an unqualified convergence promise with a local certificate. A fixed inverse-Jacobian approximation produces a contraction whose hypotheses can be checked with rational bounds.
definitions: Let f be continuously differentiable on I=[c−r,c+r], choose a nonzero constant C, and set T(x)=x−Cf(x). Assume sup_I|1−Cf′(x)|≤q<1.

result.name: One-dimensional interval Newton–Banach certificate
result.statement: If|Cf(c)|+qr≤r, then f has exactly one root inI. Starting anywhere inI, iteratingT converges to that root with geometric contraction factorq.
result.proof: The derivative bound and the mean-value theorem give|T(x)−T(y)|≤q|x−y|. Moreover|T(x)−c|≤|T(c)−c|+q|x−c|≤|Cf(c)|+qr≤r, soT maps the closed interval into itself. Completeness and the contraction theorem give a unique fixed point. SinceC≠0, fixed points are exactly zeros off. The same argument bounds the distance from an iterate to the root by|T(x)−x|/(1−q). Every hypothesis is local and explicit. A convergence plot or small residual is weaker: for example a nearly singular derivative can make a tiny residual coexist with a substantial root error. In several variables the analogous test uses a norm bound forI−CJF throughout a box and an inclusion test for its centered image. A practical certificate may choose a fixedC rather than recomputingf′(x)^{-1} at each step. This makes the map and its derivative bound uniform on the entire interval. Newton iteration with a changing inverse may converge faster, but its guarantee must be established separately or shown to stay inside the same certified domain.

example.setup: Certify the positive root off(x)=x²−2 usingc=7/5,C=5/14 andr=1/50.
example.calculation: OnI=[69/50,71/50], T′=1−5x/7 ranges from1/70 to−1/70, so q=1/70. Also|Cf(c)|=1/70. The inclusion bound is1/70+1/3500=51/3500<1/50=70/3500. Thus there is exactly one root in[1.38,1.42], and the fixed-inverse iteration converges from every point of this interval. The negative root lies outside it.
example.conclusion: Existence, uniqueness, enclosure and a convergence rate are certified by exact inequalities.

source.limits: This local theorem does not guarantee finding a valid box for every polynomial or remove global root-separation costs. The source’s universal algorithm was not retrieved as a complete implementation.
source.extension: Use an exact global root count to seed intervals, then attach such certificates to every isolated simple root and a separate multiplicity-aware certificate to repeated roots.

source.title: A p-adic completion changes convergence while keeping rational identities
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The July31 representation discussion includes rationals, reals and p-adics. A valuation makes this distinction precise: it changes which approximations are small, while preserving ordinary algebraic equalities on the embedded rational field. Root lifting provides a constructive rather than purely metaphorical example.
definitions: For a primep and nonzero rationalx, letv_p(x) be the exponent ofp in its factorization and|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}; set|0|_p=0. Q_p is the completion ofQ in this metric. Congruence modulo p^n records an error ofp-adic norm at mostp^{-n}.

result.name: Geometric convergence and simple-root lifting
result.statement: The seriesΣ_{j≥0}p^j converges inQ_p to1/(1−p). If an integer polynomialf hasf(r₁)≡0 modp andf′(r₁)≠0 modp, its root lifts uniquely through compatible congruencesr_n modulo p^n, producing a root inZ_p.
result.proof: The finite geometric identity(1−p)Σ_{j=0}^{N−1}p^j=1−p^N is valid overQ. Since|p^N|_p=p^{-N}→0, completeness gives the stated limit; the real terms instead grow and their partial sums diverge. For lifting supposef(r_n)≡0 modp^n andtryr_{n+1}=r_n+t p^n with0≤t<p. Taylor expansion modulo p^{n+1} givesf(r_{n+1})≡f(r_n)+t p^n f′(r_n). Dividing byp^n leaves one linear equation fort modulop. The derivative is a unit modulo p, so that equation has exactly one solution. The compatible sequence is Cauchy and continuity of polynomial evaluation gives a root. Uniqueness applies to the root in the chosen residue class, not every root ofthe polynomial.

example.setup: Takep=5 andf(x)=x²−6, starting withr₁=1.
example.calculation: The successive least residues are r₂=16 modulo25, r₃=16 modulo125 andr₄=516 modulo625. Their squares are6 modulo the respective moduli, and each new residue agrees with the previous one. The other root begins in the residue class−1, so the construction does not claim global uniqueness.
example.conclusion: Exact modular corrections build an infinite object with a proved convergence metric.

source.limits: A p-adic root need not be a rational number or correspond to an ordinary real approximation. No source-specific p-adic curve or regulator computation is inferred.

source.title: A cutoff theorem with the quantifiers made explicit
source.status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
source.summary: The recovered master inequality becomes useful only after the model class, data norm and quantifiers are fixed. The fundamental issue is that approximation can improve while noise amplification becomes arbitrarily large. A diagonal parameter choice reconciles these two limits without requiring a guessed convergence rate.
definitions: Let A:X→Y be bounded between normed spaces, let M⊂X be a specified nonempty class, and let R_n:Y→X be bounded linear maps. Data satisfy yδ=Ax+e with ||e||≤δ.
Define B_M(n)=sup_{x∈M}||R_nAx−x||, S(n)=||R_n||, and Eδ(R_n;M)=sup_{x∈M,||e||≤δ}||R_n(Ax+e)−x||. Assume B_M(n) is finite and tends to zero.

result.name: Uniform bias–noise decomposition and diagonal regularization
result.statement: Eδ(R_n;M)≤B_M(n)+δS(n). There exists an integer choice n(δ)→∞ with Eδ(R_{n(δ)};M)→0. Every choice with B_M(n(δ))→0 and δS(n(δ))→0 has this property.
result.proof: Add and subtract R_nAx and apply the triangle inequality and the operator norm bound. For existence choose a strictly increasing sequence n_j with B_M(n_j)≤1/j. Put s_j=max(1,S(n_1),…,S(n_j)), and choose strictly decreasing positive d_j→0 with d_j≤1/(j s_j). For d_{j+1}<δ≤d_j use n(δ)=n_j. Then δS(n(δ))≤1/j and the total bound is at most 2/j. As δ→0 the interval index j→∞, hence the result. This proof does not assume that S is monotone or that B has a power-law rate. Uniform convergence of B is a substantive hypothesis: pointwise convergence R_nAx→x for each fixed x does not imply it on an arbitrary unbounded class. If A has a nonzero kernel and M contains x and x+h with h∈ker A, a uniform error tending to zero is impossible, since the data coincide. Thus the model class must encode identifiable information as well as approximation smoothness.

example.setup: Use a diagonal inverse problem on ℓ², Av=(v_k/k), the cutoff R_N and the ellipsoid M={x:Σk²|x_k|²≤1}.
example.calculation: The tail is bounded by 1/(N+1), while S(N)=N. With N=⌊δ^(−1/2)⌋ and 0<δ≤1/4, the error is at most 1/(N+1)+δN≤2√δ. At δ=1/100, N=10 gives the sharper explicit bound 1/11+1/10=21/110.
example.conclusion: The same resolution parameter has a measurable cost and a justified accuracy bound. Unregularized inversion has unbounded norm and no such deterministic noise guarantee.

source.limits: The bound is deterministic and uniform over M. It does not estimate unknown noise, identify M from data, or imply that the two upper-bound terms can always be simultaneously attained.
source.extension: Construct a parameter rule from a known noise bound and a verifiable model hierarchy M_j, then prove an oracle inequality showing how far the selected resolution can be from the best admissible one.

A two-point indistinguishability argument supplies the lower bound, so the rate expresses an information limitation rather than only the quality of one algorithm.
definitions: Take X=Y=ℓ², Ae_k=k^(−p)e_k with p>0, and M_r={x:Σk^{2r}|x_k|²≤1}, r>0. Let R_N invert the first N coordinates and discard the rest.
The deterministic minimax error is inf over all maps T:Y→X of sup_{x∈M_r,||e||≤δ}||T(Ax+e)−x||. The map T need not be linear or continuous.

result.name: Matching polynomial upper and lower rates
result.statement: For sufficiently small δ>0, spectral cutoff with N=⌊δ^(−1/(p+r))⌋ has worst-case error O(δ^{r/(p+r)}). No reconstruction map improves this order uniformly on M_r under norm-bounded noise.
result.proof: For x∈M_r, Σ_{k>N}|x_k|²≤(N+1)^(−2r)Σ_{k>N}k^{2r}|x_k|², so B(N)≤(N+1)^(−r). Also ||R_N||=N^p, because its diagonal coefficients are k^p. The master bound is therefore (N+1)^(−r)+δN^p. The stated N balances the two terms and gives the upper order. For the lower bound put K=⌈δ^(−1/(p+r))⌉ and v=K^(−r)e_K. Both v and −v belong to M_r and ||Av||=K^(−(p+r))≤δ. The observation zero can thus arise from v with noise −Av or from −v with noise Av. For any output z=T(0), the triangle inequality gives max(||z−v||,||z+v||)≥||v||. Since K≤2δ^(−1/(p+r)) for δ≤1, this is at least 2^(−r)δ^{r/(p+r)}. This applies to every possible estimator. It also explains why stronger algorithms alone cannot remove the smoothness–noise tradeoff.

example.setup: Set p=r=1 and δ=10^(−4).
example.calculation: N=100 gives error at most 1/101+1/100<0.02. K=100 gives two opposite feasible signals ±e_100/100 that both produce zero within the noise budget. Every estimator has worst-case error at least 0.01.
example.conclusion: Cutoff is optimal up to a factor below two in this example; the exponent is exact at the level of uniform deterministic rates.

source.limits: This is a diagonal ellipsoid model. Replacing its coefficient condition by the pointwise assertion |x_k|≤Ck^(−s) changes the tail exponent to s−1/2 when s>1/2. The two smoothness conventions must not be silently identified.

source.title: Severe ill-posedness needs a logarithmic safety margin
source.status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
source.summary: A bare rule N≈(log(1/δ)/c)^{1/β} can conceal a failure: at the exact leading balance, amplified noise can remain of order one. Subtracting a log-log term yields a valid convergent rule while preserving the advertised logarithmic rate. The lower bound again follows from two indistinguishable signals.
definitions: Let Ae_k=exp(−c k^β)e_k on ℓ², with c,β>0, and use M_r={x:Σk^{2r}|x_k|²≤1}. Write L=log(1/δ).
For sufficiently large L define tδ=((L−(r/β)log L)/c)^{1/β} and Nδ=⌊tδ⌋. The subtraction is part of the parameter rule; Nδ is positive once δ is sufficiently small.

result.name: Sharp logarithmic order with a valid parameter rule
result.statement: The cutoff error is O(L^(−r/β)) for the stated Nδ. This is also the deterministic minimax order on M_r. The leading equivalence Nδ∼(L/c)^{1/β} alone does not guarantee convergence for every sequence with that equivalence.
result.proof: As before B(N)≤(N+1)^(−r), and now S(N)=exp(cN^β). Since Nδ≤tδ, δS(Nδ)≤exp(−L+L−(r/β)log L)=L^(−r/β). Because tδ∼(L/c)^{1/β}, the bias has the same order. For a lower bound take K=⌈(L/c)^{1/β}⌉ and v=K^(−r)e_K. Then ||Av||=exp(−cK^β)K^(−r)≤δ, so zero is compatible with both ±v. Every reconstruction therefore incurs error at least K^(−r), which is bounded below by a positive constant times L^(−r/β) as L→∞. To see the danger of using only the leading scale, set β=c=1, δ_j=e^(−j) and N_j=j. Then N_j exactly equals log(1/δ_j), but δ_jS(N_j)=1 for every j. A noise vector δ_je_j is amplified to a unit coordinate. The cutoff rule is consequently inconsistent at the zero signal along this subsequence despite having the expected leading asymptotic size.

example.setup: Use c=β=r=1 and δ=e^(−100).
example.calculation: The safe rule gives N=⌊100−log100⌋=95. Its bound is 1/96+e^(−5)<0.01716. The naive N=100 has noise amplification exactly1. The lower-bound signal ±e_100/100 remains indistinguishable at observation zero.
example.conclusion: A small change in resolution removes an order-one instability while keeping the optimal logarithmic information rate.

source.limits: The statements concern worst-case norm-bounded noise and a specified ellipsoid. They do not assert minimax rates for Gaussian white noise, whose effective noise size depends on dimension.
source.extension: Derive analogous safety margins for exp(−c k^β(log k)^γ), and provide a verified discrepancy rule that reaches the same order without knowledge of r.

source.title: Tikhonov filters: qualification and explicit constants
source.status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
source.summary: The filter formula in the recovered manuscript can be strengthened into an explicit theorem, including the range of smoothness for which the simple argument works. The parameter α controls both spectral bias and amplification; the source exponent determines their balance.
definitions: Let A:X→Y be bounded between Hilbert spaces and define R_α=(A* A+αI)^(−1)A*, α>0. Assume x†=(A* A)^νw, ||w||≤ρ, with 0<ν≤1.
The source condition places x† in ker(A) perpendicular and specifies spectral smoothness. Fractional powers are defined by the spectral calculus of the nonnegative bounded self-adjoint operator A* A.

result.name: Tikhonov source-condition bound
result.statement: For ||yδ−Ax†||≤δ, ||R_αyδ−x†||≤ρ cν α^ν+δ/(2√α), where cν=ν^ν(1−ν)^(1−ν) for0<ν<1 and c1=1. Forρ>0, a parameter of order (δ/ρ)^{2/(2ν+1)} gives error O(ρ^{1/(2ν+1)}δ^{2ν/(2ν+1)}).
result.proof: The residual is I−R_αA=α(A* A+αI)^(−1). On the source vector its spectral multiplier is αλ^ν/(λ+α)=α^ν t^ν/(1+t), with t=λ/α. Differentiating log(t^ν/(1+t)) gives ν/t−1/(1+t), so the maximum occurs at t=ν/(1−ν) when0<ν<1 and equals cν. Atν=1 the supremum is1. The noise multiplier is √λ/(λ+α); its derivative vanishes at λ=α and its global maximum is1/(2√α). The spectral theorem and the triangle inequality give the bound. Balancing α^νρ with δα^(−1/2) gives the parameter order and rate. The restriction ν≤1 is meaningful: forν>1 the ratio t^ν/(1+t) is unbounded on[0,∞), so this scale-free source estimate no longer follows from the same argument. A bounded spectrum gives another estimate, but it does not produce arbitrary qualification for ordinary Tikhonov regularization.

example.calculation: R_α=diag(4/5,1). The exact noiseless reconstruction is(0,1/4), so the bias is1/4, equal to c_{1/2}α^{1/2}=(1/2)(1/2). Also ||R_α||=1=1/(2√α). Noiseδe_2 aligned against the bias attains total error1/4+δ.
example.conclusion: The bias and noise constants are simultaneously sharp for this explicitly stipulated two-coordinate model.

source.limits: Ifρ=0 the source class contains onlyx†=0 and the zero reconstruction is exact. The example verifies a finite case of the spectral estimate. Choosing α from unknown noise or unknownρ requires an additional selection theorem; the bound alone is not an implementable adaptive rule.
source.extension: Compare iterated Tikhonov, whose residual is (α/(λ+α))^m, with ordinary Tikhonov and prove qualification m with explicit constants and a corresponding stopping cost.

source.title: Landweber iteration: regularization by stopping
source.status: Proved under the stated hypotheses; newly stipulated examples
source.summary: The recovered Landweber filter makes the role of iteration count precise. Increasing m shrinks the spectral residual and increases the noise norm. The same controlled-approximation principle used for spectral cutoff therefore governs an algorithm with no explicit truncation.
definitions: Let A be bounded between Hilbert spaces,0<ω≤||A||^(−2), and start x_0=0. Define x_{m+1}=x_m+ωA*(yδ−Ax_m). For A=0 the discussion is trivial, so assume ||A||>0.
Assume x†=(A*A)^νw withν>0 and||w||≤ρ. At singular valueσ>0, g_m(σ)=[1−(1−ωσ²)^m]/σ, while the residual on λ=σ² is(1−ωλ)^m.

result.name: Landweber bias–noise bound and early stopping
result.statement: For m≥1, ||x_m−x†||≤ρ(ν/(eωm))^ν+δ√(ωm). Forρ>0, choosing m of order (ρ/δ)^{2/(2ν+1)} gives the source-condition rate δ^{2ν/(2ν+1)}, with constants depending onν andω.
result.proof: Iterating the affine recurrence gives x_m=ωΣ_{j=0}^{m−1}(I−ωA*A)^jA*yδ, hence the filter. For0≤ωλ≤1, (1−ωλ)^m≤exp(−ωmλ). The maximum of λ^νexp(−ωmλ) overλ≥0 is(ν/(eωm))^ν, giving the bias estimate. For noise use1−(1−t)^m≤min(1,mt) on[0,1]. Thus |g_m(σ)|≤min(1/σ,mωσ)≤√(mω): below the crossing use the second term and above it use the first. The operator norm follows by spectral calculus. Balancing m^(−ν)ρ andδm^(1/2) gives the rate. Exact-data convergence does not justify infinite iteration withδ>0: for arbitrarily small singular values, the eventual filter approaches1/σ. Early stopping chooses how much spectral information the noisy data can support. Unlike the single-step Tikhonov estimate, this exponential-residual argument works for everyν>0.

example.setup: Use the same A=diag(1,1/2), ω=1 and m=4.
example.calculation: The first-coordinate residual is0 and the second is(3/4)^4=81/256. The second filter is2(1−81/256)=175/128, below√4=2. At the true signal x†=e_2 the exact bias is81/256. The verifier checks the recurrence and filter against each other using rational arithmetic.
example.conclusion: The iteration is exactly a family of bounded approximate inverses; stopping is the regularization parameter.

definitions: Put s(t)=(1+t)e^(−t) for t≥0, h(t)=1−√(1−s(t)), and C0=∫_0^∞h(t)dt. Then0<s(t)≤1, s is strictly decreasing for t>0, and h is decreasing from1 to0.
Let a_k=binom(2k,k)/(4^k(2k−1)) for k≥1, so1−√(1−z)=Σ_{k≥1}a_kz^k for0≤z≤1. Every coefficient is positive andΣa_k=1.

result.name: Exact bounds and a monotone rational series
result.statement: 1<C0<2 and C0=Σ_{k≥1}a_k Σ_{j=0}^k binom(k,j)j!/k^{j+1}. If S_K is the sum through K, then S_K<C0<S_K+2(1−Σ_{k≤K}a_k). All finite quantities in this enclosure are rational.
result.proof: Rationalize h=s/(1+√(1−s)). Since the denominator lies strictly between1 and2 for t>0, s/2<h<s there. The integral of s is2, proving the strict bounds and convergence. The binomial series has nonnegative terms, so monotone convergence permits integrating it term by term, including near t=0 where s=1. Expand(1+t)^k and use∫_0^∞t^j e^(−kt)dt=j!/k^{j+1}. This proves the series. For the tail, s(t)^k≤s(t) for everyk≥1; hence∫s^k≤2. Sum the omitted coefficients to obtain the rational upper error bound. The resulting enclosure is deliberately elementary rather than an efficient high-precision algorithm. For numerical work, monotonicity bounds the finite integral by left and right rectangles, whose difference is at most the step width. The tail after L is at most∫_L^∞s=(L+2)e^(−L).
