source.title: A singular descriptor matrix can encode a regular constrained system
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The August2 source correctly distinguishes differential–algebraic structure from malformed data. Singular E does not imply a singular matrix pencil. A two-dimensional exact example shows how regularization can create a large unstable eigenvalue absent from the original constrained dynamics.
definitions: Consider Eẋ=Ax. A square pencil A−λE is regular when det(A−λE) is not identically zero. Its finite generalized eigenvalues are the roots of that determinant; an infinite eigenvalue describes the missing polynomial degree relative to the matrix size.

result.name: Constraint preservation versus a spurious fast mode
result.statement: For E=diag(1,0), A=diag(−1,1), the pencil is regular, the only finite eigenvalue is−1, and consistent trajectories have x₂=0. Replacing E by E+εI, ε>0, introduces an unstable eigenvalue1/ε.
result.proof: The original equations are ẋ₁=−x₁ and0=x₂. Thus all consistent solutions are x(t)=(ae^{−t},0). The determinant det(A−λE)=−1−λ is not the zero polynomial; its degree one in a two-dimensional pencil accounts for one infinite eigenvalue. The algebraic component is a constraint, not a hidden differential state that may be evolved arbitrarily. After regularization, the equations become(1+ε)ẋ₁=−x₁ andεẋ₂=x₂, with eigenvalues−1/(1+ε) and1/ε. Any nonzero error in the constrained coordinate grows as e^{t/ε}. A pseudoinverse replacement also changes the equations unless its constraint consistency is separately enforced. Descriptor-native reduction instead retains the finite deflating subspace and algebraic constraints; an index or minimal-index assertion additionally requires the appropriate canonical data.

example.setup: Use ε=1/100 and consistent initial value(2,0), then perturb the second coordinate by10⁻⁶.
example.calculation: The original constrained solution is(2e^{−t},0). The regularized second component becomes10⁻⁶e^{100t}; at t=1/10 it is approximately0.0220. Its rapid growth is an artifact of the modified problem, even though E+εI is invertible.
example.conclusion: Regularity, constraints and numerical conditioning are separate mathematical properties.

source.title: Rank-one Rouché bounds preserve structure and leave a separate remainder obligation
source.status: Developed classical mathematics with explicit hypotheses and scoped evidence
source.summary: The August4 source reports a larger gain window for a secant surrogate, but explicitly leaves the contour supremum and the surrogate-to-target remainder unresolved. A classical determinant-lemma theorem clarifies why structure helps and what still has to be proved.
definitions: LetF(z) be a square holomorphic matrix on and inside a simple closed contourΓ, withdetF nonzero onΓ. LetΔ(z)=u(z)v(z)ᵀ be holomorphic rank at most one; the transpose is algebraic, with no z-dependent complex conjugation.

result.name: Structured root-count preservation
result.statement: If sup_Γ|vᵀF^{-1}u|<1, then det(F+Δ) anddetF have the same number of zeros insideΓ, counting multiplicity. A further perturbationR needs its own certified bound, such as sup_Γ||(F+Δ)^{-1}R||<1.
result.proof: The matrix determinant lemma givesdet(F+tuvᵀ)=detF·(1+tq), q=vᵀF^{-1}u. If|q|<1 then1+tq≠0 for0≤t≤1 onΓ. The determinant is a continuous boundary-nonvanishing homotopy, so its winding number and argument-principle zero count remain constant. There are no poles becauseF+tΔ is holomorphic, even though the quotientq may have poles inside. For a full remainderR, the factorization(F+Δ+R)=(F+Δ)[I+(F+Δ)^{-1}R] and a Neumann-series bound give a second boundary-nonvanishing homotopy. A grid of contour samples is insufficient unless a derivative or interval bound fills the gaps. The argument counts algebraic multiplicities, so it remains useful for a cluster whose individual roots cannot be tracked differentiably. The count alone does not supply a differentiable branch for each individual root, or preserve a damping ordering within the cluster. The contour must remain fixed and avoid all zeros throughout the homotopy; otherwise its integer winding number can change.

example.setup: On|z|=1 takeF(z)=diag(z,z−3), Δ=δe₂e₂ᵀ with constantδ.
example.calculation: Hereq=δ/(z−3), so|q|≤|δ|/2. Every|δ|<2 preserves the count of one root inside the unit circle. The unstructured estimate||F^{-1}||||Δ||≤|δ| would only give|δ|<1. The improvement is exact and follows from the perturbation acting only on the second coordinate.

definitions: Let π:Θ→F map parameters to their exact represented function. The semantic fiber is E(f)=π⁻¹({f}). Let D⊂Θ encode all declared deployment constraints, and let Y_H(θ) be the feasible implementation choices on a fixed target H.

definitions: For column vectors q,k,v, an attention score without positional rotations is qᵀk; after RoPE it is qᵀR_δk with R_δ orthogonal. The value/output composition is Ov.

SwiGLU allows a common hidden permutation and arbitrary nonzero diagonal rescaling of its linear U branch, compensated in D. Permutations preserving g equal sharing groups form S_r wr S_g=(S_r)^g⋊S_g.
result.proof: The score identity is qᵀAᵀA⁻ᵀk=qᵀk, while the rotated score becomes qᵀAᵀR_δA⁻ᵀk and therefore needs the commutation condition. definitions: At time t, a state s has a finite legal action set A_t(s), immediate costs c_t(s,a), deterministic successor T_t(s,a), and terminal cost h at time L. Infeasible continuations have cost+∞.

Induction proves the full continuation statement and hence equality of its minimum. For the partition direction, P refines Q precisely when every P-block lies within a Q-block; the induced map from P-blocks onto Q-blocks is surjective, so |P|≥|Q|. source.summary: The retrieved examples illustrate two forms of integer lifting: an affine line of solutions and a finite product of exponent lattices. Both require divisibility conditions, rather than a real-valued inverse followed by rounding. The exponent formulation is also the correct setting for Smith normal form compatibility tests.
definitions: A positive integer has a unique vector of nonnegative prime exponents.
A unimodular integer change of variables has determinant ±1 and preserves the integer lattice; Smith normal form diagonalizes an integer linear map using such changes.

result.name: Complete affine and multiplicative solution sets
result.statement: All integer solutions of 2x+3y=1 are (x,y)=(−1+3t,1−2t), t∈Z. The equation x²y³=2²⁰3¹² has exactly twelve positive integer solutions, indexed by 0≤r≤3 and 0≤s≤2 as x=2^(10−3r)3^(6−3s), y=2^(2r)3^(2s).
result.proof: Reducing 2x+3y=1 modulo three gives x≡−1 mod 3, so x=−1+3t; substitution forces y=1−2t. Every t works, proving completeness and injectivity. For the multiplicative equation, no prime other than two or three can divide x or y, because all exponents are nonnegative. Write x=2ᵃ3ᶜ and y=2ᵇ3ᵈ. Unique factorization gives 2a+3b=20 and 2c+3d=12. The first equation forces b even, b=2r, and then a=10−3r≥0, so r=0,1,2,3. The second similarly gives d=2s and c=6−3s≥0, so s=0,1,2. These choices are independent and unique, producing 4·3=12 solutions. More generally, if UAV=diag(d₁,…,d_r,0,…) is a Smith decomposition of an exponent map, integer solvability requires d_i to divide (Ub)_i and zero coordinates of Ub to vanish; nonnegativity is an additional constraint after applying V.

example.calculation: At (r,s)=(0,0), (x,y)=(2¹⁰3⁶,1); at (3,2), (x,y)=(2,2⁶3⁴). The address j=3r+s runs from zero to eleven; division with remainder recovers r=⌊j/3⌋ and s=j mod 3. Thus the count and inverse lookup are both exact.

definitions: Let G_n have entries gcd(i,j), 1≤i,j≤n, and E_ij=1 when j divides i, zero otherwise. Let φ be Euler’s totient.
For the second example, let L_ij=1 when j≤i and K_ij=min(i,j).

result.statement: G_n=E diag(φ(1),…,φ(n))Eᵀ, so det G_n=∏_(j=1)^nφ(j)>0. Also K=LLᵀ and K⁻¹=DᵀD, where D has diagonal one and subdiagonal −1. Its diagonal is (2,…,2,1) and its adjacent off-diagonals are −1.
result.proof: The divisor identity Σ_(d|m)φ(d)=m follows by grouping the integers 1,…,m according to their gcd with m. Hence (E diagφ Eᵀ)_ij=Σ_(d|i,d|j)φ(d)=gcd(i,j). E is lower triangular with diagonal one, proving the determinant and positive definiteness. Solving Gx=b reduces to two triangular substitutions and positive scalar divisions; the inverse incidence matrix is the divisibility Möbius matrix, by the identity Σ_(d|m)μ(d)=0 for m>1. For the chain kernel, (LLᵀ)_ij counts indices at most both i and j, giving min(i,j). D=L⁻¹ because first differences invert cumulative sums. Therefore K⁻¹=DᵀD; direct multiplication gives the stated tridiagonal entries. The last diagonal is one because the final coordinate occurs in only the last row of D.

example.calculation: K=[[1,1,1],[1,2,2],[1,2,3]] has inverse [[2,−1,0],[−1,2,−1],[0,−1,1]]. The GCD matrix [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,3]] has determinant φ(1)φ(2)φ(3)=2. Both identities are verified by exact matrix multiplication.

source.title: Superelliptic genus follows from finite and infinite ramification
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The source gives a superelliptic genus formula and its Gauss–Bonnet counterpart. Both become rigorous on the smooth compact normalization of a squarefree equation. The point at infinity must be included: overlooking its gcd contribution changes the genus.
definitions: Let P∈C[x] be squarefree of degree m≥1, let d≥2, and let C be the smooth projective normalization of yᵈ=P(x). Set δ=gcd(d,m).
The map x:C→P¹ has degree d. Curvature below is the Gaussian curvature of any smooth Riemannian metric on the compact oriented surface C.

result.name: Genus, curvature and branch monodromy
result.statement: g(C)=[(d−1)(m−1)−δ+1]/2 and ∫_C K dA=2π[d+δ−m(d−1)]. Around a simple zero of P, analytic continuation multiplies a local branch of y by exp(2πi/d).
result.proof: Near a simple zero a, write P(x)=(x−a)u(x), u(a)≠0. A holomorphic dth root of u exists locally, so a local parameter t can be chosen with x−a=tᵈ. The ramification index is d, contributing d−1 at each of the m finite branch points. At infinity the equation has orders d·ord(y)=m·ord(x); dividing by δ shows that there are δ points above infinity, each with ramification index d/δ. Their total contribution is d−δ. Riemann–Hurwitz gives 2g−2=−2d+m(d−1)+(d−δ)=m(d−1)−d−δ, which rearranges to the stated formula. Gauss–Bonnet gives ∫K=2π(2−2g), yielding the curvature expression. Finally, moving x−a once counterclockwise adds 2π to its argument, so its dth root and therefore y acquire exp(2πi/d). This is local covering monodromy, distinct from an arbitrary flat-connection holonomy.

example.setup: Compare an elliptic and a higher-genus example.
example.calculation: For y²=x³−x, d=2,m=3,δ=1 gives g=1 and total curvature zero. For y³=x⁴−1, d=3,m=4,δ=1 gives g=3 and total curvature −8π. In the latter, every finite root has local monodromy exp(2πi/3), while infinity is also totally ramified.
example.conclusion: The recovered formulas hold after the singular affine equation is replaced by its smooth compact curve.

source.limits: Repeated roots require revised local ramification data and can make the displayed genus formula false. Gauss–Bonnet controls total curvature, not a pointwise curvature sign, and an affine noncompact chart has boundary/end corrections.

source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The recovered power-chart examples admit global elementary proofs. Prime valuations establish surjectivity of the parametrization; substitution alone would show only that a proposed family gives some solutions. definitions: For a nonzero integer a and a prime p, v_p(a) is the exponent of p in |a|.
All variables in the following statements are integers; powers and signs are interpreted in Z, not merely over positive reals.

result.name: Complete cusp parametrizations
result.statement: x²=y³ if and only if (x,y)=(t³,t²) for a unique t∈Z. Also 2x²=3y³ if and only if (x,y)=(18t³,6t²) for a unique t∈Z.
result.proof: The zero case forces both coordinates to vanish. Otherwise y>0. In x²=y³, the equality 2v_p(x)=3v_p(y) implies v_p(x)=3a_p and v_p(y)=2a_p for nonnegative integers a_p. Thus y=t² and |x|=|t|³; choose the sign of t to match x. This t is unique because integer cubing is injective. For 2x²=3y³, at p=2 we have 1+2a=3b, hence b=2r+1 and a=3r+1 with r≥0. At p=3, 2a=1+3b gives b=2s+1 and a=3s+2. Every other prime again has valuations (3a_p,2a_p). Extracting these factors yields |x|=18u³ and y=6u², where u≥1 is an integer. The sign of x determines t=±u. Conversely, direct substitution gives 2·18²t⁶=3·6³t⁶, so the parametrization is exact.

example.setup: Invert a concrete point and impose an arithmetic restriction.
example.calculation: For (x,y)=(−144,24), x/18=−8 gives t=−2, and 6t²=24 checks the other coordinate. Restricting y≤150 gives |t|≤5, hence exactly eleven solutions including zero. A further congruence can be tested on the single parameter; for example x≡0 mod 5 is equivalent to t≡0 mod 5 because 18 is invertible modulo five.
example.conclusion: The nonlinear image becomes an explicitly invertible one-parameter integer population.

source.title: Squarefree quotient algebras split exceptional and regular branches by gcd
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The recovered gcd branch splitting has a clean Chinese-remainder proof. It turns an informal instruction to avoid zero denominators into an exact decomposition of a finite algebra. The squarefree hypothesis is the structural reason the branches separate.
definitions: Let K be a field, p∈K[t] squarefree, and a∈K[t]. Set g=gcd(p,a), h=p/g, with monic choices.
Write R=K[t]/(p). A component is regular for a when multiplication by a is invertible on it.

result.name: Exact regular/exceptional decomposition
result.statement: g and h are coprime, and R≅K[t]/(g)×K[t]/(h). The image of a is zero in the first factor and invertible in the second; a Bézout identity supplies its inverse there.
result.proof: Because p is squarefree, no irreducible factor dividing g can also divide h. The Chinese remainder map therefore has inverse constructed from Bézout polynomials ug+vh=1, proving the algebra isomorphism. Every factor of g divides a, so a is zero modulo g. Conversely, any common divisor of a and h would divide p and a, hence g, contradicting coprimality of g and h. Thus gcd(a,h)=1, and extended Euclid gives ra+sh=1; r is an exact inverse of a modulo h. No root approximations or heuristic branch labels enter. When g=1 there is no exceptional component; when h=1 every component is exceptional. These cases are naturally interpreted using the zero quotient factor.

example.setup: Take K=Q, p=(t−1)(t+1)(t−2) and a=t−1.
example.calculation: Here g=t−1 and h=t²−t−2. In K[t]/(h), (t−1)(t/2)=(t²−t)/2=1, so t/2 is the regular inverse. In the factor t=1, a is zero. Hence an expression b/a can be evaluated using bt/2 only on the h component; the t=1 component still requires its original undivided equation. For contrast, if p=(t−1)², then g=t−1 and h=t−1 are not coprime: the quotient contains a nonzero nilpotent and cannot be replaced by a product of two point factors.
example.conclusion: The decomposition makes every denominator decision and exceptional branch auditable.

definitions: Let Ω⊆{0,1}ⁿ be a finite nonempty population ordered lexicographically with 0 before 1. For a prefix q, let C(q) count its feasible completions.

result.statement: There is an exact bijection rank:Ω→{0,…,|Ω|−1}. At prefix q, all q0 completions occupy the first C(q0) addresses; the q1 block occupies the following C(q1). A uniform address therefore gives a uniform object.

At each step these operations are inverse translations on the two disjoint blocks, proving the global bijection. Consequently P(unrank(R)=ω)=1/|Ω| when R is uniform. source.summary: The dated synthesis lists jets and Schröder equations, while another passage warns that a seventh-order coefficient leaves six lower orders unchanged. A formal coefficient argument explains both phenomena. The chosen example is explicitly solvable and does not assume convergence of a general formal conjugacy.
definitions: Let f(x)=λx+Σ_(n≥2)f_nxⁿ over a characteristic-zero field, λ≠0. Seek h(x)=x+Σ_(n≥2)h_nxⁿ with h(f(x))=λh(x).
The N-jet is a power series modulo x^(N+1). A resonance at degree n means λⁿ=λ.

result.name: Nonresonant jet recursion
result.statement: If λⁿ≠λ for 2≤n≤N, the normalized Schröder equation has exactly one N-jet solution. Each h_n depends only on f₂,…,f_n; changing f_(N+1) cannot alter the solution through degree N.
result.proof: Assume h₂,…,h_(n−1) have been determined. In degree n, the contribution of h_nf(x)ⁿ is λⁿh_n; the right side contributes λh_n. Every remaining term uses only lower coefficients of h and coefficients of f through degree n. Thus (λⁿ−λ)h_n is a known scalar, uniquely determining h_n in the nonresonant case. Induction proves existence and uniqueness to every requested finite order and the triangular dependency. At a resonance the known scalar must vanish for solvability; if it vanishes, h_n is not determined at that order. This proves a precise obstruction rather than a general linearization promise. In particular, two maps differing first at degree seven have identical six-jets, so no procedure using only those six coefficients can distinguish them.

example.setup: Take f(x)=2x+x².
example.calculation: Here 1+f(x)=(1+x)², so h(x)=log(1+x) gives h(f(x))=2h(x) as a formal identity. Its first coefficients are x−x²/2+x³/3−x⁴/4. Direct degree-two comparison gives 1+4h₂=2h₂, hence h₂=−1/2; degree three gives 4h₂+8h₃=2h₃, hence h₃=1/3. For contrast, λ=−1 resonates at every odd degree greater than one.
example.conclusion: The example links an exact conjugacy to the finite triangular calculation and makes the identifiability limit explicit.

source.limits: Formal existence is not analytic convergence; small denominators require additional estimates. The source’s specific coefficient 1/128 cannot be independently checked without its actual input map.

source.title: A target is recoverable exactly when it factors through the observation
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The recovered kernel criterion is a complete finite-dimensional identifiability theorem. It separates state reconstruction from recovering a particular target. The distinction prevents unnecessary sensing and makes a missing-information claim testable by an explicit nullspace vector.
definitions: Let V,W,Z be finite-dimensional vector spaces over Q or R, with observation H:V→W and target G:V→Z.
The target is identifiable when Hx=Hy implies Gx=Gy for every x,y∈V.

result.name: Kernel factorization criterion
result.statement: The following are equivalent: the target is identifiable; ker H⊆ker G; and there is a linear L:W→Z such that G=LH. L is uniquely determined on im H but need not be unique on all W.
result.proof: If the target is identifiable, set y=0 and x∈ker H to obtain Gx=0. Conversely, Hx=Hy means x−y∈ker H, so kernel inclusion gives Gx=Gy. To construct L on im H, define L(Hx)=Gx. If Hx=Hy the kernel condition makes this independent of the representative, and linearity follows from the linearity of H and G. Extend a basis of im H to a basis of W and define L arbitrarily on the complement. Then G=LH. The converse factorization immediately implies kernel inclusion. A violating vector v with Hv=0 but Gv≠0 is therefore a complete impossibility certificate: x and x+v have identical data and different targets.

example.setup: Observe Hx=(x₁+x₂,x₂+x₃) and ask for Gx=x₁+2x₂+x₃.
example.calculation: Here ker H is span((1,−1,1)), and G annihilates this vector. The reconstruction is Gx=(1,1)Hx. Asking instead for x₁ fails, since its value changes along the kernel. In four dimensions, observing only the first two coordinates leaves a two-dimensional fibre; two further independent scalar linear measurements are necessary and sufficient to reconstruct the whole state, although fewer may suffice for a particular G.
example.conclusion: The theorem identifies precisely which uncertainty matters for a requested mathematical output.

source.limits: Nonlinear, noisy or restricted-state observations require revised conditions. Dimension counting is a lower bound for full linear reconstruction, not a universal lower bound for arbitrary discontinuous encodings or finite-state problems.
source.extension: Under bounded noise, minimize an explicit norm of L subject to G=LH; the resulting operator norm bounds target error and turns exact identifiability into a conditioned sensor-design problem.

source.title: Cancellation controls the condition number of an exact sum
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The retrieved condition number concerns the sum of terms, rather than the intrinsic truth of the identity. A direct perturbation bound makes its scope precise. It also explains why common-mode symbolic cancellation should occur before evaluating large nearly opposite quantities.
definitions: Let S=Σ_(j=1)^n t_j≠0 be a real or complex sum. Define κ_sum=Σ|t_j|/|S|.
Assume perturbed terms satisfy |Δt_j|≤ε|t_j|; this is an input relative-error model, separate from the additional error of the summation algorithm.

result.name: Sharp first-order relative perturbation bound
result.statement: |ΔS|/|S|≤εκ_sum. For real terms the bound can be attained by suitable independent signed perturbations. If S=0, relative conditioning is undefined and an absolute error bound must be used instead.
result.proof: The triangle inequality gives |ΣΔt_j|≤Σε|t_j|, proving the bound. For real terms, choose every Δt_j with the same sign, of magnitude ε|t_j|; then their sum has magnitude εΣ|t_j|, giving equality. Since |Σt_j|≤Σ|t_j|, κ_sum≥1. For complex terms the same upper bound holds and alignment of perturbation directions similarly attains it under the stated independent complex-error balls. This is a worst-case conditioning theorem; a particular floating-point algorithm can add further rounding errors, while correlated input errors may cancel and require a joint model. Therefore a large κ is a warning about sensitivity, not a proof that any computed value is wrong.

example.setup: Compare an unstable difference with an algebraically simplified one.
example.calculation: For t₁=10¹²+1 and t₂=−10¹², S=1 and κ_sum=2·10¹²+1. Independent relative errors of only 10⁻¹² can therefore create absolute errors around two, larger than the true result. If both terms come from the exact common expression c, computing (c+1)−c symbolically as one removes the common uncertainty before numeric evaluation. This is valid only when the two c occurrences really represent the same quantity.
example.conclusion: The condition number quantifies precisely how cancellation can magnify independent term errors.

definitions: Let ζ_N=exp(2πi/N), K=Q(ζ₁₆₈₀) and L=Q(ζ₃₀). The primitive phases are ζ_Nᵃ for gcd(a,N)=1.
Define c₃₀(n)=Σ_(a mod30,gcd(a,30)=1)ζ₃₀^(an), the Ramanujan sum.

result.name: Exact degree and trace transport
result.statement: φ(1680)=384, φ(30)=8 and [K:L]=48. The map ζ₁₆₈₀ᵃ↦ζ₃₀ᵃ sends the384 primitive phases onto the eight primitive order30 phases with exactly48 preimages each. Consequently Tr_(K/Q)(ω^(56n))=48c₃₀(n).
result.proof: The elementary totient product gives φ(1680)=1680(1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/5)(1−1/7)=384 and φ(30)=8. Its fibres are cosets of the kernel and therefore all have size384/8=48. Summing ω^(56an)=ζ₃₀^(an) over the384 embeddings of K groups the terms into these equal fibres, proving the trace identity. Equivalently, an element of L has relative trace48 times itself before taking its trace to Q.

example.calculation: Möbius inclusion–exclusion gives c₃₀(1)=μ(30)=−1, hence Tr_(K/Q)(ω⁵⁶)=−48. At n=30, every primitive η contributes one, so c₃₀(30)=8 and the K-trace is384. At n=2, the divisor formula gives c₃₀(2)=−1+2=1, so the larger-field trace is48. At n=15, every primitive order30 phase has fifteenth power−1, giving c₃₀(15)=−8 and trace−384. source.title: A 264-fold root filter differs from a degree240 field extension
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The source records the integers384,264 and240. They measure different objects: base-field degree, the number of complex roots of a power equation, and extension degree. The root-of-unity filter makes this distinction explicit and supplies a convergent exact identity.
definitions: Set q=ζ₁₆₈₀, Q=ζ₄₄₃₅₂₀ and N=264, so Qᴺ=q. Let ξ=ζ_N.
For Re(s)>1 and |z|≤1, define Li_s(z)=Σ_(n≥1)zⁿ/nˢ by its absolutely convergent series.

result.name: Full-root polylogarithm filter and primitive count
result.statement: Σ_(r=0)^(N−1)Li_s(Qξʳ)=N^(1−s)Li_s(q). There are264 distinct roots of X²⁶⁴=q, but exactly240 of them are primitive order443520 roots, and [Q(Q):Q(q)]=240.
result.proof: Absolute convergence permits the finite root sum to be interchanged with the series. The geometric sum Σ_rξ^(rn) is N when N divides n and zero otherwise. Writing n=Nℓ leaves NΣ_ℓQ^(Nℓ)/(Nℓ)ˢ=N^(1−s)Li_s(q), proving the filter with no branch continuation. All roots are Qξʳ=ζ₄₄₃₅₂₀^(1+1680r),0≤r<264. Their exponents are automatically coprime to2,3,5,7. The only possible extra common factor is11; exactly one residue class of r modulo11 makes1+1680r divisible by11, removing24 roots. Thus240 are primitive. Independently, φ(443520)=92160 and φ(1680)=384, giving the same extension degree240 by the tower law. The excluded r satisfy r≡4 mod11. The remaining240 exponents are exactly the cyclotomic automorphisms fixing q, so their sum is a relative field trace, whereas the264-term expression is a complete root filter. Filtering over only the240 primitive roots would therefore be a different sum and does not satisfy the displayed264-term identity unchanged.

example.setup: Check two elementary specializations.
example.calculation: For N=2, Li₂(z)+Li₂(−z)=½Li₂(z²), by retaining the even series terms. Also q⁴²⁰=i, so Im Li₂(q⁴²⁰)=Σ_(m≥0)(−1)ᵐ/(2m+1)², the Catalan constant. These identities follow directly from convergent series and fix the phase conventions.
example.conclusion: The power equation, primitive count and field degree are reconciled without mixing their meanings.

result.statement: S(a)=2arcsin(a/2)² for real |a|≤2. In particular, for a=2sin(π/840), S(a)=π²/352800.
result.proof: Let c_n=1/[n²binom(2n,n)]. The ratio c_(n+1)/c_n=n²/[(2n+2)(2n+1)] shows that S is analytic for |a|<2. Thus the endpoint terms are at most2/n^(3/2), a summable majorant. Dominated continuity extends the identity to a=±2. definitions: Let Φ₃₀(x)=x⁸+x⁷−x⁵−x⁴−x³+x+1 and K(x)=240x²⁹/(1−x³⁰)−Φ₃₀′(x)/Φ₃₀(x),0<x<1.
Let c₃₀(n)=Σ_(d|gcd(30,n))dμ(30/d). For Re(s)>1 set D(s)=Σ_(n≥1)[c₃₀(n)+240·1_(30|n)]/nˢ.

result.name: Exact zero and logarithmic Mellin derivative
result.statement: ∫₀¹(−log x)K(x)dx=0 and ∫₀¹(−log x)log(−log x)K(x)dx=−π²[16log2+12log3+10log5]/180.
result.proof: From the product of Φ₃₀ over its primitive roots, logarithmic differentiation gives −Φ′/Φ=Σ_(n≥1)c₃₀(n)x^(n−1) for |x|<1. The other kernel term contributes240 precisely when30 divides n. The coefficients are bounded, so integrating against (−log x)^(s−1) is justified absolutely for Re(s)>1 and gives Γ(s)D(s). Summing the divisor formula yields D(s)=ζ(s)F(s), where F(s)=240·30^(−s)+∏_(p∈{2,3,5})(p^(1−s)−1). At s=2, the product is−4/15 and240/900=4/15, hence F(2)=D(2)=0. Differentiating under the integral is legitimate near s=2 by the same absolute bound with an additional |log(−log x)| factor. The Γ′ term vanishes because D(2)=0. Convergence can also be seen directly: Φ₃₀(1)=1, so the logarithmic derivative stays bounded near one while the first kernel term is asymptotic to8/(1−x). Multiplication by−log x removes this pole, and the extra logarithm leaves an integrable log(1−x) singularity. Near zero the kernel is bounded, so its logarithmic moments are integrable there as well. Logarithmic differentiation of the finite product gives F′(2)=−(4/15)[log30+log2+½log3+¼log5]. Multiplying by ζ(2)=π²/6 produces the displayed companion.

example.setup: Check the coefficient arithmetic behind the cancellation.
example.calculation: The eight divisors of30 give Σ_(d|30)μ(30/d)/d=−1+1/2+1/3+1/5−1/6−1/10−1/15+1/30=−4/15. The exact added coefficient240/30² is4/15. Their sum vanishes before any transcendental evaluation. The cancellation does not say K is zero: its limit at zero is−1, while it is positive and unbounded sufficiently near one. The integral balances genuinely nonzero regions of opposite sign.
example.conclusion: Two recovered integral identities are fully proved with their convergence hypotheses.

source.title: The five-phase logarithmic integral equals 955π³/867 exactly
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The exact phase set makes this one of the strongest independently checkable October identities. Fourier analysis reduces the integral to a finite Bernoulli-polynomial sum. Logarithmic endpoint and interior singularities are square-integrable and are part of the proof, not exclusions from it.
definitions: Define I=∫_(−1)^1 log²|P(x)|/√(1−x²)dx, equivalently ∫₀^πlog²|P(cos t)|dt. Let B₂(u)=u²−u+1/6 and {u} denote fractional part.

result.name: Exact five-phase integral
result.statement: I=(955/867)π³. More generally I/π³=Σ_(s,r∈S)[B₂({(s−r)/17})+B₂({(s+r)/17})] for this convention of product factors.
result.proof: The factorization 2cos t−2cos θ=e^(−it)(e^(it)−e^(iθ))(e^(it)−e^(−iθ)) shows that log|2cos t−2cos θ|=−2Σ_(n≥1)cos(nt)cos(nθ)/n in L²(0,π). One can justify the boundary Fourier series by radial regularization of log|1−re^(iu)| and L² convergence of its square-summable coefficients as r↑1. Local logarithmic singularities, including the doubled endpoint singularity when θ=0, are L², so the factorization agrees with this limit. Summing over S gives −2Σa_ncos(nt)/n, where a_n=Σ_scos(nθ_s). Parseval yields I=2πΣa_n²/n². The identity2cos u cos v=cos(u−v)+cos(u+v), followed by Σ_(n≥1)cos(2πnu)/n²=π²B₂({u}), gives the finite formula. Evaluating its fifty rational B₂ terms with denominator17² gives exactly955/867. Individual B₂ terms may be negative, but the full quadratic expression is nonnegative for every phase multiset by its Parseval representation. This also checks the factor of two and shows why estimating each pair contribution independently can obscure the positivity of the original integral.

example.setup: Give a rational-only arithmetic certificate for the coefficient.
example.calculation: For residues k modulo17, B₂(k/17)=k²/289−k/17+1/6. The verifier loops over all25 ordered pairs (s,r), adds the difference and sum residues, and obtains Fraction(955,867). Root’s independent audit computes the same finite sum separately.
example.conclusion: The integral is established analytically, and its final rational coefficient is independently replayable without numerical quadrature.

source.limits: A different normalization of each product factor would add constants inside the logarithm and change the integral. No KZ or group-closure conclusion follows merely from this phase integral.
source.extension: For any finite rational phase set, derive the corresponding Bernoulli sum and classify sets with equal quadratic logarithmic energy; add higher moments only after proving convergence and the required multiple Fourier convolution identities.

definitions: Let ζ=exp(2πi/17). Assume unitary5×5 matrices R₁,R₂ satisfy the braid relation, det R_i=ζ⁹ and (R₁R₂)³=ζ⁴I.

result.statement: T_i∈SU(5), they satisfy the braid relation, and (T₁T₂)³=I. If additionally T_i³⁴=I, they define a quotient of Δ(2,3,34). Moreover G≅SU(5)×μ₁₇ as compact groups, via (S,ξ)↦ξS.
result.proof: Twisting a5×5 matrix by ζ⁵ multiplies its determinant by ζ²⁵; thus det T_i=ζ³⁴=1. Both sides of the braid relation gain the same scalar ζ¹⁵. The braid relation gives a²=b³=I, and b⁻¹a=T₁, so the extra relation T₁³⁴=I gives the triangle presentation with orders dividing2,3,34. For the group decomposition, ξ∈μ₁₇ has determinant ξ⁵. This is a continuous inverse to (S,ξ)↦ξS, and the intersection SU(5)∩μ₁₇I is trivial, proving the product isomorphism.

source.title: Shared uncertainty should be optimized jointly in a decision difference
source.status: Classical mathematics or a newly chosen finite model developed with proof; historical claims delimited
source.summary: The recovered final October target is to certify a decision using common uncertainty and the cheapest sufficient measurement. Joint modeling preserves cancellation that is destroyed by independent interval bounds. The following theorem is deterministic and concerns abstract scores, with no empirical or financial forecast assumed.
definitions: Let X be a nonempty uncertainty set and let J_A,J_B:X→R be two scores, with larger preferred. Set δ(x)=J_A(x)−J_B(x).
A strict robust certificate is a positive lower bound m≤inf_(x∈X)δ(x). Attainment of the infimum is unnecessary if a bound is proved directly.

result.name: Joint dominance and measurement certificates
result.statement: If inf_X(J_A−J_B)>0, A wins for every compatible state. In the shared model J_A=c+δ, J_B=c with δ∈[7/4,9/4], the margin is at least 7/4 regardless of the range of c. Separate interval subtraction can fail to certify the same fact.
result.proof: The first assertion is immediate from the defining inequality for every x. Its content is the order of operations: subtraction must take place at the same uncertainty state before minimization. In general inf(A−B)≥inf A−sup B, but the inequality can be strict because the separate extrema need not occur at compatible states. For c∈[0,100], separate score ranges are A∈[7/4,409/4] and B∈[0,100]; their interval difference includes −393/4, even though the exact shared difference is always positive. A new measurement with result z and error bound ε restricts X to X_z={x:|h(x)−z|≤ε}; computing the margin on X_z can only improve its lower bound because X_z⊆X. A decision-sufficient experiment is one whose every nonempty outcome fibre gives a positive margin for one of the two directions.

example.setup: Suppose δ itself is measured with absolute error at most 1/10.
example.calculation: A result z=1/4 implies δ≥z−1/10=3/20>0, certifying A. A result z=1/20 gives δ∈[−1/20,3/20], so it does not certify either direction. With several possible tests, their costs and outcome fibres can be inserted into the finite Bellman recurrence to identify the cheapest guaranteed decision procedure.
example.conclusion: The certificate exploits correlation exactly and states which remaining uncertainty matters.

source.limits: Overlapping separate intervals do not imply an undecidable joint model, while a positive estimate without an error bound is not a robust certificate. This theorem supplies no calibration of an empirical uncertainty set.
source.extension: Use polynomial or rational score models on a semialgebraic X and produce an exact positivity certificate for J_A−J_B; then optimize measurement cost subject to such certificates on every admissible outcome fibre.

source.title: Five raw observations determine the entire 107-bit generator state
source.status: New exact all-state certificate, independently replayable with standard-library Python
source.summary: The explicit recurrence allows a global theorem stronger than a collection of decoding tests. Equality of output words becomes a short-vector problem in an integer lattice. Exact dual bounds exclude every nonzero collision at once. The supplied certificate covers all 126  choices of five positions within nine steps; no enumeration of2^107 states and no trust in an LLL implementation is required.
definitions: Let M=2^107−1, A=3^121 moduloM, and b=2^26. States are integers0≤x_i<M with x_{i+1}=Ax_i moduloM; the raw observation is y_i=x_i modulo b. Since M≡1 modulo3, A is invertible moduloM.
For positions0≤p_0<⋯<p_4≤8 put g_j=p_j−p_0 and Λ_p={d∈Z^5:d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 moduloM forj=1,…,4}. Let D=⌊(M−1)/b⌋=2^81−1.

result.name: Exact raw-state observability
result.statement: For every five-position subset of{0,…,8}, the selected raw words uniquely determine the initial state. Four raw words cannot determine every state. Every supplied integer basis B_p has rows inΛ_p, |det B_p|=M^4, and DΣ_i|(B_p^(−1))_{ij}|<3/8 for each columnj.
result.proof:
The homomorphism Z^5→(Z/MZ)^4 sending d to(d_j−A^{g_j}d_0)_{j=1}^4 is onto: vary the final four coordinates while keeping d_0=0. Its kernelΛ_p therefore has indexM^4. The checker verifies lattice membership of every basis row and determinant magnitudeM^4, proving that its row lattice equalsΛ_p rather than merely a sublattice. It computes the inverse over rational numbers, verifies B_pB_p^(−1)=I, and checks the strict column bounds for all 126 position subsets. These properties alone suffice; the LLL routine used to find the bases is not trusted.

Suppose two states have the same five observed words. At each selected step their state difference is b d_j for an integerd_j with |d_j|≤D. The recurrence implies d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 moduloM because b is invertible moduloM. Hence d=cB_p for some integer rowc. Each coordinate satisfies |c_j|=|(dB_p^(−1))_j|≤DΣ_i|(B_p^(−1))_{ij}|<3/8<1. Thusc=0, all selected state differences vanish, and invertibility of A takes equality atp_0 back to equality of the initial states. Four words range over at mostb^4=2^104 possibilities, whereas even the nonzero state set has M−1>2^104 elements. Pigeonhole therefore proves four-word impossibility.

The same dual bounds yield a decoder. Write selected states as y_j+bz_j with0≤z_j≤D. Their congruences define an affine lattice v+Λ_p, using v_0=0 and v_j=b^(−1)(A^{g_j}y_0−y_j) moduloM. For z=v+cB_p, each integerc_j lies in the exact interval obtained by applying the corresponding inverse column to the box0≤z≤D. Its width is below3/8, so it contains at most one integer. Round the interval endpoints exactly, reconstruct z and check all state bounds and observations; then reverse A^{p_0}. This is an actual exact decoder, not only an existence result.

example.setup: Use each of the five states0,1,1234567890123456789,⌊M/3⌋ and M−1, and every five-position subset of the first nine raw outputs.
example.calculation: The checker verifies all 126 lattice bases with exact integers and fractions. Its decoder recovers all 630 specified state/pattern fixtures, including boundary states. The largest dual bound is checked as an exact rational number strictly below3/8; its floating display, about0.368314147, is only for reading.
example.conclusion: The universal conclusion comes from the determinant and dual-bound proof. The 630 fixtures separately verify the decoder implementation on concrete inputs.

source.limits: Raw observations are consecutive generator steps at known positions, with the source recurrence and output convention stated above. Rejected/accepted-output sequences have hidden step counts and require a different theorem. This certificate makes no claim about their six-output threshold.
source.extension: Certify additional sparse position patterns, derive the smallest alphabet width permitting five-observation recovery, and optimize the rational basis for a low-cost decoder while retaining exactly the same independent determinant/dual-bound checks.

source.title: Seven and nine raw observations have optimal one- and two-error correction
source.status: New exact all-state certificate, independently replayable with standard-library Python
source.summary: The finite-state trajectories define a code over the alphabet of26-bit words. The five-observation theorem controls its minimum Hamming distance without requiring linearity over a field. A puncturing argument then proves that the seven- and nine-word correction lengths cannot be improved for this full state population.
definitions: For5≤n≤9 let C_n={c_n(x):0≤x<M}, where c_n(x)=(y_0,…,y_{n−1}) is the raw trajectory. Hamming distance counts differing words, regardless of the bit distance within a corrupted word.

An arbitrary word corruption replaces one entire26-bit symbol. Unique correction oftcorruptions requires minimum code distance at least2t+1. Erasures at known positions are a different, easier observation model.

result.name: Exact distance and length-optimal correction
result.statement: For5≤n≤9 the minimum distance of C_n is exactlyn−4. Thus seven raw outputs correct one arbitrary word error, and nine correct two. No code representing all M states over this alphabet can correct one error with six words or two errors with eight words.
result.proof:
If two distinct state codewords agreed at five positions in any n≤9, the preceding theorem would make the states equal. They therefore agree in at most four positions, giving distance at leastn−4. Conversely, for any code of minimum distanced, puncturing d−1fixed positions leaves an injective map: otherwise two original words differed only in those positions, contradicting the distance. Hence its population is at mostb^{n−d+1}. Since M>b^4, one has n−d+1≥5, or d≤n−4. This proves equality.

Two Hamming balls of radius t are disjoint when the minimum distance exceeds2t, by the triangle inequality; hence the stated seven- and nine-word codes uniquely correct the stated errors. An explicit decoder enumerates five-position subsets, applies the certified affine-lattice decoder, re-encodes each candidate and retains a state within the permitted Hamming radius. Enough clean positions remain to produce the true candidate, and the distance proof rules out a second one. Finally any code correcting t arbitrary errors has distance at least2t+1. Puncturing2t positions must be injective, giving M≤b^{n−2t}; sinceM>b^4, necessarily n≥5+2t. This proves the requested length lower bounds without a linear-code assumption.

example.setup: Start at x=1234567890123456789. In its first seven raw words replace position2 by that word plus12345 modulo b. In its first nine words instead corrupt positions1 and7 by offsets54321 and98765 modulo b.
example.calculation: The exact subset decoder returns the original state in both cases. The verification report retains all original and corrupted words. A word can be altered in many bits and still counts as one corruption in this model.
example.conclusion: The finite decoder tests instantiate a globally proved distance theorem, and the puncturing bound proves that shorter full-population codes cannot have the same correction guarantee.

source.limits: This is a coding theorem for the stated deterministic raw trajectories. It does not assert cryptographic unpredictability, statistical randomness or a correction guarantee when output positions are hidden by rejection sampling.

bridges.title: Quotients, observability and the information a decision actually needs
bridges.kind: Proved bridge in a linear model
bridges.question: When can a target be recovered without reconstructing the entire hidden state?
bridges.text:
Let X, Y and Z be finite-dimensional vector spaces, with linear observation H:X→Y and linear target G:X→Z. Exact target recovery means that some map K on the reachable observations satisfies G=KH. The necessary and sufficient condition is ker H⊆ker G. Necessity follows immediately by applying KH to an invisible state. For sufficiency, define K(Hx)=Gx. If Hx=Hx′, then x−x′ lies in ker H and hence in ker G, so the definition is independent of the representative. It is linear on im H and may be extended linearly to Y. Thus the target descends through the observable quotient X/ker H. There is no requirement that H be injective on X.

This gives a precise relationship between algebraic quotients and experimental design. Rows of H are available measurements; rows of G are the desired quantities. The inclusion of kernels is equivalent to row(G)⊆row(H), and therefore to rank([H;G])=rank(H). A finite candidate-probe catalogue with costs becomes a discrete optimization problem: find a cheapest subset whose row span contains row(G). The lab checks every subset of six probes by exact rational elimination. The distinction between full-state observability and target observability is visible immediately: one probe x₁+x₂ suffices for the sum target even though it leaves a three-dimensional hidden subspace.

The same quotient principle applies to a deterministic machine only after its equivalence relation is specified. Histories u and v may be identified when every future continuation gives the same output; this is a congruence compatible with concatenation. For a linear realization, reachable states and unobservable states lead to the usual reachable-observable reduction. These are rigorous constructions in their respective categories. Calling any two lossy summaries the same quotient would skip the essential work of defining the objects, equivalence relation and compatible operations.

A robust decision can need less information than either absolute value. In J_A=c+δ and J_B=c, the difference is δ. Common uncertainty c disappears under the difference functional. The joint uncertainty set, rather than two marginal intervals, carries the fact that the same c appears twice. With |c|≤10 and δ∈[1,2], the individual intervals [−9,12] and [−10,10] overlap substantially, while J_A−J_B is strictly positive throughout the joint set. This is an exact cancellation theorem for the stated model. It is not an argument for canceling two unrelated uncertain inputs.

The useful general question is therefore not “How much data can we collect?” but “Which distinctions between states can alter the target?” Its answer specifies an equivalence relation and then a sufficient observation map. In nonlinear problems the linear kernel condition must be replaced by constancy of the target on observation fibres; continuity, stability and computational tractability require additional hypotheses. An algebraic factorization can exist while being numerically unstable or impractical. The atlas keeps those three questions—existence, stability and implementation—separate.

bridges.title: Local compatibility, cohomology and transport around a loop
bridges.kind: Exact finite chain model; geometric bridge under stated hypotheses
bridges.question: Why can locally consistent data fail to assemble into one global object?
bridges.text:
A cochain complex consists of groups or vector spaces Cᵏ and maps dᵏ:Cᵏ→Cᵏ⁺¹ with dᵏ⁺¹dᵏ=0. A compatible datum is a cocycle, an element of ker dᵏ. A change generated at the preceding level is a coboundary, an element of im dᵏ⁻¹. Cohomology Hᵏ=ker dᵏ/im dᵏ⁻¹ records the remaining compatible data modulo those changes. The equation d²=0 makes the quotient legitimate. This formal pattern becomes useful only when the complex is built from the actual restriction, transition or boundary maps of the problem.

For a finite oriented simplicial complex, the boundary of an oriented triangle [0,1,2] is [1,2]−[0,2]+[0,1]. Its next boundary is zero because every vertex contribution cancels with the appropriate sign. Over Q, β₁=E−rank ∂₁−rank ∂₂. The graph consisting of three edges around a triangle has β₁=1. Adding the filled two-simplex introduces a boundary generator and changes β₁ to zero. A drawing of three mutually adjacent vertices does not tell us whether the face is present. The interactive homology model makes this modeling decision explicit, which prevents confusing a graph with its clique complex.

In an additive gluing problem, differences on overlaps form a Čech 1-cocycle. If that cocycle is a coboundary, local corrections can remove it and the local sections glue. If its cohomology class is nonzero, the failure survives all allowed local corrections. This statement requires the relevant sheaf, cover and restriction maps; the abstract slogan “there is an obstruction” supplies none of them. Higher-degree classes arise when compatibility itself must be made compatible at the next level. Integer coefficients can also carry torsion that a rational rank calculation cannot detect.

Transport supplies a related but distinct view. For a local system, moving along paths gives linear maps, and concatenation becomes composition. A closed loop may return a vector transformed by a nonidentity matrix. In the lab, U=[[1,a],[0,1]] and V=[[1,0],[b,1]] give the loop UVU⁻¹V⁻¹=[[1+ab+a²b²,−a²b],[ab²,1−ab]]. Its determinant is one, but the loop can still act nontrivially. With a=2 and b=1, the result is [[7,−4],[2,−1]]. The determinant constraint alone misses the order dependence.

There are important distinctions. Holonomy is the ordered transport around a based loop. A change of fibre coordinates conjugates its matrix, so the conjugacy class is gauge invariant. For a flat connection it depends on the based homotopy class. Curvature concerns infinitesimal transport for a connection; cohomology requires its chosen differential and coefficient system. Flatness permits monodromy on spaces with nontrivial fundamental group, so zero curvature need not force trivial global transport. A finite pair of shears is an exact illustration of noncommuting composition, not a construction of a smooth connection. The bridge worth carrying forward is the explicit passage from local maps to consistency equations, and from those equations to a quotient that measures the failure of a global solution.

bridges.title: Spectra, inverse problems and why identifiability is weaker than stability
bridges.kind: Proved analytic bridge for diagonal Hilbert-space models
bridges.question: What changes when a target is uniquely determined but small noise is greatly amplified?
bridges.text:
Consider a diagonal forward operator Ae_k=σ_ke_k on a Hilbert basis. If every σ_k is positive, the noiseless data determine every coordinate x_k. Yet if σ_k→0, the formal inverse divides by smaller and smaller numbers and is unbounded on the ambient data space. Uniqueness has therefore been proved without stable inversion. This is the analytic counterpart of the finite quotient criterion: invisible directions can obstruct well-defined target recovery, while nearly invisible directions obstruct conditioning.

Assume the unknown belongs to the ellipsoid Σk≥1 k^(2r)|x_k|²≤1 and the data error has norm at most δ. The spectral cutoff inverse keeps the first N coordinates. The tail obeys ||x−P_Nx||≤(N+1)^(−r), because all discarded weights are at least (N+1)^(2r). The propagated noise obeys ||A_N^†e||≤δ/σ_N for decreasing σ_k. The triangle inequality gives the fully specified deterministic bound B(N)=(N+1)^(−r)+δ/σ_N. This is an upper bound over all admissible signals and noises, not a fitted prediction of the error in one sample.

For mildly decaying singular values σ_k=k^(−p), balancing the two terms suggests N of order δ^(−1/(p+r)) and a rate δ^(r/(p+r)). Matching lower bounds can be obtained by choosing two signals separated along a coordinate near that cutoff whose forward images differ by no more than the noise scale. Their data neighborhoods overlap, so an estimator cannot distinguish both perfectly. Such a lower-bound argument proves a limit of the information model rather than a defect of one algorithm.

For severe decay σ_k=exp(−ck), write δ=exp(−L). A leading estimate N≈L/c can make the noise term order one. To keep noise on the same polynomial scale as the bias, use a correction of the form N≈(L−r log L)/c, with integer rounding and bounded-L behavior handled explicitly. The lab displays both terms and their sum so that a visually appealing increase in resolution cannot hide noise amplification. The more general exp(−ck^β) model requires the corresponding β-dependent correction; the implemented lab intentionally fixes β=1.

Spectral gaps also govern iterative convergence, but their operators must be named. If P and Q are orthogonal projections onto distinct lines meeting at angle θ, then PQP=cos²θ P. The n-fold product has norm cos^(2n)θ on the surviving direction. A small angle gives slow convergence, even though the intersection is trivial and the limiting projection is known. The commutator norm |sin 2θ|/2 is a different quantity and is small near both alignment and orthogonality, so it cannot substitute for the contraction factor.

The shared capacity is to locate directions that a map suppresses and quantify the cost of recovering them. Inverse regularization, spectral iteration and experimental design can then exchange specific tools: singular values, principal angles, norm bounds and minimax tests. They do not become the same problem merely because an eigenvalue appears in each. The next useful experiment is always tied to a hypothesis: estimate a singular-value tail, perturb a nearly null direction, or compare a proposed cutoff with an explicit uniform error bound.

bridges.title: Exact counting, generating functions and the limits of a summary
bridges.question: When does a finite summary support a proof, and when can different objects share it?
bridges.text:
For a finite configuration set Ω and statistic T:Ω→S, exact counting produces the fibre sizes n_s=|T⁻¹(s)|. Under the uniform distribution, n_s/|Ω| is the law of T. A generating function packages those same counts as coefficients. If a weight or sampling law is changed, the induced distribution changes accordingly; counting alone does not justify a new probability model. This simple distinction connects combinatorics to inference without assuming that every enumeration is a statistically representative sample.

An optimization problem adds an objective and a feasible set. In a six-item 0–1 knapsack with weights (2,3,4,5,6,7), values (3,4,6,7,9,10), and budget 12, exhaustive enumeration finds 28 feasible subsets and a unique optimum of value 18, selecting items 1,3,5. Because all 64 masks have been checked, existence, optimality and uniqueness are separate certified statements with a transparent common witness set. Ordering feasible masks also gives a ranking and unranking operation. A larger problem may require a recurrence, decision diagram, branch bound or formal certificate instead; the six-item lab does not recover missing large-instance input data.

A summary can be exact and still incomplete. For a graph G and vertex heights h, let E_G(h)=Σ_{uv∈E(G)}(h_u−h_v)². Two explicitly recovered seven-vertex graphs have identical joint counts of Hamming weight and energy for all 128 binary assignments h∈{0,1}⁷. Consequently every invariant that is only a function of that binary census agrees on the pair. This is a rigorous information-loss result. It does not imply that the graphs agree under a richer measurement scheme.

Allow nonnegative integer heights with total mass three. The corresponding energy generating polynomials differ by q³(1−q)(1−q³)²(1−q⁴)². At q=1/2 this difference is 11025/262144, so a higher-height measurement distinguishes them. At q=1 both polynomials count the same total number of configurations, and the difference vanishes. The choice of evaluation point is therefore part of the probe. The interactive lab exposes the integer coefficient census alongside the floating evaluation, making it possible to see precisely what was counted and which information was discarded.

Cyclotomic phase fibres provide a second exact counting-to-quotient bridge. Reduction of units U(1680)→U(30) is surjective. Its fibres are cosets of a kernel and hence all have equal size. Since φ(1680)=384 and φ(30)=8, each fibre has 48 elements. The 56th powers of primitive 1680th roots correspond to the eight primitive 30th-root phases. This proves a finite phase multiplicity theorem; it does not prove density or closure of a matrix group generated by braiding operators.

A useful research discipline emerges: identify the full configuration space, the statistic, the admissible weights, and the reconstruction goal. Then ask whether the statistic separates the objects relevant to that goal. A collision is constructive evidence of a missing distinction and a guide to designing a richer probe. Exact coefficients are especially valuable because they separate a mathematical collision from a numerical tolerance accident. The source bundles preserve unrecovered-instance boundaries so that a historical claim is not silently converted into a newly verified computation.

bridges.title: Poisson structure, Moyal deformation and the first nonzero obstruction
bridges.question: How can a classical bracket agree with a deformed bracket at one order and still fail later?
bridges.text:
On the canonical plane with coordinates (q,p), the Poisson bracket is {f,g}=∂qf∂pg−∂pf∂qg. Fix the Weyl–Moyal product f⋆g=f exp[(iℏ/2)(←∂q→∂p−←∂p→∂q)]g. Its normalized commutator (f⋆g−g⋆f)/(iℏ) has only odd derivative orders, and its leading term is the Poisson bracket. For polynomials the series terminates, so the comparison is an exact finite algebraic calculation rather than a convergence claim about a formal infinite sum.

For f=q^a p^b and g=q^c p^d, define S_k=Σ_{j=0}^k(−1)^j binom(k,j)(a)_{k−j}(b)_j(c)_j(d)_{k−j}, with falling factorials zero beyond the degree. The order-k contribution for odd k is (−1)^((k−1)/2)ℏ^(k−1)S_k q^(a+c−k)p^(b+d−k)/(2^(k−1)k!). All coefficients are rational integers divided by an explicit denominator. The lab uses arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic and rational normalization, so no cancellation is decided by a numerical threshold.

For f=q³ and g=p³, the result is 9q²p²−(3/2)ℏ². This fixes the sign and normalization convention. More revealing is f=qp⁵ and g=q⁵p³: S₃=0, but S₅=201600, so the bracket is −22q⁵p⁷+105ℏ⁴qp³. Stopping after the cubic derivative test would certify the wrong conclusion. The first surviving obstruction may occur later than the first possible obstruction.

There are also infinite exact families for structural reasons. For f=qp³ and g=q^(3r+2)p^r with nonnegative integer r, the third-order coefficient cancels, and higher odd orders vanish because the relevant total degree of f is four. In this family the cancellation plus a degree cutoff is sufficient. The missing step in an informal argument is often exactly that cutoff: a vanishing coefficient proves nothing about orders that were not examined unless another theorem excludes them.

This illustrates the proper role of deformation language. A first-order Poisson structure can describe the leading deformation, while associativity and equivalence involve higher compatibility equations. An infinitesimal solution need not integrate to a global family, and a small verified monomial family need not generate a closed algebra under the desired operations. A classification must state its ambient vector space, degree bounds, closure conditions and equivalences. The new bounded sextic monomial enumeration in the algebra chapter is labeled as an atlas computation, not a historical discovery and not a classification of arbitrary sextic polynomial subspaces.

The bridge to exact certification is practical: expand the defining operator with an explicit convention, use structural vanishing to bound the search, and certify every surviving order. The bridge to geometry is conceptual but specific: the Poisson bivector is the operator contracted repeatedly in this canonical constant-coefficient model. Extending the same formula to a curved manifold without charts, connections or a compatible star-product construction would require new mathematics.

bridges.title: Arithmetic reduction, orbit completeness and finite certificates of infinite families
bridges.kind: Exact unit action with a reduction proof
bridges.question: How can a finite list certify an infinite arithmetic family?
bridges.text:
A recurrence can produce infinitely many solutions without proving that it produces all solutions. For x²−2y²=−7, multiplication of α=x+y√2 by the norm-one unit u=3+2√2 gives (x,y)↦(3x+4y,2x+3y). Direct expansion proves that x²−2y² is invariant. The inverse unit gives (x,y)↦(3x−4y,−2x+3y), again preserving integrality and the norm. This establishes a group action on the solution set. Completeness is a separate reduction theorem.

For y>0 and x>0, α>√7 and its conjugate is −7/α. Multiplying by a suitable integral power of u brings α into the half-open interval [√7,u√7). Then x=(α−7/α)/2 and y=(α+7/α)/(2√2) show that the reduced positive representative has 0≤x<8 and 0<y<6. Exact checking in that finite rectangle leaves (1,2) and (5,4). The endpoint α=√7 would give x=0, which cannot solve 2y²=7 in integers. Thus every positive solution reduces to one of those two seeds. Overall sign and signed unit powers cover the other sign choices in the corresponding real embeddings.

The numerical interval is merely a way to derive a finite search bound. The proof rests on the norm identity and the fundamental multiplicative interval, and the final candidate test is an exact integer equation. The interactive lab moves in either direction along each orbit with arbitrary-precision integers and checks the norm at every displayed point. Watching many solutions appear is useful intuition; the interval reduction is what makes the list complete.

Congruence conditions can further restrict the orbit. Reducing the recurrence matrix modulo m gives a finite permutation of its admissible residue states. One may determine which powers hit a desired residue class, then combine those periodic conditions with the unit parameter. This is a precise connection between infinite Diophantine families and finite automata. It requires a proof that all solutions have entered the chosen orbit parametrization before a residue sieve can claim completeness.

The same finite-certificate strategy appears elsewhere in arithmetic, with different hypotheses. A rational point on an elliptic curve can be checked by substitution; a claim that a point generates all rational points needs a rank and saturation argument. A finite-field group order can be checked by exhaustive counting for a small field or by a certified algorithm for a large field. A p-adic approximation is an element of a compatible residue system, and lifting a root requires its own derivative or multiplicity hypotheses. None of these certificates can be replaced by the fact that a calculation produced a plausible point.

This is a durable connection across the annual work: turn an unbounded question into finitely many representatives through a proved action, reduction or compactness argument; then verify the finite residue exactly. The bridge from arithmetic to dynamics is the explicit recurrence matrix, not a metaphor about motion. The bridge to computation is a terminating reduction algorithm plus a checkable certificate, not a claim that brute force settles every infinite search.
